Refraction: The Evidence

The strongest passages and printed tables from 23 triangulation surveys (1739 to 1908) on how refraction was measured, avoided and checked. 322 items, each quoted with its page and the page image. Click any image to open it full size.

In short

They recorded temperature and pressure with their readings, so they knew the state of the air each time. No angle came from one sighting. They repeated each one in full series at different hours of the day and at night, under different air, and averaged them. They threw out readings taken in fog, rain or shimmering air. They also measured vertical angles from both ends of each line. That gave the actual bend of the light on that line, in that air. Then they checked the horizontal angles against the triangle closures. Each triangle's three angles were measured on their own, at three different stations. Adding them up shows whether they agree with each other. Any sideways bend would make them disagree. The printed disagreements are under a second of arc per angle.

The questions

Each heading opens the items that answer it.

“They didn't take the wet term into account.” 77 items · 20 surveys

Humidity, fog, rain and vapour: what the surveyors recorded and how they treated observations made in damp air.

Short answer. Humidity was recorded and acted on, but not modelled. Schott prints hourly wet-bulb readings at Jackson Butte (1900, p. 294) and pressure and temperature for every zenith-distance line (p. 257). Delambre tested the barometer and hygrometer, found fog the main cause of large refraction (n of 0.14 to 0.17), and set the fog and rain observations aside, which moves his mean n from 0.0839 to 0.0788 (1807, pp. 775 to 776). Clarke (1858) puts the morning and evening refraction down to aqueous vapour near the ground; Lambton puts his range of 1/4 to 1/20 down to moisture and asks for a hygrometer. Struve's Finmarken journal shows readings spreading 6.6″ in thick air and 0.5″ in clear air. Instead of computing the index from humidity, the surveys measured the bend itself on each line (next question). The wet term acts mainly on vertical angles, which feed only the heights.
Zenith distances: one series of ten per target, more when doubtful; in bad weather angles were repeated instead; the zenith distance nearest in hour to the angle was used
Delambre and Méchain, meridian arc Dunkirk to Barcelona (Base du système métrique) · T1 Discours préliminaire p. 113 · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours Repetition over days and hours

Discours préliminaire, section Observations. A zenith distance is the vertical angle between the plumb-line direction straight up (the zenith) and the target. A series is a run of repeated readings on the repeating circle; ten angles means the circle was turned ten times and the total divided by ten. Delambre gives his rule and the reason: in bad weather the variations of refraction make zenith distances less sure. For steep sights he took the zenith distance just before or after the angle, or at several hours, and used the one nearest in time. Méchain repeated zenith distances more than Delambre.

“je me suis contenté de faire pour chaque distance au zénith une seule série de dix angles, excepté dans les cas où quelque circonstance rendoit l'observation douteuse. Quand le temps étoit beau, j'aimois mieux répéter l'observation des angles de position, et, s'il étoit mauvais, les variations de la réfraction terrestre auroient rendu les distances au zénith plus incertaines. Quand ces distances sont plus grandes que 91 degrés, ou plus petites que 89, il conviendroit de les observer en même temps que l'angle de position ; mais cela n'est guère possible. Il falloit donc se contenter de les observer immédiatement avant ou après, ou à plusieurs heures du jour, afin de choisir pour la réduction des angles à l'horizon la distance dont l'heure étoit la plus voisine, et où l'on avoit lieu de croire la réfraction terrestre moins différente.”
In English: “I was content to make for each zenith distance a single series of ten angles, except in cases where some circumstance made the observation doubtful. When the weather was fine I preferred to repeat the observation of the angles of position, and if it was bad, the variations of terrestrial refraction would have made the zenith distances more uncertain. When these distances are greater than 91 degrees or less than 89, they should be observed at the same time as the angle of position; but that is hardly possible. So one had to be content to observe them immediately before or after, or at several hours of the day, in order to choose for the reduction of the angles to the horizon the distance whose hour was nearest, and where there was reason to believe the terrestrial refraction least different.”
Méchain, P., & Delambre, J.-B. J. (1806). Base du système métrique décimal, ou mesure de l'arc du méridien compris entre les parallèles de Dunkerque et Barcelone (Vol. 1). Paris: Baudouin., T1 Discours préliminaire p. 113
Zenith distances at Boiscommun on seven days, each with hour, barometer, thermometer and state of the air, including 'brouillard humide'
Delambre and Méchain, meridian arc Dunkirk to Barcelona (Base du système métrique) · T1 p. 166 · strength ★★★
Raw tables of repeated measures Steady-air hours Repetition over days and hours

Tome I, station of Boiscommun (frimaire an 2, December 1793). Delambre observed the zenith distance of the weathercock of Châteauneuf on seven days, one series of ten each, and printed with each the hour, the barometer (in pouces and lignes), the thermometer (as a fraction of the ice-to-boiling interval, converted to Réaumur degrees), and the sky: rain, fine or poor horizon, damp fog. He also stayed half an hour at the telescope to see whether refraction changed the distance. This is a direct record of humidity and pressure with each vertical angle.

“24 frimaire, 12h ¼. Bar. 27p 1l9. Therm. 0.099 = 7d92. A 1h ¼ la distance étoit encore la même. ... Le baromètre et le thermomètre étoient placés environ 1t8 au-dessous de la lunette. Après ces observations je suis resté pendant une demi-heure à la lunette, pour voir si la réfraction ne changeroit pas la distance : je n'ai pas vu la moindre variation. Horizon très-pur, point de soleil. ... 25 frimaire, 3h ¾. Bar. 27p 4l. Therm. + 0.11 = 8d8. Temps pluvieux ; horizon assez beau. ... 30 frimaire, 3h ½. Bar. 27p 3l. Therm. + 0.067 = 5d36. Brouillard humide.”
In English: “24 frimaire, 12h ¼. Barometer 27 pouces 1.9 lignes. Thermometer 0.099 = 7.92 degrees. At 1h ¼ the distance was still the same. ... The barometer and thermometer were placed about 1.8 toises below the telescope. After these observations I stayed half an hour at the telescope to see whether refraction would change the distance: I did not see the least variation. Very clear horizon, no sun. ... 25 frimaire, 3h ¾. Barometer 27 pouces 4 lignes. Thermometer +0.11 = 8.8 degrees. Rainy weather; horizon fairly fine. ... 30 frimaire, 3h ½. Barometer 27 pouces 3 lignes. Thermometer +0.067 = 5.36 degrees. Damp fog.”
Reading the table. Each line: number of repetitions (10), total arc in grades, single zenith distance in grades, the same in degrees; then date, hour, barometer, thermometer, remarks. Seven series on seven days (24 to 30 frimaire) to the same target. The page continues on p. 167 with 1, 2 and 7 nivôse.
Worked out here: Seven zenith distances of the Châteauneuf weathercock range from 90° 5' 46.0" (28 frimaire) to 90° 6' 6.1" (30 frimaire, damp fog): spread 20.1".
Méchain, P., & Delambre, J.-B. J. (1806). Base du système métrique décimal, ou mesure de l'arc du méridien compris entre les parallèles de Dunkerque et Barcelone (Vol. 1). Paris: Baudouin., T1 p. 166
Méchain's zenith distances at Rieupeyroux (1798): each series dated, timed, with thermometer, wind, sun and undulations
Delambre and Méchain, meridian arc Dunkirk to Barcelona (Base du système métrique) · T1 p. 294 · strength ★★★
Raw tables of repeated measures Steady-air hours

Tome I, station of Rieupeyroux in Méchain's southern part (thermidor an 6, July-August 1798; M. et A. = Méchain and his assistant). Each target has two series of ten on different days and hours, with the thermometer reading and remarks: calm or strong wind, sun or shade, undulations or none. The mean is then corrected for half the wire thickness and for the height of the signal (dH) 'for the level difference and the refraction'.

“M. et A. 24 thermidor, à 5h ½ du soir. Thermomètre + 13d6 en 80d. Calme. L'objet est dans l'ombre ; on le voit bien. ... M. et A. 18 thermidor, à 6h ¼ du soir. Thermomètre 15d0. Soleil. Le grand vent agite le niveau, et le signal est difficile à distinguer. ... M. et A. 21 thermidor, à 7h ¾ du matin. Thermomètre 15d0. Calme. Objet assez net ; il n'y a point d'ondulations.”
In English: “M. and A., 24 thermidor, at 5h ½ in the evening. Thermometer +13.6 degrees (80-degree scale). Calm. The object is in shadow; it is seen well. ... M. and A., 18 thermidor, at 6h ¼ in the evening. Thermometer 15.0 degrees. Sun. The strong wind shakes the level, and the signal is hard to make out. ... M. and A., 21 thermidor, at 7h ¾ in the morning. Thermometer 15.0 degrees. Calm. Object fairly sharp; there are no undulations.”
Reading the table. Per target (Rodez statue, signal of La Gaste): two series of 10, each with date, hour (evening and morning), thermometer and remarks. 'Milieu des deux séries' / 'Moyenne' = mean used for the reduction to the horizon; then 'Demi-épaisseur du fil' (half wire thickness, +3") and dH (signal height correction) give the value used 'pour la différence de niveau et la réfraction'.
Worked out here: La Gaste: evening series 89° 57' 37.9", morning series 89° 57' 27.2"; difference 10.7".

Rejecting readings in unsteady air Vertical refraction coefficients Repetition over days and hours

Tome II, remarks on the n table. A hygrometer measures air humidity. Delambre repeated the reciprocal observations at Boiscommun many times to see whether changes of the barometer and hygrometer affected refraction, and left the instrument pointed at Châteauneuf for several hours. He found fog to be the main factor (n of 0.14 to 0.17) and set the fog observations aside.

“A Boiscommun j'ai répété les observations un grand nombre de fois, pour voir si les changemens du baromètre et de l'hygromètre influoient sur la réfraction : je n'ai rien pu remarquer. J'ai laissé pendant plusieurs heures l'instrument bien callé et la lunette dirigée sur Châteauneuf, dans l'intervalle des observations de distances au zénith, et je n'ai pas vu de variations sensibles dans la hauteur ... Il paroît que c'est le brouillard qui influe surtout sur les réfractions, et qui donne pour n des valeurs de 0.14 à 0.17. Je laisse donc à part les observations non numérotées de Boiscommun.”
In English: “At Boiscommun I repeated the observations a great many times to see whether changes of the barometer and the hygrometer affected refraction: I could notice nothing. I left the instrument firmly set for several hours with the telescope pointed at Châteauneuf, between the zenith-distance observations, and I saw no noticeable variation in the height ... It appears that it is fog above all that affects refraction, and gives for n values of 0.14 to 0.17. I therefore set aside the unnumbered observations of Boiscommun.”
Méchain, P., & Delambre, J.-B. J. (1807). Base du système métrique décimal, ou mesure de l'arc du méridien compris entre les parallèles de Dunkerque et Barcelone (Vol. 2). Paris: Baudouin., T2 p. 775
Mean coefficient of all 189 pairs 0.08388; 0.07876 after rejecting fog and decidedly rainy weather; more simultaneous reciprocal observations needed for more precision
Delambre and Méchain, meridian arc Dunkirk to Barcelona (Base du système métrique) · T2 p. 776 · strength ★★★
Rejecting readings in unsteady air Vertical refraction coefficients

Tome II, end of the remarks. Delambre gives the mean n of all 189 lines, then the mean after rejecting the observations made in fog and in decidedly rainy weather, and lists the rejected numbers. The 17 sea-horizon observations give nearly the same value. He states that more precise values need reciprocal observations made at the same time at both ends, in very great number.

“Le milieu entre les 189 . . . 0·08388. En rejetant les observations faites dans le brouillard et dans le temps décidément pluvieux, il restera 159 observations qui par un milieu donneront . . . 0·07876. Les 17 observations de l'horizon de la mer donnent par un milieu . . . 0·0783. J'ai rejeté de 57 à 69 inclusivement, de 71 à 75, de 76 à 88. Pour avoir quelque chose de plus précis il faudroit des observations réciproques, simultanées, en très-grand nombre.”
In English: “The mean of the 189 ... 0.08388. Rejecting the observations made in fog and in decidedly rainy weather, there remain 159 observations which give a mean of ... 0.07876. The 17 observations of the sea horizon give a mean of ... 0.0783. I rejected nos. 57 to 69 inclusive, 71 to 75, and 76 to 88. To have something more precise, reciprocal simultaneous observations in very great number would be needed.”
Worked out here: The listed ranges 57-69, 71-75, 76-88 contain 13 + 5 + 13 = 31 numbers; 189 - 31 = 158, the text prints 159.
Méchain, P., & Delambre, J.-B. J. (1807). Base du système métrique décimal, ou mesure de l'arc du méridien compris entre les parallèles de Dunkerque et Barcelone (Vol. 2). Paris: Baudouin., T2 p. 776
Instruction: zenith distances from at least three series at different hours, mainly near midday, simultaneous where possible, with barometer readings; first-order series to the twentieth repetition
Parallel of Paris, Brest to Strasbourg (Henry east part, Bonne west part), Nouvelle carte de France · 28 · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours Repetition over days and hours

Instruction of the commission of the Dépôt de la Guerre for the new map of France, printed by Puissant. It sets the observing rules for the first-order chains, including the parallel of Paris. A conjugate observation is one repetition of the angle on the repeating circle. Simultaneous observations are reciprocal zenith distances taken at both ends at the same time, so that both see the same state of the air.

“Les distances zénithales relatives à ces chaînes seront elles-mêmes le résultat de trois séries au moins, prises à des heures différentes, et surtout vers le milieu du jour, afin qu'elles puissent donner les différences de niveau avec toute l'exactitude désirable, et, autant qu'il sera possible, par le concours d'observations simultanées : celles-ci seront accompagnées d'observations barométriques. ... Toutes les séries du premier ordre seront, autant que possible, prolongées jusqu'à la vingtième observation conjuguée ; toutes celles du deuxième ordre s'arrêteront à la dixième.”
In English: “The zenith distances for these chains will themselves be the result of at least three series, taken at different hours, and above all towards the middle of the day, so that they can give the level differences with all desirable accuracy, and, as far as possible, by the combination of simultaneous observations: these will be accompanied by barometric observations. ... All first-order series will, as far as possible, be carried to the twentieth conjugate observation; all those of the second order will stop at the tenth.”
Puissant, L. (1832). Nouvelle description géométrique de la France (Première partie). Paris: Ch. Picquet., 28
Roy: conclusive refraction work needs levelled heights, barometers and thermometers at both stations, and two observers observing at the same instant
Anglo-French triangulation of 1787 (Greenwich to Paris junction), English side by Roy · p. 235 · strength ★★★

Section VII on terrestrial refraction. Terrestrial refraction is the bending of the ray between two ground stations, which makes a distant object appear higher. Roy states what a full test would need and then states what he had: reciprocal angles (each station observed from the other) taken at different times. In a footnote Maskelyne adds that a thermometer at the object as well as at the observer would allow a further correction.

“the relative heights of the stations should in strictness all have been ascertained by levelling: for purposes of this sort geometrical determinations, however good in other respects they may be, should not here be admitted, because they involve the very point in question, that is, the height, which should be obtained independently of angular measurement. Besides barometers and thermometers at both stations, two observers and two instruments of the same kind would have been necessary, for taking at the same instant the reciprocal angle of elevation and depression.”
Roy, W. (1790). An account of the trigonometrical operation, whereby the distance between the meridians of the Royal Observatories of Greenwich and Paris has been determined. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, 80, 111-270 (with Dalby, I., Remarks, pp. 593-614)., p. 235
Roy: barometer and thermometer are printed for each day, but no correction was applied without simultaneous reciprocal observations; refraction decreases with station height
Anglo-French triangulation of 1787 (Greenwich to Paris junction), English side by Roy · p. 245 · strength ★★★
Towers, scaffolds and high stations Vertical refraction coefficients

Same page. Roy records the state of the air (pressure and temperature) against each observation in the table facing p. 246, then states why he did not turn these readings into a correction: the two ends of a line were not observed at the same time with two instruments. He then states the main result of the table.

“The heights of the barometer and thermometer are inserted on the days on which the observations were made, merely to shew what was nearly the state of the atmosphere at the respective times. But we have not attempted to apply any correction on that account, because it could not be done in a satisfactory manner, and consequently could not be useful, unless the circumstances had permitted reciprocal observations to have been made at corresponding times with double sets of instruments, which in our situation was impossible. By attending to the results in the table, it will in general be seen, that terrestrial as well as celestial refraction certainly diminishes as the heights of the stations above the sea increase”
Roy, W. (1790). An account of the trigonometrical operation, whereby the distance between the meridians of the Royal Observatories of Greenwich and Paris has been determined. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, 80, 111-270 (with Dalby, I., Remarks, pp. 593-614)., p. 245

1795: bearings of church towers and other objects taken in the morning or evening, when the air was free from vapour and from the midday quivering
Trigonometrical Survey of England and Wales (Ordnance), Williams, Mudge and Dalby 1791-1799 · pp. 456-457 · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours

Account of the work of 1792. The sentence ends on p. 457 with 'without that quivering motion, which, in summer, it generally has in the middle of the day.' The observers chose the time of day by the state of the air: vapour (moisture haze) and quivering (heat shimmer) were both avoided.

“That the bearings of those might be taken with precision, the observations were made either in the morning or evening, when the air was free from vapour, and without that quivering motion, which, in summer, it generally has in the middle of the day.”
Williams, E., Mudge, W., & Dalby, I. (1795). An account of the trigonometrical survey carried on in the years 1791, 1792, 1793, and 1794. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, 85, 414-591., pp. 456-457
1795: vertical angles for the tables taken on close cloudy days or toward evening; barometer and thermometer changes cannot explain refraction on rays near the ground
Trigonometrical Survey of England and Wales (Ordnance), Williams, Mudge and Dalby 1791-1799 · p. 586 · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours Repetition over days and hours

Same remarks. The sentence before records that at one station the depression of Chanctonbury Ring varied from 1' 41" to 2' 30" (repeated observations of one angle). The authors state when the tabled observations were made, and they reject the idea that pressure and temperature at the station explain the changes when the ray runs close to the ground.

“The observations, however, on which the tables are founded, were made in close cloudy days, or toward the evenings, when the tremulous motion in the air is commonly the least. It has been conjectured, that the variations in terrestrial refraction, depend on the changes in the atmosphere indicated by the barometer and thermometer: this, however, cannot be the case when the rays of light pass near the earth's surface for any considerable distance.”
Williams, E., Mudge, W., & Dalby, I. (1795). An account of the trigonometrical survey carried on in the years 1791, 1792, 1793, and 1794. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, 85, 414-591., p. 586
1795: moist vapours near the ground named as the principal cause of unusual refraction, tested by the bending line of pickets on a dewy morning
Trigonometrical Survey of England and Wales (Ordnance), Williams, Mudge and Dalby 1791-1799 · p. 587 · strength ★★★
Towers, scaffolds and high stations

Same remarks, after Dalby's account of a hill top that seemed to lift off the ground on a dewy day in the Isle of Wight. The pickets were posts driven in a straight line 100 feet apart for the Hounslow Heath base. Seen through the telescope on a dewy, sunny morning they appeared curved; in the afternoon the curve was gone. This links the irregular refraction to moisture and evaporation over the ground.

“Here, and also on Hounslow Heath, the rays of light passed near the earth's surface a great way before they arrived at the eye; and it is more than probable, that moist vapours were the principal cause of the very unusual refractions: the truth of which conjecture seems to be verified by the following circumstance. In measuring the base on Hounslow Heath, we had driven into the ground, at the distance of 100 feet from each other, about 30 pickets, so that their heads appeared through the boning telescope to be in a right line: this was done in the afternoon. The following morning proved uncommonly dewy, and the sun shone bright; when having occasion to replace the telescope, we remarked that the heads of the pickets exhibited a curve, concave upwards, the farthermost pickets rising the highest”
Williams, E., Mudge, W., & Dalby, I. (1795). An account of the trigonometrical survey carried on in the years 1791, 1792, 1793, and 1794. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, 85, 414-591., p. 587
Mudge 1799: instructions for simultaneous reciprocal observations every hour, with watches regulated by the sun, weather, thermometer and barometer recorded
Trigonometrical Survey of England and Wales (Ordnance), Williams, Mudge and Dalby 1791-1799 · p. 183 · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours Night lamps and heliotropes

Mudge (1801), on refraction. Simultaneous reciprocal observation means that each of two stations measures the vertical angle to the other at the same moment, so that both ends see the same state of the air. Mr. Woolcot observed at one station and Mudge at the other. The times were kept by watches regulated from altitudes of the sun and by signal.

“On these occasions, the instructions which I communicated to Mr. Woolcot, and by which I governed myself, were to observe the elevation or depression of the corresponding station at the expiration of every hour, beginning at six A. M. and to have the watch well regulated from observed altitudes of the sun's limb. I requested him also to be very minute in entering on his book the state of the weather; to keep the instrument properly sheltered from the wind; to be always cautious to adjust his level; and also to insert the state of the air, as to temperature and density, by noting the thermometer and barometer.”
Mudge, W. (1801). An account of the operations carried on for accomplishing a trigonometrical survey of England and Wales, continued from the year 1797, to the end of the year 1799 (Vol. 2, from the Philosophical Transactions). London: W. Faden., p. 183

Mudge 1799: one station's angle changed while the other's did not, so a local stratum, not dew, caused it; a long series is needed
Trigonometrical Survey of England and Wales (Ordnance), Williams, Mudge and Dalby 1791-1799 · p. 188 · strength ★★★
Repetition over days and hours

Discussion of the first series. Mudge estimates the error of each angle at no more than 3". At 9 and 10 p.m. the elevation at Whiteham changed by 44" and 42" while the depression seen from White Horse Hill stayed nearly the same. Because both ends were observed at the same time, he can place the change near one station. 'Floating strata' are layers of air with different refraction.

“These changes in the observed angles of elevation at Whiteham, (44" and 42" being the differences,) without corresponding ones at White Horse Hill, prove that some partial alteration, from floating strata, had taken place in the refraction near the former station. Whoever considers the matter, must perceive a case may be constructed in which this will take place, causing a great variation in one of the angles, whilst the other apparently remains the same: and this suggested the idea, that to afford any accurate conclusions in this way, a long series of observations would be necessary. It furthermore appears, that dew could not have caused these differences at Whiteham Hill, since the same cause would equally operate to vary the observed angles at White Horse Hill; but those remained nearly the same.”
Mudge, W. (1801). An account of the operations carried on for accomplishing a trigonometrical survey of England and Wales, continued from the year 1797, to the end of the year 1799 (Vol. 2, from the Philosophical Transactions). London: W. Faden., p. 188

Ordnance Trigonometrical Survey of Great Britain and Ireland, Principal Triangulation · p. xvi · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours Vertical refraction coefficients

Introduction, paragraph on refraction. On p. xv the refraction 'in a normal state of the atmosphere' is given as 1/15.4 to 1/9.4 of the angle at the earth's centre, mean 1/12.6; the passage continues here with the extreme cases and the cause of the daily change. Aqueous vapour is water vapour, the humidity of the air.

“The great amount of refraction in the morning, its diminution towards the middle of the day, and its increase again towards evening, is obviously caused by the greater amount of aqueous vapour in the lower portion of the atmosphere in the morning and evening, as compared with the amount in the middle of the day.”

Section IV, second part: azimuthal observations in detail. Azimuth is the angle of a line from true north; it was found from the referring object and circumpolar stars at elongation (their farthest east or west point). Each row is one night's observation with its own result, so the spread can be seen. Footnote marks give the weather for individual rows. Probable error is the amount the mean is as likely to be within as outside.

“Cloudy and misty. Cloudy. Very misty; partial sun. Very clear in all directions.”
Reading the table. Columns: date (5 Aug to 14 Sep 1846); star and elongation (51 Cephei, Polaris, delta and lambda Ursae Minoris, E or W); reading of star; computed level and collimation correction; corrected reading; reading of R.O.; computed azimuth of star at elongation; resulting azimuth of R.O. (81° 52' plus 15.09" to 32.33"). Mean of eastern elongations 24.23", western 20.28", general mean 81° 52' 22".51, probable error ±0".60. The quote is the four footnotes on weather.
Clarke, A. R. (1858). Ordnance trigonometrical survey of Great Britain and Ireland: Account of the observations and calculations of the principal triangulation. London: Eyre and Spottiswoode., p. 171

Same section. A smaller zenith distance means the object looks higher, that is, more refraction. Clarke states the daily pattern from the survey records, names an exception (Hart Fell, double refraction from 1 to 3 p.m. in September), and in a footnote gives Hossard's half-hourly series at Angoulême (refraction nearly constant from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.).

“When observations are recorded as having been taken at some early hour in the morning, as 5 A.M., and from that time until 8 A.M., they almost invariably show a smaller zenith distance than during any other part of the day; sometimes the difference is very considerable, and shows that no vertical observations should be taken early in the morning.”

Russian arc of the parallel of 47.5 N, Privolzhsk triangulation (Kishinev to Astrakhan arc, eastern part) · Zapiski XXII, Otd. II, p. 13 · strength ★★★
Rejecting readings in unsteady air

Chapter I gives the year-by-year account of the Privolzhsk triangulation, the eastern part of the 47.5 N arc. The closure of a triangle is the amount by which the sum of its three measured angles differs from 180 degrees plus the spherical excess. Triangle no. 64 closed with more than 7 seconds. The computers found that the angles at the station Nomardzhin had been observed in foggy weather and judged them unreliable. In the 1856 orders on the same page, Captain Napersnikov is told to remeasure the angle at Nomardzhin of triangle no. 64.

“При вычисленіи главнаго ряда треугольниковъ оказалось, что погрѣшность суммы 3-хъ угловъ въ треугольникѣ № 64 составляла свыше 7″, по этому и почтено за необходимость переизмѣрить углы на пунктѣ Номарджинъ, оказавшіеся неблагонадежными, потому, что наблюденія на этомъ пунктѣ произведены въ туманную погоду.”
In English: “In computing the main row of triangles it was found that the error of the sum of the 3 angles in triangle no. 64 was above 7″, and for this reason it was thought necessary to remeasure the angles at the point Nomardzhin, which proved unreliable because the observations at this point had been made in foggy weather.”

Tome II, p. 21, continuing the instruction. Undulating images are images that shimmer because of unsteady air near the ground. The instruction rejected any observation made with indistinct or too undulating images. Struve states that it was followed so strictly that only in two cases is an object wholly missing from a set; incomplete sets were completed with extra observations when the object became visible again. Each object was pointed 4 times in each set, 20 times in all, against 12 in the Baltic arc.

“Enfin l'instruction fixait, que toute observation était inadmissible, si les images des objets étaient indistinctes ou trop ondulantes. Cette instruction a été suivie en Finlande à telle rigueur, qu'il ne se trouve que deux cas, où un objet manque entièrement dans une des mises à faire. ... En Finlande, chaque objet était pointé 4 fois dans chaque mise, donc en tout 20 fois, au lieu de 12 fois dans la mesure Baltique.”
In English: “Finally the instruction laid down that any observation was inadmissible if the images of the objects were indistinct or too undulating. This instruction was followed in Finland with such rigour that there are only two cases where an object is wholly missing from one of the sets to be made. ... In Finland each object was pointed 4 times in each set, so 20 times in all, instead of 12 times in the Baltic measurement.”
Struve, F. G. W. (1860). Arc du méridien de 25° 20' entre le Danube et la Mer Glaciale mesuré depuis 1816 jusqu'en 1855 (Vol. 2). Imprimerie de l'Académie impériale des sciences., T. II, p. 21

Struve Geodetic Arc (Russo-Scandinavian arc of the meridian, Danube to Fuglenaes) · T. II, p. 480 · strength ★★★
Vertical refraction coefficients

Tome II, Lindhagen's memoir on the Finmarken heights. Reciprocal zenith distances measured at the same time cancel the refraction if it is equal both ways; Lindhagen says that, when they cannot be simultaneous, they are still the best method if both are measured at the same, most favourable time of day. The great heights of the stations made the refraction very constant. Many surplus zenith distances gave a refraction constant, which was solved together with the heights. Barometer and thermometer readings were recorded at every vertical-angle measurement and were used in computing the refraction for the main net.

“In den Tagebüchern sind die Barometer- und Thermometerstände, welche zu den Zeiten der Vertikalwinkelmessungen stattfanden, regelmässig annotirt. Bei der Berechnung des Einflusses der Refraction auf die Zenithdistanzen im Hauptdreiecksnetze sind dieselben, so wie auch die Abhängigkeit der Refraction von den höheren Potenzen des Winkels, welchen die beiden Lothlinien, durch den Beobachtungsort und das Beobachtungsobject, mit einander machen, auf eine Weise berücksichtigt worden, zu deren Auseinandersetzung hier nicht der geeignete Ort ist.”
In English: “In the journals the barometer and thermometer readings that held at the times of the vertical angle measurements are regularly noted. In computing the influence of refraction on the zenith distances in the main triangle net these were taken into account, as was the dependence of the refraction on the higher powers of the angle that the two plumb lines, through the place of observation and the object observed, make with each other, in a way that this is not the proper place to set out.”
Struve, F. G. W. (1860). Arc du méridien de 25° 20' entre le Danube et la Mer Glaciale mesuré depuis 1816 jusqu'en 1855 (Vol. 2). Imprimerie de l'Académie impériale des sciences., T. II, p. 480

European arc of the parallel in 52 N, Greenwich (Feaghmain) to Warschau · p. 29 · strength ★★★
Repetition over days and hours Towers, scaffolds and high stations Night lamps and heliotropes

Heft I, § 12, the Russian (Polish) triangulation under General Tenner. In the southern Warsaw to Czenstochau connection the average number of sets was 11.4. The closures of all 219 Polish triangles give a mean angle error of ±0.73″. Tenner found this somewhat high and gave as reasons the high signals (pyramids 6 to 20 m, and 20 to 50 m in 148 cases) and measurement in unfavourable air that could not always be avoided. The rule for such air and strong wind was 18 to 24 sets. The sum of the 219 closures, +9.73″, shows no bias to positive or negative.

“Als Erklärungsgrund werden die hohen Signale, welche meist nothwendig waren, sowie die mehrfach nicht zu vermeidende Messung bei ungünstiger Luft angeführt. (Bei ungünstiger Luft und starkem Wind sollten 18—24 Sätze genommen werden.) Die Summe der 219 Widersprüche ist + 9″,73, so dass keine Neigung zu positiven oder negativen Schlussfehlern zu erkennen ist.”
In English: “The high signals, which were mostly necessary, and the measurement in unfavourable air, which several times could not be avoided, are given as the explanation. (In unfavourable air and strong wind 18 to 24 sets were to be taken.) The sum of the 219 closures is +9.73″, so that no tendency to positive or negative closure errors can be seen.”
Worked out here: √(354.1 / (219 × 3)) = √0.539 = 0.734″ (printed ±0.73″). Per direction 0.73/√2 = 0.52″ (printed).

Heft I, § 5, French channel stations of 1862. At Harlettes Beaux observed on a 21 m scaffold in wind under very unfavourable conditions, so Helmert doubled all q (halved all weights). At Cassel the weight of angle 44.42 was halved because its 60 repetitions were all obtained on a single day. A repetition is one addition of the angle on a repeating circle. The page also notes a measurement excluded because its set was spread over a whole week.

“Harlettes. Die Beobachtungen wurden 1862 von Beaux wegen Wind unter sehr ungünstigen Umständen auf einem 21 m hohen Gerüst ausgeführt, weshalb ich hier alle q verdoppelt habe. ... Letzterer Werth ist verdoppelt worden, weil jene 60 Rep. an einem einzigen Tage erhalten sind.”
In English: “Harlettes. The observations were made in 1862 by Beaux, because of wind under very unfavourable conditions, on a 21 m high scaffold, for which reason I have doubled all q here. ... The latter value has been doubled because those 60 repetitions were obtained on a single day.”

Vapour over the Madras base flat: all angles repeatedly taken; only one clear morning
Great Arc of India, Lambton's meridional arc (Coromandel coast to Punnae and north to about 18 N) · p. 165 · strength ★★★
Repetition over days and hours Rejecting readings in unsteady air

Below the triangles that connect the Madras base with St. Thomas's Mount. The two routes gave slightly different distances, and Lambton gives the reason. The vapour he describes is near-ground haze over the flat, which made the flag-staffs unsteady. His response was to repeat the angles and to use the clear morning of 7 October.

“It may be necessary to notice here, that there was great difficulty in taking all these angles, on account of the very thick vapour which constantly floated near the surface of the flat where the base line runs, almost immediately after day-light, to very near the time of sun-setting. All the angles, and particularly at the north and south end of the base line, have been repeatedly taken, and the only time when the flag-staff appeared distinctly, was in the morning of the 7th of October,”
Lambton, W. (1808). An account of the measurement of an arc on the meridian on the coast of Coromandel, and the length of a degree deduced therefrom in the latitude 12° 32'. Asiatic Researches, 8, 137 ff., p. 165
Lambton's rule: repeat hazy angles; reject any angle 10 seconds from the others until the triangle is complete
Great Arc of India, Lambton's meridional arc (Coromandel coast to Punnae and north to about 18 N) · pp. 176-177 · strength ★★★
Rejecting readings in unsteady air Repetition over days and hours

After the table of triangles 31 and 32 of the 1802-03 triangulation. Lambton states his own rule for horizontal angles taken in haze. The triangle closure (the amount by which the three observed angles, less the spherical excess, miss 180 degrees) is the test he applies before an angle is kept or rejected. The rule continues on p. 177 with the method of trying each angle in turn.

“The angles have been taken with much care, and I believe with as much accuracy as the nature of such a process admits of; difficulty, however, very frequently arose from the haziness of the weather, which rendered the objects at the very distant points extremely dull, and occasioned some irregularity in the angles. Whenever that happened, the observations were often repeated, and in case any one, in particular, was different from the other so much as ten seconds, it was rejected till the three angles of the triangle had been observed.”
Lambton, W. (1808). An account of the measurement of an arc on the meridian on the coast of Coromandel, and the length of a degree deduced therefrom in the latitude 12° 32'. Asiatic Researches, 8, 137 ff., pp. 176-177
Lambton (1814): refraction from 1/4 to 1/20 of the arc, attributed to moisture; barometer useless in the tropics, hygrometer needed
Great Arc of India, Lambton's meridional arc (Coromandel coast to Punnae and north to about 18 N) · Appendix p. 37 · strength ★★★
Vertical refraction coefficients

Appendix to GTS Vol. XII, Account of Colonel Lambton's operations, quoting a letter of 1814. Lambton reports the range of the refraction he measured on reciprocal lines over ten years, names moisture as the cause, explains why barometer readings do not help in India (pressure hardly changes), and calls for hygrometer readings and a table of low-altitude refractions from observation.

“In the course of my observations during the last ten years, I have at times found the terrestrial refraction to be as much as 1/4 of the contained arc, and occasionally as low as 1/20. This great irregularity I attribute to the different degrees of moisture in the atmosphere at different times. A knowledge of the laws of refraction is yet a desideratum in physical science. In climates remote from the equator, where the weight of the atmosphere is constantly changing, the barometer has been called in to indicate the pressure of a column of air, and rules investigated whereby to correct the mean celestial refraction according to the different heights of the mercury in the barometer. But in tropical climates this method can never apply owing to a well-known fact, that the weight of the atmosphere suffers very little variation, and while a barometer remains at the same station, it will not alter the 1/10 of an inch for several months together, excepting in the case of some great convulsion in the atmosphere. Other principles must therefore be adverted to. The hygrometer will be a necessary instrument to indicate the degree of moisture.”
Great Trigonometrical Survey of India. (1890). Account of the operations of the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India, Vol. XII: The Southern Trigon. Dehra Dun: Trigonometrical Branch, Survey of India., Appendix p. 37
Each angle measured three or four times, both microscopes read thrice, two separate field-books

GTS Vol. XII appendix summary of Lambton's 1802-03 observing of horizontal angles. A microscope here is the reading microscope on the circle; reading both, three times each, reduces reading error. Two field-books were kept independently and compared.

“The angles were all measured three or four times each; both microscopes were read off thrice every time the object was observed, and two separate field-books were kept for making out the angles. If from any marked difference between two measures of the same angle the graduation of the instrument was suspected to be in error, the division between the dots was carefully examined, as also those to the right and left, and if any error was discovered, allowance was made accordingly. Difficulties however very frequently arose from the haziness of the weather occasioning irregularity in the angles, and observations in consequence had often to be repeated.”
Great Trigonometrical Survey of India. (1890). Account of the operations of the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India, Vol. XII: The Southern Trigon. Dehra Dun: Trigonometrical Branch, Survey of India., Appendix p. 14
No heliotropes or lamps before 1832; opaque masts and flagstaves; field work began after the first heavy rain
Great Arc of India, Lambton's meridional arc (Coromandel coast to Punnae and north to about 18 N) · p. XIX · strength ★★★
Night lamps and heliotropes

Walker's introduction on the early operations. A heliotrope is a mirror that sends sunlight from the far station to the observer; a lamp does the same at night. Without them Lambton observed opaque signals, which haze made dull, and chose the rainy season because the air was then clearest.

“The difficulties which Major Lambton alludes to as arising from the haziness of the weather might have been materially diminished had he been supplied with luminous signals, such as heliotropes and lamps, to erect on the stations which he was observing; but such signals were not employed in the operations of the survey until after the year 1832, when they were introduced by Colonel Everest. For very many years the signals were “ masts, flagstaves, and other opaque objects, and then days and days often passed away without a glimpse of the distant object.” As the atmosphere in India is usually most favorable during the rainy season, for viewing such objects, it became the practice to wait for the first heavy fall of rain and then take the field,”
Walker, J. T. (1870). Account of the operations of the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India, Vol. I: Standards of measure and base-lines. Dehra Dun: Great Trigonometrical Survey., p. XIX

“The refraction is had from the tables of mean refraction, and no notice taken of the barometer or thermometer, or of the heights of the stations above the level of the sea, considering it doubtful what corrections to apply until observations are made, and tables of refraction constructed, for this climate, and for different elevations. [...] In all these observations two thermometers were used, one opposite the upper axis, the other opposite the arc,”

Introduction to the Karachi Longitudinal Series, season 1851-52. Mirage is strong refraction near hot or wet ground. The observers tried to fix the height of the Runn (a salt marsh) from Akoria station and did not use the result. The desert itself was free of mirage in that season.

“The desert was found perfectly free from mirage at the season it was visited; but the Runn of Cutch, on the southern flank of the series, was greatly affected by this atmospheric phenomenon, which prevented the ascertainment of the height of the Runn with respect to the sea level. [...] To determine this point, a secondary station was selected in the Runn, and vertical angles taken to it from Akoria station, on the edge of the tract, but the secondary point could not be connected, and the vertical angles were so affected by mirage, as to be untrustworthy.”

Part III, Rocky Mountain series (Pikes Peak to Salt Lake, stations near 3 650 m, longest side 294 km). Heliotropes are mirrors that reflect sunlight from the far station as a bright point target. A "double zenith distance" is a vertical angle read in both circle faces. This passage gives the full observing programme for both horizontal and vertical angles.

“The horizontal directions at all the stations were observed with the 50-centimetre (20-inch) theodolite, originally in 19 and later on (since 1893) in but 17 positions of the azimuth circle. The intention was to secure two full sets in each position and to balance the number of observations of the morning and evening, but on account of unavoidable broken series their numbers had generally to be increased for each position. Respecting the time of observations, they were made from sunrise till 8 o'clock, and resumed in the afternoon at half past 4 o'clock and continued till sunset. [...] To secure observations under a variety of atmospheric conditions, observations were extended over twenty or more days. Double zenith distances for heights of stations were observed at three different periods of the day, viz. between 6 1/2 and 8 o'clock in the morning, between 11 1/2 and 1 o'clock, and again between 4 1/2 and 6 o'clock in the evening. This brought to light the fact that the minimum refraction of the day occurs late in the afternoon, even after the heat of the day has passed. As a rule these vertical angle measures were spread over not less than twelve days, at least for the main lines. [...] No simultaneous reciprocal zenith distances were obtained. [...] The triangulation party also made observations of the magnetic declination, dip, and intensity, and meteorological notes were regularly kept.”
Worked out here: Minimum per direction from the stated plan: 17 positions x 2 sets = 34 observations (38 with 19 positions), each a D. and R. pair.

Weights of base-line angles carry the loss of precision from undulating signals over hot ground
Maclear's verification and extension of La Caille's arc of meridian, Cape of Good Hope · p. 338 · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours Repetition over days and hours

Section 7, part 4, of the base verification by triangulation (Zwartland base). Maclear explains how the weight of each angle was found: the square of the number of partial measures divided by twice the sum of squares of the differences from the mean. A partial measure is the mean of a group of repetitions; the weight is a number that is larger when the results agree better. He states that over flat ground the signals undulate, except in gloomy and moist weather or early morning and late evening, and that this error must enter the weights. So the state of the air is measured in the scatter of the results, not ignored.

“The weight of each angle was calculated by dividing the square of the number of partial measures by twice the sum of the squares of the differences from the mean, assuming the theodolite errors of division to be insensible, an assumption which is not strictly correct. The method pursued when measuring, of stepping the divided circle, eleminates the division errors from the mean result; they are restored in the weight as above calculated ; but that factor cannot justly be represented by the number of measures alone,—where, as in the present instance, the triangulation is carried over flat ground,—the line of sight passing in close proximity to heated sand and bush, causing the signals to undulate so much, except during gloomy and moist weather, or early in the morning and late in the evening, as to materially diminish the precision of the pointing : it is therefore necessary to introduce this element of error.”
Maclear, T. (1866). Verification and extension of La Caille's arc of meridian at the Cape of Good Hope (Vol. 1). London: Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty., p. 338

Same paragraph (p. 19). The observer was told to split the arcs between early morning and late afternoon, the hours of clearest and steadiest air, so that the mean covers two different states of the air. Morning mist and haze often stopped this. All vertical angles (angles of elevation or depression) were taken in the afternoon near sunset, with the vertical arc level read every time.

“The instructions to the observer were to observe half the arcs in the early morning and the remainder in the late afternoon, as being the hours of the day when the air might be expected to be clearest and steadiest. But it was soon found that to observe strictly in this way would be the cause of considerable delay when the morning observations were frequently quite prevented by mist and haze. The vertical angles were all observed in the afternoon as near to sunset as possible, and in repetition equivalent to the first pair of arcs as for horizontal angles, the readings of the vertical arc level being always recorded.”

Why a sight line bends: pressure and irregular heating
Middleton, Chadwick and Bogle, A Treatise on Surveying (textbook) · p. 224 · strength ★★★
Vertical refraction coefficients

Start of the section "Effect of Refraction on Vertical Angles". Air density changes with pressure and heating, so a nearly horizontal ray curves, usually concave to the ground. A target then appears higher than it is. Fig. 129 shows the true line O A, the curved path O C A, and the apparent direction A O₁. The angle O₁ A O is the refraction error.

“The effect of refraction has now to be considered. Rays of light passing through the atmosphere, nearly parallel to the earth's surface, do not travel in a straight line as they do in space (fig. 128). Owing to the varying density of the air, due to differences of pressure, and to irregular heating, they travel in a curved line. Usually, almost invariably, the path of the ray is concave towards the earth's surface, the effect of this being to make an object appear higher than it really is.”
Middleton, R. E., Chadwick, O., & Bogle, J. du T. (1904). A treatise on surveying: Part I (2nd ed.). E. & F. N. Spon., p. 224
Refraction varies with hour, temperature and pressure; horizontal deviation happens
Middleton, Chadwick and Bogle, A Treatise on Surveying (textbook) · p. 226 · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours Rejecting readings in unsteady air

The authors list what changes refraction: the hour (least about 3h 45m p.m. in the tropics), temperature and barometric pressure, and heated ground, where the ray can even curve the other way (mirage). They also state that sideways (horizontal) deviation is common. Their conclusion: under strong disturbance do not observe at all, and otherwise rely on reciprocal angles in similar conditions.

“Now the value of error of refraction though usually small, is very uncertain. It varies at different hours of the day, being least (in the tropics) at about 3h. 45m. P.M. It varies also with temperature, and barometric pressure. Over highly heated arid plains, it becomes exceedingly irregular, the curve sometimes being actually convex towards the earth, so that objects are depressed and not raised. [...] Horizontal deviation is also very common. A series of rods, ranged out in a straight line at one time, have presented the appearance of a curve at another time. When disturbance is so great as this, accurate observation of any kind is obviously impracticable. At any time, however, the effect of refraction is uncertain, and accurate results can only be arrived at, by taking reciprocal angles under similar atmospheric conditions.”
Middleton, R. E., Chadwick, O., & Bogle, J. du T. (1904). A treatise on surveying: Part I (2nd ed.). E. & F. N. Spon., p. 226
Lacaille (1740 register, extracted by Delambre): terrestrial refraction can be allowed for; the sea-horizon dip is the irregular case, partly because the air over the sea is more humid
Cassini de Thury and Lacaille, verification of the Paris meridian and the arc of the parallel near 43.5 N · T3 p. 534 · strength ★★
Vertical refraction coefficients

Delambre and Méchain, vol. 3, p. 534, quoting a note by Lacaille found in the 1740 registers. Lacaille states that terrestrial refraction is regular enough to be allowed for and too large to neglect in heights, and proposes finding it by observation and building a table. He names humidity over the sea as one cause of the irregular dip of the sea horizon. The dip is the angle by which the visible sea horizon lies below the horizontal.

“1° que cette réfraction n'est pas si irrégulière qu'on ne puisse trouver le moyen d'y avoir égard d'une manière satisfaisante ; 2° que la réfraction terrestre est trop grande pour être négligée dans le calcul des hauteurs des objets au-dessus de l'horizon ... Quand je dis que la réfraction horizontale des objets terrestres n'est pas si irrégulière qu'on pense, j'en excepte celle de l'abaissement de l'horizon de la mer. ... 2°. que l'air qui est au-dessus de la mer, est beaucoup plus humide que sur la terre.”
In English: “1st that this refraction is not so irregular that one cannot find a way to allow for it satisfactorily; 2nd that terrestrial refraction is too large to be neglected in computing the heights of objects above the horizon ... When I say that the horizontal refraction of terrestrial objects is not as irregular as people think, I except that of the dip of the sea horizon. ... 2nd that the air above the sea is much more humid than over the land.”
Méchain, P., & Delambre, J.-B. J. (1810). Base du système métrique décimal, ou mesure de l'arc du méridien compris entre les parallèles de Dunkerque et Barcelone (Vol. 3). Paris: Baudouin., T3 p. 534
Remarks on the table: a negative value in hot stormy weather between ten and eleven in the morning
Delambre and Méchain, meridian arc Dunkirk to Barcelona (Base du système métrique) · T2 p. 773 · strength ★★
Steady-air hours Rejecting readings in unsteady air

Tome II, remarks after the n table. Delambre explains the single negative n (no. 12, Fiefs-Bonnières): July, very hot and stormy weather, a poorly visible steeple. He states that refraction was nearly zero at the moment of the two observations, and notes that three observations of the same morning hour gave different refraction for different directions.

“Le 12e est négatif. Les deux observations sont du mois de juillet. A Fiefs le temps étoit très-chaud et orageux, et le clocher de Bonnières se voyoit mal. Cette dernière circonstance devoit augmenter la distance au zénith de quelques secondes. En diminuant de 9" la distance observée on auroit n = 0.0020 ; mais il n'en est pas moins sûr qu'à l'instant des deux observations la réfraction étoit à peu près nulle.”
In English: “The 12th is negative. The two observations are from July. At Fiefs the weather was very hot and stormy, and the steeple of Bonnières was poorly seen. This last circumstance must have increased the zenith distance by a few seconds. Reducing the observed distance by 9" would give n = 0.0020; but it is no less certain that at the moment of the two observations the refraction was nearly nil.”
Méchain, P., & Delambre, J.-B. J. (1807). Base du système métrique décimal, ou mesure de l'arc du méridien compris entre les parallèles de Dunkerque et Barcelone (Vol. 2). Paris: Baudouin., T2 p. 773

Rejecting readings in unsteady air

Same Instruction, added considerations. Vapours are visible moisture or haze near the ground; undulations are the trembling of the target image in unsteady air; phases are the uneven sunlight on one side of a signal that shifts its apparent centre. The rule tells observers to wait for steady, clear air before measuring angles.

“On évitera, autant que possible, de faire des observations d'angles dans les momens où il y a beaucoup de vapeurs et d'ondulations, et dans ceux où le soleil donnerait aux signaux des phases prononcées qui rendraient le pointé trop incertain.”
In English: “One will avoid, as far as possible, observing angles at moments when there are many vapours and undulations, and at those when the sun would give the signals marked phases that would make the pointing too uncertain.”

Same page. The rule for rejection was decided at the station by the observer, who wrote remarks on the air and the target against each reading (see the observation-book item). The office did not discard readings because they looked bad afterwards (p. 67 repeats this rule).

“All observations, when received in the office, are considered of equal weight, unless a remark of the observer against any observation condemns it as to be rejected. Observations under favourable circumstances are doubtless more valuable than observations under less favourable circumstances; but how to assign their relative numerical value is a question that admits of no general solution. Observations are seldom taken under decidedly unfavourable circumstances, if it can be avoided.”

Night lamps and heliotropes Steady-air hours

Tome I, p. 14, end of the signals section. A heliotrope is a mirror that reflects sunlight from the far station toward the observer, so it works only in sunshine. Struve used it for the longest distances or when a signal stood against the ground. He gives as a reason not to use it always that overcast days were either more numerous or the best for observing, because the calm of the images lasted longer.

“Un usage exclusif de l'héliotrope aurait trop arrêté la marche de l'opération, les jours couverts étant soit plus nombreux que les jours sereins, dans notre climat, soit les plus avantageux pour l'observation, par la plus longue durée du calme des images.”
In English: “An exclusive use of the heliotrope would have held up the progress of the operation too much, the overcast days being either more numerous than the clear days in our climate, or the most favourable for observation, through the longer duration of the calm of the images.”
Struve, F. G. W. (1857). Arc du méridien de 25° 20' entre le Danube et la Mer Glaciale mesuré depuis 1816 jusqu'en 1855 (Vol. 1). Imprimerie de l'Académie impériale des sciences., T. I, p. 14

Tome II, Chapter II, signals of Finland. The signals were small black posts about 12 feet high. White boards were set behind signals that stood against the ground. The heliotrope was used on 37 of the 282 directions, for the most distant stations or those not seen against the sky. Struve states that the Gulf of Bothnia triangles would hardly have succeeded without it, even through the fogs lying on the sea.

“Aussi la mesure des triangles sur le Golfe Bothnique, depuis Laton-mäki jusqu'à Tornea, n'aurait-elle guères réussi, sans l'application de ce puissant moyen de rendre visibles les stations les plus éloignées, même à travers les brouillards couchés à la surface de la mer.”
In English: “So the measurement of the triangles on the Gulf of Bothnia, from Laton-mäki to Tornea, would hardly have succeeded without the use of this powerful means of making the most distant stations visible, even through the fogs lying on the surface of the sea.”
Struve, F. G. W. (1860). Arc du méridien de 25° 20' entre le Danube et la Mer Glaciale mesuré depuis 1816 jusqu'en 1855 (Vol. 2). Imprimerie de l'Académie impériale des sciences., T. II, p. 11
Measurements of different years at one station were treated as separate stations; the state of the air is one named cause
European arc of the parallel in 52 N, Greenwich (Feaghmain) to Warschau · p. 37 · strength ★★
Night lamps and heliotropes

Heft I, § 16, end. Where a station was measured in different years, each epoch was combined on its own and then joined with weights. In the net adjustment, measurements of different years at one station were treated as measurements at different stations, because even the best measurements of different years showed large differences. Helmert names the possible causes: instruments and observers, the state of the air, centring and identity of the points, and the perception of heliotrope lights, whose appearance changes with the atmosphere.

“Für diesen Vorgang sprach das Auftreten grosser Differenzen selbst bei den besten Messungen verschiedener Jahre, wobei es allerdings unaufgeklärt geblieben ist, welches die wesentlichste Ursache dieser Unterschiede sein mag, ob die meist vorhandene Verschiedenheit der Instrumente und Beobachter, oder ein Unterschied der Luftzustände, oder in einzelnen Fällen Centrirungsmängel bezw. Nichtidentität der Punkte.”
In English: “This procedure was supported by the occurrence of large differences even in the best measurements of different years, though it has remained unexplained which is the main cause of these differences: the difference of instruments and observers that is mostly present, or a difference in the states of the air, or in single cases faults of centring or non-identity of the points.”
Helmert, F. R. (Ed.). (1893). Die europäische Längengradmessung in 52 Grad Breite von Greenwich bis Warschau. I. Heft: Hauptdreiecke und Grundlinienanschlüsse von England bis Polen. P. Stankiewicz., p. 37

US Transcontinental Triangulation, 39th parallel · p. 332 · strength ★★
Vertical refraction coefficients

Part II, heights from Round Top to Pikes Peak. Schott tabulates m for each line with the temperatures at both ends and the mean height, finds m rising as height falls except when the temperature is abnormal, and fits a formula in temperature t and height h. The formula gives the term for unequal refraction at the two ends, which is kept for these steep lines.

“An inspection of this table shows a steady increase in the coefficient of refraction as the height decreases, except where the temperature is abnormally high or low, in which case the value of m is correspondingly low or high. It was therefore decided to try to derive an expression for the coefficient of refraction of the form- m = m_0 + (t - t_0)x + (h - h_0)y [...] It was therefore concluded to use the individual values of m, disregarding the computed weights, and to derive two expressions, one for the eastern part of the triangulation from Pikes Peak to Mount Nebo and another for the remaining western part.”

Geodetic Survey of the Transvaal and Orange River Colony (Morris; preface and introduction by Gill) · p. 20 · strength ★★
Night lamps and heliotropes

Paragraph 56 (p. 20). When a distant station was often hidden, a white rod 2 to 3 miles away, in the same vertical plane, stood in for it in the round; the distant beacon was tied to the rod by micrometer whenever it could be seen. Verloren Vlei was observed this way from Mare's Kop and Langekloof.

“56. A satisfactory method of including in the round of observations a distant station which was frequently being obscured by mist or grass-fire smoke was to set up a signal, usually a straight rod, two inches in diameter and painted white, at a distance from the observing point of between 2 and 3 miles, and, as nearly as possible, in the vertical of the distant station. This rod was regarded as the distant station, and included in the usual round of observations. The beacon at the latter was then referred to the rod, at suitable opportunities, by means of the micrometer of the observing telescope, by simple vertical movement of the latter.”
Morris, W. G. (1908). Reports on the geodetic survey of the Transvaal and Orange River Colony (Geodetic Survey of South Africa, Vol. 5; preface and introduction by D. Gill). London: Harrison and Sons., p. 20

Geodetic Survey of the Transvaal and Orange River Colony (Morris; preface and introduction by Gill) · p. xxvii · strength ★★
Repetition over days and hours

Captain Gordon's report on the 1906-1907 chain joining the Transvaal survey to Simms' Rhodesia survey, printed in Gill's introduction (p. xxvii). Over the flat bushed country near the Zoutpansberg the images were unsteady from irregular refraction; haze from grass fires lasted through July and August, and rain fell from November. Each station had measures on four arcs only.

“Passing southwards through the heavy granite country of the M'Patem, one emerges on the flat heavily bushed tract which stretches continuously to the heights of the Zoutpansberg in the Transvaal. In this last country the work of observation became very tedious and difficult by reason of the unsteadiness of the images produced by irregular refraction. The absence of roads and the density of the bush in this section gave rise to much difficulty and delay in the earlier work of the reconnaissance, the trouble being in no way lightened by the constant thick haze prevailing during the months of July and August as the result of the numerous grass fires incidental to that season. During November heavy rains began to fall, and continued intermittently to the close of the work. ... Pressure of circumstances necessitated limiting the instrumental work at each station to a series of measures on four arcs only; the zero reference point of the circle being successively placed about the divisions of 0°, 45°, 90°, and 135°.”
Morris, W. G. (1908). Reports on the geodetic survey of the Transvaal and Orange River Colony (Geodetic Survey of South Africa, Vol. 5; preface and introduction by D. Gill). London: Harrison and Sons., p. xxvii

p. 208. Furber states that Struve's pressure factor, which uses the barometer reading B to refer coefficients to sea level, was not applied because the area is nearly at one level. He adds that the coefficient is the refraction at the usual observing time, 2 to 4 p.m., when it fluctuates less but is at one extreme of its daily range. “It is to be noted that, in the above discussion, Struves' pressure factor ... Where B represents the mean reading, in English inches, of the barometer at the place of observation, by which all co-efficients may be referred to sea level, has not been applied, the area covered being nearly enough at the one level to enable it to be disregarded without affecting the conclusions. It should be observed too, that the co-efficient determined above results, not the mean refraction, but the refraction at the usual time of observation, 2 to 4 p.m., when though less liable to fluctuation, it is really at one extreme of its daily range.”

Furber, T. F. (1898). The trigonometrical survey of New South Wales, with mention of similar surveys in the other Australian colonies. Report of the Australasian Association for the Advancement of Science, 7, Section A, 176-237., p. 208
“They didn't measure the refractive index along the path; crude methods.” 106 items · 22 surveys

How the bend on each line was found: reciprocal zenith distances measure the actual bend of that line, and the horizontal angles were protected by method and checked by closure.

Short answer. The surveys did not measure the refractive index along a line. They measured the bend of that line directly: the zenith distance is read from each end toward the other, and on a curved surface the pair fixes the refraction on that line in that air, ρ = (θ − (D − A)) ÷ 2 (Middleton et al., 1904, p. 225). Clarke (1858) does this for 112 lines, Delambre for 189, Maclear for 10, Schott hour by hour, with simultaneous pairs where the means allowed. For the horizontal angles there is no such measurement, so the surveys removed lateral refraction by method (hours, lights, height, repetition, rejection) and bounded what was left by the triangle closures: Clarke (1880) gives ±0.794″ per angle from 107 triangles.
Rule for refraction on computed zenith distances, founded on observations with an instrument checked by reversal
Cassini de Thury and Lacaille, verification of the Paris meridian and the arc of the parallel near 43.5 N · x (Troisième partie), with footnote; sentence ends on p. xj · strength ★★★
Vertical refraction coefficients

Same page. Where a zenith distance could not be observed at the far station, it was computed from the one observed at the near station and the itinerary arc (the arc between the two places, 1 minute for 951 toises). The authors state that refraction makes this computation inexact and give a rule: take 2 or 3 minutes off the arc when it exceeds 20 minutes. The footnote says the rule rests on observations made with a quadrant checked by reversal (turning the instrument over to remove its index error), made on purpose to measure terrestrial refraction.

“Il eft vrai que la réfraction empêche que ce calcul ne foit exact ; mais on peut y avoir égard , en quelque façon (*), en ôtant deux ou trois minutes de l'arc de la [diftance itinéraire , s'il excéde 20'] ... (*) Pour faire voir fur quoi eft fondée la correction que nous difons ici qu'on peut faire , nous allons rapporter quelques obfervations qui ont été faites avec un Inftrument vérifié exprès par le renverfement, pour connoitre la quantité de la réfraction horifontale, qui rend incertains les grands nivellemens.”
In English: “It is true that refraction prevents this calculation from being exact; but one can allow for it in some fashion (*) by taking two or three minutes off the arc of the [itinerary distance, if it exceeds 20']. (*) To show what the correction we say can be made here is founded on, we shall report some observations made with an instrument checked expressly by reversal, to learn the amount of horizontal refraction, which makes long levellings uncertain.”
Cassini de Thury, C.-F. (1744). La méridienne de l'Observatoire Royal de Paris vérifiée dans toute l'étendue du Royaume par de nouvelles observations. Paris: H.-L. Guérin & J. Guérin., x (Troisième partie), with footnote; sentence ends on p. xj
Four reciprocal zenith-distance pairs measure the total refraction on lines of 9 to 35.5 minutes of arc
Cassini de Thury and Lacaille, verification of the Paris meridian and the arc of the parallel near 43.5 N · x-xj (Troisième partie), footnote · strength ★★★

Footnote continued on p. xj. For four lines the zenith distance was observed at both ends. Reciprocal zenith distances are taken from each end of a line toward the other; their sum exceeds 180 degrees by the arc between the two verticals, less the bend of the ray at both ends, so the pair measures the refraction on that line itself. For each pair the authors print the two zenith distances, the apparent arc given by their sum, the true arc from the triangles, and the difference, which is the total refraction of both ends.

“Au fignal de Ste Victoire, la diftance apparente du fommet de la Montagne des Houpies au zenith fut obfervée de 90° 41' 40". A la Montagne des Houpies la diftance de Ste Victoire au zenith fut trouvée de 89° 43' 15". La fomme 180° 24' 55" donne 24' 55" pour l'arc itinéraire apparent, au lieu que le véritable eft de 28' 15"½. Il y avoit donc 3' 20"½ de réfraction, fur un arc de 28'.”
In English: “At the signal of Sainte-Victoire, the apparent zenith distance of the top of the Montagne des Houpies was observed as 90° 41' 40". At the Montagne des Houpies the zenith distance of Sainte-Victoire was found as 89° 43' 15". The sum 180° 24' 55" gives 24' 55" for the apparent itinerary arc, whereas the true one is 28' 15"½. So there were 3' 20"½ of refraction on an arc of 28'.”
Reading the table. Four printed pairs in running text: Sainte-Victoire / Houpies (90° 41' 40", 89° 43' 15"; 3' 20"½ on 28'); Aigues-Mortes / Houpies (89° 50' 19", 90° 40' 20"; 4' 57" on 35'½); Carcassonne / foot of Alaric signal (89° 1' 25", 91° 10' 5"; 1' 22" on 13'); Perpignan / foot of Tautavel tower (88° 36' 55", 91° 31' 20"; 43" on 9'). Each pair: zenith distance at A, zenith distance at B, apparent arc, true arc, total refraction. One value per station; the number of readings is not printed.
Worked out here: Refraction at one end as a fraction of the arc: 200.5/1695.5/2 = 0.059; 297/2136/2 = 0.070; 82/772/2 = 0.053; 43/538/2 = 0.040.

Delambre's two remedies against a possible lateral refraction: wait for favourable moments, and repeat at different hours and conditions
Delambre and Méchain, meridian arc Dunkirk to Barcelona (Base du système métrique) · T1 Discours préliminaire p. 106 · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours Repetition over days and hours Night lamps and heliotropes

Discours préliminaire, section on signals. Lateral refraction is a sideways bend of the line of sight, which would change horizontal angles. Delambre says he was at times tempted to believe in it, that night lamps would be equally subject to it, and that the defence is to observe at good moments and to repeat at other hours and in other conditions, so that a sideways error does not repeat in the same direction.

“S'il existe une réfraction latérale, comme j'ai été par fois tenté de le croire, les réverbères y seroient également sujets, et l'on n'a pour se garantir de cette illusion que deux moyens qui ne sont pas infaillibles, l'un est d'attendre les instans favorables ; l'autre, de répéter les observations à des heures et dans des circonstances différentes.”
In English: “If a lateral refraction exists, as I have at times been tempted to believe, reverberatory lamps would be equally subject to it, and there are only two means, not infallible, to guard against this illusion: one is to wait for favourable moments; the other, to repeat the observations at different hours and in different circumstances.”
Méchain, P., & Delambre, J.-B. J. (1806). Base du système métrique décimal, ou mesure de l'arc du méridien compris entre les parallèles de Dunkerque et Barcelone (Vol. 1). Paris: Baudouin., T1 Discours préliminaire p. 106
The refraction formula: reciprocal zenith distances give the refraction r on each line, assumed equal at both ends
Delambre and Méchain, meridian arc Dunkirk to Barcelona (Base du système métrique) · T2 p. 739 · strength ★★★
Vertical refraction coefficients

Tome II, chapter on inclined distances and terrestrial refraction. Reciprocal zenith distances are taken from each end of a line toward the other; their sum exceeds 180 degrees by the arc between the two verticals, less the bend of the ray at both ends, so the pair measures the refraction on that line itself. Delambre writes the observed zenith distances as δ and δ'' and the angle between the two verticals as C, and derives r, the refraction at each end. The ratio r/C is the coefficient n used in the table of 189 pairs. The only assumption is that the bend is the same at both ends.

“Ces dernières sont diminuées de la réfraction terrestre, qui est supposée proportionnelle à l'angle des deux normales ou à l'angle M, et qui par conséquent est égale pour les deux observations. Soit r cette réfraction”
In English: “These are diminished by terrestrial refraction, which is supposed proportional to the angle between the two normals or to the angle M, and which is therefore equal for the two observations. Let r be this refraction”
Worked out here: From the printed equations: 2r = 180° + C - δ - δ''; r/C = 1/2 - (δ + δ'' - 180°)/(2C) (eq. 64).
Méchain, P., & Delambre, J.-B. J. (1807). Base du système métrique décimal, ou mesure de l'arc du méridien compris entre les parallèles de Dunkerque et Barcelone (Vol. 2). Paris: Baudouin., T2 p. 739

For each line of the chain where zenith distances were taken from both ends, the table gives the factor n = r/C (refraction at one end divided by the angle between the verticals). Tome II, end of the remarks. Delambre gives the mean n of all 189 lines, then the mean after rejecting the observations made in fog and in decidedly rainy weather, and lists the rejected numbers. The 17 sea-horizon observations give nearly the same value. He states that more precise values need reciprocal observations made at the same time at both ends, in very great number.

“Le milieu entre les 189 . . . 0·08388. En rejetant les observations faites dans le brouillard et dans le temps décidément pluvieux, il restera 159 observations qui par un milieu donneront . . . 0·07876. Les 17 observations de l'horizon de la mer donnent par un milieu . . . 0·0783. J'ai rejeté de 57 à 69 inclusivement, de 71 à 75, de 76 à 88. Pour avoir quelque chose de plus précis il faudroit des observations réciproques, simultanées, en très-grand nombre.”
In English: “The mean of the 189 ... 0.08388. Rejecting the observations made in fog and in decidedly rainy weather, there remain 159 observations which give a mean of ... 0.07876. The 17 observations of the sea horizon give a mean of ... 0.0783. I rejected nos. 57 to 69 inclusive, 71 to 75, and 76 to 88. To have something more precise, reciprocal simultaneous observations in very great number would be needed.”
Worked out here: The listed ranges 57-69, 71-75, 76-88 contain 13 + 5 + 13 = 31 numbers; 189 - 31 = 158, the text prints 159.
