Instruction of the commission of the Dépôt de la Guerre for the new map of France, printed by Puissant. It sets the observing rules for the first-order chains, including the parallel of Paris. A conjugate observation is one repetition of the angle on the repeating circle. Simultaneous observations are reciprocal zenith distances taken at both ends at the same time, so that both see the same state of the air.

“Les distances zénithales relatives à ces chaînes seront elles-mêmes le résultat de trois séries au moins, prises à des heures différentes, et surtout vers le milieu du jour, afin qu'elles puissent donner les différences de niveau avec toute l'exactitude désirable, et, autant qu'il sera possible, par le concours d'observations simultanées : celles-ci seront accompagnées d'observations barométriques. ... Toutes les séries du premier ordre seront, autant que possible, prolongées jusqu'à la vingtième observation conjuguée ; toutes celles du deuxième ordre s'arrêteront à la dixième.”
In English: “The zenith distances for these chains will themselves be the result of at least three series, taken at different hours, and above all towards the middle of the day, so that they can give the level differences with all desirable accuracy, and, as far as possible, by the combination of simultaneous observations: these will be accompanied by barometric observations. ... All first-order series will, as far as possible, be carried to the twentieth conjugate observation; all those of the second order will stop at the tenth.”
Puissant, L. (1832). Nouvelle description géométrique de la France (Première partie). Paris: Ch. Picquet., 28
Night observations on lamps shortly after sunset gave much larger discordances than day observations (horizontal angles)
Parallel of Paris, Brest to Strasbourg (Henry east part, Bonne west part), Nouvelle carte de France · 35 · strength ★★★
Night lamps and heliotropes Steady-air hours

Puissant, p. 35, describing the Brest-Strasbourg line. A discordance is the disagreement between repeated measures of the same quantity. On this page the discordances belong to the night observations made with lamps as signals, that is, the angles between signals of the triangles: the next sentence turns to the zenith distances as a separate set ('C'est aussi sur cette même ligne qu'ont été observées des distances zénithales réciproques et simultanées'). Puissant confirms the reading on p. 156, where he says that with lamps 'les erreurs des triangles n'ont pas été moindres que de coutume' for the horizontal angles. The night zenith distances of the eastern part were also rejected, for their own discordance (p. 208, item fr_par_06).

“C'est sur une grande partie de cette ligne, confiée, dès l'origine des travaux, à MM. les colonels Bonne et Henry, que des réverbères ont été employés pour signaux ; mais les observations nocturnes, à peu d'intervalle du coucher du soleil, ont souvent présenté des discordances beaucoup plus considérables que celles faites de jour. C'est aussi sur cette même ligne qu'ont été observées des distances zénithales réciproques et simultanées, afin de connaître avec toute la précision désirable les hauteurs des stations depuis le Panthéon jusqu'à Brest.”
In English: “It is on a large part of this line, entrusted from the start of the work to Colonels Bonne and Henry, that lamps were used as signals; but the night observations, shortly after sunset, often showed much larger discordances than those made by day. It is also on this same line that reciprocal and simultaneous zenith distances were observed, in order to know with all desirable precision the heights of the stations from the Panthéon to Brest.”
Puissant, L. (1832). Nouvelle description géométrique de la France (Première partie). Paris: Ch. Picquet., 35
With lamps the triangle errors were no smaller than usual: night horizontal angles are as much affected by refraction as day ones, sometimes more in low places
Parallel of Paris, Brest to Strasbourg (Henry east part, Bonne west part), Nouvelle carte de France · 156 · strength ★★★
Night lamps and heliotropes Steady-air hours

Puissant, chapter on the probable error of an arc. The triangle errors (closure errors: the amount by which the three angles miss 180 degrees plus the spherical excess) are a direct test of the horizontal angles. Puissant uses them to judge the night method recommended by Laplace and finds no gain, with a larger effect in low ground between Paris and Strasbourg.

“Malgré l'usage que l'on fit de réverbères pour points de mire, dans cette partie de la méridienne, les erreurs des triangles n'ont pas été moindres que de coutume ; ainsi les observations nocturnes des angles horizontaux qui avaient été recommandées par le célèbre Laplace, sont tout aussi influencées par les effets de la réfraction atmosphérique que celles de jour, si même elles ne le sont quelquefois davantage dans les lieux bas, comme on l'a remarqué, ainsi que nous l'avons déjà dit, entre Paris et Strasbourg, lors de la mesure du parallèle compris entre ces deux villes.”
In English: “Despite the use of lamps as targets in this part of the meridian, the errors of the triangles were no smaller than usual; thus the night observations of horizontal angles, which had been recommended by the celebrated Laplace, are just as influenced by the effects of atmospheric refraction as those by day, if indeed they are not sometimes more so in low places, as was remarked, as we have already said, between Paris and Strasbourg, during the measurement of the parallel between these two towns.”
Puissant, L. (1832). Nouvelle description géométrique de la France (Première partie). Paris: Ch. Picquet., 156
Eastern part: night zenith distances rejected for enormous discordance; level differences taken from day observations
Parallel of Paris, Brest to Strasbourg (Henry east part, Bonne west part), Nouvelle carte de France · 208 · strength ★★★
Rejecting readings in unsteady air Steady-air hours Night lamps and heliotropes

Puissant, eastern part of the parallel (Colonel Henry, from 1818). The first-order angles were observed at night at Laplace's wish. Comparable zenith distances (those that should agree, such as the reciprocal pair on one line) disagreed so much that the night zenith distances were rejected and the heights were taken from day measures at second-order stations tied to the first-order ones.

“Le premier des deux tableaux ci-après présente l'ensemble des triangles du premier ordre dont les angles furent observés de nuit, dès l'année 1818, d'après le désir de l'illustre président de la commission royale, dans l'espérance qu'il en résulterait une plus grande exactitude. Mais l'énorme discordance que présentèrent sur cette ligne la plupart des distances zénithales comparables, mirent dans la nécessité de rejeter ces observations nocturnes pour déterminer les différences de niveau par d'autres mesures angulaires recueillies de jour, à différentes stations du second ordre, liées à celles du premier ordre.”
In English: “The first of the two tables below presents all the first-order triangles whose angles were observed at night, from 1818, at the wish of the illustrious president of the royal commission, in the hope of greater accuracy. But the enormous discordance shown on this line by most of the comparable zenith distances made it necessary to reject these night observations and to determine the level differences by other angular measures taken by day at various second-order stations tied to the first-order ones.”
Puissant, L. (1832). Nouvelle description géométrique de la France (Première partie). Paris: Ch. Picquet., 208
Coefficient n from reciprocal zenith distances; the two distances must belong to the same state of the air, which in general holds only when observed at the same time
Parallel of Paris, Brest to Strasbourg (Henry east part, Bonne west part), Nouvelle carte de France · 55 · strength ★★★
Vertical refraction coefficients

Puissant, Discours préliminaire, formulas of trigonometric levelling. Reciprocal zenith distances are taken from each end of a line toward the other; their sum exceeds 180 degrees by the arc between the two verticals, less the bend of the ray at both ends, so the pair measures the refraction on that line itself. The formula at the top of the page gives n from the two apparent zenith distances δ, δ' and the angle C between the verticals. Puissant states its condition: both distances must see the same atmosphere, so they should be simultaneous; he also names the constant error of the instrument as a second effect to separate.

“Il est à remarquer que les deux distances zénithales apparentes δ, δ' sont supposées répondre au même état de l'atmosphère ; circonstance qui n'a lieu en général que quand ces distances sont observées à la même époque. Il y a plus, ces mêmes distances ne sont pas seulement influencées par la réfraction, elles peuvent être affectées de l'erreur constante de l'instrument qui a servi à leur mesure”
In English: “Note that the two apparent zenith distances δ, δ' are supposed to correspond to the same state of the atmosphere; a circumstance which in general holds only when these distances are observed at the same time. Moreover, these distances are not only influenced by refraction; they may be affected by the constant error of the instrument used to measure them”
Worked out here: Printed formula: n = (½C - ½(δ + δ' - 200g))/C.
Puissant, L. (1832). Nouvelle description géométrique de la France (Première partie). Paris: Ch. Picquet., 55

Heights by reciprocal zenith distances from the Cordouan tower to Colombier and Granier; a 9 m discordance traced and removed; coefficient between 0.0563 and 0.097, generally 0.08
Brousseaud, arc of the mean parallel (45 N) across France, with link to the Austro-Sardinian chain · 160 · strength ★★★
Vertical refraction coefficients Steady-air hours

Brousseaud, p. 160. The absolute heights of the chain come from a succession of reciprocal zenith distances starting at the Cordouan lighthouse (68.445 m above mean sea, mean of four measures). Reciprocal zenith distances are taken from each end of a line toward the other; their sum exceeds 180 degrees by the arc between the two verticals, less the bend of the ray at both ends, so the pair measures the refraction on that line itself. Each height is the mean of two results that rarely differ by more than a metre. A discordance of about 9 m at the east end was traced to long sights from Bossivre and to signal caps too small to see at noon, and Puissant removed it by using heights from other stations. The coefficient of refraction found along the whole levelling lies between 0.0563 and 0.097.

“Partant de ce point, chacune des hauteurs absolues rapportées dans le deuxième tableau est la moyenne entre deux résultats, dont la différence dépasse rarement un mètre (1). ... a cependant présenté une discordance qui s'est accrue de 9m environ à l'extrémité orientale de la chaîne ... 2° que, sur toute son étendue, la valeur du coefficient de la réfraction est renfermée entre 0,0563 et 0,097, et se trouve généralement de 0,08, ainsi que Delambre l'avait déduit de ses observations.”
In English: “Starting from this point, each of the absolute heights given in the second table is the mean of two results whose difference rarely exceeds one metre (1). ... nevertheless showed a discordance that grew to about 9 m at the eastern end of the chain ... 2nd that, over its whole extent, the value of the coefficient of refraction lies between 0.0563 and 0.097, and is generally 0.08, as Delambre had deduced from his observations.”
Brousseaud (Colonel). (1839). Mesure d'un arc du parallèle moyen entre le pôle et l'équateur. Limoges: F. Chapoulaud., 160
Roy: conclusive refraction work needs levelled heights, barometers and thermometers at both stations, and two observers observing at the same instant
Anglo-French triangulation of 1787 (Greenwich to Paris junction), English side by Roy · p. 235 · strength ★★★

Section VII on terrestrial refraction. Terrestrial refraction is the bending of the ray between two ground stations, which makes a distant object appear higher. Roy states what a full test would need and then states what he had: reciprocal angles (each station observed from the other) taken at different times. In a footnote Maskelyne adds that a thermometer at the object as well as at the observer would allow a further correction.

“the relative heights of the stations should in strictness all have been ascertained by levelling: for purposes of this sort geometrical determinations, however good in other respects they may be, should not here be admitted, because they involve the very point in question, that is, the height, which should be obtained independently of angular measurement. Besides barometers and thermometers at both stations, two observers and two instruments of the same kind would have been necessary, for taking at the same instant the reciprocal angle of elevation and depression.”
Roy, W. (1790). An account of the trigonometrical operation, whereby the distance between the meridians of the Royal Observatories of Greenwich and Paris has been determined. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, 80, 111-270 (with Dalby, I., Remarks, pp. 593-614)., p. 235
Roy: measured terrestrial refraction varies from 1/3 to 1/24 of the arc, not a fixed 1/9, 1/10 or 1/14

Vertical refraction coefficients

Same section. The 'comprehended arc' (or contained arc) is the angle at the centre of the earth between the two stations. Earlier authors gave one fixed fraction of this arc for refraction. Roy's reciprocal observations showed a wide range, so a single adopted value was not reliable.

“for from these observations it will appear, that terrestrial refraction, instead of being 1/9th of the comprehended arc, according to M. Bouguer, 1/10th according to Dr. Maskelyne, 1/14th according to M. Lambert, varies from 1/3 to 1/24th part of that arc; and perhaps, if it had been possible for us to have tried it on heights considerably more elevated, we should have found it almost wholly to vanish.”
Roy, W. (1790). An account of the trigonometrical operation, whereby the distance between the meridians of the Royal Observatories of Greenwich and Paris has been determined. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, 80, 111-270 (with Dalby, I., Remarks, pp. 593-614)., p. 236

Art. II, Heights of Rook's Hill and Butser Hill. Each of three stations observed the other two, so every line has an angle from each end (reciprocal angles). From these the mean refraction of each line follows (see the rules in the 1797 item). The heights round the triangle do not close exactly: 228 feet by the lines across the water against 208 feet by the direct reciprocal line, and the authors share the 20 feet between the refractions.

“From these observations, the mean refraction between Dunnose and Rook's Hill will be found 1' 58"; between Dunnose and Butser Hill 2' 16"; and between Butser Hill and Rook's Hill 39"; which are about 1/12, 1/10, 1/15 of the contained arcs respectively, as in the table.”
Reading the table. Rows: at Dunnose, Rook's Hill and Butser Hill, the depression (or elevation) of the ground at each other station, in minutes and seconds; then the three contained arcs (23' 31", 23' 3", 9' 59"). The flagstaff at Rook's Hill was 20 feet high and the telescope axis about 5 1/2 feet above the ground. One value per direction is printed.
Worked out here: Dunnose-Rook's Hill: depressions 12' 14" + 7' 37" = 19' 51" = 1191". Reducing each to the telescope axis (5.5 ft at about 1411" x 101.4 ft = 143,100 ft subtends 7.9") removes about 16": 1175". Arc 23' 31" = 1411". (1411 - 1175)/2 = 118" = 1' 58", as printed. 118/1411 = 0.084 = 1/12.

Trigonometrical Survey of England and Wales (Ordnance), Williams, Mudge and Dalby 1791-1799 · p. 585 · strength ★★★

Art. III, Remarks on the tables. The height of Shooter's Hill from reciprocal angles (446 ft) is checked against spirit levelling from the Bull Inn (445 ft). On p. 584 the authors show that the elevation of St. Ann's Hill seen from Hampton Poor House differed widely between 1787 and 1792 with the instrument at the same height. They conclude that heights from vertical angles are good to about 10 feet unless reciprocal observations are made at the same time.

“Notwithstanding this consistency, and also that in the height of St. Ann's Hill, found by different methods, it is evident from the observations at Dunnose, Rook's Hill, and Butser Hill, that relative heights deduced from elevations, or depressions, cannot always be depended upon to less than about 10 feet, even supposing those heights are the means of two or three independent results, except, perhaps, reciprocal observations were made exactly at the same time. The very great difference in the observed elevations of St. Ann's Hill, proves that no dependance can be placed on single observations.”
Williams, E., Mudge, W., & Dalby, I. (1795). An account of the trigonometrical survey carried on in the years 1791, 1792, 1793, and 1794. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, 85, 414-591., p. 585

Steady-air hours Night lamps and heliotropes

Mudge (1801), on refraction. Simultaneous reciprocal observation means that each of two stations measures the vertical angle to the other at the same moment, so that both ends see the same state of the air. Mr. Woolcot observed at one station and Mudge at the other. The times were kept by watches regulated from altitudes of the sun and by signal.

“On these occasions, the instructions which I communicated to Mr. Woolcot, and by which I governed myself, were to observe the elevation or depression of the corresponding station at the expiration of every hour, beginning at six A. M. and to have the watch well regulated from observed altitudes of the sun's limb. I requested him also to be very minute in entering on his book the state of the weather; to keep the instrument properly sheltered from the wind; to be always cautious to adjust his level; and also to insert the state of the air, as to temperature and density, by noting the thermometer and barometer.”
Mudge, W. (1801). An account of the operations carried on for accomplishing a trigonometrical survey of England and Wales, continued from the year 1797, to the end of the year 1799 (Vol. 2, from the Philosophical Transactions). London: W. Faden., p. 183

Trigonometrical Survey of England and Wales (Ordnance), Williams, Mudge and Dalby 1791-1799 · p. 188 · strength ★★★
Repetition over days and hours

Discussion of the first series. Mudge estimates the error of each angle at no more than 3". At 9 and 10 p.m. the elevation at Whiteham changed by 44" and 42" while the depression seen from White Horse Hill stayed nearly the same. Because both ends were observed at the same time, he can place the change near one station. 'Floating strata' are layers of air with different refraction.

“These changes in the observed angles of elevation at Whiteham, (44" and 42" being the differences,) without corresponding ones at White Horse Hill, prove that some partial alteration, from floating strata, had taken place in the refraction near the former station. Whoever considers the matter, must perceive a case may be constructed in which this will take place, causing a great variation in one of the angles, whilst the other apparently remains the same: and this suggested the idea, that to afford any accurate conclusions in this way, a long series of observations would be necessary. It furthermore appears, that dew could not have caused these differences at Whiteham Hill, since the same cause would equally operate to vary the observed angles at White Horse Hill; but those remained nearly the same.”
Mudge, W. (1801). An account of the operations carried on for accomplishing a trigonometrical survey of England and Wales, continued from the year 1797, to the end of the year 1799 (Vol. 2, from the Philosophical Transactions). London: W. Faden., p. 188
Clarke 1858: Ben Macdui levelled up one side and down the other agrees with the height computed from vertical angles
Ordnance Trigonometrical Survey of Great Britain and Ireland, Principal Triangulation · p. xv · strength ★★★

Introduction. Heights of many stations were fixed by spirit levelling (a direct, step-by-step measurement of height differences with a level and staff); the vertical angles were also observed reciprocally. After the heights by vertical angles were printed, Ben Macdui was levelled, giving an independent check on the vertical-angle method over the mountain.

“Since the printing of the computed height (at page 558) of Ben Macdui, the height of that hill has been determined by spirit levelling. By levelling up the western side the height was found to be 4295.70 feet, and by levelling down the eastern side the result was 4295.76 feet. The agreements of these results with one another and also with the computed height, 4295.6 feet, are very remarkable.”
Clarke, A. R. (1858). Ordnance trigonometrical survey of Great Britain and Ireland: Account of the observations and calculations of the principal triangulation. London: Eyre and Spottiswoode., p. xv
Clarke 1858: the refraction coefficient is so variable that heights by vertical angles are secondary; reciprocal zenith distances were not simultaneous
Ordnance Trigonometrical Survey of Great Britain and Ireland, Principal Triangulation · p. 509 · strength ★★★
Vertical refraction coefficients

Opening of Section IX on zenith distances and heights. A zenith distance is the angle of a line of sight from the vertical (90° minus the elevation). The coefficient of refraction k is the refraction at one station divided by the angle at the earth's centre between the stations. Clarke shows that an error of .02 in k gives 5.1 feet in height at 14 miles but 127.4 feet at 70 miles, because the height error grows with the square of the distance.

“The co-efficient of refraction is a quantity so variable, that at great distances the average of any number of observations, however large, cannot be entirely relied upon. When the determination of altitudes becomes a matter of primary importance, the stations must be within a short distance of each other, or no very consistent or accurate results can be obtained; for the uncertainty of refraction being as the distance, the uncertainty of difference of height is as the square of the distance. ... The precision of the results is very much increased by simultaneous and reciprocal zenith distances. This case, however, does not exist in the Ordnance Survey, for the observations, though generally reciprocal, are not simultaneous.”
Clarke, A. R. (1858). Ordnance trigonometrical survey of Great Britain and Ireland: Account of the observations and calculations of the principal triangulation. London: Eyre and Spottiswoode., p. 509
Clarke 1858: k from zenith distances to stations of levelled height, 31 values on 16 lines, with number of observations
Ordnance Trigonometrical Survey of Great Britain and Ireland, Principal Triangulation · p. 542 · strength ★★★
Raw tables of repeated measures Vertical refraction coefficients

Section IX, 'Coefficient of Refraction'. Where both heights are known by levelling, the true zenith distance Z can be computed. The observed z differs from Z only by refraction, so k = (Z - z)/v is measured directly on that line. The weight w grows with the square root of the distance and with the number of observations.

“In the former case, the coefficient required is simply the ratio of the excess of the observed above the true zenith distance to the angle subtended by the two stations at the centre of the earth.”
Reading the table. Columns: number of the line; stations; levelled height (ft); observed zenith distance z; number of observations (4 to 29, e.g. Ben Nevis 19, Merrick 29, Pertinny 20); logarithmic distance; v (angle at the earth's centre, seconds); true zenith distance Z; Z - z (seconds); k; weight w; k times w. Values from 0.0649 (High Willhays) to 0.1058 (Swyre Barrow). Printed mean k = 0.0792.
Clarke, A. R. (1858). Ordnance trigonometrical survey of Great Britain and Ireland: Account of the observations and calculations of the principal triangulation. London: Eyre and Spottiswoode., p. 542
Clarke 1858: 112 reciprocal pairs of zenith distances, each giving k for that line
Ordnance Trigonometrical Survey of Great Britain and Ireland, Principal Triangulation · p. 543 · strength ★★★
Raw tables of repeated measures Vertical refraction coefficients

Next table. For two stations that observed each other, the sum of the two zenith distances exceeds 180° by the arc v when there is no refraction; refraction makes the sum smaller. So 1 - 2k = (z + z' - 180°)/v gives the bend on that line from the two angles alone, without knowing the heights. The weights follow the distance and the number of observations at each end.

“The weights assumed for the separate determinations are directly as the square root of the distance and inversely as the sum of the reciprocals of the numbers of observations at the two observing stations. The following table contains the calculation of 112 values of k:”
Reading the table. Columns: number; the two stations; observed zenith distance at each; number of observations at each (e.g. Monach 8 and Ben Clibrig 10; Corryhabbie 31 and 35; Jura 28); logarithmic distance; v; z + z' - 180°; 1 - 2k; k; weight w; kw. The table runs to p. 548. Group means printed on p. 548: 0.0801 (rays mostly over sea), 0.0778 (partly over sea), 0.0744 (inland).
Clarke, A. R. (1858). Ordnance trigonometrical survey of Great Britain and Ireland: Account of the observations and calculations of the principal triangulation. London: Eyre and Spottiswoode., p. 543
Clarke 1858: adopted k 0.0809 over sea and 0.0750 over land; short rays near the ground at least 0.1 with an uncertainty of half that
Ordnance Trigonometrical Survey of Great Britain and Ireland, Principal Triangulation · p. 550 · strength ★★★
Vertical refraction coefficients Towers, scaffolds and high stations

Conclusion of the refraction section. The levelled-height table and the reciprocal table are combined. Clarke separates rays over the sea from rays over land, and treats short lines near the ground separately because their refraction is larger and irregular.

“With one or two exceptions, all the coefficients in the preceding tables are derived from observed zenith distances of very distant objects; and the results are, upon the whole, tolerably consistent. The same consistency, however, is not found to exist among coefficients of refraction deduced from the observations of objects at short distances: the values are very irregular, and, indeed, cannot be represented with precision by any mean quantity. A great deal depends upon the nature of the ground over which the ray passes: as a general rule, when the distances are small the ray passes near the ground, which would tend to increase the coefficient of refraction, as is evident from Struve's formula (page 512); and this agrees with observation, for the mean value at short distances is certainly not under 0.1000, one-tenth of the arc-distance, with an uncertainty of at least half that quantity.”
Clarke, A. R. (1858). Ordnance trigonometrical survey of Great Britain and Ireland: Account of the observations and calculations of the principal triangulation. London: Eyre and Spottiswoode., p. 550
Clarke 1880: refraction displaces the line of sight almost wholly in the vertical plane; lateral refraction affects horizontal angles only to a very small extent
Textbook guidance of the period on terrestrial refraction · p. 280 · strength ★★★

Chapter XI, Heights of Stations. Lateral refraction is a sideways bend of the ray, which would change a horizontal angle. Clarke states that the ordinary bend is vertical, which changes zenith distances (vertical angles) but not horizontal directions.

“The displacement, resulting from refraction, of the direction of B, takes place almost wholly in the vertical plane which we may with sufficient accuracy consider common to A and B. Lateral refraction sometimes exists, affecting to a very small extent horizontal angles, but we here are concerned only with the more ordinary phenomenon which affects the measurement of zenith distances.”
Clarke, A. R. (1880). Geodesy. Oxford: Clarendon Press., p. 280
Clarke 1880: persistent lateral refraction is a constant error that only triangle closures reveal; 107 triangles give a probable error of 0.794" per angle
Textbook guidance of the period on terrestrial refraction · p. 230 · strength ★★★

Chapter on the calculation of the triangulation. The scatter of repeated readings at one station shows only errors of pointing and reading. A constant error, such as an off-centre signal, a signal lit on one side (phase), or a small persistent lateral refraction from the local ground, shows up only when the angles from different stations are combined in triangles. So Clarke takes the angle error from the triangle closures.

“In some instances local configuration of the surface may give rise to a lateral refraction, doubtless very small in amount, but persistent. ... A more trustworthy method therefore than the evidence of the observations themselves is presented by the errors in the sums of the observed angles of triangles. In the 107 triangles between Dunkirk and Formentera the mean square of error of a triangle is 4.161, hence the mean square of error of an observed angle is one third of this or 1.387: the probable error of an observed angle therefore in this work is ±.6745 √1.387 = ±0".794.”
Clarke, A. R. (1880). Geodesy. Oxford: Clarendon Press., p. 230
Clarke 1880: Ordnance Survey k values from zenith distances to stations of known height, with the number of observations; the two ends do not always agree

Pp. 282-283; the sentence begins at the foot of p. 282 ('The value of the coefficient of refraction may also be obtained from the reciprocally observed zenith distances of A and B, independently of the knowledge of the heights of those stations. “stations (and for this end the observations should be simultaneous) Z = z + kv and Z' = z' + kv, therefore z + z' + 2kv = 180° + v; ∴ 1 - 2k = (z + z' - 180°)/v.”

Table B gives the heights above the sea of the first-class points and of the Sarpinsky row. Reciprocal zenith distances are the two zenith distances of one line, one measured from each end. For each new point the table prints the zenith distance from the point to a known point (column 4) and from the known point back (column 5), the height obtained from each known point (column 6) and the mean (column 7). Two different known points give two independent heights for the same point.

“4. Зенитное разстояніе, измѣренное съ пункта опредѣляемаго на пунктъ, котораго номеръ выставленъ въ столбцѣ третьемъ. 5. Зенитное разстояніе измѣренное съ пункта, котораго № выставленъ въ столбцѣ 3-мъ на пунктъ опредѣляемый.”
In English: “4. Zenith distance measured from the point being determined to the point whose number is given in the third column. 5. Zenith distance measured from the point whose number is given in column 3 to the point being determined.”
Reading the table. Each new point is computed from two known points.

Russian arc of the parallel of 47.5 N, Privolzhsk triangulation (Kishinev to Astrakhan arc, eastern part) · Zapiski XXII, Otd. II, p. 190 · strength ★★★
Towers, scaffolds and high stations

Chapter VI, section 5. The heights of 109 points were carried by zenith distances from the New Russia points Popovka and Kadamovka to a mark on the Caspian shore at Naryshkina Kosa. This gives the difference between the levels of the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea. Struve's computation of the 1836 and 1837 Caspian to Black Sea levelling expedition (Fuss, Sabler and Savich) gives a second, independent value. The two differ by 0.643 sazhen.

“При исчисленіи высотъ 109 пунктовъ отъ начальнаго до Нарышкиной Косы, найдено, что разность поверхности морей Чернаго и Каспійскаго = — 12, 850 саж. Директоръ Пулковской Обсерваторіи Струве исчисливъ съ строжайшею точностію наблюденія, сдѣланныя въ 1836 и 1837 годахъ, для разрѣшенія ученаго вопроса относительно уровней этихъ морей нашелъ, что Каспійское море ниже Чернаго на = — 12, 207 саж. Разность обоихъ опредѣленій = 0, 643 саж.”
In English: “In computing the heights of 109 points from the starting point to Naryshkina Kosa it was found that the difference of the surfaces of the Black and Caspian Seas = -12.850 sazhen. The Director of the Pulkovo Observatory, Struve, having computed with the strictest accuracy the observations made in 1836 and 1837 to resolve the scientific question of the levels of these seas, found that the Caspian Sea is lower than the Black by -12.207 sazhen. Difference of the two determinations = 0.643 sazhen.”
Worked out here: 12.850 - 12.207 = 0.643 sazhen. 1 sazhen = 2.1336 m, so 0.643 sazhen = 1.37 m. 950 versts at 1.0668 km = about 1013 km.
Voenno-topograficheskoe depo. (1861). Zapiski Voenno-topograficheskago depo, Chast' XXII, Otd. II: Privolzhskoe trigonometricheskoe izmerenie. Voenno-topograficheskoe depo., Zapiski XXII, Otd. II, p. 190
Closures against set agreement: the extra error is assigned to signal phases; no sign of lateral refraction in the Baltic arc
Struve Geodetic Arc (Russo-Scandinavian arc of the meridian, Danube to Fuglenaes) · T. I, p. 148 · strength ★★★

Tome I, Chapter X, on the accuracy of the angles. Struve computes the probable error of an angle in two independent ways. From the agreement of the repeated sets of the same angle (5.84 sets on average) it is 0.338″. From the triangle closures it is 0.392″. The closures contain every error, including outside disturbances that are the same in all sets of one angle. Lateral refraction is a sideways bend of the line of sight by air of uneven density; it would show in the closures, not in the set agreement. Struve gives the outside part as 0.198″ per angle, names signal phases first and lateral refraction 'if it exists', and states that the Baltic arc gives no sign of lateral refraction.

“Parmi les causes des perturbations extérieures, il faut placer en premier lieu les phases des signaux, produites par une illumination latérale, puis la réfraction latérale, si elle existe. On voit par notre résultat que l'effet des phases a été réduit à un minimum, par suite de la forme et la figure exacte des signaux employés. Voyez p. 14. Quant aux réfractions latérales nous osons dire, que les opérations de l'arc Baltique n'en donnent pas le moindre indice.”
In English: “Among the causes of the external disturbances one must place first the phases of the signals, produced by a side illumination, then lateral refraction, if it exists. One sees from our result that the effect of the phases has been reduced to a minimum, owing to the form and exact shape of the signals used. See p. 14. As for lateral refractions, we dare say that the operations of the Baltic arc do not give the slightest sign of them.”
Worked out here: √(0.392² - 0.338²) = √(0.1537 - 0.1142) = 0.198″ (printed). Per direction 0.198/√2 = 0.140″.
Struve, F. G. W. (1857). Arc du méridien de 25° 20' entre le Danube et la Mer Glaciale mesuré depuis 1816 jusqu'en 1855 (Vol. 1). Imprimerie de l'Académie impériale des sciences., T. I, p. 148
Swedish part: corresponding zenith distances at every station, never fewer than 40 to 50 per station
Struve Geodetic Arc (Russo-Scandinavian arc of the meridian, Danube to Fuglenaes) · T. I, Introduction p. XXIV · strength ★★★
Repetition over days and hours

Tome I, Introduction, quoting Selander's report to the Stockholm Academy. Corresponding zenith distances are measured at both ends of a line for trigonometric levelling. From Haparanda to the Norwegian border, 40 Swedish miles, Agardh and Selander observed them at all stations with two instruments read by microscopes. The number per station was never below 40 to 50 and above 100 at some stations.

“M. Agardh, professeur d'astronomie (à l'Université de Lund), a été chargé de prendre part, des observations correspondantes des distances zénithales ont été exécutées sur toutes les stations situées depuis Haparanda jusqu'à la frontière de Norvège ... Vu que le nombre des distances zénithales, mesurées sur chaque station, n'est jamais au-dessous de 40 à 50, et s'élève pour d'autres au-delà de 100, j'ai raison d'espérer que les résultats que fournira le calcul, seront dignes de confiance.”
In English: “Mr Agardh, professor of astronomy (at the University of Lund), having been charged to take part, corresponding observations of zenith distances were made at all stations from Haparanda to the border of Norway ... Since the number of zenith distances measured at each station is never below 40 to 50, and for others rises above 100, I have reason to hope that the results the computation will give will be worthy of confidence.”
Struve, F. G. W. (1857). Arc du méridien de 25° 20' entre le Danube et la Mer Glaciale mesuré depuis 1816 jusqu'en 1855 (Vol. 1). Imprimerie de l'Académie impériale des sciences., T. I, Introduction p. XXIV
Internal check of the zenith distances: 693 values at 84 stations; probable error of one zenith distance 1.49 seconds
Struve Geodetic Arc (Russo-Scandinavian arc of the meridian, Danube to Fuglenaes) · T. II, pp. 232-233 · strength ★★★
Repetition over days and hours

Tome II, p. 233. The zenith place Z should be the same for all targets of one set if the observations were perfect and the change of terrestrial refraction (the bending of near-horizontal rays in the air) was uniform during the set. Struve uses the scatter of Z within each set as a check. At 84 stations 693 zenith distances of 335 objects were observed, about 2 per object. From the scatter he finds the probable error of a single zenith distance, from two circle positions, as 1.49″.

“Les Z qui appartiennent à la même ligne horizontale c.-à-d. à une même mise, auraient dû être identiques, si les observations avaient été d'une exactitude parfaite, et si la variation de la réfraction terrestre avait été uniforme pendant la durée de chaque mise. Les différences entre les Z de la même ligne nous font par conséquent juger de l'exactitude des distances au zénith observées”
In English: “The Z that belong to the same horizontal line, that is, to one and the same set, would have had to be identical if the observations had been of perfect accuracy and if the variation of terrestrial refraction had been uniform during each set. The differences between the Z of the same line therefore let us judge the accuracy of the observed zenith distances”
Worked out here: 693 / 335 = 2.07 observations per object (printed 2.07).
Struve, F. G. W. (1860). Arc du méridien de 25° 20' entre le Danube et la Mer Glaciale mesuré depuis 1816 jusqu'en 1855 (Vol. 2). Imprimerie de l'Académie impériale des sciences., T. II, pp. 232-233
Lindhagen: reciprocal zenith distances at the same favourable hour; barometer and thermometer recorded and used in the refraction
Struve Geodetic Arc (Russo-Scandinavian arc of the meridian, Danube to Fuglenaes) · T. II, p. 480 · strength ★★★
Vertical refraction coefficients

Tome II, Lindhagen's memoir on the Finmarken heights. Reciprocal zenith distances measured at the same time cancel the refraction if it is equal both ways; Lindhagen says that, when they cannot be simultaneous, they are still the best method if both are measured at the same, most favourable time of day. The great heights of the stations made the refraction very constant. Many surplus zenith distances gave a refraction constant, which was solved together with the heights. Barometer and thermometer readings were recorded at every vertical-angle measurement and were used in computing the refraction for the main net.

“In den Tagebüchern sind die Barometer- und Thermometerstände, welche zu den Zeiten der Vertikalwinkelmessungen stattfanden, regelmässig annotirt. Bei der Berechnung des Einflusses der Refraction auf die Zenithdistanzen im Hauptdreiecksnetze sind dieselben, so wie auch die Abhängigkeit der Refraction von den höheren Potenzen des Winkels, welchen die beiden Lothlinien, durch den Beobachtungsort und das Beobachtungsobject, mit einander machen, auf eine Weise berücksichtigt worden, zu deren Auseinandersetzung hier nicht der geeignete Ort ist.”
In English: “In the journals the barometer and thermometer readings that held at the times of the vertical angle measurements are regularly noted. In computing the influence of refraction on the zenith distances in the main triangle net these were taken into account, as was the dependence of the refraction on the higher powers of the angle that the two plumb lines, through the place of observation and the object observed, make with each other, in a way that this is not the proper place to set out.”
Struve, F. G. W. (1860). Arc du méridien de 25° 20' entre le Danube et la Mer Glaciale mesuré depuis 1816 jusqu'en 1855 (Vol. 2). Imprimerie de l'Académie impériale des sciences., T. II, p. 480
Lambton finds the refraction on the Madras line from a reciprocal elevation and depression
Great Arc of India, Lambton's meridional arc (Coromandel coast to Punnae and north to about 18 N) · p. 148 · strength ★★★
Vertical refraction coefficients

Section on the reduction of the Madras base (1802) to sea level. Lambton measured the depression of a flag on the beach from the race-stand and the elevation of the race-stand from the beach. A reciprocal pair is two vertical angles taken from each end of the same line toward the other end. The contained arc is the angle at the centre of the earth between the two stations. Half the excess of the contained arc over the sum of the two vertical angles gives the bend of the ray on that line, here 5.5 seconds.

“And the difference between the depression and elevation being 2' 58", we have (3' 9" - 2' 58")/2 = 5",5 for the terrestrial refraction.”
Worked out here: Contained arc 3' 9" = 189". Depression minus elevation as used here 2' 58" = 178". (189 - 178)/2 = 5.5". 5.5/189 = 0.029 of the contained arc.
Lambton, W. (1808). An account of the measurement of an arc on the meridian on the coast of Coromandel, and the length of a degree deduced therefrom in the latitude 12° 32'. Asiatic Researches, 8, 137 ff., p. 148

Appendix 11 of the southern arc paper. For each line, the station at which the angle was taken, the station observed, the apparent elevation (E) or depression (D), the contained arc, the refraction found from that reciprocal pair, and the height carried to the next station. The refraction is measured line by line, not assumed.

“11. Elevations and Depressions, CONTAINED Arcs, terrestrial refractions, together with the heights, above the level of the Sea, of the principal stations.”
Reading the table. Columns: Stations at; Stations observed; Apparent Elevations and Depressions (E = elevation, D = depression, degrees minutes seconds); Contained Arcs (minutes seconds, bracketed per reciprocal pair); Refraction (fraction of the contained arc, e.g. 1/12, 1/7, 1/14); Elevation above the Sea (station and height in feet). Each line is one reciprocal pair; each angle is the mean of several observations (see ga_02). Look at the spread of the refraction fractions from line to line.

Lambton (1814): refraction from 1/4 to 1/20 of the arc, attributed to moisture; barometer useless in the tropics, hygrometer needed
Great Arc of India, Lambton's meridional arc (Coromandel coast to Punnae and north to about 18 N) · Appendix p. 37 · strength ★★★
Vertical refraction coefficients

Appendix to GTS Vol. XII, Account of Colonel Lambton's operations, quoting a letter of 1814. Lambton reports the range of the refraction he measured on reciprocal lines over ten years, names moisture as the cause, explains why barometer readings do not help in India (pressure hardly changes), and calls for hygrometer readings and a table of low-altitude refractions from observation.

“In the course of my observations during the last ten years, I have at times found the terrestrial refraction to be as much as 1/4 of the contained arc, and occasionally as low as 1/20. This great irregularity I attribute to the different degrees of moisture in the atmosphere at different times. A knowledge of the laws of refraction is yet a desideratum in physical science. In climates remote from the equator, where the weight of the atmosphere is constantly changing, the barometer has been called in to indicate the pressure of a column of air, and rules investigated whereby to correct the mean celestial refraction according to the different heights of the mercury in the barometer. But in tropical climates this method can never apply owing to a well-known fact, that the weight of the atmosphere suffers very little variation, and while a barometer remains at the same station, it will not alter the 1/10 of an inch for several months together, excepting in the case of some great convulsion in the atmosphere. Other principles must therefore be adverted to. The hygrometer will be a necessary instrument to indicate the degree of moisture.”
Great Trigonometrical Survey of India. (1890). Account of the operations of the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India, Vol. XII: The Southern Trigon. Dehra Dun: Trigonometrical Branch, Survey of India., Appendix p. 37
Coast-to-coast reciprocal table: refraction per line from 1/7 to 1/40 of the arc; sea-to-sea error 8.6 ft

Table at the end of the peninsula paper. Heights start from the south end of the St. Thomas's Mount base (18.7 ft above low water) and are carried by reciprocal elevations and depressions across the peninsula to a station on the beach near Mangalore, whose height was then measured from low water on the west coast. Each bracketed pair is one line; the refraction column is the bend found on that line.

“ELEVATIONS and DEPRESSIONS, contained Arcs, terrestrial Refractions, together with the heights above the level of sea, of all the principal Stations. [...] The station on the beach above the low-water mark by measurement ...... 14.0 Difference or error ...... 8.6”
Reading the table. Columns: Stations at; Stations observed; Apparent E (elevation) and D (depression); Contained Arc (minutes seconds); Refract. (fraction of the contained arc, e.g. 1/18, 1/22, 1/7, 1/40); Elevation above the Sea (station, height in feet). 17 reciprocal pairs from St. Thomas's Mount to the Mangalore beach. Trigonometric height of the beach station 22.6 ft against 14.0 ft measured. A second table on p. 383 gives the stations off the direct line from Kylasghur.
Worked out here: 22.6 - 14.0 = 8.6 ft after a chain of 17 reciprocal lines across the peninsula.

GTS Karachi Longitudinal Series (North-West Quadrilateral) · p. 130-B · strength ★★★
Repetition over days and hours

Investigation after the sums of squares. The e.m.s. (error of mean square) of one measure and of one zero mean is computed for each group of angles by the same observer under similar conditions. The groups are split by terrain, so the larger scatter on the plains, where rays run close to the ground, is measured rather than assumed.

“The first 47 angles were measured at hill stations on 4 pairs of zeros, face right and face left, with an average of 3.14 observations on each zero; the remaining angles, 372 in number, were measured on 5 pairs of zeros with an average of 2.11 observations on each zero, at stations on hills, and sandhillocks and in the plains. The first 47 angles form a group by themselves; the remaining angles form 8 distinct groups, which again may be collected into 3 groups, in order that the relative e. m. s. of observations on hills and sand-hillocks, and in the plains, may be shown.”
Reading the table. Table columns: Group; Instrument and Observer; Position of stations (Hills, Sandhills, Plains); interval between zeros; measures on each zero (average); number of angles, single measures, zeros; e.m.s. of a single measure; e.m.s. of graduation and observation of a single zero. Compare the e.m.s. for hill groups with the plains groups.
Worked out here: e.m.s. of a single measure as printed: hills ±0.845, 0.787, 0.833, 0.760; sandhills ±0.966, 0.844; plains ±1.028, 1.252 seconds.

Mirage over the Runn of Cutch: vertical angles to the Runn judged untrustworthy
GTS Karachi Longitudinal Series (North-West Quadrilateral) · p. XI-B · strength ★★★
Rejecting readings in unsteady air

Introduction to the Karachi Longitudinal Series, season 1851-52. Mirage is strong refraction near hot or wet ground. The observers tried to fix the height of the Runn (a salt marsh) from Akoria station and did not use the result. The desert itself was free of mirage in that season.

“The desert was found perfectly free from mirage at the season it was visited; but the Runn of Cutch, on the southern flank of the series, was greatly affected by this atmospheric phenomenon, which prevented the ascertainment of the height of the Runn with respect to the sea level. [...] To determine this point, a secondary station was selected in the Runn, and vertical angles taken to it from Akoria station, on the edge of the tract, but the secondary point could not be connected, and the vertical angles were so affected by mirage, as to be untrustworthy.”
Walker, J. T. (Ed.). (1873). Account of the operations of the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India, Vol. III: The principal triangulation, North-West Quadrilateral. Dehra Dun: Great Trigonometrical Survey., p. XI-B
Over level country refraction runs from low negative to high positive; reciprocal angles days apart are mistrusted
GTS Karachi Longitudinal Series (North-West Quadrilateral) · p. (102) · strength ★★★

Walker, Vol. I, on the source of base heights. He explains why reciprocal vertical angles work in hills but not in a level country, and why spirit levels were begun in 1856 to control heights across the plains.

“But this method, though susceptible of a high degree of accuracy in a hill region, is beset with many difficulties in a level country; the rays of light, grazing the surface of the ground, pass through various gradations of refraction, from a low negative to a high positive value, during the course of the day and night; the success of the method depends on the reciprocal angles being equally refracted, which probably would not be the case even if the observations were simultaneous ; whereas from the circumstance of there being only one large theodolite with each survey party, there is always an interval of several days between the reciprocating observations, and thus there is all the more reason to mistrust the assumed equality of refraction.”
Walker, J. T. (1870). Account of the operations of the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India, Vol. I: Standards of measure and base-lines. Dehra Dun: Great Trigonometrical Survey., p. (102)
Vertical angles measured between 1 and 3 p.m., when refraction is usually a minimum, so reciprocal angles are equally refracted
GTS Bombay Longitudinal Series (Southern Trigon) · p. 22 · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours

Chapter II, section 6, reduction of vertical angles. The height formula assumes the two reciprocal angles are bent equally. The observing hour was chosen to make that assumption hold. The next paragraph explains the South Konkan revision (bo_08).

“In the preceding formulae it is assumed that the reciprocal angles are equally affected by refraction, and in order that this may be as nearly the case as possible, the vertical angles in all the modern operations are generally measured between the hours of 1 and 3 P.M., when the amount of refraction is usually a minimum.”
Great Trigonometrical Survey of India. (1890). Account of the operations of the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India, Vol. XII: The Southern Trigon. Dehra Dun: Trigonometrical Branch, Survey of India., p. 22
Coefficient of refraction found for each reciprocal pair; simultaneous re-observation on doubtful rays changed old heights by up to 43 ft
GTS Bombay Longitudinal Series (Southern Trigon) · p. 23 · strength ★★★
Vertical refraction coefficients

Continuation of bo_07. The South Konkan heights, taken 40 years earlier between the ghats and the coast, were re-observed in 1885-86 with simultaneous reciprocal angles (both ends at the same time). Then the formula: C is the contained arc, Da and Db the observed angles, beta the signal and instrument correction; phi is the mean refraction and phi/C the coefficient.

“during 1885-86, and simultaneous reciprocal observations were taken on the unfavourable rays in the hope of reducing the errors due to refraction to a minimum. A comparison between the new values and the old exhibited discrepancies with a range of 43 feet. The reciprocal angles are also employed to determine the co-efficient of refraction, to be used in reducing unreciprocated vertical angles ; [...] and φ/C gives the terrestrial refraction in decimals of contained arc—or in other words the co-efficient of refraction—for each pair of reciprocated observations.”
Worked out here: Formula as printed: φ = 1/2 {C - (Da + Db) + β}; coefficient = φ/C.
Great Trigonometrical Survey of India. (1890). Account of the operations of the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India, Vol. XII: The Southern Trigon. Dehra Dun: Trigonometrical Branch, Survey of India., p. 23
Lateral refraction named as the most important outside influence on horizontal angles; larger on plains and over jungle
GTS Bombay Longitudinal Series (Southern Trigon) · p. 100 · strength ★★★
Towers, scaffolds and high stations

Chapter III, the weights of the angles. Lateral refraction is the sideways bend of a ray passing close to ground or objects; it affects horizontal angles. The survey did not correct each angle for it; it measured its effect through the scatter of angles in each group and weighted the groups accordingly. Station height above ground is named as the control.

“Disparity of circumstance necessarily occurs whenever there are very marked variations in the general elevation of the observing and signal stations above the level of the ground; for on this condition freedom from grazing rays—and their concomitant lateral refractions—greatly depends. [...] and of these there can be little doubt that the most important is lateral refraction, which is liable to be greater in the plains than in the hills, and much greater in tracts of country which are covered with dense forest and jungle, than in tracts which are open and cultivated.”
Great Trigonometrical Survey of India. (1890). Account of the operations of the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India, Vol. XII: The Southern Trigon. Dehra Dun: Trigonometrical Branch, Survey of India., p. 100
Trigonometric heights tested against spirit-levelled stations: cumulative errors of +3, +2 and -3 ft
GTS Guzerat Longitudinal Series (South-West Quadrilateral, Vol. XIV) · p. xiii-K · strength ★★★

Same page as lo_03. The heights of the series were carried by vertical angles between stations whose heights were fixed by spirit levelling in 1875-77. The differences found at the levelled stations show the size of the error from refraction along the chain.

“The intermediate heights, of which the values were obtained trigonometrically, shewed at Poera a cumulative error of + 3 feet and at Jhinjhar and Wastrál a further error of + 2 feet, and on the section Ingrori to Sápakra of - 3 feet: these were dispersed by simple proportion.”
No page image: this source is held as a text layer only.
Great Trigonometrical Survey of India. (1890). Account of the operations of the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India, Vol. XIV: The South-West Quadrilateral (Guzerat Longitudinal Series). Dehra Dun: Trigonometrical Branch, Survey of India., p. xiii-K
Nevada series from 1880: forenoon and afternoon measures equalized to guard against lateral refraction
US Transcontinental Triangulation, 39th parallel · p. 573 · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours Repetition over days and hours

Part III, Nevada and California series. Lateral (horizontal) refraction is a sideways bend of the line of sight caused by unequal air temperature across the line, for example air heated on one side of a slope. Its sign changes between morning and afternoon heating, so equal numbers of forenoon and afternoon measures tend to cancel it.

“The equalization of the number of measures of horizontal directions at a station taken in the forenoon and in the afternoon was first put into execution in 1880 in this section; its purpose was to eliminate any effect of unequal heating of the theodolite as well as to provide against possible lateral refraction along the lines of sight. Observations of zenith distances were made at three different periods of the day, as stated in the case of the Rocky Mountain work.”
Schott, C. A. (1900). The transcontinental triangulation and the American arc of the parallel (Special Publication No. 4). U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey; Government Printing Office., p. 573
Persistent lateral deviation of the line of sight does not show at the station; it shows in the triangle closures
US Transcontinental Triangulation, 39th parallel · p. 50 · strength ★★★

Part I, on why station and net adjustments are kept separate. The station (local) adjustment compares repeated readings at one station. The net adjustment forces the triangles to close. A constant sideways bend of a line (persistent lateral refraction) affects every reading of that line equally, so it cannot appear in the station scatter; it can only appear as triangle misclosure. Schott states that the error from the closures is the larger, so the closures are the real test.

“In the latter combination of the measures new sources of error show their effects; as, for instance, the effect of the deflection of the plumb line causing the angles to be measured out of the normal horizontal plane, want of coincidence of the center of a station and of heliotropes or targets subsequently mounted over it, persistent lateral deviation of the line of sight, constant or uncompensated graduation errors of the instrument, all of which causes exert no influence on the station adjustment. It is a matter of experience that the value of the probable error of a direction derived from the measures at a station is much smaller than the same when derived from the triangle closing errors”
Schott, C. A. (1900). The transcontinental triangulation and the American arc of the parallel (Special Publication No. 4). U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey; Government Printing Office., p. 50

Part II, general remarks. The coefficient of refraction m is the bend of the line of sight expressed as a fraction of the arc between the stations (m = k/2 in the usual notation). Reciprocal zenith distances are vertical angles measured from each end of a line toward the other; from the pair, m is computed for that line, so the refraction is measured on the line itself, not assumed. Special hourly series were run day and night to find the daily cycle.

“For the sake of easy reference, we shall give here in tabular form and also exhibit by diagrams the resulting hourly values of the coefficient of refraction, m, from four experimental series [...] The tabular values were deduced under the supposition of equal refraction angles at lower and upper stations.”

Part II, appendix D. From the hourly mean zenith distances at both ends, Schott computes for each hour the difference of height (Delta h) and the coefficient m, assuming equal refraction at the two ends. Because the bend is measured from both ends, most of it cancels out of the height.

“The adopted formulae are- m = 0.5 - (zeta + zeta' - 180 deg) / 2 psi [...] The resulting hourly values for Delta h and m are given in the following table: [...] The values of Delta h are plotted on diagram (3) and show the computed difference of height between 10 a. m. and near midnight to be smaller than the mean; but the results for those hours appear remarkably consistent.”

Part II, heights across the Sacramento and San Joaquin valleys. The older long lines were observed at different hours, months and years, so equal refraction at the two ends could not be relied on. In 1898 the observers measured both ends at the same time over shorter lines, and the long lines were removed from the height results.

“The difficulty experienced when attempting the determination of heights on the crest of the Sierra Nevada by means of zenith distances measured over the long lines spanning the great valley of California rendered it necessary to supplement the older measures. This was done in the summer of 1898, by strictly simultaneous reciprocal measures over shorter lines, along which the variations of refraction are less injurious. [p. 305:] If, further, we reflect that the resulting zenith distances, as tabulated, were taken mostly at different hours of the day, in different months of the year, and in different years, with only the new (1898) measures simultaneous; it does not seem surprising that it became necessary to exclude the resulting differences of height over the several long lines across the valley which range up to 229 kilometres or 142 statute miles.”

Persistent lateral refraction along a line is a triangle-combination error, not visible in the station measures
US Eastern Oblique Arc, Calais to New Orleans · p. 26 · strength ★★★

Part I, general remarks on the adjustments. "Triangle-combination errors" are the errors that only appear when the triangles are made to close. The same rule as in the transcontinental work: a constant sideways bend on one line cannot be seen in the repeats at the station, so the closures are used to measure it.

“The errors brought to light by geometrical conditions, and which have been called triangle-combination errors, are of a different character from those developed by a comparison of the measures made at a station, where defects of centering at observing and observed stations, effects of large local deflections of the vertical at a station, persistent lateral refraction along a line, etc., do not show; that is to say, weights pertaining to one operation are not those proper for the next operation.”

Subsequent to this date all horizontal measures of the primary triangulation between these stations and the Gulf coast were made at night by Assistants F. W. Perkins and W. B. Fairfield. Repetition over days and hours

Description of the Beaufort theodolite method (p. 400). Each angle was measured by repetition, the verniers read at every tenth repetition; the mean of ten repetitions is one partial result. Maclear says the number of partial results depended on the importance of the angle and on the atmosphere. Definition is how sharp and steady the signal looks in the telescope; probable error is the error that has an even chance of being exceeded. Five results in first-rate definition (Simon's Berg, 19 November 1845) gave 0.05"; sixteen results in bad definition and lateral refraction (Kapoc Berg, 12 February 1846) gave 0.3". The footnotes giving these stations and dates are at the foot of the same page and inside the crop.

“The mean of every tenth repetition being regarded as one partial result, the required number of such results depended upon the importance of the angle, and the atmospheric circumstances during the time when measuring. The value of the latter may be gathered from the fact of five results obtained during first-rate definition, giving a probable error of 0"·05 and weight 360 (a) ; whereas during bad definition and lateral refraction, 16 results gave a probable error of 0"·3, and weight 11 (b). ... (a) Simon's Berg, Nov. 19, 1845. (b) Kapoc Berg, Feb. 12, 1846.”
Worked out here: 5 results = 50 repetitions; 16 results = 160 repetitions. Weight = 1/P^2 (p. 419): 1/0.3^2 = 11.1, printed 11. 1/0.05^2 = 400; the printed 360 corresponds to P = 0.0527, which rounds to the printed 0.05.
Maclear, T. (1866). Verification and extension of La Caille's arc of meridian at the Cape of Good Hope (Vol. 1). London: Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty., p. 400

Rule: half the arcs early morning, half late afternoon; vertical angles near sunset
Geodetic Survey of the Transvaal and Orange River Colony (Morris; preface and introduction by Gill) · p. 19 · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours

Same paragraph (p. 19). The observer was told to split the arcs between early morning and late afternoon, the hours of clearest and steadiest air, so that the mean covers two different states of the air. Morning mist and haze often stopped this. All vertical angles (angles of elevation or depression) were taken in the afternoon near sunset, with the vertical arc level read every time.

“The instructions to the observer were to observe half the arcs in the early morning and the remainder in the late afternoon, as being the hours of the day when the air might be expected to be clearest and steadiest. But it was soon found that to observe strictly in this way would be the cause of considerable delay when the morning observations were frequently quite prevented by mist and haze. The vertical angles were all observed in the afternoon as near to sunset as possible, and in repetition equivalent to the first pair of arcs as for horizontal angles, the readings of the vertical arc level being always recorded.”

Gill's finding: lateral refraction larger than pointing errors; morning and afternoon combined
Trigonometrical Survey of New South Wales · pp. 181-182 · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours

Furber, Instruments (pp. 181-182), reporting Gill's report on the Cape Colony and Natal survey. Lateral refraction is the sideways bending of the line of sight, which shifts horizontal directions. Gill found it larger than the errors of pointing and reading; a change of wind could move a distant station, and directions after noon differed from those before noon. His remedy was to vary the conditions, combining morning and afternoon work, and the probable error of an angle fell from 0.49" to 0.33". No PDF of this paper is in the project; the item points to the OCR text file, so no crop is possible. The wording was checked against page images of pp. 181-182 held elsewhere in the project.

“In this connection he states that during the course of the survey it was shown that the accidental errors of pointing or reading were less to be regarded than those caused by lateral refraction. Not only was it found that a change of wind was sometimes followed by marked change in the direction of a distant station, but that a systematic difference, small but appreciable, existed between directions measured after and before noon, and the general conclusion was come to that steps were to be taken to reduce the effects of refraction by varying the conditions under which the observations were made rather than by seeking precision from extraordinary accuracy of the instruments used. In this view a 10-inch theodolite was substituted by Dr. Gill for the 18-inch instrument previously employed, and throughout the remainder of the work morning and afternoon observations were combined, the very satisfactory result being that with an instrument of less than one-fourth the weight the probable error of an observed angle was reduced from ± 0·49″ to ± 0·33″.”

Altitudes of stations (p. 204). Furber states that simultaneous observation at both ends is the ideal, because only then is the refraction certain to be the same at both ends. That was not possible, so the reciprocal observations were made at the same time of day. Each set is two rounds of elevations, face left and face right, with a level along the line read at every sighting. He adds that more sets would be better. No PDF of this paper is in the project; the item points to the OCR text file, so no crop is possible. Quote from the text layer, one OCR word break corrected ('reciprocal observations').

“The simultaneous observation at each end of the line involved, which is necessary to an ideal determination of relative heights (for by that means only is it made certain that the co-efficients of refraction at the two ends of the line are the same) has, of course, been impracticable. The work, however, is performed always at the same time of the day, so as to secure, as far as possible, the same atmospheric conditions in the reciprocal observations. The actual field work consists in the measurement, with a theodolite having a 10-inch circle, of the elevations of all the stations in the surround, noting, at the time of sighting to each, the reading of a level the axis of which is in the direction of the line being sighted, any variations of the level being subsequently applied to the circle reading. The instrument is then reversed and a similar round taken, each such pair of rounds constituting a set from which the differences of height may be derived.”

Night lights changed how the Indian survey worked
Middleton, Chadwick and Bogle, A Treatise on Surveying (textbook) · p. 188 · strength ★★★

The book quotes Thuillier and Smyth's Manual of Surveying for India. Before Everest's vase lights (a clay dish of cotton seed and oil, burnt as a signal), the Indian survey observed in the rainy season, so that opaque flags could be seen. Lights let the observers work at night instead.

“Vase lights were invented by Colonel Everest nearly fifty years ago, and completely altered the operations of the Great Trigonometrical Survey in India, which had previously to be carried on in the unhealthy season of the rains, in order that the opaque signals, such as flags, might be clearly seen. By enabling observations to be rapidly taken at night, the progress of the work was also much accelerated.”

Steady-air hours Night lamps and heliotropes Vertical refraction coefficients

End of the quoted manual. The heliotrope limits daytime work to about 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. Vertical angles (the up-down angles used for heights) are to be taken between 2½ and 3½ p.m., the time of least refraction. The manual says vertical angles taken at other hours are so irregular that heights from them are nearly worthless. It also says luminous targets are observed more correctly than opaque ones.

“the only limit to the times at which observations can be made will be from 9 o'clock A.M. to 2½ or 3 o'clock P.M. But the heliotrope is more particularly recommended for the purpose of taking vertical angles with certainty between the hours of 2½ and 3½ afternoon, which is the time of minimum refraction, because verticals taken at any other time are subject to great irregularities, whereby heights deduced from them are nearly worthless. Luminous objects are much more correctly, rapidly, and comfortably observed than opaque ones, which, if distant, are always faint, and disappear when brought near the wire of the telescope.”
Middleton, R. E., Chadwick, O., & Bogle, J. du T. (1904). A treatise on surveying: Part I (2nd ed.). E. & F. N. Spon., pp. 190-191
Why a sight line bends: pressure and irregular heating
Middleton, Chadwick and Bogle, A Treatise on Surveying (textbook) · p. 224 · strength ★★★
Vertical refraction coefficients

Start of the section "Effect of Refraction on Vertical Angles". Air density changes with pressure and heating, so a nearly horizontal ray curves, usually concave to the ground. A target then appears higher than it is. Fig. 129 shows the true line O A, the curved path O C A, and the apparent direction A O₁. The angle O₁ A O is the refraction error.

“The effect of refraction has now to be considered. Rays of light passing through the atmosphere, nearly parallel to the earth's surface, do not travel in a straight line as they do in space (fig. 128). Owing to the varying density of the air, due to differences of pressure, and to irregular heating, they travel in a curved line. Usually, almost invariably, the path of the ray is concave towards the earth's surface, the effect of this being to make an object appear higher than it really is.”
Middleton, R. E., Chadwick, O., & Bogle, J. du T. (1904). A treatise on surveying: Part I (2nd ed.). E. & F. N. Spon., p. 224
Reciprocal angles measure the bend on each line
Middleton, Chadwick and Bogle, A Treatise on Surveying (textbook) · p. 225 · strength ★★★
Vertical refraction coefficients

The method used to find refraction on a line. The vertical angle is observed from each end toward the other (reciprocal angles). On a curved earth, the two angles and the angle θ at the earth's centre are related, so the refraction error ρ comes out of the observed angles: ρ = (θ − (D − A)) ÷ 2, where D is the depression and A the elevation. The bend is measured on that line, in that air, not taken from a model. The book adds that observing both ends at the same time, or in similar conditions on different days, determines it well enough for practical purposes.

“By taking reciprocal angles, 'refraction errors' may be eliminated, by thus ascertaining their values, and applying the same as corrections. [...] If the refraction be fairly regular, and if the reciprocal angles be observed simultaneously, or under similar conditions of the atmosphere on different days, the refraction will be determined with sufficient accuracy for all practical purposes, for the correction for refraction is usually but small. It is generally expressed as a fraction of the subtended arc, and amounts to about one-fifteenth part thereof (vide infra).”
Middleton, R. E., Chadwick, O., & Bogle, J. du T. (1904). A treatise on surveying: Part I (2nd ed.). E. & F. N. Spon., p. 225
Refraction varies with hour, temperature and pressure; horizontal deviation happens
Middleton, Chadwick and Bogle, A Treatise on Surveying (textbook) · p. 226 · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours Rejecting readings in unsteady air

The authors list what changes refraction: the hour (least about 3h 45m p.m. in the tropics), temperature and barometric pressure, and heated ground, where the ray can even curve the other way (mirage). They also state that sideways (horizontal) deviation is common. Their conclusion: under strong disturbance do not observe at all, and otherwise rely on reciprocal angles in similar conditions.

“Now the value of error of refraction though usually small, is very uncertain. It varies at different hours of the day, being least (in the tropics) at about 3h. 45m. P.M. It varies also with temperature, and barometric pressure. Over highly heated arid plains, it becomes exceedingly irregular, the curve sometimes being actually convex towards the earth, so that objects are depressed and not raised. [...] Horizontal deviation is also very common. A series of rods, ranged out in a straight line at one time, have presented the appearance of a curve at another time. When disturbance is so great as this, accurate observation of any kind is obviously impracticable. At any time, however, the effect of refraction is uncertain, and accurate results can only be arrived at, by taking reciprocal angles under similar atmospheric conditions.”
Middleton, R. E., Chadwick, O., & Bogle, J. du T. (1904). A treatise on surveying: Part I (2nd ed.). E. & F. N. Spon., p. 226
Zenith distances for the reduction to the horizon needed only 3 or 4 minutes of accuracy
Cassini de Thury and Lacaille, verification of the Paris meridian and the arc of the parallel near 43.5 N · x (Troisième partie) · strength ★★

Troisième partie, section on the reduction of the angles to the horizon. The angles between signals were taken with a quadrant in the inclined plane through the two targets. To bring an angle to the horizontal plane, the observers needed the zenith distance of each target. A zenith distance is the vertical angle between the plumb-line direction straight up (the zenith) and the target. The authors state that a coarse zenith distance is enough for this reduction, so the horizontal angles do not depend on an exact knowledge of the vertical refraction.

“En effet pour faire la réduction des angles au plan de l'Horizon, il n'étoit pas néceffaire de connoitre les diftances des objets au zenith avec une extrême précifion : il fuffifoit de les avoir à 3 ou 4 minutes près.”
In English: “Indeed, to reduce the angles to the plane of the horizon, it was not necessary to know the zenith distances of the objects with extreme precision: it was enough to have them to within 3 or 4 minutes.”
Cassini de Thury, C.-F. (1744). La méridienne de l'Observatoire Royal de Paris vérifiée dans toute l'étendue du Royaume par de nouvelles observations. Paris: H.-L. Guérin & J. Guérin., x (Troisième partie)
Refraction raises signals unequally, so the three angles of a triangle lie in different planes and are brought to one surface
Delambre and Méchain, meridian arc Dunkirk to Barcelona (Base du système métrique) · T1 Discours préliminaire p. 137 · strength ★★

Discours préliminaire, section on the reduction to the horizon. Delambre states that vertical refraction does not bend angles sideways but changes the apparent heights of the targets, so each measured angle lies in its own inclined plane. The reduction to the horizon (a small computed correction from the two zenith distances) brings all angles to one surface before the triangles are solved.

“La réfraction élève inégalement les objets terrestres ; il y a toujours une différence sensible entre la hauteur du centre du cercle et le point extérieur qui a servi de mire dans les stations circonvoisines ; il en résulte que les trois angles qui doivent former chacun des triangles, ont toujours été observés dans des plans différens. Avant que d'en faire usage, il faut donc les ramener au même plan, ou du moins à une même surface.”
In English: “Refraction raises terrestrial objects unequally; there is always a noticeable difference between the height of the centre of the circle and the outer point used as target from the surrounding stations; hence the three angles that must form each triangle were always observed in different planes. Before using them, they must therefore be brought to the same plane, or at least to the same surface.”
Méchain, P., & Delambre, J.-B. J. (1806). Base du système métrique décimal, ou mesure de l'arc du méridien compris entre les parallèles de Dunkerque et Barcelone (Vol. 1). Paris: Baudouin., T1 Discours préliminaire p. 137
