Rejecting readings in unsteady air

Same Instruction, added considerations. Vapours are visible moisture or haze near the ground; undulations are the trembling of the target image in unsteady air; phases are the uneven sunlight on one side of a signal that shifts its apparent centre. The rule tells observers to wait for steady, clear air before measuring angles.

“On évitera, autant que possible, de faire des observations d'angles dans les momens où il y a beaucoup de vapeurs et d'ondulations, et dans ceux où le soleil donnerait aux signaux des phases prononcées qui rendraient le pointé trop incertain.”
In English: “One will avoid, as far as possible, observing angles at moments when there are many vapours and undulations, and at those when the sun would give the signals marked phases that would make the pointing too uncertain.”
Puissant, L. (1832). Nouvelle description géométrique de la France (Première partie). Paris: Ch. Picquet., 28
As many reciprocal zenith distances as needed at every first-order vertex to keep level errors under two metres; Brest-Panthéon levelling by reciprocal simultaneous zenith distances by day and night
Parallel of Paris, Brest to Strasbourg (Henry east part, Bonne west part), Nouvelle carte de France · 232 · strength ★★

Puissant, section on the geodetic levelling and its precision by the formulas of probability. He states the target accuracy (level differences not wrong by more than two metres in the worst case) and that the number of reciprocal zenith distances at each vertex was set by that target. The networks control one another.

“aussi a-t-on observé à tous les sommets des triangles du 1er ordre autant de distances zénithales réciproques qu'il était nécessaire, pour que les erreurs commises sur les différences de niveau ne dépassassent pas deux mètres, dans les cas les plus défavorables. ... Tous les réseaux de triangles, qui partent de l'océan et qui s'étendent dans l'intérieur du royaume, réunissent cet avantage en se contrôlant les uns par les autres. C'est ainsi que le nivellement trigonométrique exécuté depuis Brest jusqu'au Panthéon, par des distances zénithales réciproques et simultanées, prises de jour et de nuit, a donné la hauteur absolue du sommet de cet édifice”
In English: “so at all the vertices of the first-order triangles as many reciprocal zenith distances were observed as were necessary for the errors on the level differences not to exceed two metres in the most unfavourable cases. ... All the networks of triangles that start from the ocean and extend into the interior of the kingdom have this advantage of controlling one another. Thus the trigonometric levelling carried out from Brest to the Panthéon, by reciprocal and simultaneous zenith distances taken by day and by night, gave the absolute height of the top of this building”

Puissant, p. 233. He states that he examined the original registers of the levelling by Bonne, Epailly and Béraud and judged them fully reliable, and that he measured their precision by probability formulas (probable error). He notes the missing comparison between their two repeating circles.

“En examinant avec attention les registres contenant toutes les observations et mesures relatives à ce nivellement (peut-être unique en son genre), l'on ne peut se refuser à reconnaître que cette opération, due à MM. Bonne, Epailly et Béraud, mérite une entière confiance ... In English: “Examining with care the registers containing all the observations and measures for this levelling (perhaps unique of its kind), one cannot refuse to recognise that this operation, due to Messrs Bonne, Epailly and Béraud, deserves full confidence ... Vertical refraction coefficients

Art. IV. From Dover the ground at Folkestone Turnpike was elevated 8' 37"; from Folkestone the Dover parapet was depressed 14' 17".5. With the distance 31554.6 feet, each angle gives a height difference of the two telescope axes, 108.2 feet and 104.3 feet. Without refraction they would agree; half their difference is the effect of the mean refraction on that line. On p. 240 Roy turns 1.95 feet at 31554.6 feet into 12".8, about 1/24 of the contained arc of 5' 9".4.

“In this case it is evident, that half the sum of 108.2 and 104.3, or 106.25 feet, is the difference of the relative heights of the axis at the two stations by a mean refraction; and that this mean refraction is subtended by half the difference, or”
Worked out here: (108.2 - 104.3) / 2 = 1.95 ft. 1.95 / 31554.6 = 6.18e-5 rad = 12.7 arc seconds (printed 12".8). Contained arc 5' 9".4 = 309.4"; 12.8 / 309.4 = 0.041 = 1/24.

Same section, after the table. Roy states that the ray height above the ground changes the refraction even for the same arc, and that a full study would be a separate operation on high mountains near the sea, with heights fixed by levelling (he names Ben Nevis; the 1858 account later observed there).

“If the circumstances had permitted the refraction on the distance between Dover and Calais to have been repeatedly tried, at the bottom of the cliff, at the top of the cliff, and again at the top of the castle, we should probably have found the refraction at the three stations considerably different, with the same length of arc, or one only varying insensibly. But, in order to be enabled to make conclusive observations of this sort, the operation should become a distinct one, or at most only comprehend such others as are connected with the modifications of the atmosphere.”

1795: refraction measured at both ends of the levelled Salisbury Plain base (38" and 50"), with the stated sensitivity to the height error
Trigonometrical Survey of England and Wales (Ordnance), Williams, Mudge and Dalby 1791-1799 · p. 588 · strength ★★

Same page. The two ends of the Salisbury Plain base have a height difference known from the base measurement, so the angle observed from each end can be compared with the true one. The difference is the refraction at that end. The authors state how much an error in the height difference changes the result.

“therefore two opportunities only presented themselves for determining the actual terrestrial refraction; namely, at the ends of the base of verification. From the depression taken at Beacon Hill, the refraction was 38"; but the elevation of Beacon Hill, observed at the lower end, near Old Sarum, gives 50". These deductions, perhaps, cannot be deemed very conclusive; because, as they depend on the difference in the vertical heights of the ends of the base, every 2 inches of error in that difference will produce an error of about 1" in the computed refraction.”

1797: the rules used to find the mean refraction of a line from the angle at each end
Trigonometrical Survey of England and Wales (Ordnance), Williams, Mudge and Dalby 1791-1799 · p. 470 · strength ★★

Art. II continued. The contained arc is the angle at the earth's centre between the stations. Without refraction, two depressions would add up to exactly the contained arc. The amount by which they fall short is twice the mean refraction on that line. Rule 1 first moves each angle from the ground at the far station to the telescope axis there. A footnote gives a worked example for Hensbarrow and Bodmin Down.

“2. Then, if both are depressions, subtract their sum from the contained arc, and half the remainder is the mean refraction. 3. If one is a depression and the other an elevation, take their difference. Then, if the depression is greater than the elevation, subtract the difference from the contained arc, and half the remainder is the mean refraction. But if the elevation is greatest, add the difference to the contained arc, and half the sum is the mean refraction.”
Williams, E., Mudge, W., & Dalby, I. (1797). An account of the trigonometrical survey carried on in the years 1795 and 1796. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, 87, 432-541., p. 470
Clarke 1880: terrestrial refraction follows no simple law and is most irregular when the stations are low and the ray grazes the ground
Textbook guidance of the period on terrestrial refraction · p. 280 · strength ★★
Towers, scaffolds and high stations

Same chapter. The bend depends on the air along the whole path. Clarke then describes the Indian plains, where the ground looks convex in the morning and concave at sunset, and the coefficient ranges from -0.09 to +1.21 (p. 281, citing the Indian survey).

“The amount of terrestrial refraction is very variable and not to be expressed by any simple law: the path of a ray of light, inasmuch as it depends on the refractive power of the atmosphere at every point through which it passes, is necessarily very irregular. This irregularity is very marked when the stations are low and the ray grazes the surface of the ground.”
Clarke, A. R. (1880). Geodesy. Oxford: Clarendon Press., p. 280
Clarke 1880: with mutual observations, eliminate k or weight two results by their consistency; height differences round a triangle are closed by least squares
Textbook guidance of the period on terrestrial refraction · p. 284 · strength ★★

Same chapter. Mutual observations are reciprocal ones. Formula (3) gives the height difference from the two angles with k removed. When three stations observe each other, the three height differences should add to zero; the misclosure is spread by least squares (a method that makes the sum of the weighted squared corrections as small as possible).

“When the observations at A and B are mutual, we may either eliminate the coefficient of refraction by using the formula (3), or we may get two different results from a mean assumed value of k, and then combine these results by assigning them weights deduced from the consistency of the observations from which they are separately derived ... When at each of three stations we have the observed zenith distances of the other two, the deduced differences of height will exhibit a discrepancy.”
Clarke, A. R. (1880). Geodesy. Oxford: Clarendon Press., p. 284
Airy 1848: a correction of the geodetic lines for the horizontal effect of refraction would be about 1/12 of a very small difference, and is rejected as a needless refinement

Airy's discussion of the curves used for the sides of triangles on the spheroid. The difference between the two theories of the line is itself very small; refraction would change it by about a twelfth. Airy states that such a correction is not worth making.

“If we chose to take into account the terrestrial refraction, and to suppose that refraction always bends the light towards such a shortest line, we ought to correct our results by about 1/12th of the difference between them and those obtained by the theory that we have rejected; but such a refinement would be ridiculous.”

Chapter II, continued. A zenith distance is the angle between the vertical and the line of sight to a target. Measured at both ends of a line, the two zenith distances give the height difference and show the bend of the ray on that line. The passage states that zenith distances were measured at all first-class points, and that the verification base near Astrakhan was joined to the net by three triangles whose angles were measured in 12 and more sets.

Chapter III describes the field methods. Canvas screens against wind and an umbrella against the sun protected the instrument. Horizontal angles were measured in sets by W. Struve's method: pointings left to right, then with the telescope turned through the zenith, right to left. Zenith distances for the height differences were measured with double pointing and in two positions of the vertical circle, so that the index error of the circle cancels.

“Зенитныя разстоянія, для опредѣленія разностей высотъ пунктовъ, измѣрялись двойнымъ наведеніемъ на предметы и въ двухъ различныхъ положеніяхъ вертикальнаго круга.”
In English: “The zenith distances, for determining the height differences of the points, were measured with a double pointing on the objects and in two different positions of the vertical circle.”

Chapter V, section 2. The heights above the sea were computed by the method adopted by General Vronchenko in the New Russia survey, starting from Popovka and Kadamovka. The zenith distances used were first corrected with the level readings, and the text explains how this was done for Bubnov's journal and for the other observers. Tome II, Chapter I, terrain of Finland. Between Uleaborg and Tornea the stations stand on low islands; Rontti and Ulkogrunni are only 1.2 and 3.2 toises (about 2.3 and 6.2 m) above the sea. Raw tables of repeated measures

Tome II, p. 232. Struve prints one complete vertical-angle observation at the north end of the Elimä base, 5 September 1844, true solar time 3h 26m, on three targets. For each target he gives the level readings and two vernier readings with the circle right and with the circle left, the level correction, and the means a and b. Half the difference (a - b)/2 is the zenith distance z; half the sum (a + b)/2 is the zenith place Z, the circle reading of the vertical, which should be the same for all targets of one set.

“J'ai ajouté partout dans le texte le lieu du zénith (a+b)/2 = Z, qu'a donné chaque observation complète d'un objet, en le plaçant en parenthèses, et en types mineurs, à côté de son z.”

Reading the table. Rows: level (two ends of the bubble), first and second vernier, mean, correction for the level, for circle right and circle left. Then the corrected means a and b, (a - b)/2 = zenith distance, (a + b)/2 = zenith place, the reduction to the centre of the station, and the reduced z as entered in the station table.
Worked out here: Zenith places Z for the three targets: 0°53′48.0″, 0°53′52.9″, 0°53′54.4″; spread 6.4″ within one set.

Heft I, § 16, on the weights of the station results. Helmert separates the random 'naked' observing errors from errors that stay constant in several or all observations of one direction. Among the constant ones he lists circle graduation errors, personal errors in seeing the targets, centring errors, changes of the station with time, and lateral refraction (sideways bending of the rays in the air). If these change from one group of measurements to the next, their effect is systematic and is not shown by the scatter within a station.

“ferner zeitliche Veränderungen in der Lage der Stationen aus den verschiedensten Gründen und seitliche Brechungen der Lichtstrahlen in der Luft. Wenn diese Fehler aber unter Umständen bei verschiedenen Gruppen der Winkelmessungen einer Station in von Gruppe zu Gruppe wechselnder Weise wirken, so ist ihr Einfluss ein systematischer.”
In English: “further, changes with time in the position of the stations for the most various reasons, and lateral refractions of the light rays in the air. But if these errors act, in some cases, in a way that changes from group to group of the angle measurements of a station, their influence is a systematic one.”

Heft I, § 5, Helmert's new reduction of the French repeating-circle observations of 1861-62. q is the reciprocal weight of an angle: a larger q means a smaller weight in the adjustment. For angle 50.47 at Coldham the formula gave q = 3; Helmert raised it to 5 because of the worsening state of the instrument and the danger of lateral refraction in the direction of St. Peters.

“der hieraus folgende Werth 3 wurde wegen des mehr und mehr verschlechterten Zustandes des Instruments und wegen der Gefahr von Lateralrefraktion in Richtung nach St. Peters (p. 55) auf 5 erhöht.”
In English: “the value 3 that follows from this was raised to 5 because of the more and more deteriorated state of the instrument and because of the danger of lateral refraction in the direction of St. Peters (p. 55).”
Worked out here: Weight is 1/q: from 1/3 to 1/5, a reduction to 60 percent.

Night lamps and heliotropes

Heft I, § 6. The net adjustment of the Rhenish and Hessian nets of the Prussian Geodetic Institute gives a mean error of nearly ±0.7″ for a station-adjusted direction, larger than the station scatter alone. Helmert names the causes: lateral refraction of the light, errors in perceiving the heliotrope lights (heliotropes were the targets almost everywhere), single centring uncertainties, and above all the graduation errors of the circles.

“Als Ursachen jener Erscheinung müssen, da fast ausschliesslich Heliotrope als Einstellungsobjekte benutzt sind, nächst Seitenrefraktionen des Lichtes und Auffassungsfehlern der Heliotropenlichter, sowie vielleicht einzelnen Centrirungsunsicherheiten, besonders die Theilungsfehler der Kreise betrachtet werden.”
In English: “As causes of that effect, since heliotropes were used almost exclusively as pointing targets, one must consider, besides lateral refractions of the light and errors of perception of the heliotrope lights, and perhaps single centring uncertainties, above all the graduation errors of the circles.”
Helmert, F. R. (Ed.). (1893). Die europäische Längengradmessung in 52 Grad Breite von Greenwich bis Warschau. I. Heft: Hauptdreiecke und Grundlinienanschlüsse von England bis Polen. P. Stankiewicz., p. 97
Height of every great station from the contained arcs, with the refraction observed at every station
Great Arc of India, Lambton's meridional arc (Coromandel coast to Punnae and north to about 18 N) · p. 289 · strength ★★

Opening of Lambton's paper on the arc from 10 59' to 15 6'. He states that station heights came from reciprocal vertical angles over the contained arcs, and that the refraction observed at every station across the peninsula is printed in vol. 10 (see the peninsula items).

“The perpendicular height above the sea of every great station, was determined in the usual manner, by using the contained arcs between two stations, a method so well known, that it is needless to explain it here. An account of those heights, with the terrestrial refraction as observed at every station in going direct from sea to sea, is given in the 10th volume of the Asiatick Researches.”
Lambton, W. (1816). An account of the measurement of an arc on the meridian extending from latitude 10° 59' 49" to 15° 6' 0" north. Asiatic Researches, 12, 286-356., p. 289
Old and new surveys differ more in heights than in latitude, longitude, azimuth or distance
Great Arc of India, Lambton's meridional arc (Coromandel coast to Punnae and north to about 18 N) · Appendix p. 36 · strength ★★

Same appendix, one page earlier, introducing Lambton's letter. The 1890 editors compare Lambton's heights with the modern re-survey and state that vertical (height) results disagree more than horizontal results. This separates the uncertainty of vertical refraction from the horizontal network.

“One of the greatest difficulties, that confronted all surveyors at the commencement of this century, was the satisfactory determination of the heights of their stations by means of the vertical angles. Very little was known of the laws of refraction in Europe, and still less of its effect in tropical countries. In comparing results obtained by the old and recent Trigonometrical Surveys of India, wider discrepancies are found to exist between the two values of altitude for the same station, than between those of latitude, longitude, azimuth or distance.”
Great Trigonometrical Survey of India. (1890). Account of the operations of the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India, Vol. XII: The Southern Trigon. Dehra Dun: Trigonometrical Branch, Survey of India., Appendix p. 36
Indus Series: fear of large refraction variations on grazing rays led to spirit levelling of the plains
GTS Karachi Longitudinal Series (North-West Quadrilateral) · p. VIII-D · strength ★★

Introduction to the Indus Series in the same volume. Spirit levelling measures heights directly with a level and staff, without vertical angles. It was used where rays would graze the ground over about 400 miles.

“The circumstance which has already been mentioned that nearly 400 miles of the triangulation would have to pass over a perfectly level plain, without hills and almost without any mounds, led to the initiation of operations for determining the heights of the stations in the plains by the method of spirit-leveling; for it was feared that, with rays grazing the surface of the ground so closely, the vertical angles measured in the triangulation would be so much affected by the very considerable variations of terrestrial refraction to which they would be liable, that a considerable amount of error might be generated in the course of operations carried over so great a distance under such unfavorable circumstances.”
Walker, J. T. (Ed.). (1873). Account of the operations of the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India, Vol. III: The principal triangulation, North-West Quadrilateral. Dehra Dun: Great Trigonometrical Survey., p. VIII-D
Salt Lake base net: probable error of a direction 0.09" from the stations and 0.28" from the net; the closures are computed three ways
US Transcontinental Triangulation, 39th parallel · p. 206 · strength ★★

Part I, adjustment of the Salt Lake base net. Schott computes the probable error of a direction from the station abstracts and three times from the net (from the direction corrections, the angle corrections and the triangle closing errors), then names the causes of the difference, including persistent lateral refraction.

“We thus find the probable error of a direction e_t as derived from the corrections demanded by the adjustment of the base net = +/- 0".28 and the same e_s as derived from the station adjustment = +/- 0".09; the fact that e_t is three times as great as e_s is attributed mainly to the effect of local deflections in measuring angles, the vertical axis of the theodolite being necessarily adjusted to the plumb-line. Besides, a very careful adjustment of the instrument is required when the station observed upon is considerably above or below the one occupied. Persistent lateral refraction also has a share in producing the above result.”
Worked out here: Net error not explained by station scatter: sqrt(0.28^2 - 0.09^2) = 0.27" (Schott prints the same value).
Schott, C. A. (1900). The transcontinental triangulation and the American arc of the parallel (Special Publication No. 4). U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey; Government Printing Office., p. 206
California Coast Range: how m was computed from reciprocal zenith distances, and the coast effect (0.0854 near the coast, 0.0751 inland)
US Transcontinental Triangulation, 39th parallel · pp. 276-277 · strength ★★
Vertical refraction coefficients

Part II, heights near the Coast Range. Schott states the method: m for a line comes from the two opposite zenith distances, with equal refraction assumed at both ends and m referred to the hours of minimum refraction. The regional means are then compared.

“In deducing the coefficient of refraction m, we must, as usual, make the assumption of equality of angle of refraction at the upper and lower stations, treat the observations of zenith distances as "simultaneous reciprocal," though made in different years and different months, and take m as referring to the hours of the day when the refraction is near its minimum. [p. 277:] These results are in accordance with the known influence of a coast climate on the atmospheric refraction, which is to increase it. For the 19 lines close to the coast-say within 20 or 30 kilometres of it-we find the value m = 0.0854, whereas farther inland-say within 60 or 90 kilometres-it has diminished to 0.0751.”
Reading the table. Second passage: pdf 281, crop [0.16, 0.46, 0.84, 0.57].
Schott, C. A. (1900). The transcontinental triangulation and the American arc of the parallel (Special Publication No. 4). U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey; Government Printing Office., pp. 276-277
Rocky Mountain and Great Basin: m found to depend on height and air temperature; empirical formula used for the difference of refraction at upper and lower stations
US Transcontinental Triangulation, 39th parallel · p. 332 · strength ★★
Vertical refraction coefficients

Part II, heights from Round Top to Pikes Peak. Schott tabulates m for each line with the temperatures at both ends and the mean height, finds m rising as height falls except when the temperature is abnormal, and fits a formula in temperature t and height h. The formula gives the term for unequal refraction at the two ends, which is kept for these steep lines.

“An inspection of this table shows a steady increase in the coefficient of refraction as the height decreases, except where the temperature is abnormally high or low, in which case the value of m is correspondingly low or high. It was therefore decided to try to derive an expression for the coefficient of refraction of the form- m = m_0 + (t - t_0)x + (h - h_0)y [...] It was therefore concluded to use the individual values of m, disregarding the computed weights, and to derive two expressions, one for the eastern part of the triangulation from Pikes Peak to Mount Nebo and another for the remaining western part.”
Schott, C. A. (1900). The transcontinental triangulation and the American arc of the parallel (Special Publication No. 4). U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey; Government Printing Office., p. 332
Zenith distance tables: instrument, height of the target and heliostat targets recorded
Maclear's verification and extension of La Caille's arc of meridian, Cape of Good Hope · p. 591 · strength ★★
Raw tables of repeated measures Night lamps and heliotropes

Introduction to Section 9, Observed Zenith Distances of Stations (p. 591). A zenith distance is the angle between the vertical and the line of sight. The tables name the instrument (D = Dollond repeating circle, B = Beaufort theodolite), give the height of the target above the station surface, mark heliostat targets with H, and reduce excentric set-ups to the angle point by a printed formula.

“The letters D and B in the third column distinguish the instruments employed in the measurement of the zenith distances,—viz., the Dollond repeating circle and the Beaufort theodolite. In the eighth column is given the height of the object observed above the surface of the station ; and when the object was a heliostat, the letter H is annexed to the name of the station in column five. The observations with the Dollond circle were for the most part made at excentric stations, and require on this account special reductions to the trigonometric or angle point.”
Maclear, T. (1866). Verification and extension of La Caille's arc of meridian at the Cape of Good Hope (Vol. 1). London: Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty., p. 591
Klyp Fonteyn base: zenith distances observed at both ends and the mean taken
Maclear's verification and extension of La Caille's arc of meridian, Cape of Good Hope · p. 49 · strength ★★
Towers, scaffolds and high stations

Small triangulation near Klyp Fonteyn, La Caille's base (p. 49). The relative heights of the base ends were found with an 18-inch level, and the refraction entered the computed altitudes. Zenith distances were taken from both ends of the base and the mean used, so the refraction on the line is found from the line itself.

“Lieutenant Williams and myself examined the relative heights of the base-line and corn-floor with an excellent 18-inch level, sent out by Capt. Beaufort for these inquiries. We found the north end 72·2 feet, and the south end 68·3 feet, lower than the corn-floor. The axis of the repeating circle was four feet above the floor. These quantities are taken into account in the computation of the altitudes, together with the refraction : the zenith distances having been observed at both ends of the base, the mean of the results was taken.”
Maclear, T. (1866). Verification and extension of La Caille's arc of meridian at the Cape of Good Hope (Vol. 1). London: Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty., p. 49
Gordon's Rhodesia junction chain: unsteady images from irregular refraction, grass-fire haze, rain; four arcs
Geodetic Survey of the Transvaal and Orange River Colony (Morris; preface and introduction by Gill) · p. xxvii · strength ★★
Repetition over days and hours

Captain Gordon's report on the 1906-1907 chain joining the Transvaal survey to Simms' Rhodesia survey, printed in Gill's introduction (p. xxvii). Over the flat bushed country near the Zoutpansberg the images were unsteady from irregular refraction; haze from grass fires lasted through July and August, and rain fell from November. Each station had measures on four arcs only.

“Passing southwards through the heavy granite country of the M'Patem, one emerges on the flat heavily bushed tract which stretches continuously to the heights of the Zoutpansberg in the Transvaal. In this last country the work of observation became very tedious and difficult by reason of the unsteadiness of the images produced by irregular refraction. The absence of roads and the density of the bush in this section gave rise to much difficulty and delay in the earlier work of the reconnaissance, the trouble being in no way lightened by the constant thick haze prevailing during the months of July and August as the result of the numerous grass fires incidental to that season. During November heavy rains began to fall, and continued intermittently to the close of the work. ... Pressure of circumstances necessitated limiting the instrumental work at each station to a series of measures on four arcs only; the zero reference point of the circle being successively placed about the divisions of 0°, 45°, 90°, and 135°.”
Morris, W. G. (1908). Reports on the geodetic survey of the Transvaal and Orange River Colony (Geodetic Survey of South Africa, Vol. 5; preface and introduction by D. Gill). London: Harrison and Sons., p. xxvii
Refraction named as the main difficulty in trigonometrical levelling; Bessel weights by the number of days at both ends
Trigonometrical Survey of New South Wales · p. 205 · strength ★★
Repetition over days and hours

pp. 204-205. Furber names the irregular change of refraction as the main difficulty, cites the Indian experience of zenith distances varying through nine minutes at 10 to 12 miles, and argues that a large spread is the reason to observe over more days. Bessel's weight for a reciprocal line has the factor n1 x n2, the numbers of days observed at the two ends. No PDF of this paper is in the project; the item points to the OCR text file, so no crop is possible. Quote from the text layer; the subscripts of n are garbled there and are written n₁, n₂.

“There is little doubt that the principal source of difficulty in trigonometrical levelling lies in the considerable and irregular changes in the atmospheric refraction. This cannot be better illustrated than by the experience obtained in India, where apparent zenith distances of points only 10 or 12 miles away varied under certain circumstances through a range of as much as nine minutes. At first sight it might appear to be useless to go on duplicating such apparently wild observations, yet consideration of the nature of the question will show that the great range among the observations forms, itself, the reason for extending them to cover a longer period of time. Bessel's opinion on this subject may be gathered from his estimate of the relative weights to be assigned to such observations, the principal factor in the weight being n₁ n₂, where n₁ and n₂ are the number of days on which observations are made at opposite ends of the same line.”
No page image: this source is held as a text layer only.
Furber, T. F. (1898). The trigonometrical survey of New South Wales, with mention of similar surveys in the other Australian colonies. Report of the Australasian Association for the Advancement of Science, 7, Section A, 176-237., p. 205
The reciprocal correction carries every error of observation
Middleton, Chadwick and Bogle, A Treatise on Surveying (textbook) · p. 226 · strength ★★

A caution printed right after the method: the refraction value found from reciprocal angles also contains any other error in those angles. It is a measured total, not a separated physical term. Table K (from the Manual of Surveying for India) gives the combined curvature and refraction correction for short distances in chains.

“It must not be forgotten that the correction thus obtained, includes all errors of observation. 'Refraction' has also the effect of reducing the 'curvature' already treated of. Usually it reduces it by about one-seventh of its true value.”
Reading the table. Table K: distance in chains (1 chain = 66 ft), the curvature correction in decimals of a foot, and the combined curvature-and-refraction correction. The refraction column is about 1/7 smaller than the curvature column.
Middleton, R. E., Chadwick, O., & Bogle, J. du T. (1904). A treatise on surveying: Part I (2nd ed.). E. & F. N. Spon., p. 226
“Surely they didn't take this observation a single time?” 68 items · 21 surveys

How many times each angle was measured, in how many series, on how many days, by whom.

Short answer. No angle was taken once. Typical counts printed in the sources: Schott (1900) 34 or more per direction on 17 circle positions, up to 126; Schott (1902) 20 sets of 3 direct and 3 reversed; Brousseaud 156 to 360 per angle; Puissant 100 to 294; Maclear 530 measures of one angle in 6 determinations; GTS station XCI 22 readings on 10 zeros, two seasons, three observers. Helmert halved the weight of an angle whose 60 repetitions were all taken on one day, because one day's air is one sample. Middleton et al. (1904, p. 191) state the rule: repeated methods give values more correct than is possible with one single measurement.
Zenith distances: one series of ten per target, more when doubtful; in bad weather angles were repeated instead; the zenith distance nearest in hour to the angle was used
Delambre and Méchain, meridian arc Dunkirk to Barcelona (Base du système métrique) · T1 Discours préliminaire p. 113 · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours Repetition over days and hours

Discours préliminaire, section Observations. A zenith distance is the vertical angle between the plumb-line direction straight up (the zenith) and the target. A series is a run of repeated readings on the repeating circle; ten angles means the circle was turned ten times and the total divided by ten. Delambre gives his rule and the reason: in bad weather the variations of refraction make zenith distances less sure. For steep sights he took the zenith distance just before or after the angle, or at several hours, and used the one nearest in time. Méchain repeated zenith distances more than Delambre.

“je me suis contenté de faire pour chaque distance au zénith une seule série de dix angles, excepté dans les cas où quelque circonstance rendoit l'observation douteuse. Quand le temps étoit beau, j'aimois mieux répéter l'observation des angles de position, et, s'il étoit mauvais, les variations de la réfraction terrestre auroient rendu les distances au zénith plus incertaines. Quand ces distances sont plus grandes que 91 degrés, ou plus petites que 89, il conviendroit de les observer en même temps que l'angle de position ; mais cela n'est guère possible. Il falloit donc se contenter de les observer immédiatement avant ou après, ou à plusieurs heures du jour, afin de choisir pour la réduction des angles à l'horizon la distance dont l'heure étoit la plus voisine, et où l'on avoit lieu de croire la réfraction terrestre moins différente.”
In English: “I was content to make for each zenith distance a single series of ten angles, except in cases where some circumstance made the observation doubtful. When the weather was fine I preferred to repeat the observation of the angles of position, and if it was bad, the variations of terrestrial refraction would have made the zenith distances more uncertain. When these distances are greater than 91 degrees or less than 89, they should be observed at the same time as the angle of position; but that is hardly possible. So one had to be content to observe them immediately before or after, or at several hours of the day, in order to choose for the reduction of the angles to the horizon the distance whose hour was nearest, and where there was reason to believe the terrestrial refraction least different.”
Méchain, P., & Delambre, J.-B. J. (1806). Base du système métrique décimal, ou mesure de l'arc du méridien compris entre les parallèles de Dunkerque et Barcelone (Vol. 1). Paris: Baudouin., T1 Discours préliminaire p. 113
Station register at Fiefs (July 1793): each series printed with repetitions, circle, observer, date, hours and remarks on the air; one series marked to be rejected
Delambre and Méchain, meridian arc Dunkirk to Barcelona (Base du système métrique) · T1 p. 33 · strength ★★★
Raw tables of repeated measures Rejecting readings in unsteady air Steady-air hours Repetition over days and hours

Tome I, Observations géodésiques, station of Fiefs. For each angle every series is printed: the number of repetitions, the total arc in grades, the single angle, the reduction to the centre, the observer and circle (D. = Delambre, F. = Lalande, B. = Bellet; n° 1 or n° 4 = circle number), the date and hours, and a remark on visibility, sun and wind. One series is marked 'série à rejeter' (series to be rejected) for strong wind, a faint and curved target and undulations. The remark on Sauti says that phases (the side lighting of a spire by the sun) moved the apparent target.

“D. n° 1 + première place. Grand vent ; Sauti foible et courbe ; ondulations au Mesnil ; fils en + série à rejeter. ... Le clocher de Sauti et les flèches voisines nous ont fort exercés par leurs phases différentes. ... D. n° 1. 3 juillet, 5h 40' — 7h 20'. Objets éclairés du soleil ; Sauti tout-à-fait courbe. ... F. n° 4. 4 juillet, 3h 10' — 5h 45'. Objets assez beaux en commençant ; ils l'étoient moins vers le milieu.”
In English: “D. circle no. 1, first place. Strong wind; Sauti faint and curved; undulations at Mesnil; wires in +; series to be rejected. ... The steeple of Sauti and the neighbouring spires gave us much trouble by their different phases. ... D. circle no. 1. 3 July, 5h 40' to 7h 20'. Objects lit by the sun; Sauti quite curved. ... F. circle no. 4. 4 July, 3h 10' to 5h 45'. Objects rather fine at the start; less so towards the middle.”
Reading the table. Each block is one series: first number = repetitions (20 or 12 here); then the total arc in grades, the single angle in grades, and the same in degrees; the line 'Au centre' gives the angle reduced to the centre of the station. Below: circle and observer, date, hours, remarks on the air. The angle between Mesnil and Sauti has three series of 20; the mean of the first three is reduced to the horizon (+0.58") to give 42° 59' 48.72". Bonnières-Sauti has series of 20, 20 and 12 on 3 and 4 July at different hours. A typical angle in Delambre's north part has 2 to 5 series of 12 to 30 repetitions (e.g. Dunkerque, Watten-Cassel: 20 + 16 + 30).
Worked out here: Mesnil-Sauti series reduced to centre: 42° 59' 49.68" and 42° 59' 55.07" (the rejected series is 5.4" higher).
Méchain, P., & Delambre, J.-B. J. (1806). Base du système métrique décimal, ou mesure de l'arc du méridien compris entre les parallèles de Dunkerque et Barcelone (Vol. 1). Paris: Baudouin., T1 p. 33
Instruction: zenith distances from at least three series at different hours, mainly near midday, simultaneous where possible, with barometer readings; first-order series to the twentieth repetition
Parallel of Paris, Brest to Strasbourg (Henry east part, Bonne west part), Nouvelle carte de France · 28 · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours Repetition over days and hours

Instruction of the commission of the Dépôt de la Guerre for the new map of France, printed by Puissant. It sets the observing rules for the first-order chains, including the parallel of Paris. A conjugate observation is one repetition of the angle on the repeating circle. Simultaneous observations are reciprocal zenith distances taken at both ends at the same time, so that both see the same state of the air.

“Les distances zénithales relatives à ces chaînes seront elles-mêmes le résultat de trois séries au moins, prises à des heures différentes, et surtout vers le milieu du jour, afin qu'elles puissent donner les différences de niveau avec toute l'exactitude désirable, et, autant qu'il sera possible, par le concours d'observations simultanées : celles-ci seront accompagnées d'observations barométriques. ... Toutes les séries du premier ordre seront, autant que possible, prolongées jusqu'à la vingtième observation conjuguée ; toutes celles du deuxième ordre s'arrêteront à la dixième.”
In English: “The zenith distances for these chains will themselves be the result of at least three series, taken at different hours, and above all towards the middle of the day, so that they can give the level differences with all desirable accuracy, and, as far as possible, by the combination of simultaneous observations: these will be accompanied by barometric observations. ... All first-order series will, as far as possible, be carried to the twentieth conjugate observation; all those of the second order will stop at the tenth.”
Puissant, L. (1832). Nouvelle description géométrique de la France (Première partie). Paris: Ch. Picquet., 28

Puissant prints no station registers for the parallel, but the triangle table gives for each angle the number of observations (repetitions on the repeating circle) and for each triangle the closure error. “TABLEAU DES TRIANGLES. Nomb. d'obs. ... Angles sphériques ... Erreur ... Angles moyens ... Cotés en mètres.”
In English: “TABLE OF TRIANGLES. Number of observations ... spherical angles ... error ... mean angles ... sides in metres.”
Reading the table. Columns: Nomb. d'obs. (number of observations of the angle); station names; Angles sphériques (observed angle reduced to centre and horizon, grades); Erreur (closure error of the triangle, centesimal seconds); Angles moyens (adjusted angles); Côtés en mètres. Counts on this page range from 100 to 294 per angle. Triangle errors on this page range from -14.0 to +11.1 centesimal seconds (about 4.5" to 3.6" sexagesimal).
Worked out here: 14.0 centesimal seconds x 0.324 = 4.5 sexagesimal seconds; 11.1 x 0.324 = 3.6.

At least thirty repetitions per series, series repeated at different hours and days; number of series set by the spread of the first five or six
Brousseaud, arc of the mean parallel (45 N) across France, with link to the Austro-Sardinian chain · 157 · strength ★★★
Repetition over days and hours Steady-air hours

Brousseaud, narrative of the French part (1811-1823). A repetition is one turn of the repeating circle; a series is the set of repetitions whose total gives one value of the angle. Because results sometimes varied even when the view seemed the same, the number of series for each angle was set by how far the first five or six series disagreed. The sentence continues on p. 158 (item fr_45n_02).

“A cet effet on prit la résolution, ainsi qu'il a été déjà signalé page 32, de multiplier les observations d'angles entre les objets terrestres trente fois au moins par chaque série, et de répéter ces séries à des heures et à des jours différens. On avait remarqué depuis long-temps que, malgré tous les soins apportés dans les observations angulaires, les résultats variaient quelquefois d'une quantité considérable, quoique les circonstances de la vision parussent les mêmes. En conséquence le nombre des séries jugées nécessaires à la mesure d'un angle fut déterminé par le nombre de secondes dont les cinq ou six premiers résultats différaient entre eux”
In English: “To this end it was resolved, as already noted on page 32, to multiply the observations of angles between terrestrial objects at least thirty times per series, and to repeat these series at different hours and on different days. It had long been noticed that, despite all the care taken in angular observations, the results sometimes varied by a considerable amount, although the conditions of vision seemed the same. Consequently the number of series judged necessary for the measurement of an angle was set by the number of seconds by which the first five or six results differed among themselves”
Brousseaud (Colonel). (1839). Mesure d'un arc du parallèle moyen entre le pôle et l'équateur. Limoges: F. Chapoulaud., 157
When the first six series differed by 15 to 20 seconds, the angle was carried to twelve or fifteen series; differences of 25 to 35 decimal seconds between days at the same hour
Brousseaud, arc of the mean parallel (45 N) across France, with link to the Austro-Sardinian chain · 158 · strength ★★★
Repetition over days and hours

Brousseaud, p. 158, continuing the rule of p. 157. Decimal seconds are centesimal seconds (1 decimal second = 0.324 sexagesimal second). The author reports, without hiding it, that series of the same angle at the same hour on different days differed by 25 to 35 decimal seconds even when both targets were seen well, and that more series were added to reduce these errors.

“[si, de la première à la sixième série (par exemple), les angles conclus variaient de quinze à] vingt secondes, on les continuait jusqu'à la douzième ou quinzième série afin d'atténuer le plus possible ces erreurs inexplicables. On a remarqué des différences de vingt-cinq à trente-cinq secondes décimales entre les résultats des séries d'un même angle observé à la même heure et à des jours différens, quoique les deux objets sur lesquels on pointait se vissent parfaitement dans des circonstances semblables.”
In English: “[if, from the first to the sixth series (for example), the concluded angles varied by fifteen to] twenty seconds, they were continued to the twelfth or fifteenth series in order to reduce these unexplained errors as much as possible. Differences of twenty-five to thirty-five decimal seconds were noticed between the results of series of the same angle observed at the same hour and on different days, although the two objects pointed at were seen perfectly in similar circumstances.”
Worked out here: 25 to 35 decimal seconds = 8.1" to 11.3" sexagesimal.
Brousseaud (Colonel). (1839). Mesure d'un arc du parallèle moyen entre le pôle et l'équateur. Limoges: F. Chapoulaud., 158

Brousseaud, p. 158. A zenith distance is the vertical angle between the plumb-line direction straight up (the zenith) and the target. The hours near noon were chosen because vertical refraction is then smallest and steadiest. Six to eight series of ten single angles give 60 to 80 readings per zenith distance.

“Les distances au zénith de l'extrémité des signaux ont toujours été prises entre onze heures et une heure du soir, et répétées au moins par six ou huit séries de dix angles simples chaque.”
In English: “The zenith distances of the tops of the signals were always taken between eleven o'clock and one in the afternoon, and repeated in at least six or eight series of ten single angles each.”

Repetition over days and hours Steady-air hours

Brousseaud, summary of the three parts of the arc of the mean parallel. For the French part (34 triangles, Mont Granier to Marennes) the author states the number of series and repetitions, that every series was kept in the mean without exception, and the largest triangle closure error (the amount by which the sum of the three angles missed its true value).

“Les valeurs des angles ont été déterminées par six, huit, dix, douze quatorze séries de trente à quarante répétitions chaque, faites à des jours et à des heures différens. Les distances au zénith ont aussi été répétées de soixante à cent fois, entre onze heures et midi, afin d'avoir avec exactitude la hauteur absolue des signaux placés sur les hautes montagnes de la France et de la Savoie. Le résultat adopté pour chaque angle de ces trente-quatre triangles provient de la moyenne entre tous les résultats fournis par les séries relatives à cet angle, et prises sans exception. Cependant, malgré ces soins, la plus grande erreur de la somme des trois angles des triangles s'élève encore à 4" de degré.”
In English: “The values of the angles were determined by six, eight, ten, twelve, fourteen series of thirty to forty repetitions each, made on different days and at different hours. The zenith distances were also repeated sixty to a hundred times, between eleven and noon, to obtain accurately the absolute height of the signals placed on the high mountains of France and Savoy. The result adopted for each angle of these thirty-four triangles is the mean of all the results given by the series for that angle, taken without exception. Yet, despite these precautions, the largest error of the sum of the three angles of the triangles still reaches 4" of a degree.”
Worked out here: 6 to 14 series x 30 to 40 repetitions = 180 to 560 repetitions per angle.
Brousseaud (Colonel). (1839). Mesure d'un arc du parallèle moyen entre le pôle et l'équateur. Limoges: F. Chapoulaud., 36

Roy: in hot weather only short morning and evening periods were good enough; a whole day could go for one satisfactory angle
Anglo-French triangulation of 1787 (Greenwich to Paris junction), English side by Roy · p. 170 · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours Repetition over days and hours Rejecting readings in unsteady air

Roy, Art. I of the section on the triangles, explaining why the angles were repeated less often than planned. 'Tremulous motion or boiling in the air' is the shimmer caused by heated air near the ground, which makes a distant object dance in the telescope. Roy observed only when the objects were distinct, and he did not change the zero (the starting point on the divided circle) at those times because each change needed a new levelling of the instrument.

“At particular times, especially in hot weather, there was such a tremulous motion or boiling in the air, that it was only during a very short space, chiefly in the mornings and evenings, that the objects were sufficiently distinct to be observed with accuracy. So difficult it is to do any thing perfectly good in this way, that a whole day has frequently been spent, after watching with anxious care, in obtaining a single one that was perfectly satisfactory!”
Roy, W. (1790). An account of the trigonometrical operation, whereby the distance between the meridians of the Royal Observatories of Greenwich and Paris has been determined. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, 80, 111-270 (with Dalby, I., Remarks, pp. 593-614)., p. 170
Roy: fewer repetitions than planned, but a few very good observations beat a mean of many hurried ones, as the base of verification shows
Anglo-French triangulation of 1787 (Greenwich to Paris junction), English side by Roy · p. 171 · strength ★★★
Repetition over days and hours

Same article, p. 169 to p. 171. Roy had planned to measure each angle many times on different parts of the circle (to average out errors of division of the scale). He states that this was often impossible in practice. He gives the close agreement between the measured and the computed length of the base of verification (the Romney Marsh base, computed through the triangles from the Hounslow Heath base about 70 miles away) as the test of the result. On pp. 177-178 he gives that difference as about 4 1/2 inches.

“On the whole, although, for the reasons already assigned, we have repeated the observations seldomer than was at first proposed; yet it will obviously appear from the results, and particularly from the near agreement between the measured and computed length of the base of verification, that a few very good observations are greatly preferable to a mean that might perhaps have been obtained of many made in a hurry, which at best would have been but indifferent.”
Roy, W. (1790). An account of the trigonometrical operation, whereby the distance between the meridians of the Royal Observatories of Greenwich and Paris has been determined. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, 80, 111-270 (with Dalby, I., Remarks, pp. 593-614)., p. 171
1795: angles observed on different arcs and repeated till their truth became certain; doubtful night observations re-observed with fresh lights
Trigonometrical Survey of England and Wales (Ordnance), Williams, Mudge and Dalby 1791-1799 · p. 448 · strength ★★★
Repetition over days and hours Night lamps and heliotropes

Section on the instrument and method. 'Different arcs' means different parts of the divided circle, so that errors of division average out. Staffs were poles at stations up to about fifteen miles away; lamps and white lights were used at night. When only one of two white lights was seen, the observation was kept only if it showed no error beyond the division error of the instrument; otherwise new lights were sent and the angle observed again.

“namely, that of observing the angles upon different arcs. When staffs were erected, which was generally the case when the stations were not more remote than fifteen miles, the angles were repeated till their truth became certain, and the same was also done, when angles were determined by the lamps; but it sometimes happened, that only one of the two white lights, which were burned at the distant stations, was seen; in which case, if the observation appeared to be made without any error, but that which an inequality in the division of the instrument might be supposed to produce, it was considered as sufficient; otherwise fresh lights were sent to the station and observed.”
Williams, E., Mudge, W., & Dalby, I. (1795). An account of the trigonometrical survey carried on in the years 1791, 1792, 1793, and 1794. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, 85, 414-591., p. 448
1795 station register: every reading of each angle printed with its mean; pole-star azimuth repeated morning and night on several dates; unfavourable star observations rejected

The footnote states that observations made under unfavourable conditions were rejected.

“Many observations of the star at this station, and also at Dunnose, are rejected on account of their being made under unfavourable circumstances.”

1795: heights from vertical angles agree with levelling at Shooter's Hill (446 against 445 ft), but no dependence can be placed on single observations
Trigonometrical Survey of England and Wales (Ordnance), Williams, Mudge and Dalby 1791-1799 · p. 585 · strength ★★★

Art. III, Remarks on the tables. The height of Shooter's Hill from reciprocal angles (446 ft) is checked against spirit levelling from the Bull Inn (445 ft). On p. 584 the authors show that the elevation of St. Ann's Hill seen from Hampton Poor House differed widely between 1787 and 1792 with the instrument at the same height. They conclude that heights from vertical angles are good to about 10 feet unless reciprocal observations are made at the same time.

“Notwithstanding this consistency, and also that in the height of St. Ann's Hill, found by different methods, it is evident from the observations at Dunnose, Rook's Hill, and Butser Hill, that relative heights deduced from elevations, or depressions, cannot always be depended upon to less than about 10 feet, even supposing those heights are the means of two or three independent results, except, perhaps, reciprocal observations were made exactly at the same time. The very great difference in the observed elevations of St. Ann's Hill, proves that no dependance can be placed on single observations.”
Williams, E., Mudge, W., & Dalby, I. (1795). An account of the trigonometrical survey carried on in the years 1791, 1792, 1793, and 1794. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, 85, 414-591., p. 585
Clarke 1858: the method of 'arcs': every round starts and ends on the referring object, the telescope is reversed and the circle shifted; single angles were never observed
Ordnance Trigonometrical Survey of Great Britain and Ireland, Principal Triangulation · p. 50 · strength ★★★
Repetition over days and hours

Section on the method of observing with the theodolite. The referring object (R.O.) is a fixed mark near the station. An 'arc' is one full round: the observer reads the R.O., then every object in turn, then the R.O. again; the closing reading tests the steadiness of the instrument. Between arcs the telescope is reversed and the circle turned 20 to 30 degrees, so the same directions are read on other parts of the scale. Each direction is therefore observed many times.

“The method of "arcs" has been always followed; though in the earlier operations an arc contained a smaller number of points. It has never been the practice to observe single and independent angles, as in the Indian and other geodetical operations.”
Clarke, A. R. (1858). Ordnance trigonometrical survey of Great Britain and Ireland: Account of the observations and calculations of the principal triangulation. London: Eyre and Spottiswoode., p. 50

Repetition over days and hours

Chapter VI compares the results. A probable error is the error that is as likely to be exceeded as not; here it is computed by least squares from the closures of the triangles. For all first-class triangles the probable error of one angle is 0.5997″. The main row (angles in at least 12 sets) gives 0.6019″, the Kizlyar row (6 sets) gives 0.6011″. The authors conclude that more sets did not raise the accuracy as fast as probability theory predicts, and put this down to outside conditions, above all the uneven illumination of the targets.

“Это показываетъ: что отъ увеличенія числа пріемовъ точность угла возрастаетъ не съ такою быстротою, какъ убѣждаетъ въ томъ исчисленіе вѣроятностей, и что слѣдственно тутъ, какъ надо полагать, зависитъ отъ обстоятельствъ совершенно постороннихъ, въ особенности же отъ болѣе или менѣе одинаковаго освѣщенія наблюдаемыхъ предметовъ.”
In English: “This shows that with an increase in the number of sets the accuracy of an angle grows not as fast as the calculus of probabilities leads one to expect, and that consequently it depends here, as one must suppose, on quite external circumstances, in particular on the more or less uniform illumination of the observed objects.”
Worked out here: Sum of squared closures 367.6443 for the first-class triangles. Probable error of one angle: all triangles 0.5997″; main row (119 triangles, 12 or more sets) 0.6019″; Kizlyar row (36 triangles, 6 sets) 0.6011″.
Voenno-topograficheskoe depo. (1861). Zapiski Voenno-topograficheskago depo, Chast' XXII, Otd. II: Privolzhskoe trigonometricheskoe izmerenie. Voenno-topograficheskoe depo., Zapiski XXII, Otd. II, p. 189
Livonia: measure only with distinct images, in the 2-hour afternoon calm; triangle closures show one Livonian set worth 8 of Bessel's
Struve Geodetic Arc (Russo-Scandinavian arc of the meridian, Danube to Fuglenaes) · T. I, p. 32 · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours Repetition over days and hours

Tome I, Chapter IV. A set (mise) is one complete round of pointings. Struve counts 833 sets for the 141 Livonian directions (5.91 per direction) against 41.77 per direction in Bessel's East Prussian survey. He then compares the two surveys by their triangle closures (the excess of the angle sum over 180 degrees plus the spherical excess): mean square 0.987 for 31 Livonian triangles and 1.179 for Bessel's 15. From this he finds one Livonian set equal in weight to 8.44 Prussian sets, and he states the Livonian rule: measure only with sufficiently distinct images, in practice in the 2-hour afternoon period of calm images.

“En Livonie la règle a été strictement observée, de ne jamais faire des mesures que par des images suffisamment distinctes des objets, c'est-à-dire presque exclusivement pendant la période de 2 heures des images calmes, qui d'ordinaire a lieu chaque après-midi (Gradmessung I. p. 88).”
In English: “In Livonia the rule was strictly kept never to make measurements except with sufficiently distinct images of the objects, that is, almost exclusively during the 2-hour period of calm images which usually occurs every afternoon (Gradmessung I. p. 88).”
Worked out here: 41.77 / 5.91 = 7.07 (printed 7.07). Weight ratio printed: 41.77 × 1.179 : 5.91 × 0.987 = 8.44 : 1.
Struve, F. G. W. (1857). Arc du méridien de 25° 20' entre le Danube et la Mer Glaciale mesuré depuis 1816 jusqu'en 1855 (Vol. 1). Imprimerie de l'Académie impériale des sciences., T. I, p. 32

Tome I, Introduction, quoting Selander's report to the Stockholm Academy. Corresponding zenith distances are measured at both ends of a line for trigonometric levelling. From Haparanda to the Norwegian border, 40 Swedish miles, Agardh and Selander observed them at all stations with two instruments read by microscopes. The number per station was never below 40 to 50 and above 100 at some stations.

“M. Agardh, professeur d'astronomie (à l'Université de Lund), a été chargé de prendre part, des observations correspondantes des distances zénithales ont été exécutées sur toutes les stations situées depuis Haparanda jusqu'à la frontière de Norvège ... Vu que le nombre des distances zénithales, mesurées sur chaque station, n'est jamais au-dessous de 40 à 50, et s'élève pour d'autres au-delà de 100, j'ai raison d'espérer que les résultats que fournira le calcul, seront dignes de confiance.”
In English: “Mr Agardh, professor of astronomy (at the University of Lund), having been charged to take part, corresponding observations of zenith distances were made at all stations from Haparanda to the border of Norway ... Since the number of zenith distances measured at each station is never below 40 to 50, and for others rises above 100, I have reason to hope that the results the computation will give will be worthy of confidence.”
Struve, F. G. W. (1857). Arc du méridien de 25° 20' entre le Danube et la Mer Glaciale mesuré depuis 1816 jusqu'en 1855 (Vol. 1). Imprimerie de l'Académie impériale des sciences., T. I, Introduction p. XXIV

Tome II, p. 21, continuing the instruction. Undulating images are images that shimmer because of unsteady air near the ground. The instruction rejected any observation made with indistinct or too undulating images. Struve states that it was followed so strictly that only in two cases is an object wholly missing from a set; incomplete sets were completed with extra observations when the object became visible again. Each object was pointed 4 times in each set, 20 times in all, against 12 in the Baltic arc.

“Enfin l'instruction fixait, que toute observation était inadmissible, si les images des objets étaient indistinctes ou trop ondulantes. Cette instruction a été suivie en Finlande à telle rigueur, qu'il ne se trouve que deux cas, où un objet manque entièrement dans une des mises à faire. ... En Finlande, chaque objet était pointé 4 fois dans chaque mise, donc en tout 20 fois, au lieu de 12 fois dans la mesure Baltique.”
In English: “Finally the instruction laid down that any observation was inadmissible if the images of the objects were indistinct or too undulating. This instruction was followed in Finland with such rigour that there are only two cases where an object is wholly missing from one of the sets to be made. ... In Finland each object was pointed 4 times in each set, so 20 times in all, instead of 12 times in the Baltic measurement.”
Struve, F. G. W. (1860). Arc du méridien de 25° 20' entre le Danube et la Mer Glaciale mesuré depuis 1816 jusqu'en 1855 (Vol. 2). Imprimerie de l'Académie impériale des sciences., T. II, p. 21

Tome II, pièces justificatives, explanation of the Finland station table. Three almost identical Munich universal instruments were used by Oberg, Melan and Woldstedt, each with an assistant on the lower telescope so the pointings of the two telescopes were simultaneous. Struve states that there were always 5 sets with 4 pointings on each object, each set in two halves, and that he prints the separate figures of the two halves at every station.

“Il y a eu constamment 5 mises observées, chacune à 4 pointés de chaque objet. Mais chaque mise était composée de deux moitiés, correspondantes aux deux positions renversées de la lunette supérieure. J'ai donné, à chaque station, les chiffres séparés des deux moitiés.”
In English: “There were always 5 sets observed, each with 4 pointings of each object. But each set was made of two halves, corresponding to the two reversed positions of the upper telescope. I have given, at each station, the separate figures of the two halves.”

Heft I, § 12, the Russian (Polish) triangulation under General Tenner. In the southern Warsaw to Czenstochau connection the average number of sets was 11.4. The closures of all 219 Polish triangles give a mean angle error of ±0.73″. Tenner found this somewhat high and gave as reasons the high signals (pyramids 6 to 20 m, and 20 to 50 m in 148 cases) and measurement in unfavourable air that could not always be avoided. The rule for such air and strong wind was 18 to 24 sets. The sum of the 219 closures, +9.73″, shows no bias to positive or negative.

“Als Erklärungsgrund werden die hohen Signale, welche meist nothwendig waren, sowie die mehrfach nicht zu vermeidende Messung bei ungünstiger Luft angeführt. (Bei ungünstiger Luft und starkem Wind sollten 18—24 Sätze genommen werden.) Die Summe der 219 Widersprüche ist + 9″,73, so dass keine Neigung zu positiven oder negativen Schlussfehlern zu erkennen ist.”
In English: “The high signals, which were mostly necessary, and the measurement in unfavourable air, which several times could not be avoided, are given as the explanation. (In unfavourable air and strong wind 18 to 24 sets were to be taken.) The sum of the 219 closures is +9.73″, so that no tendency to positive or negative closure errors can be seen.”
Worked out here: √(354.1 / (219 × 3)) = √0.539 = 0.734″ (printed ±0.73″). Per direction 0.73/√2 = 0.52″ (printed).

Towers, scaffolds and high stations

Heft I, § 5, French channel stations of 1862. At Harlettes Beaux observed on a 21 m scaffold in wind under very unfavourable conditions, so Helmert doubled all q (halved all weights). At Cassel the weight of angle 44.42 was halved because its 60 repetitions were all obtained on a single day. A repetition is one addition of the angle on a repeating circle. The page also notes a measurement excluded because its set was spread over a whole week.

“Harlettes. Die Beobachtungen wurden 1862 von Beaux wegen Wind unter sehr ungünstigen Umständen auf einem 21 m hohen Gerüst ausgeführt, weshalb ich hier alle q verdoppelt habe. ... Letzterer Werth ist verdoppelt worden, weil jene 60 Rep. an einem einzigen Tage erhalten sind.”
In English: “Harlettes. The observations were made in 1862 by Beaux, because of wind under very unfavourable conditions, on a 21 m high scaffold, for which reason I have doubled all q here. ... The latter value has been doubled because those 60 repetitions were obtained on a single day.”

GTS Vol. XII appendix summary of Lambton's 1802-03 observing of horizontal angles. A microscope here is the reading microscope on the circle; reading both, three times each, reduces reading error. Two field-books were kept independently and compared.

“The angles were all measured three or four times each; both microscopes were read off thrice every time the object was observed, and two separate field-books were kept for making out the angles. If from any marked difference between two measures of the same angle the graduation of the instrument was suspected to be in error, the division between the dots was carefully examined, as also those to the right and left, and if any error was discovered, allowance was made accordingly. Difficulties however very frequently arose from the haziness of the weather occasioning irregularity in the angles, and observations in consequence had often to be repeated.”

Part I, in the explanation of the station (local) adjustment. A "series" is one sweep of the telescope over all visible signals, read with the telescope direct (D.) and then reversed (R.), at one setting ("position") of the horizontal circle. Schott prints two of the 152 series observed at Mount Helena, California, as an example of the raw field record that goes into each station abstract. The counts at the foot of the next page show how many separate pointings went into each direction.

“The following portions of the local adjustment at the station Mount Helena, California, will serve to illustrate the arrangement of the numerical work. [...] In the abstract proper two series only, the thirty-third and thirty-sixth, are here given out of the 152 series shown in the original computation. The first line gives the seconds of the mean reading of the three microscopes for each signal sighted with the telescope direct. The corrections for run have already been applied. The second line gives the corresponding readings with the telescope in the reverse position, when sweeping back over the same signals in the opposite direction. The third line is the mean of the first and second.”
Reading the table. Columns: the ten signals sighted from Mount Helena (Mt. Diablo, Table Mt., Snow Mt. (E), Azimuth Mark, Marysville Butte, Lola, Pine Hill, Round Top, Monticello, Vaca). Top rows: assumed directions and their arithmetic complements. Each series block (Oct. 11 a.m., circle position 12, series 33; Oct. 12 a.m., position 13, series 36) has five lines: seconds read with telescope direct, seconds read reversed, mean of the two, mean reduced to the first signal, and the value used in the observation equations. A signal not seen in a series is left blank. The continuation on p. 44 (pdf 45) gives the "No." row, the number of pointings on each signal over all 152 series: 82, 60, 81, 122, 56, 54, 55, 50, 67, 56.
Worked out here: Sum of the "No." row on p. 44: 82+60+81+122+56+54+55+50+67+56 = 683 pointings (each one a D. and R. pair) at one station. Fewest on one signal: 50 (Round Top).
Schott, C. A. (1900). The transcontinental triangulation and the American arc of the parallel (Special Publication No. 4). U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey; Government Printing Office., p. 43

US Transcontinental Triangulation, 39th parallel · p. 47 · strength ★★★
Repetition over days and hours

Part I, rules for reading the station abstracts. Every station abstract in Part III ends with "probable error of a single observation of a direction (D. and R.)". This passage defines that unit. A probable error is the error that half the observations exceed and half do not (0.6745 times the standard error).

“The probable error of a single observation of a direction (e) is given under the list of directions at each station as a convenient index of the accuracy of the observations. When the parenthesis (D. and R.) is used, the observations were made with a direction instrument. A single observation of a direction comprises two pointings upon the signal, one with telescope direct and one with telescope reversed, and two readings (forward and backward) of each microscope, of which there are usually three, for each pointing. [...] When the parenthesis (6 D. and 6 R.) is used, the observations were made with a repeating instrument and a single observation of an angle comprises 12 pointings upon each of two signals, 6 with telescope direct and 6 reversed”
Worked out here: One (D. and R.) observation = 2 pointings x 3 microscopes x 2 readings = 12 circle readings.
Schott, C. A. (1900). The transcontinental triangulation and the American arc of the parallel (Special Publication No. 4). U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey; Government Printing Office., p. 47

Part III, introduction to the Indiana series. "Positions of the circle" are the different settings of the graduated circle, used so that graduation errors average out. "Broken series" are series in which some signals could not be seen, so the series had to be repeated.

“It was through this section that our highest towers were needed, and even then considerable cutting had to be resorted to. All the observations were made on lights at night. The total length of the series between the base-net lines is nearly 216 kilometres (or 135 statute miles); the number of stations is 15; the average length of a side is 32 kilometres (or 19.9 statute miles); the number of series of measures at a station (mean of telescope D. and R.) exceeds 34,* and the usual number of the positions of the circle is 17. [...] *The intention was to observe each direction 34 times, but owing to the presence of broken series their total number is much greater.”
Reading the table. The crop also shows the first station abstract of the series (Oblong, Illinois, 1879): dates, theodolite, telescope height above ground (30.94 m), observer, and for each direction the station-adjusted value and the corrections from the base-net and figure adjustments.
Worked out here: 34 series / 17 positions = 2 series in each circle position.

US Transcontinental Triangulation, 39th parallel · p. 553 · strength ★★★
Repetition over days and hours Steady-air hours Night lamps and heliotropes

Part III, Rocky Mountain series (Pikes Peak to Salt Lake, stations near 3 650 m, longest side 294 km). Heliotropes are mirrors that reflect sunlight from the far station as a bright point target. A "double zenith distance" is a vertical angle read in both circle faces. This passage gives the full observing programme for both horizontal and vertical angles.

“The horizontal directions at all the stations were observed with the 50-centimetre (20-inch) theodolite, originally in 19 and later on (since 1893) in but 17 positions of the azimuth circle. The intention was to secure two full sets in each position and to balance the number of observations of the morning and evening, but on account of unavoidable broken series their numbers had generally to be increased for each position. Respecting the time of observations, they were made from sunrise till 8 o'clock, and resumed in the afternoon at half past 4 o'clock and continued till sunset. [...] To secure observations under a variety of atmospheric conditions, observations were extended over twenty or more days. Double zenith distances for heights of stations were observed at three different periods of the day, viz. between 6 1/2 and 8 o'clock in the morning, between 11 1/2 and 1 o'clock, and again between 4 1/2 and 6 o'clock in the evening. This brought to light the fact that the minimum refraction of the day occurs late in the afternoon, even after the heat of the day has passed. As a rule these vertical angle measures were spread over not less than twelve days, at least for the main lines. [...] No simultaneous reciprocal zenith distances were obtained. [...] The triangulation party also made observations of the magnetic declination, dip, and intensity, and meteorological notes were regularly kept.”
Worked out here: Minimum per direction from the stated plan: 17 positions x 2 sets = 34 observations (38 with 19 positions), each a D. and R. pair.
Schott, C. A. (1900). The transcontinental triangulation and the American arc of the parallel (Special Publication No. 4). U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey; Government Printing Office., p. 553

“Assistant Boutelle generally used the large theodolite in 7 positions with 6 to 18 series, whereas Assistant Mosman with the 50-centimetre theodolite adhered to 11 positions of the circle with 3 series in each, and when using the 30-centimetre theodolite, adopted 17 positions with 2 series in each.”

Part I, Epping base net (Maine). A repeating theodolite measures one angle several times in a row on the circle and divides the total. Schott gives the probable error from the 20 measures of each angle and, separately, from the closing errors of the 46 triangles of the net. The footnote compares the two instrument types.

“In case of repetitions the probable error will depend upon the comparison of a resulting angle with each of its 20 measures (each of 3 repetitions direct and 3 repetitions reversed), from which an average and approximate value of the probable error of a single measure of an angle and of a direction has been derived [...] If we deduce the probable error of a direction from the closing errors in the sum of the angles of the 46 triangles, we find from the sum of the squares of these errors the mean closing error of a triangle = sqrt(54.49/46) = +/- 1".09, hence the probable error of a direction = 0.674 x 1.09/sqrt(6) = +/- 0".30. [...] The mean of the 4 values of e_1 derived from a single measure (D. and R.) with the 75cm theodolite is +/- 1".04 and the mean of the 5 values of e_1 derived from a single measure (3 D. and 3 R.) with the 25cm repeating theodolite is +/- 1".16, or one measure with the first instrument is about equal in accuracy to three with the latter.”
Worked out here: Per angle: 20 measures x 6 repetitions = 120 pointings on each signal.

Number of partial results set by the air; bad definition and lateral refraction cut the weight from 360 to 11
Maclear's verification and extension of La Caille's arc of meridian, Cape of Good Hope · p. 400 · strength ★★★
Repetition over days and hours

Description of the Beaufort theodolite method (p. 400). Each angle was measured by repetition, the verniers read at every tenth repetition; the mean of ten repetitions is one partial result. Maclear says the number of partial results depended on the importance of the angle and on the atmosphere. Definition is how sharp and steady the signal looks in the telescope; probable error is the error that has an even chance of being exceeded. Five results in first-rate definition (Simon's Berg, 19 November 1845) gave 0.05"; sixteen results in bad definition and lateral refraction (Kapoc Berg, 12 February 1846) gave 0.3". The footnotes giving these stations and dates are at the foot of the same page and inside the crop.

“The mean of every tenth repetition being regarded as one partial result, the required number of such results depended upon the importance of the angle, and the atmospheric circumstances during the time when measuring. The value of the latter may be gathered from the fact of five results obtained during first-rate definition, giving a probable error of 0"·05 and weight 360 (a) ; whereas during bad definition and lateral refraction, 16 results gave a probable error of 0"·3, and weight 11 (b). ... (a) Simon's Berg, Nov. 19, 1845. (b) Kapoc Berg, Feb. 12, 1846.”
Worked out here: 5 results = 50 repetitions; 16 results = 160 repetitions. Weight = 1/P^2 (p. 419): 1/0.3^2 = 11.1, printed 11. 1/0.05^2 = 400; the printed 360 corresponds to P = 0.0527, which rounds to the printed 0.05.
Maclear, T. (1866). Verification and extension of La Caille's arc of meridian at the Cape of Good Hope (Vol. 1). London: Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty., p. 400
