The printed type example for the Beaufort theodolite: the angle at Kamies-Sector Berg between the Keibiskow heliostat (about 80 miles away) and Bokkeveld Berg, 1, 3 and 4 December 1846. Each row is one partial result of 10 repetitions with the hour and a remark on the definition of the signals. The remarks record the air: wind direction, 'hot temperature: about 85 deg.', 'therm. 90 deg.', and 'Definition in the morning not good, towards 11h it became much worse'. Half the work was measured forward with the Y bearings right, half backward with Y left. The final angle comes from 260 measures with weight 131.99.

“Angle at Kamies-Sector Berg, West Rock Station; between Keibiskow and Bokkeveld Berg : measured with the Beaufort Theodolite. ... Middling definition. ... Northerly wind, perhaps 1 point E. of N. Hot temperature : about 85°. ... Bad definition and bad signaling at Bokkeveld ... Wind west, next S.W., and lastly south; this afternoon very hot, therm. 90°. ... Excellent do., points. ... Definition in the morning not good, towards 11h it became much worse. ... Resulting angle from 260 meas. = 23°32′1″·98 Weight = 131·99”
Reading the table. Columns: date (1846) and hour (A.M./P.M.); remarks on definition, wind and temperature; No. of repetitions (10 per row); pointer degrees and minutes; seconds on verniers A, D, B, C; mean reading; angle seconds for the row (left) and running mean (right), all after 23 deg 32'. Under each day: sum of squares of errors, probable error of 10 measures, probable error of the day's total, and the weight. 1 Dec: 13 rows (130 repetitions), 3 Dec: 7 rows, 4 Dec: 6 rows (130 repetitions). Row seconds range from 0.65" to 3.35". Look at how the remarks change with the hour and how the weight of each day follows its scatter.
Worked out here: Combination printed at foot: 1.96 x 75.02 = 147.039; 2.00 x 56.97 = 113.940; 75.02 + 56.97 = 131.99; 260.979 / 131.99 = 1.977 -> 1.98". The day weight above it is printed 56.77 (1/0.1327^2 = 56.8), so the 56.97 in the combination differs from it by 0.2.

Calculation of the differences of altitude (p. 598). Reciprocal zenith distances are measured from each end of the same line toward the other; their sum exceeds 180 deg by the earth's curvature minus the bending of the ray, so they give the actual refraction on that line. Maclear prints the formula for m (the coefficient of refraction as a fraction of c, the angle at the earth's centre) and the 10 lines with the zenith distance at each end, the number of observations at each end (4 to 86), z + z' - 180 deg, c and m. The values run from .0667 to .0842; the mean .0712 was adopted for the altitudes.

“The following formulæ have been employed in the calculation of the co-efficient of refraction, and the altitudes of the points observed : ... then h′—h = s cot. (z + m c — ½ c) (1 + (h′+h)/2ν). and m = ½ (1 — (z+z′—180°)/c). The calculation of m from 10 sets of reciprocal zenith distances is contained in the following table : ... The mean value of m from the above is ·0712.”
Reading the table. Columns: reference number in the preceding abstract; station (the two ends of each line); true zenith distance at each end; No. of observations at each end; log distance; z + z' - 180 deg (seconds); c (seconds); coefficient of refraction m. Observation counts per end: 68 and 82, 84 and 48, 66 and 44, 44 and 48, 48 and 86, 52 and 20, 38 and 32, 8 and 48, 8 and 12, 21 and 12.
Worked out here: East End of Base - Kapoc Berg: m = 0.5 x (1 - 646.1/746.2) = 0.5 x 0.13415 = 0.0671 (printed .0671). In the usual k = 2m form the mean is 0.1424.

Morris's report, paragraph 53 (p. 19). An arc is one complete measure of the round of directions with the circle set to a given zero; CL and CR are circle left and circle right (the telescope turned over). Captain Gordon and Mr. Simms used eight arcs at every point, with zeros near 0, 45, 90, 135, 23, 67, 113 and 157 deg. When an arc was repeated, the same circle readings were kept.

“53. Captain Gordon and Mr. Simms observed at all points of their work with the zeros of the horizontal arc set as follows :— Arc 1 {C L 0 C R 180} Arc 2 {C R 270 C L 90} Arc 3 {C L 45 C R 225} Arc 4 {C R 315 C L 135} Arc 5 {C L 23 C R 203} Arc 6 {C R 293 C L 113} Arc 7 {C L 67 C R 247} Arc 8 {C R 337 C L 157} not, of necessity, accurately to the foregoing, but in their near proximity; and whenever any particular arc had to be repeated, either as a whole, or partially, the circle readings for that arc as recorded were always adhered to.”

Extract from the field book of the 12-inch instrument at Dromedary station, 1851 (p. 95). It shows the vernier readings of a horizontal angle measured with 1 and then 7 repetitions, star elongations (a star at its greatest east or west position, used for the meridian), and the vertical angle to Rumney's Hill from six readings. The barometer (27.016 inches) and the attached and detached thermometers (46 deg) were recorded with the vertical angle, which is the information needed for a refraction allowance.

Trigonometrical Survey of New South Wales · p. 182 · strength ★★★
Repetition over days and hours

Measurement of angles (p. 182). A round is one sighting of every station in azimuth order; a double set is a round in one face and the return round with the telescope reversed. Rounds were spread over different parts of the graduated circle to remove graduation errors. No PDF of this paper is in the project; the item points to the OCR text file, so no crop is possible. Wording checked against a page image of p. 182 held elsewhere in the project.

“The method of measuring angles, followed during the earlier years of the survey of New South Wales, was to observe the direction of one point as a referring mark and then to sight to each station consecutively in order of azimuth, completing the surround by again observing the referring mark ; the instrument was then reversed and the same round of stations was observed in this position, similar rounds being taken after moving the graduated circle so that each station was observed upon different parts of the arc in order to eliminate graduation errors. About twenty observations on to each station were deemed sufficient. In the later angle measures, the method has been to reverse the telescope after each round and observe in reverse order of azimuth back to referring mark, twenty such double sets being altogether observed on different parts of the circle.”

An angle is never taken from one single measurement
Middleton, Chadwick and Bogle, A Treatise on Surveying (textbook) · p. 191 · strength ★★★
Repetition over days and hours

The book's rule for measuring angles: two methods, repetition and reiteration, both measure the angle many times. In repetition the angle is added up on the circle several times and the total is divided by the number of readings. In reiteration the angle is measured separately at different parts of the circle (a different zero each time) and the results are averaged.

“It will be assumed therefore that before commencing the observation of angles, it is practically in perfect adjustment. There are two methods of observing angles, by which more correct values can be obtained than is possible with one single measurement. These are 'repetition' and 'reiteration.'”
Middleton, R. E., Chadwick, O., & Bogle, J. du T. (1904). A treatise on surveying: Part I (2nd ed.). E. & F. N. Spon., p. 191
From no. 135 the zenith distances are Méchain's: always several series per distance, mostly on mountains where the ray did not graze the ground

Repetition over days and hours Towers, scaffolds and high stations

Tome II, remarks on the n table. Delambre states how the southern zenith distances were taken: by Méchain, with several series for each distance, rarely after October, and from mountain stations where the line of sight stayed clear of the ground.

“A commencer de 135 toutes les observations sont de M. Méchain qui a toujours fait plusieurs séries pour la même distance, et qui, à l'exception de quelques stations de Nore au Vernet, n'a guère observé passé le mois d'octobre, et presque toujours sur des montagnes où le rayon visuel ne rasoit pas le sol.”
In English: “From 135 on, all the observations are by M. Méchain, who always made several series for the same distance, and who, except for some stations from Nore to Le Vernet, hardly observed after October, and almost always on mountains where the line of sight did not graze the ground.”
Méchain, P., & Delambre, J.-B. J. (1807). Base du système métrique décimal, ou mesure de l'arc du méridien compris entre les parallèles de Dunkerque et Barcelone (Vol. 2). Paris: Baudouin., T2 p. 776
As many reciprocal zenith distances as needed at every first-order vertex to keep level errors under two metres; Brest-Panthéon levelling by reciprocal simultaneous zenith distances by day and night
Parallel of Paris, Brest to Strasbourg (Henry east part, Bonne west part), Nouvelle carte de France · 232 · strength ★★

Puissant, section on the geodetic levelling and its precision by the formulas of probability. He states the target accuracy (level differences not wrong by more than two metres in the worst case) and that the number of reciprocal zenith distances at each vertex was set by that target. The networks control one another.

“aussi a-t-on observé à tous les sommets des triangles du 1er ordre autant de distances zénithales réciproques qu'il était nécessaire, pour que les erreurs commises sur les différences de niveau ne dépassassent pas deux mètres, dans les cas les plus défavorables. ... Tous les réseaux de triangles, qui partent de l'océan et qui s'étendent dans l'intérieur du royaume, réunissent cet avantage en se contrôlant les uns par les autres. C'est ainsi que le nivellement trigonométrique exécuté depuis Brest jusqu'au Panthéon, par des distances zénithales réciproques et simultanées, prises de jour et de nuit, a donné la hauteur absolue du sommet de cet édifice”
In English: “so at all the vertices of the first-order triangles as many reciprocal zenith distances were observed as were necessary for the errors on the level differences not to exceed two metres in the most unfavourable cases. ... All the networks of triangles that start from the ocean and extend into the interior of the kingdom have this advantage of controlling one another. Thus the trigonometric levelling carried out from Brest to the Panthéon, by reciprocal and simultaneous zenith distances taken by day and by night, gave the absolute height of the top of this building”
Puissant, L. (1832). Nouvelle description géométrique de la France (Première partie). Paris: Ch. Picquet., 232
Roy: the refraction results are not offered as free from error; many repetitions would have been needed
Anglo-French triangulation of 1787 (Greenwich to Paris junction), English side by Roy · p. 245 · strength ★★
Repetition over days and hours

Art. VII, General Remarks, introducing the refraction table. 'Double observations' are an elevation and a depression on the same line, one from each end. Roy states that refraction was a secondary object of the operation and that his table shows mainly how variable refraction is.

“These results are not however offered as being free from error; on the contrary, if the circumstances had permitted this to become a principal object in our operation, the successive repetition of the observations for many times would, no doubt, have furnished still more satisfactory conclusions. It is hoped, nevertheless, that these, such as they are, may have their use, were it only by shewing the variableness of terrestrial refraction”
Roy, W. (1790). An account of the trigonometrical operation, whereby the distance between the meridians of the Royal Observatories of Greenwich and Paris has been determined. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, 80, 111-270 (with Dalby, I., Remarks, pp. 593-614)., p. 245

Ordnance Trigonometrical Survey of Great Britain and Ireland, Principal Triangulation · p. 52 · strength ★★
Night lamps and heliotropes Repetition over days and hours

Section on observing. A heliostat is a mirror that reflects the sun from a distant station so that it shows as a bright point. Rewards were paid for each sighting, graded by distance, with smaller sums for the second and third arcs on the same day. The passage shows the effort to get repeated observations on long lines.

“A watch is always kept in the camp for distant heliostats. ... The propriety of this allowance will be readily admitted when it is remembered that as long a period as a month has very frequently occurred between consecutive observations of very distant points.”
Clarke, A. R. (1858). Ordnance trigonometrical survey of Great Britain and Ireland: Account of the observations and calculations of the principal triangulation. London: Eyre and Spottiswoode., p. 52

Repetition over days and hours

Same page. The vertical circle was read after the horizontal reading in each observation (p. 510), so the zenith distances come in the same arcs as the horizontal directions. 'Under all circumstances' means at all hours and in all weather in which horizontal work was done, so the mean includes the daily range.

“The vertical observations with the larger theodolites are generally numerous (at least in the more modern observations), and taken under all circumstances.”
Clarke, A. R. (1858). Ordnance trigonometrical survey of Great Britain and Ireland: Account of the observations and calculations of the principal triangulation. London: Eyre and Spottiswoode., p. 509

Chapter II, the general review of the work. A set (приёмъ) is one complete round of pointings on the targets in both positions of the telescope; the angle is the mean of all sets. The passage gives the instruments used at the 161 first-class points and the minimum number of sets per angle: 12 in the Main and Krasnoyarsk rows, 6 in the Kizlyar row.

“Измѣреніе на нихъ первоклассныхъ угловъ произведено: на 74-хъ универсальными инструментами, на 70-ти терристрическимъ теодолитомъ и на 16-ти теодолитомъ Порта, дѣлая для каждаго угла въ Главномъ и Красноярскомъ ряду не менѣе 12 пріемовъ, а въ Кизлярскомъ не менѣе 6.”
In English: “The measurement of the first-class angles at them was made: at 74 with universal instruments, at 70 with the terrestrial theodolite and at 16 with Porta's theodolite, making for each angle in the Main and Krasnoyarsk rows not fewer than 12 sets, and in the Kizlyar row not fewer than 6.”

Russian arc of the parallel of 47.5 N, Privolzhsk triangulation (Kishinev to Astrakhan arc, eastern part) · Zapiski XXII, Otd. II, p. 22 · strength ★★
Repetition over days and hours

Chapter III describes the field methods. Canvas screens against wind and an umbrella against the sun protected the instrument. Horizontal angles were measured in sets by W. Struve's method: pointings left to right, then with the telescope turned through the zenith, right to left. Zenith distances for the height differences were measured with double pointing and in two positions of the vertical circle, so that the index error of the circle cancels.

“Зенитныя разстоянія, для опредѣленія разностей высотъ пунктовъ, измѣрялись двойнымъ наведеніемъ на предметы и въ двухъ различныхъ положеніяхъ вертикальнаго круга.”
In English: “The zenith distances, for determining the height differences of the points, were measured with a double pointing on the objects and in two different positions of the vertical circle.”
Voenno-topograficheskoe depo. (1861). Zapiski Voenno-topograficheskago depo, Chast' XXII, Otd. II: Privolzhskoe trigonometricheskoe izmerenie. Voenno-topograficheskoe depo., Zapiski XXII, Otd. II, p. 22
Lithuania (Tenner): each angle in two series of 20 repetitions, with three instruments
Struve Geodetic Arc (Russo-Scandinavian arc of the meridian, Danube to Fuglenaes) · T. I, p. 148 · strength ★★
Repetition over days and hours

Tome I, p. 148, § 39. Tenner's southern section used the repetition method: the angle is added on the circle many times and the total is divided by the number of repetitions. Each angle had two series of 20 repetitions, and from 1827 the repetitions were made in both directions of rotation. The difference of the two series gives an estimate of the probable error of the final angle.

“En général, il y a eu pour chaque angle deux séries, chacune de 20 répétitions. La comparaison des deux valeurs du même angle conduit à une évaluation de l'erreur probable de l'angle définitif qui est la moyenne des deux valeurs isolées.”
In English: “In general there were for each angle two series, each of 20 repetitions. The comparison of the two values of the same angle leads to an estimate of the probable error of the final angle, which is the mean of the two separate values.”
Struve, F. G. W. (1857). Arc du méridien de 25° 20' entre le Danube et la Mer Glaciale mesuré depuis 1816 jusqu'en 1855 (Vol. 1). Imprimerie de l'Académie impériale des sciences., T. I, p. 148
Finland instruction: 5 sets 18 degrees apart on the circle, each set in two halves with the telescope reversed
Struve Geodetic Arc (Russo-Scandinavian arc of the meridian, Danube to Fuglenaes) · T. II, p. 20 · strength ★★
Repetition over days and hours

Tome II, Chapter V, § 78, observing methods of Finland. Horizontal angles were measured by reiteration: each set starts on a different part of the circle, so graduation errors average out. Struve replaced the 6 sets of the Baltic arc by 5 sets 18 degrees apart. Each set has two halves (vertical circle east, then west), and in each half every object is pointed twice with the two opposite motions of the slow-motion screw. The pointing order is reversed in the second half.

“Seulement je remplaçai les 6 mises, adoptées pour l'arc Baltique, par 5 mises, distantes de 18° à 18° sur le limbe, chaque mise étant partagée en deux moitiés, relatives aux deux positions de l'axe horizontal, le cercle vertical étant ou à l'est, ou à l'ouest. Dans ces moitiés chaque objet fut observé deux fois de suite, par les deux mouvements opposés de la vis de rappel.”
In English: “Only I replaced the 6 sets adopted for the Baltic arc by 5 sets, 18° apart on the circle, each set being divided into two halves, relating to the two positions of the horizontal axis, the vertical circle being either east or west. In these halves each object was observed twice in succession, by the two opposite motions of the slow-motion screw.”
Struve, F. G. W. (1860). Arc du méridien de 25° 20' entre le Danube et la Mer Glaciale mesuré depuis 1816 jusqu'en 1855 (Vol. 2). Imprimerie de l'Académie impériale des sciences., T. II, p. 20

European arc of the parallel in 52 N, Greenwich (Feaghmain) to Warschau · p. 20 · strength ★★
Repetition over days and hours

Heft I, § 7. The Rhenish, Hessian and Märkisch-Thuringian nets were observed under General Baeyer's instruction of 9 April 1868. It prescribes direction observations after Bessel, with a zero mark (a distant fixed target in every set) and 36 pointings in 18 sets on each object, on 6 circle positions 30 degrees apart. Bessel's East Prussian arc used 12 sets 15 degrees apart.

“unterscheidet sich aber von Bessels Methode einestheils durch die Einführung der Nullmarke, einem einige Kilometer entfernten, meist künstlichen Objekt, welches in jedem Satze Aufnahme finden sollte, anderntheils durch Vertheilung der 36 Einstellungen (in 18 Sätzen) für jedes Objekt auf nur 6 Stände des Horizontalkreises mit 30° Intervall.”
In English: “but differs from Bessel's method partly by the introduction of the zero mark, an object some kilometres away, usually artificial, which was to be included in every set, and partly by the distribution of the 36 pointings (in 18 sets) for each object over only 6 positions of the horizontal circle at 30° intervals.”
Helmert, F. R. (Ed.). (1893). Die europäische Längengradmessung in 52 Grad Breite von Greenwich bis Warschau. I. Heft: Hauptdreiecke und Grundlinienanschlüsse von England bis Polen. P. Stankiewicz., p. 20

Same page as ga_01. Lambton states how the vertical angles for the Madras height were taken. Collimation error is the small offset of the telescope line of sight; turning the telescope over and the circle half round cancels it. He also records the weather during these observations.

Walker on the Great Arc south of Daumergida. The Royal Society recommended re-measurement; the Bangalore base was already checked. He states that the early triangles had fewer observations and sometimes only two measured angles, which later practice replaced with three angles and polygonal figures.

“The sections of the Great Arc from Daumergida southwards to Punnoe are being re-measured at the present time, at the recommendation of the President and Council of the Royal Society, but the undertaking is not yet sufficiently advanced to permit of the results being closely compared with those of the early operations, excepting at the Bangalore base, the error of which has been found to be about the 1/12,000th part of it's length. [...] It is known that in the early operations the observations were very few and not so systematic as afterwards; in several cases only two of the angles of the principal triangles were measured, whereas subsequently all three angles were measured,”

Walker quotes Lambton's manuscript General Report on how he measured the horizontal angles of this period (1802-1808). It adds his method when a triangle did not close: each angle in turn was held correct and the sides were recomputed, and no angle was dropped without cause.

““ As to the angles in general they have been taken three and four times, and every time that the object was observed, both microscopes were read off thrice, and two separate field-books kept for making out the angles. One-third of the spherical excess is the correction applied to each angle after the error of observation is removed, in proportion to the weight of each angle.”
Reading the table. Columns: no. of triangle; angular points; no. of repetitions; spherical excess; observed angle (sum 180 deg 0' 1.6"); corrected angle; reduced from spherical excess; sine of angle; log of sides; sides in feet.
Worked out here: 41.2 + 38.8 + 41.6 = 121.6" -> sum 180 0 1.6; spherical excess 3.1"; error 3.1 - 1.6 = 1.5" (printed 1.5).
Cotton, H. C. (1855). On the trigonometrical survey of Van Diemen's Land. Papers and Proceedings of the Royal Society of Van Diemen's Land, 3, 82-107., p. 96
Refraction named as the main difficulty in trigonometrical levelling; Bessel weights by the number of days at both ends
Trigonometrical Survey of New South Wales · p. 205 · strength ★★
Repetition over days and hours

pp. 204-205. Furber names the irregular change of refraction as the main difficulty, cites the Indian experience of zenith distances varying through nine minutes at 10 to 12 miles, and argues that a large spread is the reason to observe over more days. Bessel's weight for a reciprocal line has the factor n1 x n2, the numbers of days observed at the two ends. No PDF of this paper is in the project; the item points to the OCR text file, so no crop is possible. Quote from the text layer; the subscripts of n are garbled there and are written n₁, n₂.

“There is little doubt that the principal source of difficulty in trigonometrical levelling lies in the considerable and irregular changes in the atmospheric refraction. This cannot be better illustrated than by the experience obtained in India, where apparent zenith distances of points only 10 or 12 miles away varied under certain circumstances through a range of as much as nine minutes. At first sight it might appear to be useless to go on duplicating such apparently wild observations, yet consideration of the nature of the question will show that the great range among the observations forms, itself, the reason for extending them to cover a longer period of time. Bessel's opinion on this subject may be gathered from his estimate of the relative weights to be assigned to such observations, the principal factor in the weight being n₁ n₂, where n₁ and n₂ are the number of days on which observations are made at opposite ends of the same line.”
No page image: this source is held as a text layer only.
Furber, T. F. (1898). The trigonometrical survey of New South Wales, with mention of similar surveys in the other Australian colonies. Report of the Australasian Association for the Advancement of Science, 7, Section A, 176-237., p. 205
What repeating an angle does and does not remove
Middleton, Chadwick and Bogle, A Treatise on Surveying (textbook) · p. 191 · strength ★★
Repetition over days and hours

The authors explain the limits of repetition: it reduces graduation and pointing errors, but past a point it stops helping, and it cannot remove a displaced signal. This is why the surveys also changed the circle zero, the hour and the day, rather than only repeating on one occasion.

“There is a limit beyond which repetition produces no improvement. Errors due to slip and flexure, accumulate and prevent extreme accuracy, though a moderate number of repetitions reduce graduation error, by measuring the angle at different parts of the circle. To some extent it reduces errors in bisecting the objects aimed at, for it is reasonable to suppose that the cross-wire will not be always laid on the same side of the true centre. Repetition, however, does not eliminate the most serious source of error of all, namely displacement of the signal observed to.”
Middleton, R. E., Chadwick, O., & Bogle, J. du T. (1904). A treatise on surveying: Part I (2nd ed.). E. & F. N. Spon., p. 191
“I'd like to see the raw measurement data and the results for all the tests.” 62 items · 21 surveys

The printed tables of individual readings, series, reciprocal zenith distances and closures, with what each column means.

Short answer. The printed records are below, cropped from the scans: Schott's microscope readings at Mount Helena (152 series) and 14 days of hourly zenith distances at Round Top; Delambre's Fiefs register with series, hours and air remarks; Struve's half-set values at Ristisaari; the Russian field journals with hour, barometer, thermometer and "object steady"; GTS Vol. XII with every single reading; the Karachi vertical-angle tables with hours and negative refractions; Clarke's Ben Nevis observation book; Roy's refraction table; Mudge's simultaneous hourly tables of 1799. The full scans of every volume are available, and 8,734 directions are transcribed station by station.
Four reciprocal zenith-distance pairs measure the total refraction on lines of 9 to 35.5 minutes of arc
Cassini de Thury and Lacaille, verification of the Paris meridian and the arc of the parallel near 43.5 N · x-xj (Troisième partie), footnote · strength ★★★
Raw tables of repeated measures Vertical refraction coefficients

Footnote continued on p. xj. For four lines the zenith distance was observed at both ends. Reciprocal zenith distances are taken from each end of a line toward the other; their sum exceeds 180 degrees by the arc between the two verticals, less the bend of the ray at both ends, so the pair measures the refraction on that line itself. For each pair the authors print the two zenith distances, the apparent arc given by their sum, the true arc from the triangles, and the difference, which is the total refraction of both ends.

“Au fignal de Ste Victoire, la diftance apparente du fommet de la Montagne des Houpies au zenith fut obfervée de 90° 41' 40". A la Montagne des Houpies la diftance de Ste Victoire au zenith fut trouvée de 89° 43' 15". La fomme 180° 24' 55" donne 24' 55" pour l'arc itinéraire apparent, au lieu que le véritable eft de 28' 15"½. Il y avoit donc 3' 20"½ de réfraction, fur un arc de 28'.”
In English: “At the signal of Sainte-Victoire, the apparent zenith distance of the top of the Montagne des Houpies was observed as 90° 41' 40". At the Montagne des Houpies the zenith distance of Sainte-Victoire was found as 89° 43' 15". The sum 180° 24' 55" gives 24' 55" for the apparent itinerary arc, whereas the true one is 28' 15"½. So there were 3' 20"½ of refraction on an arc of 28'.”
Reading the table. Four printed pairs in running text: Sainte-Victoire / Houpies (90° 41' 40", 89° 43' 15"; 3' 20"½ on 28'); Aigues-Mortes / Houpies (89° 50' 19", 90° 40' 20"; 4' 57" on 35'½); Carcassonne / foot of Alaric signal (89° 1' 25", 91° 10' 5"; 1' 22" on 13'); Perpignan / foot of Tautavel tower (88° 36' 55", 91° 31' 20"; 43" on 9'). Each pair: zenith distance at A, zenith distance at B, apparent arc, true arc, total refraction. One value per station; the number of readings is not printed.
Worked out here: Refraction at one end as a fraction of the arc: 200.5/1695.5/2 = 0.059; 297/2136/2 = 0.070; 82/772/2 = 0.053; 43/538/2 = 0.040.

Tome I, Observations géodésiques, station of Fiefs. For each angle every series is printed: the number of repetitions, the total arc in grades, the single angle, the reduction to the centre, the observer and circle (D. = Delambre, F. = Lalande, B. = Bellet; n° 1 or n° 4 = circle number), the date and hours, and a remark on visibility, sun and wind. One series is marked 'série à rejeter' (series to be rejected) for strong wind, a faint and curved target and undulations. The remark on Sauti says that phases (the side lighting of a spire by the sun) moved the apparent target.

“D. n° 1 + première place. Grand vent ; Sauti foible et courbe ; ondulations au Mesnil ; fils en + série à rejeter. ... Le clocher de Sauti et les flèches voisines nous ont fort exercés par leurs phases différentes. ... D. n° 1. 3 juillet, 5h 40' — 7h 20'. Objets éclairés du soleil ; Sauti tout-à-fait courbe. ... F. n° 4. 4 juillet, 3h 10' — 5h 45'. Objets assez beaux en commençant ; ils l'étoient moins vers le milieu.”
In English: “D. circle no. 1, first place. Strong wind; Sauti faint and curved; undulations at Mesnil; wires in +; series to be rejected. ... The steeple of Sauti and the neighbouring spires gave us much trouble by their different phases. ... D. circle no. 1. 3 July, 5h 40' to 7h 20'. Objects lit by the sun; Sauti quite curved. ... F. circle no. 4. 4 July, 3h 10' to 5h 45'. Objects rather fine at the start; less so towards the middle.”
Reading the table. Each block is one series: first number = repetitions (20 or 12 here); then the total arc in grades, the single angle in grades, and the same in degrees; the line 'Au centre' gives the angle reduced to the centre of the station. Below: circle and observer, date, hours, remarks on the air. The angle between Mesnil and Sauti has three series of 20; the mean of the first three is reduced to the horizon (+0.58") to give 42° 59' 48.72". Bonnières-Sauti has series of 20, 20 and 12 on 3 and 4 July at different hours. A typical angle in Delambre's north part has 2 to 5 series of 12 to 30 repetitions (e.g. Dunkerque, Watten-Cassel: 20 + 16 + 30).
Worked out here: Mesnil-Sauti series reduced to centre: 42° 59' 49.68" and 42° 59' 55.07" (the rejected series is 5.4" higher).

Tome I, station of Boiscommun (frimaire an 2, December 1793). Delambre observed the zenith distance of the weathercock of Châteauneuf on seven days, one series of ten each, and printed with each the hour, the barometer (in pouces and lignes), the thermometer (as a fraction of the ice-to-boiling interval, converted to Réaumur degrees), and the sky: rain, fine or poor horizon, damp fog. He also stayed half an hour at the telescope to see whether refraction changed the distance. This is a direct record of humidity and pressure with each vertical angle.

“24 frimaire, 12h ¼. Bar. 27p 1l9. Therm. 0.099 = 7d92. A 1h ¼ la distance étoit encore la même. ... Le baromètre et le thermomètre étoient placés environ 1t8 au-dessous de la lunette. Après ces observations je suis resté pendant une demi-heure à la lunette, pour voir si la réfraction ne changeroit pas la distance : je n'ai pas vu la moindre variation. Horizon très-pur, point de soleil. ... 25 frimaire, 3h ¾. Bar. 27p 4l. Therm. + 0.11 = 8d8. Temps pluvieux ; horizon assez beau. ... 30 frimaire, 3h ½. Bar. 27p 3l. Therm. + 0.067 = 5d36. Brouillard humide.”
In English: “24 frimaire, 12h ¼. Barometer 27 pouces 1.9 lignes. Thermometer 0.099 = 7.92 degrees. At 1h ¼ the distance was still the same. ... The barometer and thermometer were placed about 1.8 toises below the telescope. After these observations I stayed half an hour at the telescope to see whether refraction would change the distance: I did not see the least variation. Very clear horizon, no sun. ... 25 frimaire, 3h ¾. Barometer 27 pouces 4 lignes. Thermometer +0.11 = 8.8 degrees. Rainy weather; horizon fairly fine. ... 30 frimaire, 3h ½. Barometer 27 pouces 3 lignes. Thermometer +0.067 = 5.36 degrees. Damp fog.”
Reading the table. Each line: number of repetitions (10), total arc in grades, single zenith distance in grades, the same in degrees; then date, hour, barometer, thermometer, remarks. Seven series on seven days (24 to 30 frimaire) to the same target. The page continues on p. 167 with 1, 2 and 7 nivôse.
Worked out here: Seven zenith distances of the Châteauneuf weathercock range from 90° 5' 46.0" (28 frimaire) to 90° 6' 6.1" (30 frimaire, damp fog): spread 20.1".

“M. et A. 24 thermidor, à 5h ½ du soir. Thermomètre + 13d6 en 80d. Calme. L'objet est dans l'ombre ; on le voit bien. ... M. et A. 18 thermidor, à 6h ¼ du soir. Thermomètre 15d0. Soleil. Le grand vent agite le niveau, et le signal est difficile à distinguer. ... M. et A. 21 thermidor, à 7h ¾ du matin. Thermomètre 15d0. Calme. Objet assez net ; il n'y a point d'ondulations.”
In English: “M. and A., 24 thermidor, at 5h ½ in the evening. Thermometer +13.6 degrees (80-degree scale). Calm. The object is in shadow; it is seen well. ... M. and A., 18 thermidor, at 6h ¼ in the evening. Thermometer 15.0 degrees. Sun. The strong wind shakes the level, and the signal is hard to make out. ... M. and A., 21 thermidor, at 7h ¾ in the morning. Thermometer 15.0 degrees. Calm. Object fairly sharp; there are no undulations.”
Reading the table. Per target (Rodez statue, signal of La Gaste): two series of 10, each with date, hour (evening and morning), thermometer and remarks. 'Milieu des deux séries' / 'Moyenne' = mean used for the reduction to the horizon; then 'Demi-épaisseur du fil' (half wire thickness, +3") and dH (signal height correction) give the value used 'pour la différence de niveau et la réfraction'.

Tome I, Tableau des triangles. For each triangle the table gives the observed angles with the register page, the spherical excess (the amount by which the angles of a triangle on the curved earth exceed 180 degrees) and the 'Somme des erreurs', which is the closure error: the sum of the three observed angles minus 180 degrees minus the excess. A star marks an angle concluded, not observed. Closure errors are a direct internal check on the horizontal angles.

“Somme des erreurs . . — 1"18 ... L'astérisque est la marque d'un angle conclu.”
In English: “Sum of the errors -1.18" ... The asterisk marks a concluded angle.”
Reading the table. Columns: No. of triangle; station names; register page; observed angles; spherical excess; spherical angles; angles of the chords; mean angles. Under each fully observed triangle, 'Somme des erreurs' gives the closure error. Triangle 1 (Dunkerque, Watten, Cassel): -1.18"; triangle 3 (Watten, Cassel, Fiefs): -0.90".

Art. II, Calculation of the Triangles, the first page of the table that runs to p. 182. Spherical excess is the amount by which the three angles of a triangle on a curved surface exceed 180 degrees; it is computed from the area. Reading the table. Columns: 'Between' (the two objects of the angle, or the date and time for the star); degrees, minutes, seconds of each separate observation (seconds to 0.25"); 'Mean' (bracketed mean of the values). At Dean Hill and Old Sarum most angles have 2 to 4 values, for example Beacon Hill and Four Mile Stone at Old Sarum: 21.5, 21.75, 22.25, 23.75, mean 22.5. The pole-star angle has 7 values from 26 Jul to 11 Aug. Typical spread of the values for one angle: 1 to 3 seconds.

Printed as the form of the observation book. The booker wrote every microscope reading in ink as the observer called it out. Each object line also carries the ground depression read on the vertical circle. The footnote explains the abbreviations for the air.

“This, together with some other similar abbreviations, as (m.m.) (f.) are used to denote any atmospheric circumstance peculiar to the observation, as very hazy, much motion, faint.”
Reading the table. Header: instrument (Royal Society's theodolite), station, date. Second column: barometer 25.466 in, attached thermometer 40°; each object (pile on a hill) with the ground depression read at verniers A and B (e.g. Ben Wyvis 359° 28' 51" and 49"). Then degrees and minutes, and the seconds of five microscopes A to E, and their mean (filled in at the office). The R.O. is read at the start (19.40") and the end (19.60") of the arc. '(v.h.)' marks very hazy objects.

Section IV, extracts from the general abstracts. For each station the instrument, the dates, the observer and every object are listed. The range is the difference between the greatest and least single observation of that direction. The reciprocal of weight is larger for directions with fewer or more scattered observations. Footnotes reduce bearings taken to an object off the station to the station itself.

“From 20th January to 29th March 1843. Observer: Serg. Donelan, R.S.M.”
Reading the table. Arbury Hill, 3-ft theodolite, 20 Jan to 29 Mar 1843, observer Serg. Donelan. Columns: object; bearing (degrees, minutes, seconds, from an approximate south meridian); number of observations; range in seconds; reciprocal of weight. Number of observations per direction here: 2 to 15, and 102 for the referring object. Ranges 0.78" to 9.43". The quote is the station heading. The Section IV introduction (p. 71) states that only the mean bearing, the number of observations, the range and the weight are printed.

Section IV, second part: azimuthal observations in detail. Azimuth is the angle of a line from true north; it was found from the referring object and circumpolar stars at elongation (their farthest east or west point). Each row is one night's observation with its own result, so the spread can be seen. Footnote marks give the weather for individual rows. Probable error is the amount the mean is as likely to be within as outside.

“Cloudy and misty. Cloudy. Very misty; partial sun. Very clear in all directions.”
Reading the table. Columns: date (5 Aug to 14 Sep 1846); star and elongation (51 Cephei, Polaris, delta and lambda Ursae Minoris, E or W); reading of star; computed level and collimation correction; corrected reading; reading of R.O.; computed azimuth of star at elongation; resulting azimuth of R.O. (81° 52' plus 15.09" to 32.33"). Mean of eastern elongations 24.23", western 20.28", general mean 81° 52' 22".51, probable error ±0".60. The quote is the four footnotes on weather.

Ordnance Trigonometrical Survey of Great Britain and Ireland, Principal Triangulation · p. 542 · strength ★★★
Raw tables of repeated measures Vertical refraction coefficients

Section IX, 'Coefficient of Refraction'. Where both heights are known by levelling, the true zenith distance Z can be computed. The observed z differs from Z only by refraction, so k = (Z - z)/v is measured directly on that line. The weight w grows with the square root of the distance and with the number of observations.

“In the former case, the coefficient required is simply the ratio of the excess of the observed above the true zenith distance to the angle subtended by the two stations at the centre of the earth.”
Reading the table. Columns: number of the line; stations; levelled height (ft); observed zenith distance z; number of observations (4 to 29, e.g. Ben Nevis 19, Merrick 29, Pertinny 20); logarithmic distance; v (angle at the earth's centre, seconds); true zenith distance Z; Z - z (seconds); k; weight w; k times w. Values from 0.0649 (High Willhays) to 0.1058 (Swyre Barrow). Printed mean k = 0.0792.
Clarke, A. R. (1858). Ordnance trigonometrical survey of Great Britain and Ireland: Account of the observations and calculations of the principal triangulation. London: Eyre and Spottiswoode., p. 542
Clarke 1858: 112 reciprocal pairs of zenith distances, each giving k for that line
Ordnance Trigonometrical Survey of Great Britain and Ireland, Principal Triangulation · p. 543 · strength ★★★
Raw tables of repeated measures Vertical refraction coefficients

Next table. For two stations that observed each other, the sum of the two zenith distances exceeds 180° by the arc v when there is no refraction; refraction makes the sum smaller. So 1 - 2k = (z + z' - 180°)/v gives the bend on that line from the two angles alone, without knowing the heights. The weights follow the distance and the number of observations at each end.

“The weights assumed for the separate determinations are directly as the square root of the distance and inversely as the sum of the reciprocals of the numbers of observations at the two observing stations. The following table contains the calculation of 112 values of k:”
Reading the table. Columns: number; the two stations; observed zenith distance at each; number of observations at each (e.g. Monach 8 and Ben Clibrig 10; Corryhabbie 31 and 35; Jura 28); logarithmic distance; v; z + z' - 180°; 1 - 2k; k; weight w; kw. The table runs to p. 548. Group means printed on p. 548: 0.0801 (rays mostly over sea), 0.0778 (partly over sea), 0.0744 (inland).
Clarke, A. R. (1858). Ordnance trigonometrical survey of Great Britain and Ireland: Account of the observations and calculations of the principal triangulation. London: Eyre and Spottiswoode., p. 543

Table B gives the heights above the sea of the first-class points and of the Sarpinsky row. Reciprocal zenith distances are the two zenith distances of one line, one measured from each end. For each new point the table prints the zenith distance from the point to a known point (column 4) and from the known point back (column 5), the height obtained from each known point (column 6) and the mean (column 7). Two different known points give two independent heights for the same point.

“4. Зенитное разстояніе, измѣренное съ пункта опредѣляемаго на пунктъ, котораго номеръ выставленъ въ столбцѣ третьемъ. 5. Зенитное разстояніе измѣренное съ пункта, котораго № выставленъ въ столбцѣ 3-мъ на пунктъ опредѣляемый.”
In English: “4. Zenith distance measured from the point being determined to the point whose number is given in the third column. 5. Zenith distance measured from the point whose number is given in column 3 to the point being determined.”
Reading the table. Columns: 1 number; 2 point; 3 known point it is computed from; 4 forward zenith distance; 5 backward zenith distance; 6 height of the signal top from that known point (sazhen); 7 mean of the two heights; 8 height of the foot of the pyramid. Each new point is computed from two known points.

Table of pole-star observations for the meridian at Yerracondah (January 1804). A referring lamp is a lamp set up as a fixed night mark near the station; the angle from the star to the lamp is measured each night and the lamp is then tied to a survey station by day. The note below says no double azimuths were possible because vapour hid the pole star by day.

“Pole-Star Observations at Yerracondah Station, reduced for determining the position of the Meridian. [...] It may be remarked here, that no double azimuths have been taken. The pole-star being so low, and the vapour in the atmosphere so great in general, that I have never, except in two instances, been able to discern it while the sun was above the horizon.”
Reading the table. Columns: date (15 to 27 January 1804, 9 nights); apparent polar distance of the star; latitude; azimuth of the star; angle between the pole star and the referring lamp; angle between the north pole and the referring lamp. Look at the last column: 9 independent nightly values from 7 16 31.49 to 7 16 36.08, mean 7 16 33.64.
Worked out here: Spread of the nightly values: 36.08 - 31.49 = 4.59".

US Transcontinental Triangulation, 39th parallel · p. 43 · strength ★★★

Part I, in the explanation of the station (local) adjustment. A "series" is one sweep of the telescope over all visible signals, read with the telescope direct (D.) and then reversed (R.), at one setting ("position") of the horizontal circle. Schott prints two of the 152 series observed at Mount Helena, California, as an example of the raw field record that goes into each station abstract. The counts at the foot of the next page show how many separate pointings went into each direction.

“The following portions of the local adjustment at the station Mount Helena, California, will serve to illustrate the arrangement of the numerical work. [...] In the abstract proper two series only, the thirty-third and thirty-sixth, are here given out of the 152 series shown in the original computation. The first line gives the seconds of the mean reading of the three microscopes for each signal sighted with the telescope direct. The corrections for run have already been applied. The second line gives the corresponding readings with the telescope in the reverse position, when sweeping back over the same signals in the opposite direction. The third line is the mean of the first and second.”
Reading the table. Columns: the ten signals sighted from Mount Helena (Mt. Diablo, Table Mt., Snow Mt. (E), Azimuth Mark, Marysville Butte, Lola, Pine Hill, Round Top, Monticello, Vaca). Top rows: assumed directions and their arithmetic complements. Each series block (Oct. 11 a.m., circle position 12, series 33; Oct. 12 a.m., position 13, series 36) has five lines: seconds read with telescope direct, seconds read reversed, mean of the two, mean reduced to the first signal, and the value used in the observation equations. A signal not seen in a series is left blank. The continuation on p. 44 (pdf 45) gives the "No." row, the number of pointings on each signal over all 152 series: 82, 60, 81, 122, 56, 54, 55, 50, 67, 56.
Worked out here: Sum of the "No." row on p. 44: 82+60+81+122+56+54+55+50+67+56 = 683 pointings (each one a D. and R. pair) at one station. Fewest on one signal: 50 (Round Top).

US Transcontinental Triangulation, 39th parallel · p. 613 · strength ★★★
Raw tables of repeated measures

Part III, summary of angular results. The closing error of a triangle is 180 degrees plus the spherical excess minus the sum of the three measured angles; it is a check that is independent of the station repeats. Schott lists, per series and base net, how many triangles closed plus and minus, the sums of the plus and minus errors, the mean error of an angle and the probable error of an adjusted direction.

“With respect to the closure of the triangles (pi plus spherical excess minus the sum of the angles), we find the number of cases in excess to those in defect in the ratio 36 to 34, nearly.”
Reading the table. Columns: locality; number of positive and negative closing errors; sum of positive and sum of negative closing errors (seconds); number of triangles; mean error of an angle; probable error of a resulting direction. Totals: 357 positive, 343 negative, 701 triangles (one closes exactly), mean error of an angle +/- 0.77", probable error of a direction from 1 660 directions +/- 0.44". The intro sentence is on p. 612 (pdf 642).
Worked out here: Mean closing error per triangle from sums: (383.21 + 359.60) / 701 = 1.06" (average size of a closure, sign ignored).
Schott, C. A. (1900). The transcontinental triangulation and the American arc of the parallel (Special Publication No. 4). U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey; Government Printing Office., p. 613

US Transcontinental Triangulation, 39th parallel · p. 255 · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours Vertical refraction coefficients Raw tables of repeated measures

Part II, general remarks. The coefficient of refraction m is the bend of the line of sight expressed as a fraction of the arc between the stations (m = k/2 in the usual notation). Reciprocal zenith distances are vertical angles measured from each end of a line toward the other; from the pair, m is computed for that line, so the refraction is measured on the line itself, not assumed. Special hourly series were run day and night to find the daily cycle.

“For the sake of easy reference, we shall give here in tabular form and also exhibit by diagrams the resulting hourly values of the coefficient of refraction, m, from four experimental series [...] The tabular values were deduced under the supposition of equal refraction angles at lower and upper stations.”
Reading the table. Table 1: local hour (midnight to midnight) against m for Bodega Head-Ross Mountain (22.48 km, 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. only), Martinez East-Mount Diablo (24.26 km), Jackson Butte-Round Top (72.37 km) and the sea horizon from Ragged Mountain. Table 2: hourly departure from the daily mean. Daily means: 0.1000, 0.0646, 0.0849; daily ranges 0.0333, 0.0168, 0.0293. The first sentence of the quote is on p. 254 (pdf 257).
Worked out here: Jackson Butte-Round Top: maximum 0.0711 (2 a.m.), minimum 0.0557 (2 to 3 p.m.).
Schott, C. A. (1900). The transcontinental triangulation and the American arc of the parallel (Special Publication No. 4). U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey; Government Printing Office., p. 255

Part II, eastern Colorado. These abstracts are printed for every vertical-angle station from First View to the Pacific. Each row is one line. The pressure and temperature columns are the readings used to judge the air on each line; the note under each station gives the hours.

“These abstracts require but little explanation. The first column gives the number of days upon which observations were made (since the resulting zeta's were combined by days); the observed zenith distances are reduced to the ground at both stations; the columns headed P and T contain the rough values of the atmospheric pressure expressed in millimetres and of the atmospheric temperature expressed in degrees Centigrade; the log. of the distance s between the stations is given for metres. Notes appended state the extremes of time between which observations were obtained. No rejections were made of micrometric measures of differences of height.”
Reading the table. Pikes Peak 1895: 9 to 13 days per line, P 459-460 mm, T 5.1 to 6.7 C. Note: observations between 11 h 45 m a.m. and 1 h 20 m p.m., and between 4 h 30 m and 7 h 5 m p.m.

Maclear's verification and extension of La Caille's arc of meridian, Cape of Good Hope · p. 419 · strength ★★★

Opening of Section 3, Observed Horizontal Angles (p. 419). Maclear describes the record: 24 field-books for the Fuller theodolite and 2 for the Beaufort, copied into five folio volumes in which all the arithmetic was repeated and compared with the field-books. Further books hold the zenith distance measures. He prints only the means for every angle, plus the complete record of one angle by each instrument (see items cape_06 and cape_07) as the type of the whole.

“It was the general practice on the survey, when measuring angles, to call out the reading of each microscope or vernier to an amanuensis, who repeated the numbers aloud while recording them in the field-book ; and during the evening or other leisure moments the observer computed and applied the corrections for micrometer runs, and calculated the means. Twenty-four field-books contain the Fuller theodolite measures, and the Beaufort theodolite work occupies two. These books were afterwards transcribed at the Observatory into five pretty thick folio volumes, where the whole of the arithmetic was repeated, and carefully compared with the field-books. Exclusive of these books, there are others, which contain zenith distance measures for time and relative heights. The printing of such a mass of figures would incur an unwarrantable expense, and few persons would take the trouble to consult them ; therefore, after due consideration, it has been decided to print the mean results only, first placing in evidence the details of one angle by each instrument, which may be taken as the general type of the whole.”
Maclear, T. (1866). Verification and extension of La Caille's arc of meridian at the Cape of Good Hope (Vol. 1). London: Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty., p. 419

The printed type example for the Beaufort theodolite: the angle at Kamies-Sector Berg between the Keibiskow heliostat (about 80 miles away) and Bokkeveld Berg, 1, 3 and 4 December 1846. Each row is one partial result of 10 repetitions with the hour and a remark on the definition of the signals. The remarks record the air: wind direction, 'hot temperature: about 85 deg.', 'therm. 90 deg.', and 'Definition in the morning not good, towards 11h it became much worse'. Half the work was measured forward with the Y bearings right, half backward with Y left. The final angle comes from 260 measures with weight 131.99.

“Angle at Kamies-Sector Berg, West Rock Station; between Keibiskow and Bokkeveld Berg : measured with the Beaufort Theodolite. ... Middling definition. ... Northerly wind, perhaps 1 point E. of N. Hot temperature : about 85°. ... Bad definition and bad signaling at Bokkeveld ... Wind west, next S.W., and lastly south; this afternoon very hot, therm. 90°. ... Excellent do., points. ... Definition in the morning not good, towards 11h it became much worse. ... Resulting angle from 260 meas. = 23°32′1″·98 Weight = 131·99”
Reading the table. Columns: date (1846) and hour (A.M./P.M.); remarks on definition, wind and temperature; No. of repetitions (10 per row); pointer degrees and minutes; seconds on verniers A, D, B, C; mean reading; angle seconds for the row (left) and running mean (right), all after 23 deg 32'. Under each day: sum of squares of errors, probable error of 10 measures, probable error of the day's total, and the weight. 1 Dec: 13 rows (130 repetitions), 3 Dec: 7 rows, 4 Dec: 6 rows (130 repetitions). Row seconds range from 0.65" to 3.35". Look at how the remarks change with the hour and how the weight of each day follows its scatter.
Worked out here: Combination printed at foot: 1.96 x 75.02 = 147.039; 2.00 x 56.97 = 113.940; 75.02 + 56.97 = 131.99; 260.979 / 131.99 = 1.977 -> 1.98". The day weight above it is printed 56.77 (1/0.1327^2 = 56.8), so the 56.97 in the combination differs from it by 0.2.

The printed type example for the Fuller theodolite (pp. 422-426): the angle at Riebeek's Kasteel between the Kapoc Berg signal rock heliostat and the east end of the base, 17 to 26 February 1842. Each block is a couplet: the angle measured twice with the circle stepped, giving one partial mean. The remarks column gives the definition ('Beautiful definition', 'Good definition. Calm.', 'Excellent definition.', 'Light north air.'), and some couplets are marked 'Repeated on the 19th'. The last page (shown) gives the total, 54 couplets, and the weather diary: misty horizon, dense fog in the afternoon on the 20th, and a gale with bad images on the 26th.

“54 Couplets = 33°50′58″·524. ☾ 20th February.—In general cloudy, with misty horizon,—none of the heliostats now visible at the same time. Cape Town seen twice, Kapoc Berg once, east end of Base for an hour. N.W. wind and dense fog in the afternoon. ♄ 26th February.—Violent wind from E. by S. came on, on Thursday night and continued until 9 o'clock yesterday morning, then died away; but towards 4 o'clock it returned, last night and this morning it may be called a strong gale. Yesterday and last night the canvas and instrument were removed for security, but time being valuable, an attempt to observe was made at 10h 30m this morning. Bad images, the instrument not free from danger.”
Reading the table. Columns: date and hour (1842); reference to the observation book page; remarks; pointer degrees and minutes; seconds on microscopes A, B, C; runs (micrometer run correction, +1.15"); mean reading; angle seconds after 33 deg 50' for each measure and for the couplet (bracketed). The record runs over pdf pp. 469-473 (printed pp. 422-426); the crop shows the last page. Reading the table. Columns (page turned sideways): date; hour; instrument (D or B); number for reference; station observed, with H for heliostat and the angle gamma at the angle point; observed zenith distance; No. of observations; height of object above the surface (feet); correction to the zenith distance (seconds). Look at East End of Base to Kapoc Berg: six sets, 20+10+10+8+4+16 = 68 observations, values from 89 deg 7' 56.2" to 89 deg 8' 46.6" (spread 50" between morning and afternoon).
Worked out here: 20 + 10 + 10 + 8 + 4 + 16 = 68 observations, the same count printed for this line on p. 598.

Coefficient of refraction computed from 10 sets of reciprocal zenith distances (mean m = .0712)
Maclear's verification and extension of La Caille's arc of meridian, Cape of Good Hope · p. 598 · strength ★★★
Vertical refraction coefficients Raw tables of repeated measures

Calculation of the differences of altitude (p. 598). Reciprocal zenith distances are measured from each end of the same line toward the other; their sum exceeds 180 deg by the earth's curvature minus the bending of the ray, so they give the actual refraction on that line. Maclear prints the formula for m (the coefficient of refraction as a fraction of c, the angle at the earth's centre) and the 10 lines with the zenith distance at each end, the number of observations at each end (4 to 86), z + z' - 180 deg, c and m. The values run from .0667 to .0842; the mean .0712 was adopted for the altitudes.

“The following formulæ have been employed in the calculation of the co-efficient of refraction, and the altitudes of the points observed : ... then h′—h = s cot. (z + m c — ½ c) (1 + (h′+h)/2ν). and m = ½ (1 — (z+z′—180°)/c). The calculation of m from 10 sets of reciprocal zenith distances is contained in the following table : ... The mean value of m from the above is ·0712.”
Reading the table. Columns: reference number in the preceding abstract; station (the two ends of each line); true zenith distance at each end; No. of observations at each end; log distance; z + z' - 180 deg (seconds); c (seconds); coefficient of refraction m. Observation counts per end: 68 and 82, 84 and 48, 66 and 44, 44 and 48, 48 and 86, 52 and 20, 38 and 32, 8 and 48, 8 and 12, 21 and 12.
Worked out here: East End of Base - Kapoc Berg: m = 0.5 x (1 - 646.1/746.2) = 0.5 x 0.13415 = 0.0671 (printed .0671). In the usual k = 2m form the mean is 0.1424.
Maclear, T. (1866). Verification and extension of La Caille's arc of meridian at the Cape of Good Hope (Vol. 1). London: Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty., p. 598

Robinson's report on the computations, (h) Abstract of triangular errors (p. 59). The triangular error is the amount by which the sum of the observed angles differs from 180 deg plus the spherical excess. For each of the three observers the table counts triangles in half-second steps and gives the probable error of a single angle. Table (i) below gives the size of the corrections the adjustment applied to 784 angles.

“(h) Abstract of Triangular Errors. ... Captain Gordon 102 54 35 8 2 2 1 ±0·30 Mr. Simms 87 36 35 15 1 .. .. ±0·29 Captain Ley 71 23 21 19 6 2 .. ±0·39 Thus the probable error of a single angle, measured on eight arcs, is ... ± 0″·30 and the probable error of a single angle, measured on four arcs, is ... ± 0″·39”
Reading the table. Table (h) columns: observer; number of triangles; number of triangles with error 0.0-0.5", 0.5-1.0", 1.0-1.5", 1.5-2.0", 2.0-2.5", 2.5-3.0"; probable error of a single angle. Table (i): for each chain, the number of angles whose adjustment correction fell in 0.25" steps, and the total number of angles (784). In this scan the figures 3 and 8 look alike; Ley's first count is read as 23 because the row must sum to 71.
Worked out here: Row sums: 54+35+8+2+2+1 = 102; 36+35+15+1 = 87; 23+21+19+6+2 = 71. Triangles with error under 1.0": 89 + 71 + 44 = 204 of 260 (78 per cent).

Geodetic Survey of the Transvaal and Orange River Colony (Morris; preface and introduction by Gill) · p. 151 · strength ★★★
Vertical refraction coefficients Raw tables of repeated measures Rejecting readings in unsteady air

Vertical heights (p. 151). Mutual vertical angles are elevation angles measured from each end of a line toward the other. The formula h' - h = s tan 1/2 (alpha - alpha') uses both, and the refraction drops out when it is the same at both ends. Table M gives the coefficient of refraction found on each line, so the bend was measured line by line. Values in brackets were left out of the chain mean; on this page they are all lines of 4.9 to 12.9 miles. The definition of the coefficient is not printed in the report.

“17. The differences of height were computed by the formula h′ — h = s . tan ½ (α — α′) where s = the length of the line in feet α, α′ = the angles of elevation of each point from the other. ... 1. The coefficients of refraction and the mean coefficient for each chain Quantities in brackets are omitted in the mean (Table M). ... Table M. Coefficients of Refraction determined from Mutual Vertical Angles.”
Reading the table. Three column groups, each: numbers of the two stations; coefficient of refraction; distance in miles. Chains on this page: Newcastle to Belfast (two columns, mean .065 at 27.5 miles average) and Belfast to Ottoshoop (mean .065, 37.9 miles). About 85 lines on this page. Bracketed (omitted) values: (.097) 12.9 mi, (.096) 7.7 mi, (.028) 4.9 mi, (.128) 10.8 mi. Table M continues on pp. 152-153.

Extract from the field book of the 12-inch instrument at Dromedary station, 1851 (p. 95). Struve Geodetic Arc (Russo-Scandinavian arc of the meridian, Danube to Fuglenaes) · T. II, p. 232 · strength ★★
Raw tables of repeated measures

Tome II, p. 232. Struve prints one complete vertical-angle observation at the north end of the Elimä base, 5 September 1844, true solar time 3h 26m, on three targets. For each target he gives the level readings and two vernier readings with the circle right and with the circle left, the level correction, and the means a and b. Half the difference (a - b)/2 is the zenith distance z; half the sum (a + b)/2 is the zenith place Z, the circle reading of the vertical, which should be the same for all targets of one set.

“J'ai ajouté partout dans le texte le lieu du zénith (a+b)/2 = Z, qu'a donné chaque observation complète d'un objet, en le plaçant en parenthèses, et en types mineurs, à côté de son z.”
In English: “I have added everywhere in the text the zenith place (a+b)/2 = Z given by each complete observation of an object, placing it in parentheses and in small type beside its z.”
Reading the table. Rows: level (two ends of the bubble), first and second vernier, mean, correction for the level, for circle right and circle left. Then the corrected means a and b, (a - b)/2 = zenith distance, (a + b)/2 = zenith place, the reduction to the centre of the station, and the reduced z as entered in the station table.
Worked out here: Zenith places Z for the three targets: 0°53′48.0″, 0°53′52.9″, 0°53′54.4″; spread 6.4″ within one set.

Paragraph 54 (p. 19). A bisection is one setting of the cross-wire on the target. The number per pointing depended on how steady and sharp the heliograph light or beacon was, and every single reading went into the field book.

“In the observations of the horizontal angles, a number of bisections of the heliograph light, or beacon, were made, depending on their steadiness and definition in the field of view, the separate readings being recorded in the field book.”

“Just numbers on paper, no validation.” 141 items · 23 surveys

The checks printed in the sources themselves: triangle closures, probable errors, measured bases compared with the triangles, re-observation of doubtful angles.

Short answer. Each survey carries its own tests. Closures: every triangle's three angles, measured at three stations, must sum to 180° plus the excess; Schott (1900, p. 613) summarises 701 triangles. Bases: a base length computed through the chain from another measured base is compared with its own measurement: Atlanta to Dauphin Island, 677 km apart, agree to about 1 part in 2.9 million (Schott, 1902); Perpignan through 53 triangles from Melun, 11 pouces (Delambre); Karachi 10.45 inches, 23 parts in a million (GTS). Heights: trigonometric heights against spirit levelling: Mount Lola 2,786.8 m against 2,787.5 m (Schott, 1900); Ben Macdui 4,295.6 ft against 4,295.7 ft (Clarke, 1858); Karachi to Attok 3.2 ft over 706 miles; the Russian chain against the Caspian levelling, 0.643 sazhen over about 950 versts.
Two chains of triangles checked against each other, and a base computed through the chain agrees with the measured base to about one foot
Cassini de Thury and Lacaille, verification of the Paris meridian and the arc of the parallel near 43.5 N · 24 (Discours) · strength ★★★

Discours, p. 24. The authors describe two checks. A second chain of triangles from Dunkirk to Amiens differed from the first by five toises over the whole distance. A base near Paris, computed through the triangles, came out about one foot shorter than its measured length, for bases 60 leagues apart. A base computed through the triangles and compared with a measured base tests all the angles between them.

“CETTE fuite de triangles fut vérifiée par une autre dont les objets paroiffoient encore mieux difpofés ... dont elle ne différoit que de cinq toifes, fur toute la diftance de Dunkerke à Amiens. ... Nous parvînmes ainfi à la nouvelle bafe de Paris, qui s'eft trouvée, fuivant le calcul, plus petite feulement d'environ un pied, que celle qui avoit été mefurée. Cet accord de deux bafes éloignées l'une de l'autre de 60 lieues”
In English: “THIS chain of triangles was checked by another whose objects seemed even better placed ... from which it differed by only five toises over the whole distance from Dunkirk to Amiens. ... We thus reached the new base of Paris, which was found, by calculation, smaller by only about one foot than the measured one. This agreement of two bases 60 leagues apart”
Cassini de Thury, C.-F. (1744). La méridienne de l'Observatoire Royal de Paris vérifiée dans toute l'étendue du Royaume par de nouvelles observations. Paris: H.-L. Guérin & J. Guérin., 24 (Discours)

Tome I, Tableau des triangles. For each triangle the table gives the observed angles with the register page, the spherical excess (the amount by which the angles of a triangle on the curved earth exceed 180 degrees) and the 'Somme des erreurs', which is the closure error: the sum of the three observed angles minus 180 degrees minus the excess. A star marks an angle concluded, not observed. Closure errors are a direct internal check on the horizontal angles.

“Somme des erreurs . . — 1"18 ... L'astérisque est la marque d'un angle conclu.”
In English: “Sum of the errors -1.18" ... The asterisk marks a concluded angle.”
Reading the table. Columns: No. of triangle; station names; register page; observed angles; spherical excess; spherical angles; angles of the chords; mean angles. Under each fully observed triangle, 'Somme des erreurs' gives the closure error. Triangle 1 (Dunkerque, Watten, Cassel): -1.18"; triangle 3 (Watten, Cassel, Fiefs): -0.90".
Worked out here: Triangle 1: observed sum 180° 0' 0.00", excess 1.18", closure -1.18". Triangle 3: observed sum 180° 0' 0.77", excess 1.67", closure -0.90".
Méchain, P., & Delambre, J.-B. J. (1806). Base du système métrique décimal, ou mesure de l'arc du méridien compris entre les parallèles de Dunkerque et Barcelone (Vol. 1). Paris: Baudouin., T1 p. 513
Base-to-base check: the Perpignan base computed through 53 triangles from Melun differs from its measured length by 0.160 demi-module (11 pouces)
Delambre and Méchain, meridian arc Dunkirk to Barcelona (Base du système métrique) · T3 p. 418 (sentence begins on p. 417) · strength ★★★

Tome III, report of the commission on the final result. A base is a line measured on the ground with rods; the whole chain is computed from it. The Perpignan base, measured at the south end, was also computed from the Melun base through fifty-three triangles. The two values differ by 0.160 demi-module (one demi-module is one toise), about 11 pouces, for bases about 33 000 toises apart. The commission states it did not adjust any angle to improve this agreement.

“de celle de Melun réduite en arc, se trouve, par le calcul, de . . . 6006·089 demi-modules. La base de Perpignan réduite en arc, se trouve, par la mesure actuelle, de . . . 6006·249. La différence est de . . . 0·160. Ce qui, traduit en anciennes mesures, fait 11 pouces”
In English: “[The Perpignan base, deduced by a chain of fifty-three triangles] from that of Melun, reduced to arc, is found by calculation to be 6006.089 demi-modules. The Perpignan base reduced to arc is found by the actual measurement to be 6006.249. The difference is 0.160. Which, in old measures, makes 11 pouces”
Worked out here: 0.160 / 6006.249 = 2.7e-5, about 1 part in 37 500.
Méchain, P., & Delambre, J.-B. J. (1810). Base du système métrique décimal, ou mesure de l'arc du méridien compris entre les parallèles de Dunkerque et Barcelone (Vol. 3). Paris: Baudouin., T3 p. 418 (sentence begins on p. 417)
Montjouy tower: six sea-horizon heights compared with a direct levelling; the levelling is kept
Delambre and Méchain, meridian arc Dunkirk to Barcelona (Base du système métrique) · T2 p. 759 · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours Raw tables of repeated measures

Tome II, heights above the Mediterranean. The height of the battlements of the Montjouy tower had been measured by direct levelling (105.1 toises). Delambre computes it again from six zenith distances of the sea horizon and prints each result. The mean agrees with the levelling within 0.5 toise, but single values scatter. He states the observations were all near sunset, when refraction raises the sea, and that one isolated sea-horizon observation can be wrong by 5 to 6 toises; he keeps the levelling.

“toutes ces observations ayant été faites vers le coucher du soleil, la réfraction devoit élever la mer plus que dans l'état moyen et faire paroître la hauteur de la tour trop petite. Elles prouvent qu'une observation de l'horizon de la mer prise isolément peut donner une erreur de 5 à 6 toises. Nous nous en tiendrons donc au résultat du nivellement”
In English: “all these observations having been made towards sunset, refraction must have raised the sea more than in the mean state and made the height of the tower appear too small. They prove that an isolated observation of the sea horizon can give an error of 5 to 6 toises. We shall therefore keep to the result of the levelling”
Reading the table. Columns: zenith distance of the sea horizon (90° 23' to 90° 25'); height computed with n = 0.08 and the correction for each; resulting height H in toises (100.5 to 107.5). Milieu 105.2; plus 0.4 for half the wire thickness gives 105.6, against Nivellement 105.1; difference 0.5 toise.

With lamps the triangle errors were no smaller than usual: night horizontal angles are as much affected by refraction as day ones, sometimes more in low places

Night lamps and heliotropes Steady-air hours

Puissant, chapter on the probable error of an arc. The triangle errors (closure errors: the amount by which the three angles miss 180 degrees plus the spherical excess) are a direct test of the horizontal angles. Puissant uses them to judge the night method recommended by Laplace and finds no gain, with a larger effect in low ground between Paris and Strasbourg.

“Malgré l'usage que l'on fit de réverbères pour points de mire, dans cette partie de la méridienne, les erreurs des triangles n'ont pas été moindres que de coutume ; ainsi les observations nocturnes des angles horizontaux qui avaient été recommandées par le célèbre Laplace, sont tout aussi influencées par les effets de la réfraction atmosphérique que celles de jour, si même elles ne le sont quelquefois davantage dans les lieux bas, comme on l'a remarqué, ainsi que nous l'avons déjà dit, entre Paris et Strasbourg, lors de la mesure du parallèle compris entre ces deux villes.”
In English: “Despite the use of lamps as targets in this part of the meridian, the errors of the triangles were no smaller than usual; thus the night observations of horizontal angles, which had been recommended by the celebrated Laplace, are just as influenced by the effects of atmospheric refraction as those by day, if indeed they are not sometimes more so in low places, as was remarked, as we have already said, between Paris and Strasbourg, during the measurement of the parallel between these two towns.”

Repetition over days and hours

Brousseaud, p. 158, continuing the rule of p. 157. Decimal seconds are centesimal seconds (1 decimal second = 0.324 sexagesimal second). The author reports, without hiding it, that series of the same angle at the same hour on different days differed by 25 to 35 decimal seconds even when both targets were seen well, and that more series were added to reduce these errors.

“[si, de la première à la sixième série (par exemple), les angles conclus variaient de quinze à] vingt secondes, on les continuait jusqu'à la douzième ou quinzième série afin d'atténuer le plus possible ces erreurs inexplicables. On a remarqué des différences de vingt-cinq à trente-cinq secondes décimales entre les résultats des séries d'un même angle observé à la même heure et à des jours différens, quoique les deux objets sur lesquels on pointait se vissent parfaitement dans des circonstances semblables.”
In English: “[if, from the first to the sixth series (for example), the concluded angles varied by fifteen to] twenty seconds, they were continued to the twelfth or fifteenth series in order to reduce these unexplained errors as much as possible. Differences of twenty-five to thirty-five decimal seconds were noticed between the results of series of the same angle observed at the same hour and on different days, although the two objects pointed at were seen perfectly in similar circumstances.”
Worked out here: 25 to 35 decimal seconds = 8.1" to 11.3" sexagesimal.

Brousseaud, summary of the three parts of the arc of the mean parallel. For the French part (34 triangles, Mont Granier to Marennes) the author states the number of series and repetitions, that every series was kept in the mean without exception, and the largest triangle closure error (the amount by which the sum of the three angles missed its true value).

“Les valeurs des angles ont été déterminées par six, huit, dix, douze quatorze séries de trente à quarante répétitions chaque, faites à des jours et à des heures différens. Les distances au zénith ont aussi été répétées de soixante à cent fois, entre onze heures et midi, afin d'avoir avec exactitude la hauteur absolue des signaux placés sur les hautes montagnes de la France et de la Savoie. Le résultat adopté pour chaque angle de ces trente-quatre triangles provient de la moyenne entre tous les résultats fournis par les séries relatives à cet angle, et prises sans exception. Cependant, malgré ces soins, la plus grande erreur de la somme des trois angles des triangles s'élève encore à 4" de degré.”
In English: “The values of the angles were determined by six, eight, ten, twelve, fourteen series of thirty to forty repetitions each, made on different days and at different hours. The zenith distances were also repeated sixty to a hundred times, between eleven and noon, to obtain accurately the absolute height of the signals placed on the high mountains of France and Savoy. The result adopted for each angle of these thirty-four triangles is the mean of all the results given by the series for that angle, taken without exception. Yet, despite these precautions, the largest error of the sum of the three angles of the triangles still reaches 4" of a degree.”
Worked out here: 6 to 14 series x 30 to 40 repetitions = 180 to 560 repetitions per angle.

Reading the table. Four comparisons: Ticino from Bordeaux (150 triangles) +0.201 m; Gourbera from Bordeaux (23 triangles) +0.302 m; Bordeaux from Gourbera +0.349 m; Ticino from Gourbera +0.032 m. Each: computed length, measured length, difference.

Heights by reciprocal zenith distances from the Cordouan tower to Colombier and Granier; a 9 m discordance traced and removed; coefficient between 0.0563 and 0.097, generally 0.08
Brousseaud, arc of the mean parallel (45 N) across France, with link to the Austro-Sardinian chain · 160 · strength ★★★
Vertical refraction coefficients Steady-air hours

Brousseaud, p. 160. The absolute heights of the chain come from a succession of reciprocal zenith distances starting at the Cordouan lighthouse (68.445 m above mean sea, mean of four measures). Reciprocal zenith distances are taken from each end of a line toward the other; their sum exceeds 180 degrees by the arc between the two verticals, less the bend of the ray at both ends, so the pair measures the refraction on that line itself. Each height is the mean of two results that rarely differ by more than a metre. A discordance of about 9 m at the east end was traced to long sights from Bossivre and to signal caps too small to see at noon, and Puissant removed it by using heights from other stations. The coefficient of refraction found along the whole levelling lies between 0.0563 and 0.097.

“Partant de ce point, chacune des hauteurs absolues rapportées dans le deuxième tableau est la moyenne entre deux résultats, dont la différence dépasse rarement un mètre (1). ... a cependant présenté une discordance qui s'est accrue de 9m environ à l'extrémité orientale de la chaîne ... 2° que, sur toute son étendue, la valeur du coefficient de la réfraction est renfermée entre 0,0563 et 0,097, et se trouve généralement de 0,08, ainsi que Delambre l'avait déduit de ses observations.”
In English: “Starting from this point, each of the absolute heights given in the second table is the mean of two results whose difference rarely exceeds one metre (1). ... nevertheless showed a discordance that grew to about 9 m at the eastern end of the chain ... 2nd that, over its whole extent, the value of the coefficient of refraction lies between 0.0563 and 0.097, and is generally 0.08, as Delambre had deduced from his observations.”
Brousseaud (Colonel). (1839). Mesure d'un arc du parallèle moyen entre le pôle et l'équateur. Limoges: F. Chapoulaud., 160
