Roy: fewer repetitions than planned, but a few very good observations beat a mean of many hurried ones, as the base of verification shows
Anglo-French triangulation of 1787 (Greenwich to Paris junction), English side by Roy · p. 171 · strength ★★★
Repetition over days and hours

Same article, p. 169 to p. 171. Roy had planned to measure each angle many times on different parts of the circle (to average out errors of division of the scale). He states that this was often impossible in practice. He gives the close agreement between the measured and the computed length of the base of verification (the Romney Marsh base, computed through the triangles from the Hounslow Heath base about 70 miles away) as the test of the result. On pp. 177-178 he gives that difference as about 4 1/2 inches.

“On the whole, although, for the reasons already assigned, we have repeated the observations seldomer than was at first proposed; yet it will obviously appear from the results, and particularly from the near agreement between the measured and computed length of the base of verification, that a few very good observations are greatly preferable to a mean that might perhaps have been obtained of many made in a hurry, which at best would have been but indifferent.”
Roy, W. (1790). An account of the trigonometrical operation, whereby the distance between the meridians of the Royal Observatories of Greenwich and Paris has been determined. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, 80, 111-270 (with Dalby, I., Remarks, pp. 593-614)., p. 171

Anglo-French triangulation of 1787 (Greenwich to Paris junction), English side by Roy · p. 172 · strength ★★★
Raw tables of repeated measures

Art. II, Calculation of the Triangles, the first page of the table that runs to p. 182. Spherical excess is the amount by which the three angles of a triangle on a curved surface exceed 180 degrees; it is computed from the area. The 'error' is the difference between the observed excess and the computed one, so it is a check on each triangle. On p. 169 Roy introduces the table: 'a column is inserted containing the spherical excess; and another for the difference or error between that and the excess of the sum of the observed angles above 180°'.

“Art. II. Calculation of the Triangles.”
Reading the table. Columns: number of the triangle; names of the stations; observed angles (degrees, minutes, seconds) with their sum below; spherical excess in seconds; difference or error in seconds; angles corrected for calculation; distances in feet. Triangle I: observed sum 179 59 59, excess 0.29, error -1.29. Triangle II: sum 179 59 59.6, excess 0.21, error -0.61. Each angle is a single printed value (Roy gives the means only); the error column is the test.
Roy, W. (1790). An account of the trigonometrical operation, whereby the distance between the meridians of the Royal Observatories of Greenwich and Paris has been determined. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, 80, 111-270 (with Dalby, I., Remarks, pp. 593-614)., p. 172
Roy: the Hounslow Heath and Romney Marsh bases measure each other within a few inches; triangle errors are very small
Anglo-French triangulation of 1787 (Greenwich to Paris junction), English side by Roy · p. 247 · strength ★★★
Night lamps and heliotropes

Opening of Section VIII. A base is a line measured on the ground with a chain or rods; the other sides are computed from it through the angles. Roy measured two bases about 70 miles apart and computed each from the other through the triangles. On pp. 177-178 he gives the difference as about 4 1/2 inches. He also states that the lights and the instrument were placed over the same station mark, so that no eccentricity (offset of the target or instrument from the station point) entered.

“the same excellent instrument having been placed at every station on our side of the Channel, and all the angles observed with the utmost care, it hath consequently followed, that the base on Hounslow Heath, and that in Romney Marsh, reciprocally measure each other within a few inches of the truth, which is an instance of such exactness as probably never occurred in any former operation of this sort. The extreme smallness of the error on the sum of the three angles of each triangle sufficiently proves that the general result would not have differed greatly, if only two of the angles had actually been observed.”
Roy, W. (1790). An account of the trigonometrical operation, whereby the distance between the meridians of the Royal Observatories of Greenwich and Paris has been determined. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, 80, 111-270 (with Dalby, I., Remarks, pp. 593-614)., p. 247
1795: the Salisbury Plain base computed from the Hounslow Heath base by several triangle routes comes within about an inch of its measurement
Trigonometrical Survey of England and Wales (Ordnance), Williams, Mudge and Dalby 1791-1799 · p. 499 · strength ★★★

Art. IV, the length of the base of verification deduced from Hounslow Heath. The base of verification on Salisbury Plain (Beacon Hill to Old Sarum) was measured with a steel chain in 1794 and also computed through the triangles from the Hounslow Heath base. Different routes through the triangles give 36573.8 to 36574.9 feet. The authors also say which triangles they trust less (an acute angle at Highclere, and a strained clamp at Thorney Down).

“Lastly;—if the computations are carried directly from one base to the other, independent of the mean distances and the 14 and 15th triangles, the greatest and least results will be 36574,8, and 36573,8, the mean being 36574,3 feet, or about an inch short of the measurement.”

Raw tables of repeated measures Vertical refraction coefficients

Art. II, Heights of Rook's Hill and Butser Hill. Each of three stations observed the other two, so every line has an angle from each end (reciprocal angles). From these the mean refraction of each line follows (see the rules in the 1797 item). The heights round the triangle do not close exactly: 228 feet by the lines across the water against 208 feet by the direct reciprocal line, and the authors share the 20 feet between the refractions.

“From these observations, the mean refraction between Dunnose and Rook's Hill will be found 1' 58"; between Dunnose and Butser Hill 2' 16"; and between Butser Hill and Rook's Hill 39"; which are about 1/12, 1/10, 1/15 of the contained arcs respectively, as in the table.”
Reading the table. Rows: at Dunnose, Rook's Hill and Butser Hill, the depression (or elevation) of the ground at each other station, in minutes and seconds; then the three contained arcs (23' 31", 23' 3", 9' 59"). The flagstaff at Rook's Hill was 20 feet high and the telescope axis about 5 1/2 feet above the ground. One value per direction is printed.
Worked out here: Dunnose-Rook's Hill: depressions 12' 14" + 7' 37" = 19' 51" = 1191". Reducing each to the telescope axis (5.5 ft at about 1411" x 101.4 ft = 143,100 ft subtends 7.9") removes about 16": 1175". Arc 23' 31" = 1411". (1411 - 1175)/2 = 118" = 1' 58", as printed. 118/1411 = 0.084 = 1/12.
Williams, E., Mudge, W., & Dalby, I. (1795). An account of the trigonometrical survey carried on in the years 1791, 1792, 1793, and 1794. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, 85, 414-591., p. 580
1795: heights from vertical angles agree with levelling at Shooter's Hill (446 against 445 ft), but no dependence can be placed on single observations
Trigonometrical Survey of England and Wales (Ordnance), Williams, Mudge and Dalby 1791-1799 · p. 585 · strength ★★★

Art. III, Remarks on the tables. The height of Shooter's Hill from reciprocal angles (446 ft) is checked against spirit levelling from the Bull Inn (445 ft). On p. 584 the authors show that the elevation of St. Ann's Hill seen from Hampton Poor House differed widely between 1787 and 1792 with the instrument at the same height. They conclude that heights from vertical angles are good to about 10 feet unless reciprocal observations are made at the same time.

“Notwithstanding this consistency, and also that in the height of St. Ann's Hill, found by different methods, it is evident from the observations at Dunnose, Rook's Hill, and Butser Hill, that relative heights deduced from elevations, or depressions, cannot always be depended upon to less than about 10 feet, even supposing those heights are the means of two or three independent results, except, perhaps, reciprocal observations were made exactly at the same time. The very great difference in the observed elevations of St. Ann's Hill, proves that no dependance can be placed on single observations.”
Williams, E., Mudge, W., & Dalby, I. (1795). An account of the trigonometrical survey carried on in the years 1791, 1792, 1793, and 1794. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, 85, 414-591., p. 585

Ordnance Trigonometrical Survey of Great Britain and Ireland, Principal Triangulation · p. xiv · strength ★★★

Introduction by Colonel James. Two main bases (Salisbury Plain and Lough Foyle, about 7 and 8 miles) were measured with Colby's compensation bars; four more with steel chains. Each base was also computed from the others through the whole triangulation. The difference between measured and computed lengths is the strongest check on the angles, since every angle on the route enters the computed length.

“The difference between the measured lengths and their lengths as computed through the Triangulation is ± 0.4178 feet, or about 5 inches. ... Four other base-lines were measured with Ramsden's 100-feet Steel Chains,—one on Hounslow Heath, one at Misterton Carr near Doncaster, and one at Belhelvie in Aberdeenshire,—and the greatest difference between the measured lengths and the computed lengths of these bases from the mean base does not amount to 3 inches. ... the sum of the angles in the triangles rarely differed 3".4 from the true sum.”
Clarke, A. R. (1858). Ordnance trigonometrical survey of Great Britain and Ireland: Account of the observations and calculations of the principal triangulation. London: Eyre and Spottiswoode., p. xiv

Ordnance Trigonometrical Survey of Great Britain and Ireland, Principal Triangulation · p. xv · strength ★★★

Introduction. Heights of many stations were fixed by spirit levelling (a direct, step-by-step measurement of height differences with a level and staff); the vertical angles were also observed reciprocally. After the heights by vertical angles were printed, Ben Macdui was levelled, giving an independent check on the vertical-angle method over the mountain.

“Since the printing of the computed height (at page 558) of Ben Macdui, the height of that hill has been determined by spirit levelling. By levelling up the western side the height was found to be 4295.70 feet, and by levelling down the eastern side the result was 4295.76 feet. The agreements of these results with one another and also with the computed height, 4295.6 feet, are very remarkable.”
Clarke, A. R. (1858). Ordnance trigonometrical survey of Great Britain and Ireland: Account of the observations and calculations of the principal triangulation. London: Eyre and Spottiswoode., p. xv

Raw tables of repeated measures Repetition over days and hours

Section IV, second part: azimuthal observations in detail. Azimuth is the angle of a line from true north; it was found from the referring object and circumpolar stars at elongation (their farthest east or west point). Each row is one night's observation with its own result, so the spread can be seen. Footnote marks give the weather for individual rows. Probable error is the amount the mean is as likely to be within as outside.

“Cloudy and misty. Cloudy. Very misty; partial sun. Very clear in all directions.”
Reading the table. Columns: date (5 Aug to 14 Sep 1846); star and elongation (51 Cephei, Polaris, delta and lambda Ursae Minoris, E or W); reading of star; computed level and collimation correction; corrected reading; reading of R.O.; computed azimuth of star at elongation; resulting azimuth of R.O. (81° 52' plus 15.09" to 32.33"). Mean of eastern elongations 24.23", western 20.28", general mean 81° 52' 22".51, probable error ±0".60. The quote is the four footnotes on weather.
Clarke, A. R. (1858). Ordnance trigonometrical survey of Great Britain and Ireland: Account of the observations and calculations of the principal triangulation. London: Eyre and Spottiswoode., p. 171
Clarke 1858: k from zenith distances to stations of levelled height, 31 values on 16 lines, with number of observations
Ordnance Trigonometrical Survey of Great Britain and Ireland, Principal Triangulation · p. 542 · strength ★★★
Raw tables of repeated measures Vertical refraction coefficients

Section IX, 'Coefficient of Refraction'. Where both heights are known by levelling, the true zenith distance Z can be computed. The observed z differs from Z only by refraction, so k = (Z - z)/v is measured directly on that line. The weight w grows with the square root of the distance and with the number of observations.

“In the former case, the coefficient required is simply the ratio of the excess of the observed above the true zenith distance to the angle subtended by the two stations at the centre of the earth.”
Reading the table. Columns: number of the line; stations; levelled height (ft); observed zenith distance z; number of observations (4 to 29, e.g. Ben Nevis 19, Merrick 29, Pertinny 20); logarithmic distance; v (angle at the earth's centre, seconds); true zenith distance Z; Z - z (seconds); k; weight w; k times w. Values from 0.0649 (High Willhays) to 0.1058 (Swyre Barrow). Printed mean k = 0.0792.
Clarke, A. R. (1858). Ordnance trigonometrical survey of Great Britain and Ireland: Account of the observations and calculations of the principal triangulation. London: Eyre and Spottiswoode., p. 542
Clarke 1858: Salisbury Plain base as measured exceeds its length computed from Lough Foyle by 4.7 inches
Ordnance Trigonometrical Survey of Great Britain and Ireland, Principal Triangulation · p. 419 · strength ★★★

Calculation of distances. The Lough Foyle base in Ireland and the Salisbury Plain base in England are joined by the whole triangulation across the Irish Sea. Clarke computes Salisbury Plain from Lough Foyle and compares it with the measurement. On p. 421 he estimates the probable error of such a computed length through a single chain of triangles as about ±1.09 feet, so the 4.7 inch difference is well inside it.

“The difference between the lengths of the Salisbury Plain base as measured (M), and as calculated (C) from the Lough Foyle base, is given by the equation ... M = C + 4.6956 inches”
Clarke, A. R. (1858). Ordnance trigonometrical survey of Great Britain and Ireland: Account of the observations and calculations of the principal triangulation. London: Eyre and Spottiswoode., p. 419
Clarke 1880: persistent lateral refraction is a constant error that only triangle closures reveal; 107 triangles give a probable error of 0.794" per angle
Textbook guidance of the period on terrestrial refraction · p. 230 · strength ★★★

Chapter on the calculation of the triangulation. The scatter of repeated readings at one station shows only errors of pointing and reading. A constant error, such as an off-centre signal, a signal lit on one side (phase), or a small persistent lateral refraction from the local ground, shows up only when the angles from different stations are combined in triangles. So Clarke takes the angle error from the triangle closures.

“In some instances local configuration of the surface may give rise to a lateral refraction, doubtless very small in amount, but persistent. ... A more trustworthy method therefore than the evidence of the observations themselves is presented by the errors in the sums of the observed angles of triangles. In the 107 triangles between Dunkirk and Formentera the mean square of error of a triangle is 4.161, hence the mean square of error of an observed angle is one third of this or 1.387: the probable error of an observed angle therefore in this work is ±.6745 √1.387 = ±0".794.”
Clarke, A. R. (1880). Geodesy. Oxford: Clarendon Press., p. 230
Clarke 1880: mean of 144 Ordnance Survey values k = .0771, probable error of one value ±.0035; .0750 over land, .0809 over sea
Textbook guidance of the period on terrestrial refraction · p. 283 · strength ★★★
Vertical refraction coefficients

Same chapter. Clarke sorts the 144 values: the central 72 lie between .0733 and .0804. The probable error of a single determination of k (±.0035) states how far one line's value is likely to be from the mean. He separates rays over the sea from rays over land and cites Massachusetts values for comparison.

“From the mean of 144 values of k determined from the observations of the Ordnance Survey it appears that the mean coefficient of refraction is .0771. If we arrange the different values in order of magnitude, the extremes are .0320 and .1058, while the 72 which hold the central position are contained between .0733 and .0804, the mean of these 72, viz. .0768 differing but little from the general mean. Thus it would appear that the probable error of a single determination of k is about ±.0035. But it is necessary to discriminate between rays which cross the sea and those which do not.”
Clarke, A. R. (1880). Geodesy. Oxford: Clarendon Press., p. 283
A triangle that closed badly was traced to angles observed in fog, and those angles were measured again
Russian arc of the parallel of 47.5 N, Privolzhsk triangulation (Kishinev to Astrakhan arc, eastern part) · Zapiski XXII, Otd. II, p. 13 · strength ★★★
Rejecting readings in unsteady air

Chapter I gives the year-by-year account of the Privolzhsk triangulation, the eastern part of the 47.5 N arc. The closure of a triangle is the amount by which the sum of its three measured angles differs from 180 degrees plus the spherical excess. Triangle no. 64 closed with more than 7 seconds. The computers found that the angles at the station Nomardzhin had been observed in foggy weather and judged them unreliable. In the 1856 orders on the same page, Captain Napersnikov is told to remeasure the angle at Nomardzhin of triangle no. 64.

“При вычисленіи главнаго ряда треугольниковъ оказалось, что погрѣшность суммы 3-хъ угловъ въ треугольникѣ № 64 составляла свыше 7″, по этому и почтено за необходимость переизмѣрить углы на пунктѣ Номарджинъ, оказавшіеся неблагонадежными, потому, что наблюденія на этомъ пунктѣ произведены въ туманную погоду.”
In English: “In computing the main row of triangles it was found that the error of the sum of the 3 angles in triangle no. 64 was above 7″, and for this reason it was thought necessary to remeasure the angles at the point Nomardzhin, which proved unreliable because the observations at this point had been made in foggy weather.”
Voenno-topograficheskoe depo. (1861). Zapiski Voenno-topograficheskago depo, Chast' XXII, Otd. II: Privolzhskoe trigonometricheskoe izmerenie. Voenno-topograficheskoe depo., Zapiski XXII, Otd. II, p. 13

Chapter V. The net was computed from a side of the New Russia survey (Popovka to Kadamovskaya) along the main row to its end points Mokon and Kushlet, which gives a length for the Astrakhan verification base. That base was also measured directly on the ground. The printed difference between the computed and the measured value is the independent check of all the angles in about 90 triangles.

“откуда выведена длина Астраханскаго повѣрительнаго базиса = 3947, 568 саженей изъ дѣйствительнаго измѣренія = 3947, 027 ——— Разность = 0, 541 сажени, что составляетъ 0, 0001370652 цѣлаго или 5, 7567 дюймовъ на версту.”
In English: “from which the length of the Astrakhan verification base is derived = 3947.568 sazhen; from the actual measurement = 3947.027; difference = 0.541 sazhen, which is 0.0001370652 of the whole, or 5.7567 inches per verst.”
Worked out here: 0.541 / 3947.027 = 1.371 × 10^-4 (printed 0.0001370652). After this check the difference was spread over the angles (0.28″ per angle, p. 131, Table A column 5); the base value printed in Chapter VI (p. 189) is therefore an adjusted value, not a second independent check.

Table B gives the heights above the sea of the first-class points and of the Sarpinsky row. Reciprocal zenith distances are the two zenith distances of one line, one measured from each end. For each new point the table prints the zenith distance from the point to a known point (column 4) and from the known point back (column 5), the height obtained from each known point (column 6) and the mean (column 7). Two different known points give two independent heights for the same point.

“4. Зенитное разстояніе, измѣренное съ пункта опредѣляемаго на пунктъ, котораго номеръ выставленъ въ столбцѣ третьемъ. 5. Зенитное разстояніе измѣренное съ пункта, котораго № выставленъ въ столбцѣ 3-мъ на пунктъ опредѣляемый.”
In English: “4. Zenith distance measured from the point being determined to the point whose number is given in the third column. 5. Zenith distance measured from the point whose number is given in column 3 to the point being determined.”
Reading the table. Columns: 1 number; 2 point; 3 known point it is computed from; 4 forward zenith distance; 5 backward zenith distance; 6 height of the signal top from that known point (sazhen); 7 mean of the two heights; 8 height of the foot of the pyramid. Each new point is computed from two known points.
Worked out here: Two heights per point (sazhen): Mokry Log 76.871 and 76.145 (difference 0.726); Melekhovskaya 60.955 and 60.866 (0.089); Razdorskaya 70.191 and 70.188 (0.003); Krymskaya 85.484 and 85.404 (0.080).

Probable errors from 156 triangle closures; 12-set and 6-set rows give the same accuracy
Russian arc of the parallel of 47.5 N, Privolzhsk triangulation (Kishinev to Astrakhan arc, eastern part) · Zapiski XXII, Otd. II, p. 189 · strength ★★★
Repetition over days and hours

Chapter VI compares the results. A probable error is the error that is as likely to be exceeded as not; here it is computed by least squares from the closures of the triangles. For all first-class triangles the probable error of one angle is 0.5997″. The main row (angles in at least 12 sets) gives 0.6019″, the Kizlyar row (6 sets) gives 0.6011″. The authors conclude that more sets did not raise the accuracy as fast as probability theory predicts, and put this down to outside conditions, above all the uneven illumination of the targets.

“Это показываетъ: что отъ увеличенія числа пріемовъ точность угла возрастаетъ не съ такою быстротою, какъ убѣждаетъ въ томъ исчисленіе вѣроятностей, и что слѣдственно тутъ, какъ надо полагать, зависитъ отъ обстоятельствъ совершенно постороннихъ, въ особенности же отъ болѣе или менѣе одинаковаго освѣщенія наблюдаемыхъ предметовъ.”
In English: “This shows that with an increase in the number of sets the accuracy of an angle grows not as fast as the calculus of probabilities leads one to expect, and that consequently it depends here, as one must suppose, on quite external circumstances, in particular on the more or less uniform illumination of the observed objects.”
Worked out here: Sum of squared closures 367.6443 for the first-class triangles. Probable error of one angle: all triangles 0.5997″; main row (119 triangles, 12 or more sets) 0.6019″; Kizlyar row (36 triangles, 6 sets) 0.6011″.
Voenno-topograficheskoe depo. (1861). Zapiski Voenno-topograficheskago depo, Chast' XXII, Otd. II: Privolzhskoe trigonometricheskoe izmerenie. Voenno-topograficheskoe depo., Zapiski XXII, Otd. II, p. 189
Trigonometric heights over about 950 versts agree with the Caspian levelling to 0.643 sazhen
Russian arc of the parallel of 47.5 N, Privolzhsk triangulation (Kishinev to Astrakhan arc, eastern part) · Zapiski XXII, Otd. II, p. 190 · strength ★★★
Towers, scaffolds and high stations

Chapter VI, section 5. The heights of 109 points were carried by zenith distances from the New Russia points Popovka and Kadamovka to a mark on the Caspian shore at Naryshkina Kosa. This gives the difference between the levels of the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea. Struve's computation of the 1836 and 1837 Caspian to Black Sea levelling expedition (Fuss, Sabler and Savich) gives a second, independent value. The two differ by 0.643 sazhen.

“При исчисленіи высотъ 109 пунктовъ отъ начальнаго до Нарышкиной Косы, найдено, что разность поверхности морей Чернаго и Каспійскаго = — 12, 850 саж. Директоръ Пулковской Обсерваторіи Струве исчисливъ съ строжайшею точностію наблюденія, сдѣланныя въ 1836 и 1837 годахъ, для разрѣшенія ученаго вопроса относительно уровней этихъ морей нашелъ, что Каспійское море ниже Чернаго на = — 12, 207 саж. Разность обоихъ опредѣленій = 0, 643 саж.”
In English: “In computing the heights of 109 points from the starting point to Naryshkina Kosa it was found that the difference of the surfaces of the Black and Caspian Seas = -12.850 sazhen. The Director of the Pulkovo Observatory, Struve, having computed with the strictest accuracy the observations made in 1836 and 1837 to resolve the scientific question of the levels of these seas, found that the Caspian Sea is lower than the Black by -12.207 sazhen. Difference of the two determinations = 0.643 sazhen.”
Worked out here: 12.850 - 12.207 = 0.643 sazhen. 1 sazhen = 2.1336 m, so 0.643 sazhen = 1.37 m. 950 versts at 1.0668 km = about 1013 km.
Voenno-topograficheskoe depo. (1861). Zapiski Voenno-topograficheskago depo, Chast' XXII, Otd. II: Privolzhskoe trigonometricheskoe izmerenie. Voenno-topograficheskoe depo., Zapiski XXII, Otd. II, p. 190
Livonia: measure only with distinct images, in the 2-hour afternoon calm; triangle closures show one Livonian set worth 8 of Bessel's
Struve Geodetic Arc (Russo-Scandinavian arc of the meridian, Danube to Fuglenaes) · T. I, p. 32 · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours Repetition over days and hours

Tome I, Chapter IV. A set (mise) is one complete round of pointings. Struve counts 833 sets for the 141 Livonian directions (5.91 per direction) against 41.77 per direction in Bessel's East Prussian survey. He then compares the two surveys by their triangle closures (the excess of the angle sum over 180 degrees plus the spherical excess): mean square 0.987 for 31 Livonian triangles and 1.179 for Bessel's 15. From this he finds one Livonian set equal in weight to 8.44 Prussian sets, and he states the Livonian rule: measure only with sufficiently distinct images, in practice in the 2-hour afternoon period of calm images.

“En Livonie la règle a été strictement observée, de ne jamais faire des mesures que par des images suffisamment distinctes des objets, c'est-à-dire presque exclusivement pendant la période de 2 heures des images calmes, qui d'ordinaire a lieu chaque après-midi (Gradmessung I. p. 88).”
In English: “In Livonia the rule was strictly kept never to make measurements except with sufficiently distinct images of the objects, that is, almost exclusively during the 2-hour period of calm images which usually occurs every afternoon (Gradmessung I. p. 88).”
Worked out here: 41.77 / 5.91 = 7.07 (printed 7.07). Weight ratio printed: 41.77 × 1.179 : 5.91 × 0.987 = 8.44 : 1.
Struve, F. G. W. (1857). Arc du méridien de 25° 20' entre le Danube et la Mer Glaciale mesuré depuis 1816 jusqu'en 1855 (Vol. 1). Imprimerie de l'Académie impériale des sciences., T. I, p. 32
Closures against set agreement: the extra error is assigned to signal phases; no sign of lateral refraction in the Baltic arc
Struve Geodetic Arc (Russo-Scandinavian arc of the meridian, Danube to Fuglenaes) · T. I, p. 148 · strength ★★★

Tome I, Chapter X, on the accuracy of the angles. Struve computes the probable error of an angle in two independent ways. From the agreement of the repeated sets of the same angle (5.84 sets on average) it is 0.338″. From the triangle closures it is 0.392″. The closures contain every error, including outside disturbances that are the same in all sets of one angle. Lateral refraction is a sideways bend of the line of sight by air of uneven density; it would show in the closures, not in the set agreement. Struve gives the outside part as 0.198″ per angle, names signal phases first and lateral refraction 'if it exists', and states that the Baltic arc gives no sign of lateral refraction.

“Parmi les causes des perturbations extérieures, il faut placer en premier lieu les phases des signaux, produites par une illumination latérale, puis la réfraction latérale, si elle existe. On voit par notre résultat que l'effet des phases a été réduit à un minimum, par suite de la forme et la figure exacte des signaux employés. Voyez p. 14. Quant aux réfractions latérales nous osons dire, que les opérations de l'arc Baltique n'en donnent pas le moindre indice.”
In English: “Among the causes of the external disturbances one must place first the phases of the signals, produced by a side illumination, then lateral refraction, if it exists. One sees from our result that the effect of the phases has been reduced to a minimum, owing to the form and exact shape of the signals used. See p. 14. As for lateral refractions, we dare say that the operations of the Baltic arc do not give the slightest sign of them.”
Worked out here: √(0.392² - 0.338²) = √(0.1537 - 0.1142) = 0.198″ (printed). Per direction 0.198/√2 = 0.140″.
Struve, F. G. W. (1857). Arc du méridien de 25° 20' entre le Danube et la Mer Glaciale mesuré depuis 1816 jusqu'en 1855 (Vol. 1). Imprimerie de l'Académie impériale des sciences., T. I, p. 148
Base-to-base check over five groups: computed against measured bases, with the expected error printed beside the actual one
Struve Geodetic Arc (Russo-Scandinavian arc of the meridian, Danube to Fuglenaes) · T. I, p. 155 · strength ★★★

Tome I, § 42. The southern arc has six measured bases. Each group of triangles between two bases is computed from the base before and from the base after; U is the logarithmic difference between the computed and the measured value of a base. W² is the square of the difference expected from the probable errors of the base measurements and of the angles. The table gives U² and W² for the five groups from Simonis to Taschbunar.

“Par conséquent ces U expriment aussi la différence logarithmique entre la valeur d'une base calculée sur la base précédente et sa valeur trouvée par la mesure directe.”
In English: “Consequently these U also express the logarithmic difference between the value of a base computed from the preceding base and its value found by direct measurement.”
Reading the table. Upper table: squared mean error, mean error and probable error of an angle for each region (Baltic, Lithuania, Volhynia, Bessarabia, triangles T. 460 and T. 461), first as observed, then corrected to 180 degrees plus the excess. Lower table: for each pair of bases, the actual square U² and the expected square W² (units of the 7th decimal of the logarithm, squared). In three groups U² is below W², in two it is above.
Worked out here: Sum of U² = 74794; sum of W² = 88245; ratio 0.847 (printed on p. 156).
Struve, F. G. W. (1857). Arc du méridien de 25° 20' entre le Danube et la Mer Glaciale mesuré depuis 1816 jusqu'en 1855 (Vol. 1). Imprimerie de l'Académie impériale des sciences., T. I, p. 155
Conclusion: the agreement of computed and measured bases is as close as the stated accuracy predicts
Struve Geodetic Arc (Russo-Scandinavian arc of the meridian, Danube to Fuglenaes) · T. I, p. 156 · strength ★★★

Tome I, p. 156, continuing the base comparison on p. 155. The ratio of the actual to the expected squared differences is 0.847, and of the differences 0.920, both below 1. Struve concludes that the base agreement is very nearly what the accuracies of the bases and angles predict, and that the comparisons give no sign that the adopted mean errors are too small.

“Nous voilà donc parvenus à la conclusion importante, que l'accord des bases calculées et mesurées est de très-près tel qu'il fallait l'attendre, d'après les degrés d'exactitude assignés par nos recherches, § 24, § 25 et § 37 à § 41, aux mesures des bases et des angles. En tout cas les comparaisons ne fournissent aucun indice, que les différentes erreurs moyennes que nous avons adoptées, soient trop faibles.”
In English: “We have thus reached the important conclusion that the agreement of the computed and measured bases is very nearly what was to be expected from the degrees of accuracy assigned by our investigations, § 24, § 25 and § 37 to § 41, to the measurements of the bases and the angles. In any case the comparisons give no sign that the various mean errors we have adopted are too small.”
Worked out here: 74794 / 88245 = 0.8476; √0.8476 = 0.921 (printed 0.847 and 0.920).
Struve, F. G. W. (1857). Arc du méridien de 25° 20' entre le Danube et la Mer Glaciale mesuré depuis 1816 jusqu'en 1855 (Vol. 1). Imprimerie de l'Académie impériale des sciences., T. I, p. 156
Internal check of the zenith distances: 693 values at 84 stations; probable error of one zenith distance 1.49 seconds
Struve Geodetic Arc (Russo-Scandinavian arc of the meridian, Danube to Fuglenaes) · T. II, pp. 232-233 · strength ★★★
Repetition over days and hours

Tome II, p. 233. The zenith place Z should be the same for all targets of one set if the observations were perfect and the change of terrestrial refraction (the bending of near-horizontal rays in the air) was uniform during the set. Struve uses the scatter of Z within each set as a check. At 84 stations 693 zenith distances of 335 objects were observed, about 2 per object. From the scatter he finds the probable error of a single zenith distance, from two circle positions, as 1.49″.

“Les Z qui appartiennent à la même ligne horizontale c.-à-d. à une même mise, auraient dû être identiques, si les observations avaient été d'une exactitude parfaite, et si la variation de la réfraction terrestre avait été uniforme pendant la durée de chaque mise. Les différences entre les Z de la même ligne nous font par conséquent juger de l'exactitude des distances au zénith observées”
In English: “The Z that belong to the same horizontal line, that is, to one and the same set, would have had to be identical if the observations had been of perfect accuracy and if the variation of terrestrial refraction had been uniform during each set. The differences between the Z of the same line therefore let us judge the accuracy of the observed zenith distances”
Worked out here: 693 / 335 = 2.07 observations per object (printed 2.07).
Struve, F. G. W. (1860). Arc du méridien de 25° 20' entre le Danube et la Mer Glaciale mesuré depuis 1816 jusqu'en 1855 (Vol. 2). Imprimerie de l'Académie impériale des sciences., T. II, pp. 232-233

Heft I, p. 14. A second table gives the mean angle errors of the channel nets and the connections to Warsaw, partly from the Geodetic Institute and partly from the Russian Zapiski, vol. 47. Helmert then states the result of the base connections: where the net is joined to the measured bases in Belgium and Prussia, the bases confirm the stated accuracy of the angles from south-east England to the Prussian-Russian border, while in the Russian part the base connections show a lower actual accuracy (see the base table of p. 30).

“Es kann gleich hier im voraus noch bemerkt werden, dass die Anschlüsse des Dreiecksnetzes an die Grundlinien in Belgien und Preussen die angegebene Genauigkeit der Winkelmessung vom südöstlichen England bis an die preussisch-russische Grenze im wesentlichen bestätigen, während im russischen Theile der Längengradmessung die Basisanschlüsse eine erheblich geringere thatsächliche Genauigkeit erkennen lassen”
In English: “It may be noted here in advance that the connections of the triangle net to the bases in Belgium and Prussia essentially confirm the stated accuracy of the angle measurement from south-east England to the Prussian-Russian border, while in the Russian part of the longitude arc the base connections show a considerably lower actual accuracy”
Reading the table. Table: English channel net 1861, 17 triangles, ±1.08″; French channel net 1861-62, 8 triangles, ±0.51″; southern Silesian-Posen net 1877, ±0.70″; Czenstochau to Warsaw connections ±0.68″ and ±0.80″; new Berlin base net ±0.68″.
Helmert, F. R. (Ed.). (1893). Die europäische Längengradmessung in 52 Grad Breite von Greenwich bis Warschau. I. Heft: Hauptdreiecke und Grundlinienanschlüsse von England bis Polen. P. Stankiewicz., p. 14
Polish chains: 219 triangle closures give ±0.73 seconds; in unfavourable air and strong wind 18 to 24 sets were to be taken
European arc of the parallel in 52 N, Greenwich (Feaghmain) to Warschau · p. 29 · strength ★★★
Repetition over days and hours Towers, scaffolds and high stations Night lamps and heliotropes

Heft I, § 12, the Russian (Polish) triangulation under General Tenner. In the southern Warsaw to Czenstochau connection the average number of sets was 11.4. The closures of all 219 Polish triangles give a mean angle error of ±0.73″. Tenner found this somewhat high and gave as reasons the high signals (pyramids 6 to 20 m, and 20 to 50 m in 148 cases) and measurement in unfavourable air that could not always be avoided. The rule for such air and strong wind was 18 to 24 sets. The sum of the 219 closures, +9.73″, shows no bias to positive or negative.

“Als Erklärungsgrund werden die hohen Signale, welche meist nothwendig waren, sowie die mehrfach nicht zu vermeidende Messung bei ungünstiger Luft angeführt. (Bei ungünstiger Luft und starkem Wind sollten 18—24 Sätze genommen werden.) Die Summe der 219 Widersprüche ist + 9″,73, so dass keine Neigung zu positiven oder negativen Schlussfehlern zu erkennen ist.”
In English: “The high signals, which were mostly necessary, and the measurement in unfavourable air, which several times could not be avoided, are given as the explanation. (In unfavourable air and strong wind 18 to 24 sets were to be taken.) The sum of the 219 closures is +9.73″, so that no tendency to positive or negative closure errors can be seen.”
Worked out here: √(354.1 / (219 × 3)) = √0.539 = 0.734″ (printed ±0.73″). Per direction 0.73/√2 = 0.52″ (printed).
Helmert, F. R. (Ed.). (1893). Die europäische Längengradmessung in 52 Grad Breite von Greenwich bis Warschau. I. Heft: Hauptdreiecke und Grundlinienanschlüsse von England bis Polen. P. Stankiewicz., p. 29
Base-to-base check Warsaw to Czenstochau: misclosures 1.51 and 0.44 times the expected error
European arc of the parallel in 52 N, Greenwich (Feaghmain) to Warschau · p. 29 · strength ★★★

Heft I, p. 29. Two chains join the Warsaw base net to the Czenstochau base net. Carried through the triangles, the base length disagrees with the measured one by -135.5 (southern chain, 36 triangles) and -51.8 (northern chain, 43 triangles) units of the 7th decimal of the logarithm of the sides. Helmert compares these with the mean errors expected from the closure-based accuracy of the angles: they are 1.51 and 0.44 times as large, which he calls entirely satisfactory.

“Diese Widersprüche von 135.5 und 51.8 Einheiten der 7. Decimalstelle werden mit den mittleren Fehlern nach Maassgabe der aus den Dreieckswidersprüchen abgeleiteten Genauigkeit der Winkelmessung verglichen, wobei sie sich bezw. 1,51- und 0,44-mal so gross als leztere herausstellen, was durchaus befriedigt.”
In English: “These misclosures of 135.5 and 51.8 units of the 7th decimal are compared with the mean errors according to the accuracy of the angle measurement derived from the triangle closures, and they turn out to be 1.51 and 0.44 times as large as the latter, which is entirely satisfactory.”
Worked out here: 135.5 units of the 7th decimal of a logarithm = relative length error 135.5 × 10^-7 × 2.3026 = 3.1 × 10^-5. 51.8 units = 1.2 × 10^-5.

Heft I, § 5, French channel stations of 1862. At Harlettes Beaux observed on a 21 m scaffold in wind under very unfavourable conditions, so Helmert doubled all q (halved all weights). At Cassel the weight of angle 44.42 was halved because its 60 repetitions were all obtained on a single day. A repetition is one addition of the angle on a repeating circle. The page also notes a measurement excluded because its set was spread over a whole week.

“Harlettes. Die Beobachtungen wurden 1862 von Beaux wegen Wind unter sehr ungünstigen Umständen auf einem 21 m hohen Gerüst ausgeführt, weshalb ich hier alle q verdoppelt habe. ... Letzterer Werth ist verdoppelt worden, weil jene 60 Rep. an einem einzigen Tage erhalten sind.”
In English: “Harlettes. The observations were made in 1862 by Beaux, because of wind under very unfavourable conditions, on a 21 m high scaffold, for which reason I have doubled all q here. ... The latter value has been doubled because those 60 repetitions were obtained on a single day.”

European arc of the parallel in 52 N, Greenwich (Feaghmain) to Warschau · p. 186 · strength ★★★
Rejecting readings in unsteady air Steady-air hours Night lamps and heliotropes Repetition over days and hours

Heft I, Kap. 3, station record of Golmberg. In 1880 each angle was measured twice on 8 circle positions, a full set of 24 pointings per direction. The angle Collm to Golmberg differed by 2.61″ from 1871. Helmert examined the possible causes: the 1880 sights were spread over only three days, and the brightly lit tower at Collm may have pulled the pointing, since the observations were as usual made in the afternoon. General Schreiber ordered a remeasurement in 1889: 32 measurements on 16 circle positions over several days, the first 16 rejected for poor lights. The new result confirms 1880 to 0.85″.

“General Schreiber ordnete eine Neumessung des letzteren an, die im Juni und Juli 1889 durch den Landesvermessungsrath Erfurth erfolgte. Es wurden 32 Messungen angestellt, die sich auf 16 Kreisstände vertheilten und 149° 16′ 49″,72 als Resultat ergaben, dessen m. F. nach Maassgabe der Abweichungen der 16 Mittel aus Hin- und Hergang vom Gesammtmittel ± 0″,20 beträgt. (Die ersten 16 Beobachtungen sind wegen mangelhafter Lichter verworfen; sie geben 49″,74.)”
In English: “General Schreiber ordered a remeasurement of the latter, which was made in June and July 1889 by Landesvermessungsrath Erfurth. 32 measurements were made, distributed over 16 circle positions, and gave 149° 16′ 49.72″ as the result, whose mean error, from the deviations of the 16 means of forward and return runs from the overall mean, is ±0.20″. (The first 16 observations were rejected because of poor lights; they give 49.74″.)”
Reading the table. The small table in the middle of the page lists the values of the angle Collm to Golmberg: 1871 from 3 circle positions with 4 and 6 pointings (50.67″, 52.01″) and from the other angles of a pentagon (51.34″); 1880 from 16 direct measurements and from the two part angles (48.65″, 49.21″) and from a quadrilateral (51.24″).
Worked out here: 1889: 49.72″; 1880 mean 48.87″; difference 0.85″ (printed). 1871 mean 51.48″.

A 10-second reading error found from disagreement; after correction two routes agree within 0.4 ft and 0.14 ft
Great Arc of India, Lambton's meridional arc (Coromandel coast to Punnae and north to about 18 N) · p. 166 · strength ★★★
Rejecting readings in unsteady air

Continuation of ga_03. Lambton found that all angles referred to the south end of the base at Perumbauk hill were 10 to 12 seconds too large, a micrometer reading error. He replaced those angles by the supplement of the other corrected angles. A side computed through two different triangles is a check: if the angles are good, both routes give the same length.

“It was discovered, that at Perumbauk hill, there had been an error in reading off the south end of the base, most probably of 10" from the micrometers, as all the angles which had a reference to that point, exceeded what they ought to have been by ten or twelve seconds. In consequence of this disagreement, I chose to take the supplemental angle in the second and fourth triangles, after the other angles had been corrected. [...] it appears that the latter distance comes out within 0,4 of a foot to what had been brought by the first triangle; and that, the distance from the south end of the base to Perumbauk hill, derived from the second and fourth triangles, differ only ,14 of a foot.”
Lambton, W. (1808). An account of the measurement of an arc on the meridian on the coast of Coromandel, and the length of a degree deduced therefrom in the latitude 12° 32'. Asiatic Researches, 8, 137 ff., p. 166
Lambton's rule: repeat hazy angles; reject any angle 10 seconds from the others until the triangle is complete
Great Arc of India, Lambton's meridional arc (Coromandel coast to Punnae and north to about 18 N) · pp. 176-177 · strength ★★★
Rejecting readings in unsteady air Repetition over days and hours

After the table of triangles 31 and 32 of the 1802-03 triangulation. Lambton states his own rule for horizontal angles taken in haze. The triangle closure (the amount by which the three observed angles, less the spherical excess, miss 180 degrees) is the test he applies before an angle is kept or rejected. The rule continues on p. 177 with the method of trying each angle in turn.

“The angles have been taken with much care, and I believe with as much accuracy as the nature of such a process admits of; difficulty, however, very frequently arose from the haziness of the weather, which rendered the objects at the very distant points extremely dull, and occasioned some irregularity in the angles. Whenever that happened, the observations were often repeated, and in case any one, in particular, was different from the other so much as ten seconds, it was rejected till the three angles of the triangle had been observed.”
Lambton, W. (1808). An account of the measurement of an arc on the meridian on the coast of Coromandel, and the length of a degree deduced therefrom in the latitude 12° 32'. Asiatic Researches, 8, 137 ff., pp. 176-177

End of the triangle tables of the southern arc (Punnae to Putchapolliam). A base of verification is a second measured base: its length carried through the triangles from the first base is compared with its measured length. The table also shows the method: observed angles, the difference column, the spherical excess, and the error (closure) of each triangle, for example +0.83" and +2.46".

“In the two last triangles, the distance Sekundermalli from Suddragherry will be found common: then, by taking the mean and referring to the 29th triangle, it will appear, that there is a difference of 4 1/10 feet, in the same side Suddragherry from Sekundermalli; from whence it may be inferred, that had the base been computed from bringing down the triangles from the northward, it would have exceeded the measurement by 10 inches, nearly.”

GTS Vol. XII appendix on Lambton's 1805-06 work between Mysore and the Malabar coast. GTS Karachi Longitudinal Series (North-West Quadrilateral) · p. 130-B · strength ★★★
Repetition over days and hours

Investigation after the sums of squares. The e.m.s. (error of mean square) of one measure and of one zero mean is computed for each group of angles by the same observer under similar conditions. The groups are split by terrain, so the larger scatter on the plains, where rays run close to the ground, is measured rather than assumed.

“The first 47 angles were measured at hill stations on 4 pairs of zeros, face right and face left, with an average of 3.14 observations on each zero; the remaining angles, 372 in number, were measured on 5 pairs of zeros with an average of 2.11 observations on each zero, at stations on hills, and sandhillocks and in the plains. The first 47 angles form a group by themselves; the remaining angles form 8 distinct groups, which again may be collected into 3 groups, in order that the relative e. m. s. of observations on hills and sand-hillocks, and in the plains, may be shown.”
Reading the table. Table columns: Group; Instrument and Observer; Position of stations (Hills, Sandhills, Plains); interval between zeros; measures on each zero (average); number of angles, single measures, zeros; e.m.s. of a single measure; e.m.s. of graduation and observation of a single zero. Compare the e.m.s. for hill groups with the plains groups.
Worked out here: e.m.s. of a single measure as printed: hills ±0.845, 0.787, 0.833, 0.760; sandhills ±0.966, 0.844; plains ±1.028, 1.252 seconds.

GTS Bombay Longitudinal Series (Southern Trigon) · p. 23 · strength ★★★
Vertical refraction coefficients

Continuation of bo_07. The South Konkan heights, taken 40 years earlier between the ghats and the coast, were re-observed in 1885-86 with simultaneous reciprocal angles (both ends at the same time). Then the formula: C is the contained arc, Da and Db the observed angles, beta the signal and instrument correction; phi is the mean refraction and phi/C the coefficient.

“during 1885-86, and simultaneous reciprocal observations were taken on the unfavourable rays in the hope of reducing the errors due to refraction to a minimum. A comparison between the new values and the old exhibited discrepancies with a range of 43 feet. The reciprocal angles are also employed to determine the co-efficient of refraction, to be used in reducing unreciprocated vertical angles ; [...] and φ/C gives the terrestrial refraction in decimals of contained arc—or in other words the co-efficient of refraction—for each pair of reciprocated observations.”
Worked out here: Formula as printed: φ = 1/2 {C - (Da + Db) + β}; coefficient = φ/C.

Persistent lateral deviation of the line of sight does not show at the station; it shows in the triangle closures
US Transcontinental Triangulation, 39th parallel · p. 50 · strength ★★★

Part I, on why station and net adjustments are kept separate. The station (local) adjustment compares repeated readings at one station. The net adjustment forces the triangles to close. A constant sideways bend of a line (persistent lateral refraction) affects every reading of that line equally, so it cannot appear in the station scatter; it can only appear as triangle misclosure. Schott states that the error from the closures is the larger, so the closures are the real test.

“In the latter combination of the measures new sources of error show their effects; as, for instance, the effect of the deflection of the plumb line causing the angles to be measured out of the normal horizontal plane, want of coincidence of the center of a station and of heliotropes or targets subsequently mounted over it, persistent lateral deviation of the line of sight, constant or uncompensated graduation errors of the instrument, all of which causes exert no influence on the station adjustment. It is a matter of experience that the value of the probable error of a direction derived from the measures at a station is much smaller than the same when derived from the triangle closing errors”
Schott, C. A. (1900). The transcontinental triangulation and the American arc of the parallel (Special Publication No. 4). U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey; Government Printing Office., p. 50
Summary of triangle closing errors for all 11 series and 10 base nets: 701 triangles, mean error of an angle 0.77"

Raw tables of repeated measures

Part III, summary of angular results. The closing error of a triangle is 180 degrees plus the spherical excess minus the sum of the three measured angles; it is a check that is independent of the station repeats. Schott lists, per series and base net, how many triangles closed plus and minus, the sums of the plus and minus errors, the mean error of an angle and the probable error of an adjusted direction.

“With respect to the closure of the triangles (pi plus spherical excess minus the sum of the angles), we find the number of cases in excess to those in defect in the ratio 36 to 34, nearly.”
Reading the table. Columns: locality; number of positive and negative closing errors; sum of positive and sum of negative closing errors (seconds); number of triangles; mean error of an angle; probable error of a resulting direction. Totals: 357 positive, 343 negative, 701 triangles (one closes exactly), mean error of an angle +/- 0.77", probable error of a direction from 1 660 directions +/- 0.44". The intro sentence is on p. 612 (pdf 642).
Worked out here: Mean closing error per triangle from sums: (383.21 + 359.60) / 701 = 1.06" (average size of a closure, sign ignored).

Part III, section I. Ten bases were measured with bars or tapes across the continent. Between two adjacent bases, the length of one is computed from the other through the chain of triangles, using the angles from the station adjustments before the triangles were closed. The table gives the disagreement in the seventh decimal of the logarithm and as a fraction of the length.

“In the adjustment of the triangulation between two adjacent base nets the length equation has been derived from the angles as given by the station adjustments previous to any further adjustment, the triangles not even having been closed. [...] The following table shows the discord in length between adjacent base lines as computed through the intervening triangulation, derived in the manner explained above.”
Reading the table. Columns: pair of bases; discrepancy in units of the seventh decimal of the logarithm; the same as one part in N. Values run from 1 in 724 000 (Olney and American Bottom) to 1 in 25 700 (Versailles and Salina). The explanation of the method is at the foot of p. 613 (pdf 643, crop [0.12, 0.645, 0.88, 0.87]).
Worked out here: A logarithm difference of d units in the 7th decimal is a length ratio of d x 1e-7 x ln 10 = d x 2.303e-7. For +169 units: 3.89e-5 = 1 part in 25 700, as printed.

Part II, appendix D. From the hourly mean zenith distances at both ends, Schott computes for each hour the difference of height (Delta h) and the coefficient m, assuming equal refraction at the two ends. Because the bend is measured from both ends, most of it cancels out of the height.

“The adopted formulae are- m = 0.5 - (zeta + zeta' - 180 deg) / 2 psi [...] The resulting hourly values for Delta h and m are given in the following table: [...] The values of Delta h are plotted on diagram (3) and show the computed difference of height between 10 a. m. and near midnight to be smaller than the mean; but the results for those hours appear remarkably consistent.”
Reading the table. Columns: hour; Delta h (m); difference from mean (m); m. Mean Delta h = 2 463.51 m +/- 0.28 m; mean m = 0.0646. The top of the crop gives facts (a) to (c) on the diurnal variation: range nearly 51" at the lower and 38" at the upper station; maximum zenith distance 2 to 3 p.m.; little change from 11 a.m. to 4 1/2 p.m.
Worked out here: Over 24 hours m runs from 0.0557 to 0.0711 (a change of 28 percent), while Delta h runs from 2 461.65 m (1 p.m.) to 2 466.89 m (2 a.m.): 5.24 m, or 0.21 percent of 2 463.5 m.
Schott, C. A. (1900). The transcontinental triangulation and the American arc of the parallel (Special Publication No. 4). U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey; Government Printing Office., p. 286
Sierra Nevada: 1898 strictly simultaneous reciprocal measures over shorter lines; long valley lines (up to 229 km) excluded
US Transcontinental Triangulation, 39th parallel · pp. 304-305 · strength ★★★
Rejecting readings in unsteady air

Part II, heights across the Sacramento and San Joaquin valleys. The older long lines were observed at different hours, months and years, so equal refraction at the two ends could not be relied on. In 1898 the observers measured both ends at the same time over shorter lines, and the long lines were removed from the height results.

“The difficulty experienced when attempting the determination of heights on the crest of the Sierra Nevada by means of zenith distances measured over the long lines spanning the great valley of California rendered it necessary to supplement the older measures. This was done in the summer of 1898, by strictly simultaneous reciprocal measures over shorter lines, along which the variations of refraction are less injurious. [p. 305:] If, further, we reflect that the resulting zenith distances, as tabulated, were taken mostly at different hours of the day, in different months of the year, and in different years, with only the new (1898) measures simultaneous; it does not seem surprising that it became necessary to exclude the resulting differences of height over the several long lines across the valley which range up to 229 kilometres or 142 statute miles.”
Reading the table. Second passage: pdf 310, crop [0.15, 0.12, 0.83, 0.84] (includes the sketch of the lines).

Part II, Sierra Nevada heights. The heights of Round Top and Mount Lola were carried up more than 2 100 m from Pine Hill by reciprocal zenith distances, with a term for unequal refraction at upper and lower stations. Mount Lola was also reached by spirit levelling (railroad levels to Truckee and Gilbert's 1898 levels), so the trigonometric height can be checked against an independent levelled height.

“As already stated, the long lines stretching across the valley give too discordant results to be used, and the heights of Mount Lola and Round Top are made to depend entirely upon the intermediate station, Pine Hill. For its height we have six values, two of which are very doubtful and are therefore rejected. [...] The height of Mount Lola from the railroad levels to Truckee (h = 1 773.66 metres) and Assistant J. J. Gilbert's levels of 1898 from Truckee to Mount Lola (Delta h = 1 013.87 metres) is 2 787.5 metres.”
Reading the table. Upper table: six determinations of Pine Hill (two marked "reject"). Middle table: observed differences of height, weights, observation equations, adjusted values and discrepancies (0.08 m to 0.75 m). Lower table: adjusted heights, Mount Lola 2 786.8 m.
Worked out here: Levelled 2 787.5 m minus trigonometric 2 786.8 m = 0.7 m, after a rise of 2 159 m from Pine Hill (0.03 percent).
Schott, C. A. (1900). The transcontinental triangulation and the American arc of the parallel (Special Publication No. 4). U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey; Government Printing Office., p. 311
Persistent lateral refraction along a line is a triangle-combination error, not visible in the station measures
US Eastern Oblique Arc, Calais to New Orleans · p. 26 · strength ★★★

Part I, general remarks on the adjustments. "Triangle-combination errors" are the errors that only appear when the triangles are made to close. The same rule as in the transcontinental work: a constant sideways bend on one line cannot be seen in the repeats at the station, so the closures are used to measure it.

“The errors brought to light by geometrical conditions, and which have been called triangle-combination errors, are of a different character from those developed by a comparison of the measures made at a station, where defects of centering at observing and observed stations, effects of large local deflections of the vertical at a station, persistent lateral refraction along a line, etc., do not show; that is to say, weights pertaining to one operation are not those proper for the next operation.”
Schott, C. A. (1902). The eastern oblique arc of the United States and osculating spheroid (Special Publication No. 7). U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey; Government Printing Office., p. 26
Epping base net: every angle 20 measures of 3 direct and 3 reversed repetitions; 46 triangle closures; one 75 cm direction measure equals three 25 cm repeater measures
US Eastern Oblique Arc, Calais to New Orleans · p. 29 · strength ★★★
Repetition over days and hours

Part I, Epping base net (Maine). A repeating theodolite measures one angle several times in a row on the circle and divides the total. Schott gives the probable error from the 20 measures of each angle and, separately, from the closing errors of the 46 triangles of the net. The footnote compares the two instrument types.

“In case of repetitions the probable error will depend upon the comparison of a resulting angle with each of its 20 measures (each of 3 repetitions direct and 3 repetitions reversed), from which an average and approximate value of the probable error of a single measure of an angle and of a direction has been derived [...] If we deduce the probable error of a direction from the closing errors in the sum of the angles of the 46 triangles, we find from the sum of the squares of these errors the mean closing error of a triangle = sqrt(54.49/46) = +/- 1".09, hence the probable error of a direction = 0.674 x 1.09/sqrt(6) = +/- 0".30. [...] The mean of the 4 values of e_1 derived from a single measure (D. and R.) with the 75cm theodolite is +/- 1".04 and the mean of the 5 values of e_1 derived from a single measure (3 D. and 3 R.) with the 25cm repeating theodolite is +/- 1".16, or one measure with the first instrument is about equal in accuracy to three with the latter.”
Worked out here: Per angle: 20 measures x 6 repetitions = 120 pointings on each signal.
Schott, C. A. (1902). The eastern oblique arc of the United States and osculating spheroid (Special Publication No. 7). U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey; Government Printing Office., p. 29

Weights of base-line angles carry the loss of precision from undulating signals over hot ground
Maclear's verification and extension of La Caille's arc of meridian, Cape of Good Hope · p. 338 · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours Repetition over days and hours

Section 7, part 4, of the base verification by triangulation (Zwartland base). Maclear explains how the weight of each angle was found: the square of the number of partial measures divided by twice the sum of squares of the differences from the mean. A partial measure is the mean of a group of repetitions; the weight is a number that is larger when the results agree better. He states that over flat ground the signals undulate, except in gloomy and moist weather or early morning and late evening, and that this error must enter the weights. So the state of the air is measured in the scatter of the results, not ignored.

“The weight of each angle was calculated by dividing the square of the number of partial measures by twice the sum of the squares of the differences from the mean, assuming the theodolite errors of division to be insensible, an assumption which is not strictly correct. The method pursued when measuring, of stepping the divided circle, eleminates the division errors from the mean result; they are restored in the weight as above calculated ; but that factor cannot justly be represented by the number of measures alone,—where, as in the present instance, the triangulation is carried over flat ground,—the line of sight passing in close proximity to heated sand and bush, causing the signals to undulate so much, except during gloomy and moist weather, or early in the morning and late in the evening, as to materially diminish the precision of the pointing : it is therefore necessary to introduce this element of error.”
Maclear, T. (1866). Verification and extension of La Caille's arc of meridian at the Cape of Good Hope (Vol. 1). London: Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty., p. 338
Number of partial results set by the air; bad definition and lateral refraction cut the weight from 360 to 11
Maclear's verification and extension of La Caille's arc of meridian, Cape of Good Hope · p. 400 · strength ★★★
Repetition over days and hours

Description of the Beaufort theodolite method (p. 400). Each angle was measured by repetition, the verniers read at every tenth repetition; the mean of ten repetitions is one partial result. Maclear says the number of partial results depended on the importance of the angle and on the atmosphere. Definition is how sharp and steady the signal looks in the telescope; probable error is the error that has an even chance of being exceeded. Five results in first-rate definition (Simon's Berg, 19 November 1845) gave 0.05"; sixteen results in bad definition and lateral refraction (Kapoc Berg, 12 February 1846) gave 0.3". The footnotes giving these stations and dates are at the foot of the same page and inside the crop.

“The mean of every tenth repetition being regarded as one partial result, the required number of such results depended upon the importance of the angle, and the atmospheric circumstances during the time when measuring. The value of the latter may be gathered from the fact of five results obtained during first-rate definition, giving a probable error of 0"·05 and weight 360 (a) ; whereas during bad definition and lateral refraction, 16 results gave a probable error of 0"·3, and weight 11 (b). ... (a) Simon's Berg, Nov. 19, 1845. (b) Kapoc Berg, Feb. 12, 1846.”
Worked out here: 5 results = 50 repetitions; 16 results = 160 repetitions. Weight = 1/P^2 (p. 419): 1/0.3^2 = 11.1, printed 11. 1/0.05^2 = 400; the printed 360 corresponds to P = 0.0527, which rounds to the printed 0.05.
Maclear, T. (1866). Verification and extension of La Caille's arc of meridian at the Cape of Good Hope (Vol. 1). London: Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty., p. 400
Every reading called out and recorded; all arithmetic repeated and compared; one full angle per instrument printed
Maclear's verification and extension of La Caille's arc of meridian, Cape of Good Hope · p. 419 · strength ★★★

Opening of Section 3, Observed Horizontal Angles (p. 419). Maclear describes the record: 24 field-books for the Fuller theodolite and 2 for the Beaufort, copied into five folio volumes in which all the arithmetic was repeated and compared with the field-books. Further books hold the zenith distance measures. He prints only the means for every angle, plus the complete record of one angle by each instrument (see items cape_06 and cape_07) as the type of the whole.

“It was the general practice on the survey, when measuring angles, to call out the reading of each microscope or vernier to an amanuensis, who repeated the numbers aloud while recording them in the field-book ; and during the evening or other leisure moments the observer computed and applied the corrections for micrometer runs, and calculated the means. Twenty-four field-books contain the Fuller theodolite measures, and the Beaufort theodolite work occupies two. These books were afterwards transcribed at the Observatory into five pretty thick folio volumes, where the whole of the arithmetic was repeated, and carefully compared with the field-books. Exclusive of these books, there are others, which contain zenith distance measures for time and relative heights. The printing of such a mass of figures would incur an unwarrantable expense, and few persons would take the trouble to consult them ; therefore, after due consideration, it has been decided to print the mean results only, first placing in evidence the details of one angle by each instrument, which may be taken as the general type of the whole.”
Maclear, T. (1866). Verification and extension of La Caille's arc of meridian at the Cape of Good Hope (Vol. 1). London: Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty., p. 419
Definition of the angle weights: reciprocal of the squared probable error from the partial results
Maclear's verification and extension of La Caille's arc of meridian, Cape of Good Hope · p. 419 · strength ★★★
Repetition over days and hours

Same page. For the Beaufort theodolite the weight of an angle is 1/P^2, where P is the probable error computed from the spread of the partial results (each partial result = 10 repetitions). For the Fuller theodolite, where errors from the atmosphere and the eye are mixed with instrument errors, the weight is the number of partial means. Maclear states that the two methods are not homogeneous. This rule is why angles measured in unsteady air (larger scatter) count less in the adjustment.

“The weight annexed to each angle observed with the Beaufort theodolite is the reciprocal of the square of the probable error (P), derived from the formula : P = √(Σ.ε × 0·454936 / (n²—n)) where Σ.ε is the sum of the squares of the differences from the mean of each partial result,—10 repetitions being taken for the unit; 0·454936 = 2 ρ², derived from the theory of probabilities (ρ = ·476936). The weight annexed to the final determination of an angle is the sum of the weights of the separate determinations. ... With respect to the Fuller theodolite, the errors depending upon the state of the atmosphere and the eye, are mixed up with instrumental errors of a different order to errors of observation. The precision of the partial measures have therefore been regarded as equal, and the weight annexed to each angle is the sum of the partial means from which it is derived.”
Worked out here: Check with the 1 December 1846 group on p. 421: n = 13 partial results, sum of squares 4.5708. P = sqrt(4.5708 x 0.454936 / (169 - 13)) = sqrt(0.013330) = 0.1155 (printed 0.1155). Weight = 1/0.1155^2 = 75.0 (printed 75.02).
Maclear, T. (1866). Verification and extension of La Caille's arc of meridian at the Cape of Good Hope (Vol. 1). London: Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty., p. 419

Register of horizontal angles at Kapoc Berg (p. 449), the form used for every station on pp. 427-474. F and B mark the Fuller and Beaufort theodolites; E and C mark an excentric (off-centre) or central set-up, with the reduction to the centre. The angle Winter Berg to Sneeuw Kop was measured in six separate determinations of 50 to 100 measures (530 in all); the six values lie between 56.66" and 58.01". Several angles were measured with both instruments. This answers how many times an angle was taken.

“Horizontal Angles observed at Kapoc Berg Signal Station. ... Winter Berg, heliostat.. and Sneeuw Kop, heliostat... B E 77·54·27·020 —29·684 77·53·57·336 50 3·08 ... (Mean) B (77·53·57·470) 530 57·68”
Reading the table. Columns: signals between which the angle lies; F (Fuller) or B (Beaufort); E (excentric) or C (central); angle observed at the excentric position; reduction to centre; angle at the centre; No. of observations; weights (Beaufort) or partial means (Fuller). Typical counts are 20 to 160 measures per determination. For Winter Berg-Sneeuw Kop the six B determinations have 50, 80, 100, 100, 100, 100 measures.
Worked out here: 50 + 80 + 100 + 100 + 100 + 100 = 530 measures (printed 530). Spread of the six values: 58.010 - 56.660 = 1.35".
Maclear, T. (1866). Verification and extension of La Caille's arc of meridian at the Cape of Good Hope (Vol. 1). London: Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty., p. 449
Base verified by triangulation: measured and calculated section lengths agree within 0.055 foot
Maclear's verification and extension of La Caille's arc of meridian, Cape of Good Hope · p. 343 · strength ★★★
Raw tables of repeated measures

Section 7, 'Verification of the Base by Triangulation' (p. 343). The Zwartland base was divided into six sections, and a small triangulation computed each section from section 1. The table compares the measured and calculated lengths. The sum of sections 3 to 6 computed through the triangle C, G, K is 29137.595 feet against 29137.455 measured. This is an independent check of the angles measured over the same hot, flat ground as item cape_01.

“The following results are deduced from the foregoing table :— Measured. Calculated. Differences. Section 1 = 6436·529 Base. 2 = 7245·045 7245·060 — ·015 3 = 5145·030 5145·050 — ·020 5 & 6 = 17797·343 17797·398 — ·055 5 = 8085·046 8085·042 + ·004 6 = 9712·297 9712·256 + ·041 3, 4 & 5 = 19425·157 19425·156 + ·001 ... the sum of the sections 3, 4, 5, and 6, is 29137·595, the measured length is 29137·455.”
Reading the table. Columns: section; measured length (feet); length calculated through the triangles from section 1 (feet); difference (foot). Section 1 is the given base of the small triangulation.
Worked out here: Largest difference 0.055 ft in 17797 ft = 1 part in 324,000. Sections 3-6: 29137.595 - 29137.455 = 0.140 ft = 1.7 inches, 1 part in 208,000.

Triangle errors per observer: 260 triangles sorted by size of closure error
Geodetic Survey of the Transvaal and Orange River Colony (Morris; preface and introduction by Gill) · p. 59 · strength ★★★
Raw tables of repeated measures

Robinson's report on the computations, (h) Abstract of triangular errors (p. 59). The triangular error is the amount by which the sum of the observed angles differs from 180 deg plus the spherical excess. For each of the three observers the table counts triangles in half-second steps and gives the probable error of a single angle. Table (i) below gives the size of the corrections the adjustment applied to 784 angles.

“(h) Abstract of Triangular Errors. ... Captain Gordon 102 54 35 8 2 2 1 ±0·30 Mr. Simms 87 36 35 15 1 .. .. ±0·29 Captain Ley 71 23 21 19 6 2 .. ±0·39 Thus the probable error of a single angle, measured on eight arcs, is ... ± 0″·30 and the probable error of a single angle, measured on four arcs, is ... ± 0″·39”
Reading the table. Table (h) columns: observer; number of triangles; number of triangles with error 0.0-0.5", 0.5-1.0", 1.0-1.5", 1.5-2.0", 2.0-2.5", 2.5-3.0"; probable error of a single angle. Table (i): for each chain, the number of angles whose adjustment correction fell in 0.25" steps, and the total number of angles (784). In this scan the figures 3 and 8 look alike; Ley's first count is read as 23 because the row must sum to 71.
Worked out here: Row sums: 54+35+8+2+2+1 = 102; 36+35+15+1 = 87; 23+21+19+6+2 = 71. Triangles with error under 1.0": 89 + 71 + 44 = 204 of 260 (78 per cent).
Morris, W. G. (1908). Reports on the geodetic survey of the Transvaal and Orange River Colony (Geodetic Survey of South Africa, Vol. 5; preface and introduction by D. Gill). London: Harrison and Sons., p. 59
Two independent surveys meet at Standaus-Wedza: scale discordance 2.64 inches on the side
Geodetic Survey of the Transvaal and Orange River Colony (Morris; preface and introduction by Gill) · p. xxix · strength ★★★

Gill's introduction (p. xxix). The Transvaal survey (from the south, through Gordon's chain) and Simms' Rhodesia survey (from Salisbury) were computed independently and compared at their common side Standaus-Wedza. Latitude and longitude differ by 0.6 to 3.5", the bearing by 8.9" (Gill names cumulative error and local attraction at Salisbury as possible causes), and the scale by 2.64 inches. The 38 and 42 foot height differences come from the two different height data (railway bench mark at Bulawayo against levelling from the sea at Lourenco Marques), as the page states.

“The agreement between the Scales of the two independent Surveys is remarkable, and indeed the circuit angle-corrections of Gordon's triangles would be absolutely negligible if the angles of his chain had only been recorded to the first decimal of a second of arc. ... Standaus. Gordon-Simms. Latitude ... 3·503 Longitude ... 0·602 Bearing of Wedza ... 8·89 Height... ... 38 feet ... Wedza. Gordon-Simms. Latitude ... 3·543 Longitude ... 0·627 Bearing of Standaus ... 8·86 Height... ... 42 feet The adjustment for discordance of scale amounts only to 2·64 inches on the side Standaus-Wedza.”
Reading the table. Rows: latitude, longitude, bearing (seconds of arc) and height (feet), Gordon value minus Simms value, at each end of the common side.

Robinson's report, paragraphs 20-21 (p. 165). Heights carried by vertical angles from Zwartkop, Natal, are compared with heights from spirit levelling from Delagoa Bay at four stations, next to the theoretical probable error (0.35 foot per mile times the square root of the miles). The differences L - V are of the size of the theoretical probable errors. This tests the vertical-angle heights, and so the refraction treatment, against an independent method.

“20. Assuming the average probable error of an adjusted difference of height to be ± 0·35 feet per mile, it is interesting to compare the theoretical probable errors with discordances between results from vertical angles and from actual levelling from Delagoa Bay. Taking Zwartkop, Natal, where the discordance is only 1·6 feet, as a datum, we have the following comparisons at other stations :— ... S. end Belfast base .. 280 6391·4 6399·9 + 8·5 ± 5·8 Muckleneuk .. .. 400 4739·8 4748·6 + 8·8 ± 7·0 Observatory Hill .. 460 5930·0 5936·1 + 6·1 ± 7·5 E. end Kroonstad base 670 4691·7 4684·4 — 7·3 ± 9·1”
Reading the table. Columns: station; distance from Zwartkop through the chains (miles); height from vertical angles (feet); height by levelling (feet); L - V (feet); theoretical probable error of the vertical height (feet). The second table gives the probable errors of the five base heights (5.8 to 10.1 feet).
Worked out here: 0.35 x sqrt(280) = 5.86 (printed 5.8); 0.35 x sqrt(670) = 9.06 (printed 9.1). 8.5 ft in 6399.9 ft of height after 280 miles of chain; 7.3 ft after 670 miles.

“Many repetitions were made of every angle with reverse observations, and every possible attention to ensure an accurate mean; and the result has been most satisfactory. The greatest error in the sum of the angles of one triangle was 3·3 seconds, and this was in a triangle of nearly forty miles sides.”

Gill's finding: lateral refraction larger than pointing errors; morning and afternoon combined
Trigonometrical Survey of New South Wales · pp. 181-182 · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours

Furber, Instruments (pp. 181-182), reporting Gill's report on the Cape Colony and Natal survey. Lateral refraction is the sideways bending of the line of sight, which shifts horizontal directions. Gill found it larger than the errors of pointing and reading; a change of wind could move a distant station, and directions after noon differed from those before noon. His remedy was to vary the conditions, combining morning and afternoon work, and the probable error of an angle fell from 0.49" to 0.33". No PDF of this paper is in the project; the item points to the OCR text file, so no crop is possible. The wording was checked against page images of pp. 181-182 held elsewhere in the project.

“In this connection he states that during the course of the survey it was shown that the accidental errors of pointing or reading were less to be regarded than those caused by lateral refraction. Not only was it found that a change of wind was sometimes followed by marked change in the direction of a distant station, but that a systematic difference, small but appreciable, existed between directions measured after and before noon, and the general conclusion was come to that steps were to be taken to reduce the effects of refraction by varying the conditions under which the observations were made rather than by seeking precision from extraordinary accuracy of the instruments used. In this view a 10-inch theodolite was substituted by Dr. Gill for the 18-inch instrument previously employed, and throughout the remainder of the work morning and afternoon observations were combined, the very satisfactory result being that with an instrument of less than one-fourth the weight the probable error of an observed angle was reduced from ± 0·49″ to ± 0·33″.”
No page image: this source is held as a text layer only.
Furber, T. F. (1898). The trigonometrical survey of New South Wales, with mention of similar surveys in the other Australian colonies. Report of the Australasian Association for the Advancement of Science, 7, Section A, 176-237., pp. 181-182
