The authors warn that the printed zenith distances are not precise enough for mountain heights
Cassini de Thury and Lacaille, verification of the Paris meridian and the arc of the parallel near 43.5 N · xj (Troisième partie) · strength ★★

Troisième partie, p. xj. The authors state the limits of their own vertical angles: difficult stations, and a plumb line hung from a point about 3.5 lignes above the plane of the quadrant. This tells the reader which numbers can be used for heights and which only for the reduction to the horizon.

“Nous devons avertir auffi que les diftances au zenith, qui font marquées à la fin de chaque ftation, n'ont pas été toutes obfervées avec une précifion fuffifante, pour en conclure la hauteur des Montagnes au-deffus du niveau de la Mer, parce que l'incommodité des lieux n'a fouvent pas permis d'y prendre les précautions néceffaires”
In English: “We must also warn that the zenith distances given at the end of each station were not all observed with sufficient precision to conclude from them the height of the mountains above sea level, because the inconvenience of the places often did not allow the necessary precautions there”
Cassini de Thury, C.-F. (1744). La méridienne de l'Observatoire Royal de Paris vérifiée dans toute l'étendue du Royaume par de nouvelles observations. Paris: H.-L. Guérin & J. Guérin., xj (Troisième partie)
Delambre (1810) recomputes the 1739 sea-horizon heights: refraction had been neglected, so heights came out too large
Cassini de Thury and Lacaille, verification of the Paris meridian and the arc of the parallel near 43.5 N · T3 p. 145 · strength ★★
Vertical refraction coefficients

Delambre and Méchain, vol. 3, review of the 1739 meridian. Delambre takes five 1739 observations of the sea horizon from the terrace of the Sainte-Victoire hermitage and computes the terrace height with mean refraction. The five results agree within about 7 toises, and their mean is 42 toises below the height printed in 1744. He states that the 1744 calculation neglected terrestrial refraction, and that with the mean coefficient 0.08 the heights come much closer.

“Mais, dans le calcul, on négligeoit la réfraction terrestre : ainsi l'on trouvoit toutes les hauteurs trop grandes. C'est ce qu'on peut aussi remarquer dans la méridienne de 1718. En refaisant tous les calculs avec la réfraction moyenne 0.08, j'ai trouvé des nombres beaucoup plus rapprochés de ceux qu'on a vus”
In English: “But in the calculation terrestrial refraction was neglected: so all the heights were found too large. This can also be seen in the meridian of 1718. Redoing all the calculations with the mean refraction 0.08, I found numbers much closer to those we have seen”
Worked out here: Five heights 444.3, 447.4, 440.0, 446.3, 440.9 toises; range 7.4 toises; mean 443.8 against 486.0 printed, difference 42.2 toises (printed).
Méchain, P., & Delambre, J.-B. J. (1810). Base du système métrique décimal, ou mesure de l'arc du méridien compris entre les parallèles de Dunkerque et Barcelone (Vol. 3). Paris: Baudouin., T3 p. 145
Night lamps compared with day signals: no better agreement between series; undulations seen on lamps and on day signals
Delambre and Méchain, meridian arc Dunkirk to Barcelona (Base du système métrique) · T1 Discours préliminaire p. 106 · strength ★★
Night lamps and heliotropes

Discours préliminaire. Méchain used reverberatory lamps (oil lamps with a reflector) as night targets in Spain. Delambre compares the series (sets of repeated readings) of the same angle and finds no better agreement than with day signals. Undulations are the visible trembling or slow swaying of a target image caused by unsteady air.

“En examinant les diverses séries d'un même angle ou les diverses parties de la même série, je n'y vois pas plus d'accord, peut-être même un peu moins que quand il observoit des signaux ordinaires. Nous avons dit ci-dessus que le réverbère allumé à Montmartre le 11 et le 15 août 1792 étoit sujet à des ondulations très-sensibles, qui faisoient osciller le lieu apparent autour du véritable. C'est un inconvénient au reste qui paroît inhérent aux signaux de toute espèce, je l'ai éprouvé bien souvent sur les signaux de jour”
In English: “Examining the different series of the same angle or the different parts of the same series, I see no more agreement, perhaps even a little less, than when he observed ordinary signals. We said above that the lamp lit at Montmartre on 11 and 15 August 1792 was subject to very noticeable undulations, which made the apparent place oscillate around the true one. This drawback seems inherent in signals of every kind; I experienced it very often with day signals”
Méchain, P., & Delambre, J.-B. J. (1806). Base du système métrique décimal, ou mesure de l'arc du méridien compris entre les parallèles de Dunkerque et Barcelone (Vol. 1). Paris: Baudouin., T1 Discours préliminaire p. 106
Adopted n = 0.08 can vary from 0.07 to 0.09 and sometimes 0.10; heights fixed from two points are sure, from one point doubtful
Delambre and Méchain, meridian arc Dunkirk to Barcelona (Base du système métrique) · T2 p. 768 · strength ★★
Vertical refraction coefficients

Tome II, table of heights. Delambre states the range of the coefficient n over the arc and the size of the error it can cause (one or two toises at 18 000 toises). He separates heights found from two different points, which check each other, from heights found from a single point.

“Le coefficient n, que nous avons supposé 0.08, pouvant varier de 0.07 à 0.09, et même quelquefois à 0.10 ... ce qui peut produire une ou deux toises d'erreur quand la distance est de 18000 toises. ... Presque toutes les hauteurs de la table précédente ont été déterminées de deux points différens. On peut les regarder comme sûres dans les limites que nous avons dites ; celles qui n'ont été déterminées que d'un seul point peuvent être douteuses, non seulement parce que la réfraction peut avoir été assez différente de la moyenne”
In English: “The coefficient n, which we have supposed 0.08, being able to vary from 0.07 to 0.09, and even sometimes to 0.10 ... which can produce one or two toises of error when the distance is 18000 toises. ... Almost all the heights of the preceding table were determined from two different points. They can be regarded as sure within the limits we have given; those determined from a single point may be doubtful, not only because the refraction may have been rather different from the mean”
Méchain, P., & Delambre, J.-B. J. (1807). Base du système métrique décimal, ou mesure de l'arc du méridien compris entre les parallèles de Dunkerque et Barcelone (Vol. 2). Paris: Baudouin., T2 p. 768
As many reciprocal zenith distances as needed at every first-order vertex to keep level errors under two metres; Brest-Panthéon levelling by reciprocal simultaneous zenith distances by day and night
Parallel of Paris, Brest to Strasbourg (Henry east part, Bonne west part), Nouvelle carte de France · 232 · strength ★★

Puissant, section on the geodetic levelling and its precision by the formulas of probability. He states the target accuracy (level differences not wrong by more than two metres in the worst case) and that the number of reciprocal zenith distances at each vertex was set by that target. The networks control one another.

“aussi a-t-on observé à tous les sommets des triangles du 1er ordre autant de distances zénithales réciproques qu'il était nécessaire, pour que les erreurs commises sur les différences de niveau ne dépassassent pas deux mètres, dans les cas les plus défavorables. ... Tous les réseaux de triangles, qui partent de l'océan et qui s'étendent dans l'intérieur du royaume, réunissent cet avantage en se contrôlant les uns par les autres. C'est ainsi que le nivellement trigonométrique exécuté depuis Brest jusqu'au Panthéon, par des distances zénithales réciproques et simultanées, prises de jour et de nuit, a donné la hauteur absolue du sommet de cet édifice”
In English: “so at all the vertices of the first-order triangles as many reciprocal zenith distances were observed as were necessary for the errors on the level differences not to exceed two metres in the most unfavourable cases. ... All the networks of triangles that start from the ocean and extend into the interior of the kingdom have this advantage of controlling one another. Thus the trigonometric levelling carried out from Brest to the Panthéon, by reciprocal and simultaneous zenith distances taken by day and by night, gave the absolute height of the top of this building”
Puissant, L. (1832). Nouvelle description géométrique de la France (Première partie). Paris: Ch. Picquet., 232
Puissant examined the registers of the Brest-Panthéon levelling and applied the calculus of probabilities because the reciprocal observations were simultaneous
Parallel of Paris, Brest to Strasbourg (Henry east part, Bonne west part), Nouvelle carte de France · 233 · strength ★★

Puissant, p. 233. He states that he examined the original registers of the levelling by Bonne, Epailly and Béraud and judged them fully reliable, and that he measured their precision by probability formulas (probable error). He notes the missing comparison between their two repeating circles.

“En examinant avec attention les registres contenant toutes les observations et mesures relatives à ce nivellement (peut-être unique en son genre), l'on ne peut se refuser à reconnaître que cette opération, due à MM. Bonne, Epailly et Béraud, mérite une entière confiance ... Pour appliquer à ce nivellement le calcul des probabilités, j'ai eu recours à la formule (18) de la page 161, parce que les observations réciproques ont été simultanées”
In English: “Examining with care the registers containing all the observations and measures for this levelling (perhaps unique of its kind), one cannot refuse to recognise that this operation, due to Messrs Bonne, Epailly and Béraud, deserves full confidence ... To apply the calculus of probabilities to this levelling I used formula (18) of page 161, because the reciprocal observations were simultaneous”

Anglo-French triangulation of 1787 (Greenwich to Paris junction), English side by Roy · pp. 170-171 · strength ★★
Rejecting readings in unsteady air

Same page, at the foot. The 'column of observed angles' is in the triangle tables that follow (pp. 172-182). The sentence continues on p. 171: 'But no bad consequence has arisen on that account, there being always such other checks from the collateral stations, as to leave nothing doubtful.' Collateral stations are neighbouring stations whose angles close the same figures.

“Sometimes an observation has been entirely lost, or at least that which had been obtained was not thought a very good one. In such cases a blank has been left in the column of observed angles, and also in that expressing the error.”
Roy, W. (1790). An account of the trigonometrical operation, whereby the distance between the meridians of the Royal Observatories of Greenwich and Paris has been determined. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, 80, 111-270 (with Dalby, I., Remarks, pp. 593-614)., pp. 170-171
1795: refraction measured at both ends of the levelled Salisbury Plain base (38" and 50"), with the stated sensitivity to the height error
Trigonometrical Survey of England and Wales (Ordnance), Williams, Mudge and Dalby 1791-1799 · p. 588 · strength ★★

Same page. The two ends of the Salisbury Plain base have a height difference known from the base measurement, so the angle observed from each end can be compared with the true one. The difference is the refraction at that end. The authors state how much an error in the height difference changes the result.

“therefore two opportunities only presented themselves for determining the actual terrestrial refraction; namely, at the ends of the base of verification. From the depression taken at Beacon Hill, the refraction was 38"; but the elevation of Beacon Hill, observed at the lower end, near Old Sarum, gives 50". These deductions, perhaps, cannot be deemed very conclusive; because, as they depend on the difference in the vertical heights of the ends of the base, every 2 inches of error in that difference will produce an error of about 1" in the computed refraction.”
Williams, E., Mudge, W., & Dalby, I. (1795). An account of the trigonometrical survey carried on in the years 1791, 1792, 1793, and 1794. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, 85, 414-591., p. 588

End of Mudge's refraction article. He compares the difference of height of the stations found from the angles with that found from the barometer readings, on the two arcs where the remarks show quiet air. The two methods differ, and he states that more work is needed.

“The little done on this subject, points out the necessity of doing more”
Reading the table. Columns: arc; difference of height from the observed angles (317 and 60 ft); from the barometer (282 and 15 ft); difference (35 and 45 ft).

Next page. To estimate the probable error of the computed base, Clarke takes one chain of 16 triangles linking the two bases and prints the error of each triangle's angle sum (the observed sum against 180° plus the spherical excess).

“For this purpose, take the triangles contained in the following table.”
Reading the table. Columns (twice across): number; names of the three stations; angles (minutes and seconds); error of sum in seconds. Errors from +0.02" (Precelly, Dunkery, Cradle) to -5.83" (Slieve Donard, Snowdon, Kippure); triangle 8 has one angle not observed. On p. 421 the sum of squares of the errors for 15 triangles is 129.16, giving a mean error of 2.93".

Clarke 1880: with mutual observations, eliminate k or weight two results by their consistency; height differences round a triangle are closed by least squares
Textbook guidance of the period on terrestrial refraction · p. 284 · strength ★★

Same chapter. Mutual observations are reciprocal ones. Formula (3) gives the height difference from the two angles with k removed. When three stations observe each other, the three height differences should add to zero; the misclosure is spread by least squares (a method that makes the sum of the weighted squared corrections as small as possible).

“When the observations at A and B are mutual, we may either eliminate the coefficient of refraction by using the formula (3), or we may get two different results from a mean assumed value of k, and then combine these results by assigning them weights deduced from the consistency of the observations from which they are separately derived ... When at each of three stations we have the observed zenith distances of the other two, the deduced differences of height will exhibit a discrepancy.”
Clarke, A. R. (1880). Geodesy. Oxford: Clarendon Press., p. 284
The closure of each triangle was shared among its angles in proportion to the scatter of their sets
Russian arc of the parallel of 47.5 N, Privolzhsk triangulation (Kishinev to Astrakhan arc, eastern part) · Zapiski XXII, Otd. II, p. 130 · strength ★★
Repetition over days and hours

Chapter V, computation of the triangulation. m is the mean deviation of the single sets of an angle from the mean of all its sets. The closure error of each triangle was divided among its three angles in proportion to their m, so a less consistent angle took a larger share. The worked example is triangle 52: closure -3.35″, m = 2.0, 1.0 and 1.1, corrections -1.63″, -0.82″ and -0.90″.

“чтобы соразмѣрять поправку съ достоинствомъ его измѣренія, принималось во вниманіе среднее ариѳметическое число, получаемое изъ разностей каждаго пріема съ среднимъ изъ всѣхъ пріемовъ одного и того же угла. Если это среднее ариѳметическое число означимъ чрезъ m, то погрѣшность суммы угловъ разлагалась пропорціонально тремъ m;”
In English: “to make the correction proportional to the quality of its measurement, account was taken of the arithmetic mean obtained from the differences of each set from the mean of all sets of one and the same angle. If this arithmetic mean is denoted by m, the error of the sum of the angles was distributed in proportion to the three m;”
Worked out here: -3.35 × 2.0/4.1 = -1.63; -3.35 × 1.0/4.1 = -0.82; -3.35 × 1.1/4.1 = -0.90 (sum of m = 4.1).
Voenno-topograficheskoe depo. (1861). Zapiski Voenno-topograficheskago depo, Chast' XXII, Otd. II: Privolzhskoe trigonometricheskoe izmerenie. Voenno-topograficheskoe depo., Zapiski XXII, Otd. II, p. 130
The authors attribute the base difference to the accumulation of small angle errors, most of all to the illumination of the targets
Russian arc of the parallel of 47.5 N, Privolzhsk triangulation (Kishinev to Astrakhan arc, eastern part) · Zapiski XXII, Otd. II, p. 131 · strength ★★
Night lamps and heliotropes

Chapter V, continued from the base comparison. The authors list the sources of the 0.541 sazhen difference: pointing, circle graduation, vernier reading and, they suppose, mostly the illumination of the targets. Because the Privolzhsk and New Russia surveys must agree with both measured bases (Novocherkassk and Astrakhan), the difference was spread over about 90 triangles as a correction of 0.28″ per angle.

“Эта разность вывода длины одной и той же линіи, полученной изъ тригонометрической сѣти и изъ дѣйствительнаго измѣренія, происходитъ отъ накопленія весьма малыхъ погрѣшностей, не избѣжныхъ при измѣреніи угловъ, зависящихъ частію отъ неточности визированія наблюдателя, невѣрности дѣленій лимба, не совершенно-точнаго отсчитыванія по ноніусамъ, а наиболѣе, какъ можно полагать, отъ освѣщенія предметовъ.”
In English: “This difference in the length of one and the same line, obtained from the trigonometric net and from the actual measurement, arises from the accumulation of very small errors, unavoidable in the measurement of angles, depending partly on inexact pointing by the observer, incorrect divisions of the circle, not quite exact reading of the verniers, and most of all, as one may suppose, on the illumination of the targets.”
Voenno-topograficheskoe depo. (1861). Zapiski Voenno-topograficheskago depo, Chast' XXII, Otd. II: Privolzhskoe trigonometricheskoe izmerenie. Voenno-topograficheskoe depo., Zapiski XXII, Otd. II, p. 131

F.) and their ratio. “Es dürften wohl verschiedene Identitätsfehler in den Dreieckspunkten beim Zusammenhang von Messungen aus verschiedenen Epochen zur Erklärung heranzuziehen sein.”
In English: “Various identity errors in the triangle points, where measurements of different epochs are joined, may well have to be called on for the explanation.”
Reading the table. Rows from Orsk (east) to Czenstochau (west). Columns: number of triangles; distance in 100 km; misclosure (units of the 7th decimal); mean error expected; ratio misclosure : mean error. Ratios: 6.8, 2.1, 2.5, 3.5 east of Rohatschew; 0.8, 0.4, 0.4, 1.5 from Rohatschew to Czenstochau.
Helmert, F. R. (Ed.). (1893). Die europäische Längengradmessung in 52 Grad Breite von Greenwich bis Warschau. I. Heft: Hauptdreiecke und Grundlinienanschlüsse von England bis Polen. P. Stankiewicz., p. 30
Helmert lists lateral refraction of the rays among the constant errors that act systematically on a direction
European arc of the parallel in 52 N, Greenwich (Feaghmain) to Warschau · p. 35 · strength ★★

Heft I, § 16, on the weights of the station results. Helmert separates the random 'naked' observing errors from errors that stay constant in several or all observations of one direction. Among the constant ones he lists circle graduation errors, personal errors in seeing the targets, centring errors, changes of the station with time, and lateral refraction (sideways bending of the rays in the air). If these change from one group of measurements to the next, their effect is systematic and is not shown by the scatter within a station.

“ferner zeitliche Veränderungen in der Lage der Stationen aus den verschiedensten Gründen und seitliche Brechungen der Lichtstrahlen in der Luft. Wenn diese Fehler aber unter Umständen bei verschiedenen Gruppen der Winkelmessungen einer Station in von Gruppe zu Gruppe wechselnder Weise wirken, so ist ihr Einfluss ein systematischer.”
In English: “further, changes with time in the position of the stations for the most various reasons, and lateral refractions of the light rays in the air. But if these errors act, in some cases, in a way that changes from group to group of the angle measurements of a station, their influence is a systematic one.”
Helmert, F. R. (Ed.). (1893). Die europäische Längengradmessung in 52 Grad Breite von Greenwich bis Warschau. I. Heft: Hauptdreiecke und Grundlinienanschlüsse von England bis Polen. P. Stankiewicz., p. 35
Measurements of different years at one station were treated as separate stations; the state of the air is one named cause
European arc of the parallel in 52 N, Greenwich (Feaghmain) to Warschau · p. 37 · strength ★★
Night lamps and heliotropes

Heft I, § 16, end. Where a station was measured in different years, each epoch was combined on its own and then joined with weights. In the net adjustment, measurements of different years at one station were treated as measurements at different stations, because even the best measurements of different years showed large differences. Helmert names the possible causes: instruments and observers, the state of the air, centring and identity of the points, and the perception of heliotrope lights, whose appearance changes with the atmosphere.

“Für diesen Vorgang sprach das Auftreten grosser Differenzen selbst bei den besten Messungen verschiedener Jahre, wobei es allerdings unaufgeklärt geblieben ist, welches die wesentlichste Ursache dieser Unterschiede sein mag, ob die meist vorhandene Verschiedenheit der Instrumente und Beobachter, oder ein Unterschied der Luftzustände, oder in einzelnen Fällen Centrirungsmängel bezw. Nichtidentität der Punkte.”
In English: “This procedure was supported by the occurrence of large differences even in the best measurements of different years, though it has remained unexplained which is the main cause of these differences: the difference of instruments and observers that is mostly present, or a difference in the states of the air, or in single cases faults of centring or non-identity of the points.”
Helmert, F. R. (Ed.). (1893). Die europäische Längengradmessung in 52 Grad Breite von Greenwich bis Warschau. I. Heft: Hauptdreiecke und Grundlinienanschlüsse von England bis Polen. P. Stankiewicz., p. 37
French channel net: an angle at Coldham was given a lower weight for the danger of lateral refraction toward St. Peters
European arc of the parallel in 52 N, Greenwich (Feaghmain) to Warschau · p. 60 · strength ★★

Heft I, § 5, Helmert's new reduction of the French repeating-circle observations of 1861-62. q is the reciprocal weight of an angle: a larger q means a smaller weight in the adjustment. For angle 50.47 at Coldham the formula gave q = 3; Helmert raised it to 5 because of the worsening state of the instrument and the danger of lateral refraction in the direction of St. Peters.

“der hieraus folgende Werth 3 wurde wegen des mehr und mehr verschlechterten Zustandes des Instruments und wegen der Gefahr von Lateralrefraktion in Richtung nach St. Peters (p. 55) auf 5 erhöht.”
In English: “the value 3 that follows from this was raised to 5 because of the more and more deteriorated state of the instrument and because of the danger of lateral refraction in the direction of St. Peters (p. 55).”
Worked out here: Weight is 1/q: from 1/3 to 1/5, a reduction to 60 percent.
Helmert, F. R. (Ed.). (1893). Die europäische Längengradmessung in 52 Grad Breite von Greenwich bis Warschau. I. Heft: Hauptdreiecke und Grundlinienanschlüsse von England bis Polen. P. Stankiewicz., p. 60
Rhenish and Hessian nets: lateral refraction named first among the causes of the ±0.7 seconds direction error
European arc of the parallel in 52 N, Greenwich (Feaghmain) to Warschau · p. 97 · strength ★★
Night lamps and heliotropes

Heft I, § 6. The net adjustment of the Rhenish and Hessian nets of the Prussian Geodetic Institute gives a mean error of nearly ±0.7″ for a station-adjusted direction, larger than the station scatter alone. Helmert names the causes: lateral refraction of the light, errors in perceiving the heliotrope lights (heliotropes were the targets almost everywhere), single centring uncertainties, and above all the graduation errors of the circles.

“Als Ursachen jener Erscheinung müssen, da fast ausschliesslich Heliotrope als Einstellungsobjekte benutzt sind, nächst Seitenrefraktionen des Lichtes und Auffassungsfehlern der Heliotropenlichter, sowie vielleicht einzelnen Centrirungsunsicherheiten, besonders die Theilungsfehler der Kreise betrachtet werden.”
In English: “As causes of that effect, since heliotropes were used almost exclusively as pointing targets, one must consider, besides lateral refractions of the light and errors of perception of the heliotrope lights, and perhaps single centring uncertainties, above all the graduation errors of the circles.”
Helmert, F. R. (Ed.). (1893). Die europäische Längengradmessung in 52 Grad Breite von Greenwich bis Warschau. I. Heft: Hauptdreiecke und Grundlinienanschlüsse von England bis Polen. P. Stankiewicz., p. 97

Triangles 33 and 34 on the Carangooly to Maillacherry line, used for the degree perpendicular to the meridian. Lambton computed the side Curnatighur to Carangooly from a northern chain started on another side and compared it with the value from the main chain.

“Upon the distance from Curnatighur to Maillacherry as a base, the distance from Curnatighur to Carangooly has been computed, and differs only two feet from that derived from the side Carangooly and Maillacherry Droog: but there was some variation in the angles taken at Poonauk hill, which renders it doubtful, for the present, which to select; I have therefore relied on the single distance given in the thirty-fourth triangle.”

Old and new surveys differ more in heights than in latitude, longitude, azimuth or distance
Great Arc of India, Lambton's meridional arc (Coromandel coast to Punnae and north to about 18 N) · Appendix p. 36 · strength ★★

Same appendix, one page earlier, introducing Lambton's letter. The 1890 editors compare Lambton's heights with the modern re-survey and state that vertical (height) results disagree more than horizontal results. This separates the uncertainty of vertical refraction from the horizontal network.

“One of the greatest difficulties, that confronted all surveyors at the commencement of this century, was the satisfactory determination of the heights of their stations by means of the vertical angles. Very little was known of the laws of refraction in Europe, and still less of its effect in tropical countries. In comparing results obtained by the old and recent Trigonometrical Surveys of India, wider discrepancies are found to exist between the two values of altitude for the same station, than between those of latitude, longitude, azimuth or distance.”

Walker on the Great Arc south of Daumergida. The Royal Society recommended re-measurement; the Bangalore base was already checked. He states that the early triangles had fewer observations and sometimes only two measured angles, which later practice replaced with three angles and polygonal figures.

“The sections of the Great Arc from Daumergida southwards to Punnoe are being re-measured at the present time, at the recommendation of the President and Council of the Royal Society, but the undertaking is not yet sufficiently advanced to permit of the results being closely compared with those of the early operations, excepting at the Bangalore base, the error of which has been found to be about the 1/12,000th part of it's length. [...] It is known that in the early operations the observations were very few and not so systematic as afterwards; in several cases only two of the angles of the principal triangles were measured, whereas subsequently all three angles were measured,”

Walker quotes Lambton's manuscript General Report on how he measured the horizontal angles of this period (1802-1808). It adds his method when a triangle did not close: each angle in turn was held correct and the sides were recomputed, and no angle was dropped without cause.

““ As to the angles in general they have been taken three and four times, and every time that the object was observed, both microscopes were read off thrice, and two separate field-books kept for making out the angles. [...] This however has rarely happened, and when it did, great precaution was used, and no angle was rejected without some reason appeared to render it doubtful”.”

GTS Karachi Longitudinal Series (North-West Quadrilateral) · p. VIII-D · strength ★★

Introduction to the Indus Series in the same volume. Spirit levelling measures heights directly with a level and staff, without vertical angles. It was used where rays would graze the ground over about 400 miles.

“The circumstance which has already been mentioned that nearly 400 miles of the triangulation would have to pass over a perfectly level plain, without hills and almost without any mounds, led to the initiation of operations for determining the heights of the stations in the plains by the method of spirit-leveling; for it was feared that, with rays grazing the surface of the ground so closely, the vertical angles measured in the triangulation would be so much affected by the very considerable variations of terrestrial refraction to which they would be liable, that a considerable amount of error might be generated in the course of operations carried over so great a distance under such unfavorable circumstances.”
Walker, J. T. (Ed.). (1873). Account of the operations of the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India, Vol. III: The principal triangulation, North-West Quadrilateral. Dehra Dun: Great Trigonometrical Survey., p. VIII-D

Preface to Vol. III. The absolute heights are referred to Karachi mean sea level; between stations fixed by spirit levelling, the error that the vertical angles produced is spread over the intermediate stations.

“and the remainder by referring the trigonometrical differences of height to the nearest stations whose absolute heights were determined by the spirit-leveling operations. The errors generated trigonometrically, between any two spirit-leveled stations, have been dispersed by simple proportion over the intermediate trigonometrical values.”
Walker, J. T. (Ed.). (1873). Account of the operations of the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India, Vol. III: The principal triangulation, North-West Quadrilateral. Dehra Dun: Great Trigonometrical Survey., p. xiii

Mount Diablo was occupied in three different years by different observers, so its directions rest on independent campaigns.

Part I, adjustment of the Salt Lake base net. Schott computes the probable error of a direction from the station abstracts and three times from the net (from the direction corrections, the angle corrections and the triangle closing errors), then names the causes of the difference, including persistent lateral refraction.

“We thus find the probable error of a direction e_t as derived from the corrections demanded by the adjustment of the base net = +/- 0".28 and the same e_s as derived from the station adjustment = +/- 0".09; the fact that e_t is three times as great as e_s is attributed mainly to the effect of local deflections in measuring angles, the vertical axis of the theodolite being necessarily adjusted to the plumb-line. Besides, a very careful adjustment of the instrument is required when the station observed upon is considerably above or below the one occupied. Persistent lateral refraction also has a share in producing the above result.”
Worked out here: Net error not explained by station scatter: sqrt(0.28^2 - 0.09^2) = 0.27" (Schott prints the same value).
Schott, C. A. (1900). The transcontinental triangulation and the American arc of the parallel (Special Publication No. 4). U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey; Government Printing Office., p. 206

Before 1890 Peirce's criterion used to reject directions; since 1890 no rejections and least-squares figure adjustment
Trigonometrical Survey of New South Wales · pp. 182-183 · strength ★★
Rejecting readings in unsteady air

Computation of triangulation (pp. 182-183). Before 1890 observed directions were tested with Peirce's criterion for rejection. After 1890 the practice of other major surveys was followed: no rejection for apparent discordance (disagreement), local adjustment at each station, and adjustment of the figures by least squares. No PDF of this paper is in the project; the item points to the OCR text file, so no crop is possible. The p. 182 part was checked against a page image held elsewhere in the project; the p. 183 part is from the text layer.

“Prior to 1890, when the survey was resumed after having been in abeyance some years, the azimuthal directions derived immediately from the observations were tabulated, without adjustment for correction of reading or bisection of referring mark, and Peirce's criterion was applied in order to determine whether any should be rejected; also, in the computation, no adjustment for "figure" conditions was made except in the case of one or two quadrilaterals. In the primary work done since the year named, the practice in other surveys of similar importance of making local adjustment and permitting no rejections on account of apparent discordance has been followed, and, in the series of triangles south from the Lake George base to the boundary of the Colony, adjustment to meet the geometrical conditions of such figure has been made by the method of least squares.”

What repeating an angle does and does not remove
Middleton, Chadwick and Bogle, A Treatise on Surveying (textbook) · p. 191 · strength ★★
Repetition over days and hours

The authors explain the limits of repetition: it reduces graduation and pointing errors, but past a point it stops helping, and it cannot remove a displaced signal. This is why the surveys also changed the circle zero, the hour and the day, rather than only repeating on one occasion.

“There is a limit beyond which repetition produces no improvement. Errors due to slip and flexure, accumulate and prevent extreme accuracy, though a moderate number of repetitions reduce graduation error, by measuring the angle at different parts of the circle. To some extent it reduces errors in bisecting the objects aimed at, for it is reasonable to suppose that the cross-wire will not be always laid on the same side of the true centre. Repetition, however, does not eliminate the most serious source of error of all, namely displacement of the signal observed to.”
Middleton, R. E., Chadwick, O., & Bogle, J. du T. (1904). A treatise on surveying: Part I (2nd ed.). E. & F. N. Spon., p. 191
The reciprocal correction carries every error of observation
Middleton, Chadwick and Bogle, A Treatise on Surveying (textbook) · p. 226 · strength ★★

A caution printed right after the method: the refraction value found from reciprocal angles also contains any other error in those angles. It is a measured total, not a separated physical term. Table K (from the Manual of Surveying for India) gives the combined curvature and refraction correction for short distances in chains.

“It must not be forgotten that the correction thus obtained, includes all errors of observation. 'Refraction' has also the effect of reducing the 'curvature' already treated of. Usually it reduces it by about one-seventh of its true value.”
Reading the table. Table K: distance in chains (1 chain = 66 ft), the curvature correction in decimals of a foot, and the combined curvature-and-refraction correction. The refraction column is about 1/7 smaller than the curvature column.

By method

Steady-air hours 72 items · 20 surveys

Observing only in the hours when the air near the ground was calmest.

Delambre's two remedies against a possible lateral refraction: wait for favourable moments, and repeat at different hours and conditions
Delambre and Méchain, meridian arc Dunkirk to Barcelona (Base du système métrique) · T1 Discours préliminaire p. 106 · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours Repetition over days and hours Night lamps and heliotropes

Discours préliminaire, section on signals. Lateral refraction is a sideways bend of the line of sight, which would change horizontal angles. Delambre says he was at times tempted to believe in it, that night lamps would be equally subject to it, and that the defence is to observe at good moments and to repeat at other hours and in other conditions, so that a sideways error does not repeat in the same direction.

“S'il existe une réfraction latérale, comme j'ai été par fois tenté de le croire, les réverbères y seroient également sujets, et l'on n'a pour se garantir de cette illusion que deux moyens qui ne sont pas infaillibles, l'un est d'attendre les instans favorables ; l'autre, de répéter les observations à des heures et dans des circonstances différentes.”
In English: “If a lateral refraction exists, as I have at times been tempted to believe, reverberatory lamps would be equally subject to it, and there are only two means, not infallible, to guard against this illusion: one is to wait for favourable moments; the other, to repeat the observations at different hours and in different circumstances.”
Méchain, P., & Delambre, J.-B. J. (1806). Base du système métrique décimal, ou mesure de l'arc du méridien compris entre les parallèles de Dunkerque et Barcelone (Vol. 1). Paris: Baudouin., T1 Discours préliminaire p. 106
Zenith distances: one series of ten per target, more when doubtful; in bad weather angles were repeated instead; the zenith distance nearest in hour to the angle was used
Delambre and Méchain, meridian arc Dunkirk to Barcelona (Base du système métrique) · T1 Discours préliminaire p. 113 · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours Repetition over days and hours

Discours préliminaire, section Observations. A zenith distance is the vertical angle between the plumb-line direction straight up (the zenith) and the target. A series is a run of repeated readings on the repeating circle; ten angles means the circle was turned ten times and the total divided by ten. Delambre gives his rule and the reason: in bad weather the variations of refraction make zenith distances less sure. For steep sights he took the zenith distance just before or after the angle, or at several hours, and used the one nearest in time. Méchain repeated zenith distances more than Delambre.

“je me suis contenté de faire pour chaque distance au zénith une seule série de dix angles, excepté dans les cas où quelque circonstance rendoit l'observation douteuse. Quand le temps étoit beau, j'aimois mieux répéter l'observation des angles de position, et, s'il étoit mauvais, les variations de la réfraction terrestre auroient rendu les distances au zénith plus incertaines. Quand ces distances sont plus grandes que 91 degrés, ou plus petites que 89, il conviendroit de les observer en même temps que l'angle de position ; mais cela n'est guère possible. Il falloit donc se contenter de les observer immédiatement avant ou après, ou à plusieurs heures du jour, afin de choisir pour la réduction des angles à l'horizon la distance dont l'heure étoit la plus voisine, et où l'on avoit lieu de croire la réfraction terrestre moins différente.”
In English: “I was content to make for each zenith distance a single series of ten angles, except in cases where some circumstance made the observation doubtful. When the weather was fine I preferred to repeat the observation of the angles of position, and if it was bad, the variations of terrestrial refraction would have made the zenith distances more uncertain. When these distances are greater than 91 degrees or less than 89, they should be observed at the same time as the angle of position; but that is hardly possible. So one had to be content to observe them immediately before or after, or at several hours of the day, in order to choose for the reduction of the angles to the horizon the distance whose hour was nearest, and where there was reason to believe the terrestrial refraction least different.”
Méchain, P., & Delambre, J.-B. J. (1806). Base du système métrique décimal, ou mesure de l'arc du méridien compris entre les parallèles de Dunkerque et Barcelone (Vol. 1). Paris: Baudouin., T1 Discours préliminaire p. 113

“D. n° 1 + première place. Grand vent ; Sauti foible et courbe ; ondulations au Mesnil ; fils en + série à rejeter. ... Le clocher de Sauti et les flèches voisines nous ont fort exercés par leurs phases différentes. ... D. n° 1. 3 juillet, 5h 40' — 7h 20'. Objets éclairés du soleil ; Sauti tout-à-fait courbe. ... F. n° 4. 4 juillet, 3h 10' — 5h 45'. Objets assez beaux en commençant ; ils l'étoient moins vers le milieu.”
In English: “D. circle no. 1, first place. Strong wind; Sauti faint and curved; undulations at Mesnil; wires in +; series to be rejected. ... The steeple of Sauti and the neighbouring spires gave us much trouble by their different phases. ... D. circle no. 1. 3 July, 5h 40' to 7h 20'. Objects lit by the sun; Sauti quite curved. ... F. circle no. 4. 4 July, 3h 10' to 5h 45'. Objects rather fine at the start; less so towards the middle.”
Reading the table. Each block is one series: first number = repetitions (20 or 12 here); then the total arc in grades, the single angle in grades, and the same in degrees; the line 'Au centre' gives the angle reduced to the centre of the station. Below: circle and observer, date, hours, remarks on the air. The angle between Mesnil and Sauti has three series of 20; the mean of the first three is reduced to the horizon (+0.58") to give 42° 59' 48.72". Bonnières-Sauti has series of 20, 20 and 12 on 3 and 4 July at different hours. A typical angle in Delambre's north part has 2 to 5 series of 12 to 30 repetitions (e.g. Dunkerque, Watten-Cassel: 20 + 16 + 30).
Worked out here: Mesnil-Sauti series reduced to centre: 42° 59' 49.68" and 42° 59' 55.07" (the rejected series is 5.4" higher).

Tome I, station of Boiscommun (frimaire an 2, December 1793). Delambre observed the zenith distance of the weathercock of Châteauneuf on seven days, one series of ten each, and printed with each the hour, the barometer (in pouces and lignes), the thermometer (as a fraction of the ice-to-boiling interval, converted to Réaumur degrees), and the sky: rain, fine or poor horizon, damp fog. He also stayed half an hour at the telescope to see whether refraction changed the distance. This is a direct record of humidity and pressure with each vertical angle.

“24 frimaire, 12h ¼. Bar. 27p 1l9. Therm. 0.099 = 7d92. A 1h ¼ la distance étoit encore la même. ... Le baromètre et le thermomètre étoient placés environ 1t8 au-dessous de la lunette. Après ces observations je suis resté pendant une demi-heure à la lunette, pour voir si la réfraction ne changeroit pas la distance : je n'ai pas vu la moindre variation. Horizon très-pur, point de soleil. ... 25 frimaire, 3h ¾. Bar. 27p 4l. Therm. + 0.11 = 8d8. Temps pluvieux ; horizon assez beau. ... 30 frimaire, 3h ½. Bar. 27p 3l. Therm. + 0.067 = 5d36. Brouillard humide.”
In English: “24 frimaire, 12h ¼. Barometer 27 pouces 1.9 lignes. Thermometer 0.099 = 7.92 degrees. At 1h ¼ the distance was still the same. ... The barometer and thermometer were placed about 1.8 toises below the telescope. After these observations I stayed half an hour at the telescope to see whether refraction would change the distance: I did not see the least variation. Very clear horizon, no sun. ... 25 frimaire, 3h ¾. Barometer 27 pouces 4 lignes. Thermometer +0.11 = 8.8 degrees. Rainy weather; horizon fairly fine. ... 30 frimaire, 3h ½. Barometer 27 pouces 3 lignes. Thermometer +0.067 = 5.36 degrees. Damp fog.”
Reading the table. Each line: number of repetitions (10), total arc in grades, single zenith distance in grades, the same in degrees; then date, hour, barometer, thermometer, remarks. Seven series on seven days (24 to 30 frimaire) to the same target. The page continues on p. 167 with 1, 2 and 7 nivôse.
Worked out here: Seven zenith distances of the Châteauneuf weathercock range from 90° 5' 46.0" (28 frimaire) to 90° 6' 6.1" (30 frimaire, damp fog): spread 20.1".

Tome I, station of Rieupeyroux in Méchain's southern part (thermidor an 6, July-August 1798; M. et A. = Méchain and his assistant). Each target has two series of ten on different days and hours, with the thermometer reading and remarks: calm or strong wind, sun or shade, undulations or none. The mean is then corrected for half the wire thickness and for the height of the signal (dH) 'for the level difference and the refraction'.

“M. et A. 24 thermidor, à 5h ½ du soir. Thermomètre + 13d6 en 80d. Calme. L'objet est dans l'ombre ; on le voit bien. ... M. et A. 18 thermidor, à 6h ¼ du soir. Thermomètre 15d0. Soleil. Le grand vent agite le niveau, et le signal est difficile à distinguer. ... M. et A. 21 thermidor, à 7h ¾ du matin. Thermomètre 15d0. Calme. Objet assez net ; il n'y a point d'ondulations.”
In English: “M. and A., 24 thermidor, at 5h ½ in the evening. Thermometer +13.6 degrees (80-degree scale). Calm. The object is in shadow; it is seen well. ... M. and A., 18 thermidor, at 6h ¼ in the evening. Thermometer 15.0 degrees. Sun. The strong wind shakes the level, and the signal is hard to make out. ... M. and A., 21 thermidor, at 7h ¾ in the morning. Thermometer 15.0 degrees. Calm. Object fairly sharp; there are no undulations.”
Reading the table. Per target (Rodez statue, signal of La Gaste): two series of 10, each with date, hour (evening and morning), thermometer and remarks. 'Milieu des deux séries' / 'Moyenne' = mean used for the reduction to the horizon; then 'Demi-épaisseur du fil' (half wire thickness, +3") and dH (signal height correction) give the value used 'pour la différence de niveau et la réfraction'.
Worked out here: La Gaste: evening series 89° 57' 37.9", morning series 89° 57' 27.2"; difference 10.7".

Montjouy tower: six sea-horizon heights compared with a direct levelling; the levelling is kept
Delambre and Méchain, meridian arc Dunkirk to Barcelona (Base du système métrique) · T2 p. 759 · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours Raw tables of repeated measures

Tome II, heights above the Mediterranean. The height of the battlements of the Montjouy tower had been measured by direct levelling (105.1 toises). Delambre computes it again from six zenith distances of the sea horizon and prints each result. The mean agrees with the levelling within 0.5 toise, but single values scatter. He states the observations were all near sunset, when refraction raises the sea, and that one isolated sea-horizon observation can be wrong by 5 to 6 toises; he keeps the levelling.

“toutes ces observations ayant été faites vers le coucher du soleil, la réfraction devoit élever la mer plus que dans l'état moyen et faire paroître la hauteur de la tour trop petite. Elles prouvent qu'une observation de l'horizon de la mer prise isolément peut donner une erreur de 5 à 6 toises. Nous nous en tiendrons donc au résultat du nivellement”
In English: “all these observations having been made towards sunset, refraction must have raised the sea more than in the mean state and made the height of the tower appear too small. They prove that an isolated observation of the sea horizon can give an error of 5 to 6 toises. We shall therefore keep to the result of the levelling”
Reading the table. Columns: zenith distance of the sea horizon (90° 23' to 90° 25'); height computed with n = 0.08 and the correction for each; resulting height H in toises (100.5 to 107.5). Milieu 105.2; plus 0.4 for half the wire thickness gives 105.6, against Nivellement 105.1; difference 0.5 toise.

Instruction of the commission of the Dépôt de la Guerre for the new map of France, printed by Puissant. It sets the observing rules for the first-order chains, including the parallel of Paris. A conjugate observation is one repetition of the angle on the repeating circle. Simultaneous observations are reciprocal zenith distances taken at both ends at the same time, so that both see the same state of the air.

“Les distances zénithales relatives à ces chaînes seront elles-mêmes le résultat de trois séries au moins, prises à des heures différentes, et surtout vers le milieu du jour, afin qu'elles puissent donner les différences de niveau avec toute l'exactitude désirable, et, autant qu'il sera possible, par le concours d'observations simultanées : celles-ci seront accompagnées d'observations barométriques. ... Toutes les séries du premier ordre seront, autant que possible, prolongées jusqu'à la vingtième observation conjuguée ; toutes celles du deuxième ordre s'arrêteront à la dixième.”
In English: “The zenith distances for these chains will themselves be the result of at least three series, taken at different hours, and above all towards the middle of the day, so that they can give the level differences with all desirable accuracy, and, as far as possible, by the combination of simultaneous observations: these will be accompanied by barometric observations. ... All first-order series will, as far as possible, be carried to the twentieth conjugate observation; all those of the second order will stop at the tenth.”
Puissant, L. (1832). Nouvelle description géométrique de la France (Première partie). Paris: Ch. Picquet., 28
Night observations on lamps shortly after sunset gave much larger discordances than day observations (horizontal angles)

Puissant, p. 35, describing the Brest-Strasbourg line. A discordance is the disagreement between repeated measures of the same quantity. On this page the discordances belong to the night observations made with lamps as signals, that is, the angles between signals of the triangles: the next sentence turns to the zenith distances as a separate set ('C'est aussi sur cette même ligne qu'ont été observées des distances zénithales réciproques et simultanées'). Puissant confirms the reading on p. 156, where he says that with lamps 'les erreurs des triangles n'ont pas été moindres que de coutume' for the horizontal angles. The night zenith distances of the eastern part were also rejected, for their own discordance (p. 208, item fr_par_06).

“C'est sur une grande partie de cette ligne, confiée, dès l'origine des travaux, à MM. les colonels Bonne et Henry, que des réverbères ont été employés pour signaux ; mais les observations nocturnes, à peu d'intervalle du coucher du soleil, ont souvent présenté des discordances beaucoup plus considérables que celles faites de jour. C'est aussi sur cette même ligne qu'ont été observées des distances zénithales réciproques et simultanées, afin de connaître avec toute la précision désirable les hauteurs des stations depuis le Panthéon jusqu'à Brest.”
In English: “It is on a large part of this line, entrusted from the start of the work to Colonels Bonne and Henry, that lamps were used as signals; but the night observations, shortly after sunset, often showed much larger discordances than those made by day. It is also on this same line that reciprocal and simultaneous zenith distances were observed, in order to know with all desirable precision the heights of the stations from the Panthéon to Brest.”
Puissant, L. (1832). Nouvelle description géométrique de la France (Première partie). Paris: Ch. Picquet., 35
With lamps the triangle errors were no smaller than usual: night horizontal angles are as much affected by refraction as day ones, sometimes more in low places
Parallel of Paris, Brest to Strasbourg (Henry east part, Bonne west part), Nouvelle carte de France · 156 · strength ★★★
Night lamps and heliotropes Steady-air hours

Puissant, chapter on the probable error of an arc. The triangle errors (closure errors: the amount by which the three angles miss 180 degrees plus the spherical excess) are a direct test of the horizontal angles. Puissant uses them to judge the night method recommended by Laplace and finds no gain, with a larger effect in low ground between Paris and Strasbourg.

“Malgré l'usage que l'on fit de réverbères pour points de mire, dans cette partie de la méridienne, les erreurs des triangles n'ont pas été moindres que de coutume ; ainsi les observations nocturnes des angles horizontaux qui avaient été recommandées par le célèbre Laplace, sont tout aussi influencées par les effets de la réfraction atmosphérique que celles de jour, si même elles ne le sont quelquefois davantage dans les lieux bas, comme on l'a remarqué, ainsi que nous l'avons déjà dit, entre Paris et Strasbourg, lors de la mesure du parallèle compris entre ces deux villes.”
In English: “Despite the use of lamps as targets in this part of the meridian, the errors of the triangles were no smaller than usual; thus the night observations of horizontal angles, which had been recommended by the celebrated Laplace, are just as influenced by the effects of atmospheric refraction as those by day, if indeed they are not sometimes more so in low places, as was remarked, as we have already said, between Paris and Strasbourg, during the measurement of the parallel between these two towns.”
Puissant, L. (1832). Nouvelle description géométrique de la France (Première partie). Paris: Ch. Picquet., 156

Puissant, eastern part of the parallel (Colonel Henry, from 1818). The first-order angles were observed at night at Laplace's wish. Comparable zenith distances (those that should agree, such as the reciprocal pair on one line) disagreed so much that the night zenith distances were rejected and the heights were taken from day measures at second-order stations tied to the first-order ones.

“Le premier des deux tableaux ci-après présente l'ensemble des triangles du premier ordre dont les angles furent observés de nuit, dès l'année 1818, d'après le désir de l'illustre président de la commission royale, dans l'espérance qu'il en résulterait une plus grande exactitude. Mais l'énorme discordance que présentèrent sur cette ligne la plupart des distances zénithales comparables, mirent dans la nécessité de rejeter ces observations nocturnes pour déterminer les différences de niveau par d'autres mesures angulaires recueillies de jour, à différentes stations du second ordre, liées à celles du premier ordre.”
In English: “The first of the two tables below presents all the first-order triangles whose angles were observed at night, from 1818, at the wish of the illustrious president of the royal commission, in the hope of greater accuracy. But the enormous discordance shown on this line by most of the comparable zenith distances made it necessary to reject these night observations and to determine the level differences by other angular measures taken by day at various second-order stations tied to the first-order ones.”
Puissant, L. (1832). Nouvelle description géométrique de la France (Première partie). Paris: Ch. Picquet., 208

Brousseaud, narrative of the French part (1811-1823). A repetition is one turn of the repeating circle; a series is the set of repetitions whose total gives one value of the angle. Because results sometimes varied even when the view seemed the same, the number of series for each angle was set by how far the first five or six series disagreed. The sentence continues on p. 158 (item fr_45n_02).

“A cet effet on prit la résolution, ainsi qu'il a été déjà signalé page 32, de multiplier les observations d'angles entre les objets terrestres trente fois au moins par chaque série, et de répéter ces séries à des heures et à des jours différens. On avait remarqué depuis long-temps que, malgré tous les soins apportés dans les observations angulaires, les résultats variaient quelquefois d'une quantité considérable, quoique les circonstances de la vision parussent les mêmes. En conséquence le nombre des séries jugées nécessaires à la mesure d'un angle fut déterminé par le nombre de secondes dont les cinq ou six premiers résultats différaient entre eux”
In English: “To this end it was resolved, as already noted on page 32, to multiply the observations of angles between terrestrial objects at least thirty times per series, and to repeat these series at different hours and on different days. It had long been noticed that, despite all the care taken in angular observations, the results sometimes varied by a considerable amount, although the conditions of vision seemed the same. Consequently the number of series judged necessary for the measurement of an angle was set by the number of seconds by which the first five or six results differed among themselves”
Brousseaud (Colonel). (1839). Mesure d'un arc du parallèle moyen entre le pôle et l'équateur. Limoges: F. Chapoulaud., 157

Brousseaud, p. 158. A zenith distance is the vertical angle between the plumb-line direction straight up (the zenith) and the target. The hours near noon were chosen because vertical refraction is then smallest and steadiest. Six to eight series of ten single angles give 60 to 80 readings per zenith distance.

“Les distances au zénith de l'extrémité des signaux ont toujours été prises entre onze heures et une heure du soir, et répétées au moins par six ou huit séries de dix angles simples chaque.”
In English: “The zenith distances of the tops of the signals were always taken between eleven o'clock and one in the afternoon, and repeated in at least six or eight series of ten single angles each.”

Brousseaud, summary of the three parts of the arc of the mean parallel. For the French part (34 triangles, Mont Granier to Marennes) the author states the number of series and repetitions, that every series was kept in the mean without exception, and the largest triangle closure error (the amount by which the sum of the three angles missed its true value).

“Les valeurs des angles ont été déterminées par six, huit, dix, douze quatorze séries de trente à quarante répétitions chaque, faites à des jours et à des heures différens. Les distances au zénith ont aussi été répétées de soixante à cent fois, entre onze heures et midi, afin d'avoir avec exactitude la hauteur absolue des signaux placés sur les hautes montagnes de la France et de la Savoie. Le résultat adopté pour chaque angle de ces trente-quatre triangles provient de la moyenne entre tous les résultats fournis par les séries relatives à cet angle, et prises sans exception. Cependant, malgré ces soins, la plus grande erreur de la somme des trois angles des triangles s'élève encore à 4" de degré.”
In English: “The values of the angles were determined by six, eight, ten, twelve, fourteen series of thirty to forty repetitions each, made on different days and at different hours. The zenith distances were also repeated sixty to a hundred times, between eleven and noon, to obtain accurately the absolute height of the signals placed on the high mountains of France and Savoy. The result adopted for each angle of these thirty-four triangles is the mean of all the results given by the series for that angle, taken without exception. Yet, despite these precautions, the largest error of the sum of the three angles of the triangles still reaches 4" of a degree.”
Worked out here: 6 to 14 series x 30 to 40 repetitions = 180 to 560 repetitions per angle.

Heights by reciprocal zenith distances from the Cordouan tower to Colombier and Granier; a 9 m discordance traced and removed; coefficient between 0.0563 and 0.097, generally 0.08
Brousseaud, arc of the mean parallel (45 N) across France, with link to the Austro-Sardinian chain · 160 · strength ★★★
Vertical refraction coefficients Steady-air hours

Brousseaud, p. 160. The absolute heights of the chain come from a succession of reciprocal zenith distances starting at the Cordouan lighthouse (68.445 m above mean sea, mean of four measures). Reciprocal zenith distances are taken from each end of a line toward the other; their sum exceeds 180 degrees by the arc between the two verticals, less the bend of the ray at both ends, so the pair measures the refraction on that line itself. Each height is the mean of two results that rarely differ by more than a metre. A discordance of about 9 m at the east end was traced to long sights from Bossivre and to signal caps too small to see at noon, and Puissant removed it by using heights from other stations. The coefficient of refraction found along the whole levelling lies between 0.0563 and 0.097.

“Partant de ce point, chacune des hauteurs absolues rapportées dans le deuxième tableau est la moyenne entre deux résultats, dont la différence dépasse rarement un mètre (1). ... a cependant présenté une discordance qui s'est accrue de 9m environ à l'extrémité orientale de la chaîne ... 2° que, sur toute son étendue, la valeur du coefficient de la réfraction est renfermée entre 0,0563 et 0,097, et se trouve généralement de 0,08, ainsi que Delambre l'avait déduit de ses observations.”
In English: “Starting from this point, each of the absolute heights given in the second table is the mean of two results whose difference rarely exceeds one metre (1). ... nevertheless showed a discordance that grew to about 9 m at the eastern end of the chain ... 2nd that, over its whole extent, the value of the coefficient of refraction lies between 0.0563 and 0.097, and is generally 0.08, as Delambre had deduced from his observations.”
Brousseaud (Colonel). (1839). Mesure d'un arc du parallèle moyen entre le pôle et l'équateur. Limoges: F. Chapoulaud., 160
Roy: in hot weather only short morning and evening periods were good enough; a whole day could go for one satisfactory angle
Anglo-French triangulation of 1787 (Greenwich to Paris junction), English side by Roy · p. 170 · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours Repetition over days and hours Rejecting readings in unsteady air

Roy, Art. I of the section on the triangles, explaining why the angles were repeated less often than planned. 'Tremulous motion or boiling in the air' is the shimmer caused by heated air near the ground, which makes a distant object dance in the telescope. Roy observed only when the objects were distinct, and he did not change the zero (the starting point on the divided circle) at those times because each change needed a new levelling of the instrument.

“At particular times, especially in hot weather, there was such a tremulous motion or boiling in the air, that it was only during a very short space, chiefly in the mornings and evenings, that the objects were sufficiently distinct to be observed with accuracy. So difficult it is to do any thing perfectly good in this way, that a whole day has frequently been spent, after watching with anxious care, in obtaining a single one that was perfectly satisfactory!”
Roy, W. (1790). An account of the trigonometrical operation, whereby the distance between the meridians of the Royal Observatories of Greenwich and Paris has been determined. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, 80, 111-270 (with Dalby, I., Remarks, pp. 593-614)., p. 170

Steady-air hours

Account of the work of 1792. The sentence ends on p. 457 with 'without that quivering motion, which, in summer, it generally has in the middle of the day.' The observers chose the time of day by the state of the air: vapour (moisture haze) and quivering (heat shimmer) were both avoided.

“That the bearings of those might be taken with precision, the observations were made either in the morning or evening, when the air was free from vapour, and without that quivering motion, which, in summer, it generally has in the middle of the day.”
Williams, E., Mudge, W., & Dalby, I. (1795). An account of the trigonometrical survey carried on in the years 1791, 1792, 1793, and 1794. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, 85, 414-591., pp. 456-457

Art. on the angles observed in 1793. For each station the angle between two objects is printed with each separate value read and the mean in the right-hand column. Reading the table. Same remarks. The sentence before records that at one station the depression of Chanctonbury Ring varied from 1' 41" to 2' 30" (repeated observations of one angle). The authors state when the tabled observations were made, and they reject the idea that pressure and temperature at the station explain the changes when the ray runs close to the ground.

“The observations, however, on which the tables are founded, were made in close cloudy days, or toward the evenings, when the tremulous motion in the air is commonly the least. It has been conjectured, that the variations in terrestrial refraction, depend on the changes in the atmosphere indicated by the barometer and thermometer: this, however, cannot be the case when the rays of light pass near the earth's surface for any considerable distance.”

Mudge (1801), on refraction. Simultaneous reciprocal observation means that each of two stations measures the vertical angle to the other at the same moment, so that both ends see the same state of the air. Mr. Woolcot observed at one station and Mudge at the other. The times were kept by watches regulated from altitudes of the sun and by signal.

“On these occasions, the instructions which I communicated to Mr. Woolcot, and by which I governed myself, were to observe the elevation or depression of the corresponding station at the expiration of every hour, beginning at six A. M. and to have the watch well regulated from observed altitudes of the sun's limb. I requested him also to be very minute in entering on his book the state of the weather; to keep the instrument properly sheltered from the wind; to be always cautious to adjust his level; and also to insert the state of the air, as to temperature and density, by noting the thermometer and barometer.”
Mudge, W. (1801). An account of the operations carried on for accomplishing a trigonometrical survey of England and Wales, continued from the year 1797, to the end of the year 1799 (Vol. 2, from the Philosophical Transactions). London: W. Faden., p. 183

Introduction, paragraph on refraction. On p. xv the refraction 'in a normal state of the atmosphere' is given as 1/15.4 to 1/9.4 of the angle at the earth's centre, mean 1/12.6; the passage continues here with the extreme cases and the cause of the daily change. Aqueous vapour is water vapour, the humidity of the air.

“The great amount of refraction in the morning, its diminution towards the middle of the day, and its increase again towards evening, is obviously caused by the greater amount of aqueous vapour in the lower portion of the atmosphere in the morning and evening, as compared with the amount in the middle of the day.”

Steady-air hours

Same section. A smaller zenith distance means the object looks higher, that is, more refraction. Clarke states the daily pattern from the survey records, names an exception (Hart Fell, double refraction from 1 to 3 p.m. in September), and in a footnote gives Hossard's half-hourly series at Angoulême (refraction nearly constant from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.).

“When observations are recorded as having been taken at some early hour in the morning, as 5 A.M., and from that time until 8 A.M., they almost invariably show a smaller zenith distance than during any other part of the day; sometimes the difference is very considerable, and shows that no vertical observations should be taken early in the morning.”
Clarke, A. R. (1858). Ordnance trigonometrical survey of Great Britain and Ireland: Account of the observations and calculations of the principal triangulation. London: Eyre and Spottiswoode., p. 511
Clarke 1880: the daily cycle of refraction, greatest at daybreak and nearly constant from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.
Textbook guidance of the period on terrestrial refraction · p. 281 · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours

Same chapter. This gives the observing window used to choose hours for vertical angles: refraction changes fast in the early morning and is steady in the middle of the day.

“In Great Britain the refraction is greatest in the early mornings; towards the middle of the day it decreases, again to increase in the evenings—but this rule is not without remarkable exceptions. From a series of carefully conducted observations by Colonel Hossard at Angouleme it appeared that refraction is greatest about daybreak; from 5 or 6 A.M. until 8 A.M. it diminishes very rapidly; from 8 A.M. until 10 A.M. the diminution is slow; from this hour until 4 P.M. the refraction remains nearly constant; after that it commences to increase.”
Clarke, A. R. (1880). Geodesy. Oxford: Clarendon Press., p. 281

Tome I, Chapter I, on the signals of the Baltic arc. The signals were painted dark so that the vertical beam, not the sunlit face of the pyramid, was pointed. A phase is a false apparent centre of a target caused by side lighting. Struve states that angle measurement had already stopped before sunset, because the images then always undulate, and gives the summer period of calm images as 0.5 to 0.8 of the interval from noon to sunset.

“Mais à cette époque la mesure des angles a déjà cessé, parce que près du coucher du soleil les objets sont toujours très ondulants, le calme des images ayant lieu en été, dans nos climats, entre 0,5 à 0,8 de l'intervalle de temps entre midi et le coucher du soleil.”
In English: “But at that time the measurement of the angles has already stopped, because near sunset the objects are always very undulating, the calm of the images taking place in summer, in our climates, between 0.5 and 0.8 of the interval of time between noon and sunset.”
Struve, F. G. W. (1857). Arc du méridien de 25° 20' entre le Danube et la Mer Glaciale mesuré depuis 1816 jusqu'en 1855 (Vol. 1). Imprimerie de l'Académie impériale des sciences., T. I, p. 14

Struve Geodetic Arc (Russo-Scandinavian arc of the meridian, Danube to Fuglenaes) · T. I, p. 32 · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours Repetition over days and hours

Tome I, Chapter IV. A set (mise) is one complete round of pointings. Struve counts 833 sets for the 141 Livonian directions (5.91 per direction) against 41.77 per direction in Bessel's East Prussian survey. He then compares the two surveys by their triangle closures (the excess of the angle sum over 180 degrees plus the spherical excess): mean square 0.987 for 31 Livonian triangles and 1.179 for Bessel's 15. From this he finds one Livonian set equal in weight to 8.44 Prussian sets, and he states the Livonian rule: measure only with sufficiently distinct images, in practice in the 2-hour afternoon period of calm images.

“En Livonie la règle a été strictement observée, de ne jamais faire des mesures que par des images suffisamment distinctes des objets, c'est-à-dire presque exclusivement pendant la période de 2 heures des images calmes, qui d'ordinaire a lieu chaque après-midi (Gradmessung I. p. 88).”
In English: “In Livonia the rule was strictly kept never to make measurements except with sufficiently distinct images of the objects, that is, almost exclusively during the 2-hour period of calm images which usually occurs every afternoon (Gradmessung I. p. 88).”
Worked out here: 41.77 / 5.91 = 7.07 (printed 7.07). Weight ratio printed: 41.77 × 1.179 : 5.91 × 0.987 = 8.44 : 1.
Struve, F. G. W. (1857). Arc du méridien de 25° 20' entre le Danube et la Mer Glaciale mesuré depuis 1816 jusqu'en 1855 (Vol. 1). Imprimerie de l'Académie impériale des sciences., T. I, p. 32

Heft I, Kap. 3, station record of Golmberg. In 1880 each angle was measured twice on 8 circle positions, a full set of 24 pointings per direction. The angle Collm to Golmberg differed by 2.61″ from 1871. Helmert examined the possible causes: the 1880 sights were spread over only three days, and the brightly lit tower at Collm may have pulled the pointing, since the observations were as usual made in the afternoon. General Schreiber ordered a remeasurement in 1889: 32 measurements on 16 circle positions over several days, the first 16 rejected for poor lights. The new result confirms 1880 to 0.85″.

“General Schreiber ordnete eine Neumessung des letzteren an, die im Juni und Juli 1889 durch den Landesvermessungsrath Erfurth erfolgte. Es wurden 32 Messungen angestellt, die sich auf 16 Kreisstände vertheilten und 149° 16′ 49″,72 als Resultat ergaben, dessen m. F. nach Maassgabe der Abweichungen der 16 Mittel aus Hin- und Hergang vom Gesammtmittel ± 0″,20 beträgt. (Die ersten 16 Beobachtungen sind wegen mangelhafter Lichter verworfen; sie geben 49″,74.)”
In English: “General Schreiber ordered a remeasurement of the latter, which was made in June and July 1889 by Landesvermessungsrath Erfurth. 32 measurements were made, distributed over 16 circle positions, and gave 149° 16′ 49.72″ as the result, whose mean error, from the deviations of the 16 means of forward and return runs from the overall mean, is ±0.20″. (The first 16 observations were rejected because of poor lights; they give 49.74″.)”
Reading the table. The small table in the middle of the page lists the values of the angle Collm to Golmberg: 1871 from 3 circle positions with 4 and 6 pointings (50.67″, 52.01″) and from the other angles of a pentagon (51.34″); 1880 from 16 direct measurements and from the two part angles (48.65″, 49.21″) and from a quadrilateral (51.24″).
Worked out here: 1889: 49.72″; 1880 mean 48.87″; difference 0.85″ (printed). 1871 mean 51.48″.

Walker, section on the reduction of base-lines to sea level, where the source of base heights is discussed. He separates the Lambton period, when vertical angles were taken at any hour and often at night, from the later rule that kept them to the daily time of minimum refraction.

“During the immediately preceding period of about twenty years the rule had been followed of restricting the observations of vertical angles as closely as possible to the time of minimum refraction, which occurs daily between the hours of 1 and 3 p.m. apparent time ; the back angle was also measured at nearly the same interval from apparent noon as the forward angle. But during the operations of the period between 1800 and 1836 the observations were taken at any hour of the day and often during the night.”

Part III, Rocky Mountain series (Pikes Peak to Salt Lake, stations near 3 650 m, longest side 294 km). Heliotropes are mirrors that reflect sunlight from the far station as a bright point target. A "double zenith distance" is a vertical angle read in both circle faces. This passage gives the full observing programme for both horizontal and vertical angles.

“The horizontal directions at all the stations were observed with the 50-centimetre (20-inch) theodolite, originally in 19 and later on (since 1893) in but 17 positions of the azimuth circle. The intention was to secure two full sets in each position and to balance the number of observations of the morning and evening, but on account of unavoidable broken series their numbers had generally to be increased for each position. Respecting the time of observations, they were made from sunrise till 8 o'clock, and resumed in the afternoon at half past 4 o'clock and continued till sunset. [...] To secure observations under a variety of atmospheric conditions, observations were extended over twenty or more days. Double zenith distances for heights of stations were observed at three different periods of the day, viz. between 6 1/2 and 8 o'clock in the morning, between 11 1/2 and 1 o'clock, and again between 4 1/2 and 6 o'clock in the evening. This brought to light the fact that the minimum refraction of the day occurs late in the afternoon, even after the heat of the day has passed. As a rule these vertical angle measures were spread over not less than twelve days, at least for the main lines. [...] No simultaneous reciprocal zenith distances were obtained. [...] The triangulation party also made observations of the magnetic declination, dip, and intensity, and meteorological notes were regularly kept.”
Worked out here: Minimum per direction from the stated plan: 17 positions x 2 sets = 34 observations (38 with 19 positions), each a D. and R. pair.

Part III, Nevada and California series. Lateral (horizontal) refraction is a sideways bend of the line of sight caused by unequal air temperature across the line, for example air heated on one side of a slope. Its sign changes between morning and afternoon heating, so equal numbers of forenoon and afternoon measures tend to cancel it.

“The equalization of the number of measures of horizontal directions at a station taken in the forenoon and in the afternoon was first put into execution in 1880 in this section; its purpose was to eliminate any effect of unequal heating of the theodolite as well as to provide against possible lateral refraction along the lines of sight. Observations of zenith distances were made at three different periods of the day, as stated in the case of the Rocky Mountain work.”
Schott, C. A. (1900). The transcontinental triangulation and the American arc of the parallel (Special Publication No. 4). U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey; Government Printing Office., p. 573

Part II, general remarks. The coefficient of refraction m is the bend of the line of sight expressed as a fraction of the arc between the stations (m = k/2 in the usual notation). Reciprocal zenith distances are vertical angles measured from each end of a line toward the other; from the pair, m is computed for that line, so the refraction is measured on the line itself, not assumed. Special hourly series were run day and night to find the daily cycle.

“For the sake of easy reference, we shall give here in tabular form and also exhibit by diagrams the resulting hourly values of the coefficient of refraction, m, from four experimental series [...] The tabular values were deduced under the supposition of equal refraction angles at lower and upper stations.”
Reading the table. Table 1: local hour (midnight to midnight) against m for Bodega Head-Ross Mountain (22.48 km, 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. only), Martinez East-Mount Diablo (24.26 km), Jackson Butte-Round Top (72.37 km) and the sea horizon from Ragged Mountain. Table 2: hourly departure from the daily mean. Daily means: 0.1000, 0.0646, 0.0849; daily ranges 0.0333, 0.0168, 0.0293. The first sentence of the quote is on p. 254 (pdf 257).
Worked out here: Jackson Butte-Round Top: maximum 0.0711 (2 a.m.), minimum 0.0557 (2 to 3 p.m.).
Schott, C. A. (1900). The transcontinental triangulation and the American arc of the parallel (Special Publication No. 4). U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey; Government Printing Office., p. 255
Conclusion from the hourly series: 10 a.m. to 5 1/2 p.m. is the best window for zenith distances; noon images are unsteady
