Steady-air hours Vertical refraction coefficients

Part II, directly after the hourly table. Schott draws the observing rule from the measured cycle: refraction is largest and most irregular at night and changes little through the middle of the day.

“It shows that the refraction is greater and more irregular during the night hours than during the day; the maximum value is reached within two or three hours from midnight and the minimum value at sometime within 2 hours from noon-before noon at the coast stations after noon at the interior stations. The average amount (mean of 24 hours) is greater the nearer the line of sight is to the sea level, being some function of the altitude. The refraction changes but little, comparatively, between the hours of 10 a. m. and 5 1/2 p. m. and the intervening time is best suited for observing zenith distances for altitudes, so far as refraction is concerned; but in other respects, as for telescopic visions, the hours about noon are unfavorable on account of faint, unsteady, and distorted images being then more prevalent.”
Schott, C. A. (1900). The transcontinental triangulation and the American arc of the parallel (Special Publication No. 4). U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey; Government Printing Office., p. 256

The two passages show that the observers knew the warm air layer at the ground changes the bend of short, low lines, and that they dropped observations taken while refraction was far above its daily minimum.

“The tabular values of m show an apparent dependence upon the length of lines s, viz: the shorter s, the smaller m. This fact may be explained by the circumstance of the line of sight being nearer the heated ground the shorter the distance. The comparatively warm stratum of air is quite close to the ground, particularly during insolation. [...] The ground is barren and treeless over the entire region and the climate is very dry, especially during the summer. The instrument was only elevated sufficiently to overcome the earth's curvature and permit the visibility of the distant object. Part II, appendix D. From the hourly mean zenith distances at both ends, Schott computes for each hour the difference of height (Delta h) and the coefficient m, assuming equal refraction at the two ends. Because the bend is measured from both ends, most of it cancels out of the height.

“The adopted formulae are- m = 0.5 - (zeta + zeta' - 180 deg) / 2 psi [...] The resulting hourly values for Delta h and m are given in the following table: [...] The values of Delta h are plotted on diagram (3) and show the computed difference of height between 10 a. m. and near midnight to be smaller than the mean; but the results for those hours appear remarkably consistent.”

Weights of base-line angles carry the loss of precision from undulating signals over hot ground
Maclear's verification and extension of La Caille's arc of meridian, Cape of Good Hope · p. 338 · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours Repetition over days and hours

Section 7, part 4, of the base verification by triangulation (Zwartland base). Maclear explains how the weight of each angle was found: the square of the number of partial measures divided by twice the sum of squares of the differences from the mean. A partial measure is the mean of a group of repetitions; the weight is a number that is larger when the results agree better. He states that over flat ground the signals undulate, except in gloomy and moist weather or early morning and late evening, and that this error must enter the weights. So the state of the air is measured in the scatter of the results, not ignored.

“The weight of each angle was calculated by dividing the square of the number of partial measures by twice the sum of the squares of the differences from the mean, assuming the theodolite errors of division to be insensible, an assumption which is not strictly correct. The method pursued when measuring, of stepping the divided circle, eleminates the division errors from the mean result; they are restored in the weight as above calculated ; but that factor cannot justly be represented by the number of measures alone,—where, as in the present instance, the triangulation is carried over flat ground,—the line of sight passing in close proximity to heated sand and bush, causing the signals to undulate so much, except during gloomy and moist weather, or early in the morning and late in the evening, as to materially diminish the precision of the pointing : it is therefore necessary to introduce this element of error.”
Maclear, T. (1866). Verification and extension of La Caille's arc of meridian at the Cape of Good Hope (Vol. 1). London: Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty., p. 338

The printed type example for the Beaufort theodolite: the angle at Kamies-Sector Berg between the Keibiskow heliostat (about 80 miles away) and Bokkeveld Berg, 1, 3 and 4 December 1846. Each row is one partial result of 10 repetitions with the hour and a remark on the definition of the signals. The remarks record the air: wind direction, 'hot temperature: about 85 deg.', 'therm. 90 deg.', and 'Definition in the morning not good, towards 11h it became much worse'. Half the work was measured forward with the Y bearings right, half backward with Y left. The final angle comes from 260 measures with weight 131.99.

“Angle at Kamies-Sector Berg, West Rock Station; between Keibiskow and Bokkeveld Berg : measured with the Beaufort Theodolite. ... Middling definition. ... Northerly wind, perhaps 1 point E. of N. Hot temperature : about 85°. ... Bad definition and bad signaling at Bokkeveld ... Wind west, next S.W., and lastly south; this afternoon very hot, therm. 90°. ... Excellent do., points. ... Definition in the morning not good, towards 11h it became much worse. ... Resulting angle from 260 meas. = 23°32′1″·98 Weight = 131·99”

Same paragraph (p. 19). The observer was told to split the arcs between early morning and late afternoon, the hours of clearest and steadiest air, so that the mean covers two different states of the air. Morning mist and haze often stopped this. All vertical angles (angles of elevation or depression) were taken in the afternoon near sunset, with the vertical arc level read every time.

“The instructions to the observer were to observe half the arcs in the early morning and the remainder in the late afternoon, as being the hours of the day when the air might be expected to be clearest and steadiest. But it was soon found that to observe strictly in this way would be the cause of considerable delay when the morning observations were frequently quite prevented by mist and haze. The vertical angles were all observed in the afternoon as near to sunset as possible, and in repetition equivalent to the first pair of arcs as for horizontal angles, the readings of the vertical arc level being always recorded.”
Morris, W. G. (1908). Reports on the geodetic survey of the Transvaal and Orange River Colony (Geodetic Survey of South Africa, Vol. 5; preface and introduction by D. Gill). London: Harrison and Sons., p. 19

Trigonometrical Survey of New South Wales · pp. 181-182 · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours

Furber, Instruments (pp. 181-182), reporting Gill's report on the Cape Colony and Natal survey. Lateral refraction is the sideways bending of the line of sight, which shifts horizontal directions. Gill found it larger than the errors of pointing and reading; a change of wind could move a distant station, and directions after noon differed from those before noon. His remedy was to vary the conditions, combining morning and afternoon work, and the probable error of an angle fell from 0.49" to 0.33". No PDF of this paper is in the project; the item points to the OCR text file, so no crop is possible. The wording was checked against page images of pp. 181-182 held elsewhere in the project.

“In this connection he states that during the course of the survey it was shown that the accidental errors of pointing or reading were less to be regarded than those caused by lateral refraction. Not only was it found that a change of wind was sometimes followed by marked change in the direction of a distant station, but that a systematic difference, small but appreciable, existed between directions measured after and before noon, and the general conclusion was come to that steps were to be taken to reduce the effects of refraction by varying the conditions under which the observations were made rather than by seeking precision from extraordinary accuracy of the instruments used. In this view a 10-inch theodolite was substituted by Dr. Gill for the 18-inch instrument previously employed, and throughout the remainder of the work morning and afternoon observations were combined, the very satisfactory result being that with an instrument of less than one-fourth the weight the probable error of an observed angle was reduced from ± 0·49″ to ± 0·33″.”

Heights from zenith distances at both ends, always at the same time of day; sets of two rounds with level read
Trigonometrical Survey of New South Wales · p. 204 · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours Repetition over days and hours

Altitudes of stations (p. 204). Furber states that simultaneous observation at both ends is the ideal, because only then is the refraction certain to be the same at both ends. That was not possible, so the reciprocal observations were made at the same time of day. Each set is two rounds of elevations, face left and face right, with a level along the line read at every sighting. He adds that more sets would be better. No PDF of this paper is in the project; the item points to the OCR text file, so no crop is possible. Quote from the text layer, one OCR word break corrected ('reciprocal observations').

“The simultaneous observation at each end of the line involved, which is necessary to an ideal determination of relative heights (for by that means only is it made certain that the co-efficients of refraction at the two ends of the line are the same) has, of course, been impracticable. The work, however, is performed always at the same time of the day, so as to secure, as far as possible, the same atmospheric conditions in the reciprocal observations. The actual field work consists in the measurement, with a theodolite having a 10-inch circle, of the elevations of all the stations in the surround, noting, at the time of sighting to each, the reading of a level the axis of which is in the direction of the line being sighted, any variations of the level being subsequently applied to the circle reading. The instrument is then reversed and a similar round taken, each such pair of rounds constituting a set from which the differences of height may be derived.”

Night lights changed how the Indian survey worked
Middleton, Chadwick and Bogle, A Treatise on Surveying (textbook) · p. 188 · strength ★★★
Night lamps and heliotropes Steady-air hours

The book quotes Thuillier and Smyth's Manual of Surveying for India. Before Everest's vase lights (a clay dish of cotton seed and oil, burnt as a signal), the Indian survey observed in the rainy season, so that opaque flags could be seen. Lights let the observers work at night instead.

“Vase lights were invented by Colonel Everest nearly fifty years ago, and completely altered the operations of the Great Trigonometrical Survey in India, which had previously to be carried on in the unhealthy season of the rains, in order that the opaque signals, such as flags, might be clearly seen. By enabling observations to be rapidly taken at night, the progress of the work was also much accelerated.”
Middleton, R. E., Chadwick, O., & Bogle, J. du T. (1904). A treatise on surveying: Part I (2nd ed.). E. & F. N. Spon., p. 188
Vertical angles only between 2½ and 3½ p.m.: other hours make heights "nearly worthless"
Middleton, Chadwick and Bogle, A Treatise on Surveying (textbook) · pp. 190-191 · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours Night lamps and heliotropes Vertical refraction coefficients

End of the quoted manual. The heliotrope limits daytime work to about 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. Vertical angles (the up-down angles used for heights) are to be taken between 2½ and 3½ p.m., the time of least refraction. The manual says vertical angles taken at other hours are so irregular that heights from them are nearly worthless. It also says luminous targets are observed more correctly than opaque ones.

“the only limit to the times at which observations can be made will be from 9 o'clock A.M. to 2½ or 3 o'clock P.M. But the heliotrope is more particularly recommended for the purpose of taking vertical angles with certainty between the hours of 2½ and 3½ afternoon, which is the time of minimum refraction, because verticals taken at any other time are subject to great irregularities, whereby heights deduced from them are nearly worthless. Luminous objects are much more correctly, rapidly, and comfortably observed than opaque ones, which, if distant, are always faint, and disappear when brought near the wire of the telescope.”
Middleton, R. E., Chadwick, O., & Bogle, J. du T. (1904). A treatise on surveying: Part I (2nd ed.). E. & F. N. Spon., pp. 190-191
When the air "boils", do not observe
Middleton, Chadwick and Bogle, A Treatise on Surveying (textbook) · p. 195 · strength ★★★
Rejecting readings in unsteady air Steady-air hours

Under the margin heading "Perturbation of Atmosphere in Hot Climates". Boiling is the shimmer of heated air near the ground. The instruction is to stop observing while it lasts, because the signal moves about and accurate work is impossible.

“In hot climates the atmosphere often 'boils' at certain times of the day. When this takes place it is useless to observe, the signal will dance about and become distorted in so erratic a manner, that accurate work is impossible. To attempt to observe under these conditions merely amounts to loss of time and temper.”
Middleton, R. E., Chadwick, O., & Bogle, J. du T. (1904). A treatise on surveying: Part I (2nd ed.). E. & F. N. Spon., p. 195
Refraction varies with hour, temperature and pressure; horizontal deviation happens
Middleton, Chadwick and Bogle, A Treatise on Surveying (textbook) · p. 226 · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours Rejecting readings in unsteady air

The authors list what changes refraction: the hour (least about 3h 45m p.m. in the tropics), temperature and barometric pressure, and heated ground, where the ray can even curve the other way (mirage). They also state that sideways (horizontal) deviation is common. Their conclusion: under strong disturbance do not observe at all, and otherwise rely on reciprocal angles in similar conditions.

“Now the value of error of refraction though usually small, is very uncertain. It varies at different hours of the day, being least (in the tropics) at about 3h. 45m. P.M. It varies also with temperature, and barometric pressure. Over highly heated arid plains, it becomes exceedingly irregular, the curve sometimes being actually convex towards the earth, so that objects are depressed and not raised. [...] Horizontal deviation is also very common. A series of rods, ranged out in a straight line at one time, have presented the appearance of a curve at another time. When disturbance is so great as this, accurate observation of any kind is obviously impracticable. At any time, however, the effect of refraction is uncertain, and accurate results can only be arrived at, by taking reciprocal angles under similar atmospheric conditions.”
Middleton, R. E., Chadwick, O., & Bogle, J. du T. (1904). A treatise on surveying: Part I (2nd ed.). E. & F. N. Spon., p. 226

Tome II, remarks after the n table. Delambre explains the single negative n (no. 12, Fiefs-Bonnières): July, very hot and stormy weather, a poorly visible steeple. He states that refraction was nearly zero at the moment of the two observations, and notes that three observations of the same morning hour gave different refraction for different directions.

“Le 12e est négatif. Les deux observations sont du mois de juillet. A Fiefs le temps étoit très-chaud et orageux, et le clocher de Bonnières se voyoit mal. Cette dernière circonstance devoit augmenter la distance au zénith de quelques secondes. En diminuant de 9" la distance observée on auroit n = 0.0020 ; mais il n'en est pas moins sûr qu'à l'instant des deux observations la réfraction étoit à peu près nulle.”
In English: “The 12th is negative. The two observations are from July. At Fiefs the weather was very hot and stormy, and the steeple of Bonnières was poorly seen. This last circumstance must have increased the zenith distance by a few seconds. Reducing the observed distance by 9" would give n = 0.0020; but it is no less certain that at the moment of the two observations the refraction was nearly nil.”

Same page. A flag-staff is a pole set over the station; to 'bisect' it is to set the telescope cross-wire on its centre. White lights were short-burning flares fired at agreed times at the distant stations. Roy compares the two kinds of target and states which lines needed the night lights.

“In very favourable circumstances of the weather a good observation by day is preferable to one by the white lights at night; because, in the first case, the observer has time at his leisure nicely to bisect a fine flag-staff, and repeatedly to read off the angle; whereas, in the short duration of the burning of the light, he is somewhat hurried, from the fear of losing some of the lights at other distant stations, if two of them happened to come together, which now and then they did, from the irregularity of the rates of the watches of the artillery-men attending at the different stations. It was, however, by the assistance of the white lights only, that the most distant stations could be rendered visible”

Airy's account of the Indian arc. Night signals are lamps observed after dark. Larger refraction at night lifts the line of sight, so distant low stations come into view; the steadier night air is the reason for the choice.

Night lamps and heliotropes Steady-air hours

Tome I, p. 14, end of the signals section. A heliotrope is a mirror that reflects sunlight from the far station toward the observer, so it works only in sunshine. Struve used it for the longest distances or when a signal stood against the ground. He gives as a reason not to use it always that overcast days were either more numerous or the best for observing, because the calm of the images lasted longer.

“Un usage exclusif de l'héliotrope aurait trop arrêté la marche de l'opération, les jours couverts étant soit plus nombreux que les jours sereins, dans notre climat, soit les plus avantageux pour l'observation, par la plus longue durée du calme des images.”
In English: “An exclusive use of the heliotrope would have held up the progress of the operation too much, the overcast days being either more numerous than the clear days in our climate, or the most favourable for observation, through the longer duration of the calm of the images.”

Historic abstract, January 1847, Boschluis station in the Bushman Flat (p. 415). The heliostat on Keibiskow, about 80 miles away, rose above the horizon only in the early morning, when the vertical refraction was largest, so this angle could be measured only then. The margin note reads 'Effect of mirage on the Keibiskow light'. This shows the observers watched the change of refraction through the day and timed the work to it.

“The angle between the Keibiskow and Kamies-Sector Berg station detained me there until the 11th, for the top of Keibiskow could only be seen during the maximum refraction. Shortly after daybreak, the culminating top of the mountain gradually ascended above the horizon ; at sunrise, the heliostat light entered the telescope like a diffused, orange-coloured nebula, which gradually contracted to a brilliant point, equal to a star of the 5th magnitude.”

“It is to be noted that, in the above discussion, Struves' pressure factor ... Where B represents the mean reading, in English inches, of the barometer at the place of observation, by which all co-efficients may be referred to sea level, has not been applied, the area covered being nearly enough at the one level to enable it to be disregarded without affecting the conclusions. It should be observed too, that the co-efficient determined above results, not the mean refraction, but the refraction at the usual time of observation, 2 to 4 p.m., when though less liable to fluctuation, it is really at one extreme of its daily range.”

Delambre's two remedies against a possible lateral refraction: wait for favourable moments, and repeat at different hours and conditions
Delambre and Méchain, meridian arc Dunkirk to Barcelona (Base du système métrique) · T1 Discours préliminaire p. 106 · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours Repetition over days and hours Night lamps and heliotropes

Discours préliminaire, section on signals. Lateral refraction is a sideways bend of the line of sight, which would change horizontal angles. Delambre says he was at times tempted to believe in it, that night lamps would be equally subject to it, and that the defence is to observe at good moments and to repeat at other hours and in other conditions, so that a sideways error does not repeat in the same direction.

“S'il existe une réfraction latérale, comme j'ai été par fois tenté de le croire, les réverbères y seroient également sujets, et l'on n'a pour se garantir de cette illusion que deux moyens qui ne sont pas infaillibles, l'un est d'attendre les instans favorables ; l'autre, de répéter les observations à des heures et dans des circonstances différentes.”
In English: “If a lateral refraction exists, as I have at times been tempted to believe, reverberatory lamps would be equally subject to it, and there are only two means, not infallible, to guard against this illusion: one is to wait for favourable moments; the other, to repeat the observations at different hours and in different circumstances.”
Méchain, P., & Delambre, J.-B. J. (1806). Base du système métrique décimal, ou mesure de l'arc du méridien compris entre les parallèles de Dunkerque et Barcelone (Vol. 1). Paris: Baudouin., T1 Discours préliminaire p. 106

Puissant, p. 35, describing the Brest-Strasbourg line. A discordance is the disagreement between repeated measures of the same quantity. On this page the discordances belong to the night observations made with lamps as signals, that is, the angles between signals of the triangles: the next sentence turns to the zenith distances as a separate set ('C'est aussi sur cette même ligne qu'ont été observées des distances zénithales réciproques et simultanées'). Puissant confirms the reading on p. 156, where he says that with lamps 'les erreurs des triangles n'ont pas été moindres que de coutume' for the horizontal angles. The night zenith distances of the eastern part were also rejected, for their own discordance (p. 208, item fr_par_06).

“C'est sur une grande partie de cette ligne, confiée, dès l'origine des travaux, à MM. les colonels Bonne et Henry, que des réverbères ont été employés pour signaux ; mais les observations nocturnes, à peu d'intervalle du coucher du soleil, ont souvent présenté des discordances beaucoup plus considérables que celles faites de jour. C'est aussi sur cette même ligne qu'ont été observées des distances zénithales réciproques et simultanées, afin de connaître avec toute la précision désirable les hauteurs des stations depuis le Panthéon jusqu'à Brest.”
In English: “It is on a large part of this line, entrusted from the start of the work to Colonels Bonne and Henry, that lamps were used as signals; but the night observations, shortly after sunset, often showed much larger discordances than those made by day. It is also on this same line that reciprocal and simultaneous zenith distances were observed, in order to know with all desirable precision the heights of the stations from the Panthéon to Brest.”
Puissant, L. (1832). Nouvelle description géométrique de la France (Première partie). Paris: Ch. Picquet., 35

Night lamps and heliotropes Steady-air hours

Puissant, chapter on the probable error of an arc. The triangle errors (closure errors: the amount by which the three angles miss 180 degrees plus the spherical excess) are a direct test of the horizontal angles. Puissant uses them to judge the night method recommended by Laplace and finds no gain, with a larger effect in low ground between Paris and Strasbourg.

“Malgré l'usage que l'on fit de réverbères pour points de mire, dans cette partie de la méridienne, les erreurs des triangles n'ont pas été moindres que de coutume ; ainsi les observations nocturnes des angles horizontaux qui avaient été recommandées par le célèbre Laplace, sont tout aussi influencées par les effets de la réfraction atmosphérique que celles de jour, si même elles ne le sont quelquefois davantage dans les lieux bas, comme on l'a remarqué, ainsi que nous l'avons déjà dit, entre Paris et Strasbourg, lors de la mesure du parallèle compris entre ces deux villes.”
In English: “Despite the use of lamps as targets in this part of the meridian, the errors of the triangles were no smaller than usual; thus the night observations of horizontal angles, which had been recommended by the celebrated Laplace, are just as influenced by the effects of atmospheric refraction as those by day, if indeed they are not sometimes more so in low places, as was remarked, as we have already said, between Paris and Strasbourg, during the measurement of the parallel between these two towns.”
Puissant, L. (1832). Nouvelle description géométrique de la France (Première partie). Paris: Ch. Picquet., 156

Puissant, eastern part of the parallel (Colonel Henry, from 1818). The first-order angles were observed at night at Laplace's wish. Comparable zenith distances (those that should agree, such as the reciprocal pair on one line) disagreed so much that the night zenith distances were rejected and the heights were taken from day measures at second-order stations tied to the first-order ones.

“Le premier des deux tableaux ci-après présente l'ensemble des triangles du premier ordre dont les angles furent observés de nuit, dès l'année 1818, d'après le désir de l'illustre président de la commission royale, dans l'espérance qu'il en résulterait une plus grande exactitude. Mais l'énorme discordance que présentèrent sur cette ligne la plupart des distances zénithales comparables, mirent dans la nécessité de rejeter ces observations nocturnes pour déterminer les différences de niveau par d'autres mesures angulaires recueillies de jour, à différentes stations du second ordre, liées à celles du premier ordre.”
In English: “The first of the two tables below presents all the first-order triangles whose angles were observed at night, from 1818, at the wish of the illustrious president of the royal commission, in the hope of greater accuracy. But the enormous discordance shown on this line by most of the comparable zenith distances made it necessary to reject these night observations and to determine the level differences by other angular measures taken by day at various second-order stations tied to the first-order ones.”

Roy: the Hounslow Heath and Romney Marsh bases measure each other within a few inches; triangle errors are very small
Anglo-French triangulation of 1787 (Greenwich to Paris junction), English side by Roy · p. 247 · strength ★★★
Night lamps and heliotropes

Opening of Section VIII. A base is a line measured on the ground with a chain or rods; the other sides are computed from it through the angles. Roy measured two bases about 70 miles apart and computed each from the other through the triangles. On pp. 177-178 he gives the difference as about 4 1/2 inches. He also states that the lights and the instrument were placed over the same station mark, so that no eccentricity (offset of the target or instrument from the station point) entered.

“the same excellent instrument having been placed at every station on our side of the Channel, and all the angles observed with the utmost care, it hath consequently followed, that the base on Hounslow Heath, and that in Romney Marsh, reciprocally measure each other within a few inches of the truth, which is an instance of such exactness as probably never occurred in any former operation of this sort. The extreme smallness of the error on the sum of the three angles of each triangle sufficiently proves that the general result would not have differed greatly, if only two of the angles had actually been observed.”
Roy, W. (1790). An account of the trigonometrical operation, whereby the distance between the meridians of the Royal Observatories of Greenwich and Paris has been determined. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, 80, 111-270 (with Dalby, I., Remarks, pp. 593-614)., p. 247

Trigonometrical Survey of England and Wales (Ordnance), Williams, Mudge and Dalby 1791-1799 · p. 448 · strength ★★★
Repetition over days and hours Night lamps and heliotropes

Section on the instrument and method. 'Different arcs' means different parts of the divided circle, so that errors of division average out. Staffs were poles at stations up to about fifteen miles away; lamps and white lights were used at night. When only one of two white lights was seen, the observation was kept only if it showed no error beyond the division error of the instrument; otherwise new lights were sent and the angle observed again.

“namely, that of observing the angles upon different arcs. When staffs were erected, which was generally the case when the stations were not more remote than fifteen miles, the angles were repeated till their truth became certain, and the same was also done, when angles were determined by the lamps; but it sometimes happened, that only one of the two white lights, which were burned at the distant stations, was seen; in which case, if the observation appeared to be made without any error, but that which an inequality in the division of the instrument might be supposed to produce, it was considered as sufficient; otherwise fresh lights were sent to the station and observed.”
Williams, E., Mudge, W., & Dalby, I. (1795). An account of the trigonometrical survey carried on in the years 1791, 1792, 1793, and 1794. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, 85, 414-591., p. 448
Mudge 1799: instructions for simultaneous reciprocal observations every hour, with watches regulated by the sun, weather, thermometer and barometer recorded
Trigonometrical Survey of England and Wales (Ordnance), Williams, Mudge and Dalby 1791-1799 · p. 183 · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours Night lamps and heliotropes

Mudge (1801), on refraction. Simultaneous reciprocal observation means that each of two stations measures the vertical angle to the other at the same moment, so that both ends see the same state of the air. Mr. Woolcot observed at one station and Mudge at the other. The times were kept by watches regulated from altitudes of the sun and by signal.

“On these occasions, the instructions which I communicated to Mr. Woolcot, and by which I governed myself, were to observe the elevation or depression of the corresponding station at the expiration of every hour, beginning at six A. M. and to have the watch well regulated from observed altitudes of the sun's limb. I requested him also to be very minute in entering on his book the state of the weather; to keep the instrument properly sheltered from the wind; to be always cautious to adjust his level; and also to insert the state of the air, as to temperature and density, by noting the thermometer and barometer.”
Mudge, W. (1801). An account of the operations carried on for accomplishing a trigonometrical survey of England and Wales, continued from the year 1797, to the end of the year 1799 (Vol. 2, from the Philosophical Transactions). London: W. Faden., p. 183

Tome I, Chapter I, on the signals of the Baltic arc. The signals were painted dark so that the vertical beam, not the sunlit face of the pyramid, was pointed. A phase is a false apparent centre of a target caused by side lighting. Struve states that angle measurement had already stopped before sunset, because the images then always undulate, and gives the summer period of calm images as 0.5 to 0.8 of the interval from noon to sunset.

“Mais à cette époque la mesure des angles a déjà cessé, parce que près du coucher du soleil les objets sont toujours très ondulants, le calme des images ayant lieu en été, dans nos climats, entre 0,5 à 0,8 de l'intervalle de temps entre midi et le coucher du soleil.”
In English: “But at that time the measurement of the angles has already stopped, because near sunset the objects are always very undulating, the calm of the images taking place in summer, in our climates, between 0.5 and 0.8 of the interval of time between noon and sunset.”

Heft I, § 12, the Russian (Polish) triangulation under General Tenner. In the southern Warsaw to Czenstochau connection the average number of sets was 11.4. The closures of all 219 Polish triangles give a mean angle error of ±0.73″. Tenner found this somewhat high and gave as reasons the high signals (pyramids 6 to 20 m, and 20 to 50 m in 148 cases) and measurement in unfavourable air that could not always be avoided. The rule for such air and strong wind was 18 to 24 sets. The sum of the 219 closures, +9.73″, shows no bias to positive or negative.

“Als Erklärungsgrund werden die hohen Signale, welche meist nothwendig waren, sowie die mehrfach nicht zu vermeidende Messung bei ungünstiger Luft angeführt. (Bei ungünstiger Luft und starkem Wind sollten 18—24 Sätze genommen werden.) Die Summe der 219 Widersprüche ist + 9″,73, so dass keine Neigung zu positiven oder negativen Schlussfehlern zu erkennen ist.”
In English: “The high signals, which were mostly necessary, and the measurement in unfavourable air, which several times could not be avoided, are given as the explanation. (In unfavourable air and strong wind 18 to 24 sets were to be taken.) The sum of the 219 closures is +9.73″, so that no tendency to positive or negative closure errors can be seen.”
Worked out here: √(354.1 / (219 × 3)) = √0.539 = 0.734″ (printed ±0.73″). Per direction 0.73/√2 = 0.52″ (printed).

Heft I, Kap. 3, station record of Golmberg. In 1880 each angle was measured twice on 8 circle positions, a full set of 24 pointings per direction. The angle Collm to Golmberg differed by 2.61″ from 1871. Helmert examined the possible causes: the 1880 sights were spread over only three days, and the brightly lit tower at Collm may have pulled the pointing, since the observations were as usual made in the afternoon. General Schreiber ordered a remeasurement in 1889: 32 measurements on 16 circle positions over several days, the first 16 rejected for poor lights. The new result confirms 1880 to 0.85″.

“General Schreiber ordnete eine Neumessung des letzteren an, die im Juni und Juli 1889 durch den Landesvermessungsrath Erfurth erfolgte. Es wurden 32 Messungen angestellt, die sich auf 16 Kreisstände vertheilten und 149° 16′ 49″,72 als Resultat ergaben, dessen m. F. nach Maassgabe der Abweichungen der 16 Mittel aus Hin- und Hergang vom Gesammtmittel ± 0″,20 beträgt. (Die ersten 16 Beobachtungen sind wegen mangelhafter Lichter verworfen; sie geben 49″,74.)”
In English: “General Schreiber ordered a remeasurement of the latter, which was made in June and July 1889 by Landesvermessungsrath Erfurth. 32 measurements were made, distributed over 16 circle positions, and gave 149° 16′ 49.72″ as the result, whose mean error, from the deviations of the 16 means of forward and return runs from the overall mean, is ±0.20″. (The first 16 observations were rejected because of poor lights; they give 49.74″.)”
Reading the table. Great Arc of India, Lambton's meridional arc (Coromandel coast to Punnae and north to about 18 N) · p. XIX · strength ★★★
Night lamps and heliotropes

Walker's introduction on the early operations. A heliotrope is a mirror that sends sunlight from the far station to the observer; a lamp does the same at night. Without them Lambton observed opaque signals, which haze made dull, and chose the rainy season because the air was then clearest.

“The difficulties which Major Lambton alludes to as arising from the haziness of the weather might have been materially diminished had he been supplied with luminous signals, such as heliotropes and lamps, to erect on the stations which he was observing; but such signals were not employed in the operations of the survey until after the year 1832, when they were introduced by Colonel Everest. For very many years the signals were “ masts, flagstaves, and other opaque objects, and then days and days often passed away without a glimpse of the distant object.” As the atmosphere in India is usually most favorable during the rainy season, for viewing such objects, it became the practice to wait for the first heavy fall of rain and then take the field,”
Walker, J. T. (1870). Account of the operations of the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India, Vol. I: Standards of measure and base-lines. Dehra Dun: Great Trigonometrical Survey., p. XIX

Table of pole-star observations for the meridian at Yerracondah (January 1804). A referring lamp is a lamp set up as a fixed night mark near the station; the angle from the star to the lamp is measured each night and the lamp is then tied to a survey station by day. The note below says no double azimuths were possible because vapour hid the pole star by day.

“Pole-Star Observations at Yerracondah Station, reduced for determining the position of the Meridian. [...] It may be remarked here, that no double azimuths have been taken. The pole-star being so low, and the vapour in the atmosphere so great in general, that I have never, except in two instances, been able to discern it while the sun was above the horizon.”

Repetition over days and hours Steady-air hours Night lamps and heliotropes

Part III, Rocky Mountain series (Pikes Peak to Salt Lake, stations near 3 650 m, longest side 294 km). Heliotropes are mirrors that reflect sunlight from the far station as a bright point target. A "double zenith distance" is a vertical angle read in both circle faces. This passage gives the full observing programme for both horizontal and vertical angles.

“The horizontal directions at all the stations were observed with the 50-centimetre (20-inch) theodolite, originally in 19 and later on (since 1893) in but 17 positions of the azimuth circle. The intention was to secure two full sets in each position and to balance the number of observations of the morning and evening, but on account of unavoidable broken series their numbers had generally to be increased for each position. Respecting the time of observations, they were made from sunrise till 8 o'clock, and resumed in the afternoon at half past 4 o'clock and continued till sunset. [...] To secure observations under a variety of atmospheric conditions, observations were extended over twenty or more days. Double zenith distances for heights of stations were observed at three different periods of the day, viz. between 6 1/2 and 8 o'clock in the morning, between 11 1/2 and 1 o'clock, and again between 4 1/2 and 6 o'clock in the evening. This brought to light the fact that the minimum refraction of the day occurs late in the afternoon, even after the heat of the day has passed. As a rule these vertical angle measures were spread over not less than twelve days, at least for the main lines. [...] No simultaneous reciprocal zenith distances were obtained. [...] The triangulation party also made observations of the magnetic declination, dip, and intensity, and meteorological notes were regularly kept.”
Worked out here: Minimum per direction from the stated plan: 17 positions x 2 sets = 34 observations (38 with 19 positions), each a D. and R. pair.
Schott, C. A. (1900). The transcontinental triangulation and the American arc of the parallel (Special Publication No. 4). U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey; Government Printing Office., p. 553

Part II, third section west of the Atlanta base. Observing at night on lamps avoids the daytime heating of the ground and the boiling images it causes.

“The observations of 1888 at stations Laurel and Horn by Assistant F. W. Perkins were made at night upon lights. Subsequent to this date all horizontal measures of the primary triangulation between these stations and the Gulf coast were made at night by Assistants F. W. Perkins and W. B. Fairfield. Advantage was thus taken of the greater transparency of the atmosphere and of the better seeing during the night as compared with the day. On long or difficult lines two or three lights arranged vertically were shown at the same station.”

Part II, fifth section to Mobile Bay. The probable errors from the triangle closures are compared across four sections observed by different observers, instruments, heights and hours.

“The country being well timbered and cutting impracticable, it was necessary to elevate the theodolite on scaffolds ranging from 12m.4 to 46m.5 in height, with several 37m high. All observing was done at night on signal lights. The mean closing error derived from 28 triangles composing the figure equals sqrt(38.23/28) = +/- 1".17; the mean error of an angle is +/- 0".68, and the probable error of a direction, 0.674 x 1.17/sqrt(6) = +/- 0".34. For the several sections these last values are very nearly equal notwithstanding the number of observers, of instruments, and methods, and other circumstances, such as elevation of instruments, day or night observations, etc. The values of the probable error of a direction for the second, third, fourth, and fifth sections average +/- 0".34, which indicates that the triangulation of Alabama is of a high degree of accuracy.”

Middleton, Chadwick and Bogle, A Treatise on Surveying (textbook) · p. 188 · strength ★★★
Night lamps and heliotropes Steady-air hours

The book quotes Thuillier and Smyth's Manual of Surveying for India. Before Everest's vase lights (a clay dish of cotton seed and oil, burnt as a signal), the Indian survey observed in the rainy season, so that opaque flags could be seen. Lights let the observers work at night instead.

“Vase lights were invented by Colonel Everest nearly fifty years ago, and completely altered the operations of the Great Trigonometrical Survey in India, which had previously to be carried on in the unhealthy season of the rains, in order that the opaque signals, such as flags, might be clearly seen. By enabling observations to be rapidly taken at night, the progress of the work was also much accelerated.”
Middleton, R. E., Chadwick, O., & Bogle, J. du T. (1904). A treatise on surveying: Part I (2nd ed.). E. & F. N. Spon., p. 188
Vertical angles only between 2½ and 3½ p.m.: other hours make heights "nearly worthless"
Middleton, Chadwick and Bogle, A Treatise on Surveying (textbook) · pp. 190-191 · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours Night lamps and heliotropes Vertical refraction coefficients

End of the quoted manual. The heliotrope limits daytime work to about 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. Vertical angles (the up-down angles used for heights) are to be taken between 2½ and 3½ p.m., the time of least refraction. The manual says vertical angles taken at other hours are so irregular that heights from them are nearly worthless. It also says luminous targets are observed more correctly than opaque ones.

“the only limit to the times at which observations can be made will be from 9 o'clock A.M. to 2½ or 3 o'clock P.M. But the heliotrope is more particularly recommended for the purpose of taking vertical angles with certainty between the hours of 2½ and 3½ afternoon, which is the time of minimum refraction, because verticals taken at any other time are subject to great irregularities, whereby heights deduced from them are nearly worthless. Luminous objects are much more correctly, rapidly, and comfortably observed than opaque ones, which, if distant, are always faint, and disappear when brought near the wire of the telescope.”
Middleton, R. E., Chadwick, O., & Bogle, J. du T. (1904). A treatise on surveying: Part I (2nd ed.). E. & F. N. Spon., pp. 190-191
Night lamps compared with day signals: no better agreement between series; undulations seen on lamps and on day signals
Delambre and Méchain, meridian arc Dunkirk to Barcelona (Base du système métrique) · T1 Discours préliminaire p. 106 · strength ★★
Night lamps and heliotropes

Discours préliminaire. Méchain used reverberatory lamps (oil lamps with a reflector) as night targets in Spain. Delambre compares the series (sets of repeated readings) of the same angle and finds no better agreement than with day signals. Undulations are the visible trembling or slow swaying of a target image caused by unsteady air.

“En examinant les diverses séries d'un même angle ou les diverses parties de la même série, je n'y vois pas plus d'accord, peut-être même un peu moins que quand il observoit des signaux ordinaires. Nous avons dit ci-dessus que le réverbère allumé à Montmartre le 11 et le 15 août 1792 étoit sujet à des ondulations très-sensibles, qui faisoient osciller le lieu apparent autour du véritable. C'est un inconvénient au reste qui paroît inhérent aux signaux de toute espèce, je l'ai éprouvé bien souvent sur les signaux de jour”
In English: “Examining the different series of the same angle or the different parts of the same series, I see no more agreement, perhaps even a little less, than when he observed ordinary signals. We said above that the lamp lit at Montmartre on 11 and 15 August 1792 was subject to very noticeable undulations, which made the apparent place oscillate around the true one. This drawback seems inherent in signals of every kind; I experienced it very often with day signals”

Same page. A flag-staff is a pole set over the station; to 'bisect' it is to set the telescope cross-wire on its centre. White lights were short-burning flares fired at agreed times at the distant stations. Roy compares the two kinds of target and states which lines needed the night lights.

“In very favourable circumstances of the weather a good observation by day is preferable to one by the white lights at night; because, in the first case, the observer has time at his leisure nicely to bisect a fine flag-staff, and repeatedly to read off the angle; whereas, in the short duration of the burning of the light, he is somewhat hurried, from the fear of losing some of the lights at other distant stations, if two of them happened to come together, which now and then they did, from the irregularity of the rates of the watches of the artillery-men attending at the different stations. It was, however, by the assistance of the white lights only, that the most distant stations could be rendered visible”

Section on placing the instrument. Raising the instrument lifts the line of sight clear of the ground over flat country. The inner scaffold for the instrument was separate from the outer one for the observer, so neither the observer's movements nor the wind on the hut reached the instrument.

“The high stage used for the great instruments is 32 feet high, but has been only used in cases of absolute necessity. ... Many instances of high scaffolding occurred in the triangulation of the Eastern Counties, where, the country being flat, the stations were over church-towers. ... Thus the instrument, at the height of 178 feet above ground, was insulated, and not affected by the movements of the observer, or the action of the wind upon the observatory.”

Airy's account of the Indian arc. Night signals are lamps observed after dark. Larger refraction at night lifts the line of sight, so distant low stations come into view; the steadier night air is the reason for the choice.

Tome I, p. 14, end of the signals section. A heliotrope is a mirror that reflects sunlight from the far station toward the observer, so it works only in sunshine. Struve used it for the longest distances or when a signal stood against the ground. He gives as a reason not to use it always that overcast days were either more numerous or the best for observing, because the calm of the images lasted longer.

“Un usage exclusif de l'héliotrope aurait trop arrêté la marche de l'opération, les jours couverts étant soit plus nombreux que les jours sereins, dans notre climat, soit les plus avantageux pour l'observation, par la plus longue durée du calme des images.”

Heft I, § 16, end. Where a station was measured in different years, each epoch was combined on its own and then joined with weights. In the net adjustment, measurements of different years at one station were treated as measurements at different stations, because even the best measurements of different years showed large differences. Helmert names the possible causes: instruments and observers, the state of the air, centring and identity of the points, and the perception of heliotrope lights, whose appearance changes with the atmosphere.

“Für diesen Vorgang sprach das Auftreten grosser Differenzen selbst bei den besten Messungen verschiedener Jahre, wobei es allerdings unaufgeklärt geblieben ist, welches die wesentlichste Ursache dieser Unterschiede sein mag, ob die meist vorhandene Verschiedenheit der Instrumente und Beobachter, oder ein Unterschied der Luftzustände, oder in einzelnen Fällen Centrirungsmängel bezw. Nichtidentität der Punkte.”
In English: “This procedure was supported by the occurrence of large differences even in the best measurements of different years, though it has remained unexplained which is the main cause of these differences: the difference of instruments and observers that is mostly present, or a difference in the states of the air, or in single cases faults of centring or non-identity of the points.”
Helmert, F. R. (Ed.). (1893). Die europäische Längengradmessung in 52 Grad Breite von Greenwich bis Warschau. I. Heft: Hauptdreiecke und Grundlinienanschlüsse von England bis Polen. P. Stankiewicz., p. 37

Heft I, § 6. The net adjustment of the Rhenish and Hessian nets of the Prussian Geodetic Institute gives a mean error of nearly ±0.7″ for a station-adjusted direction, larger than the station scatter alone. Helmert names the causes: lateral refraction of the light, errors in perceiving the heliotrope lights (heliotropes were the targets almost everywhere), single centring uncertainties, and above all the graduation errors of the circles.

“Als Ursachen jener Erscheinung müssen, da fast ausschliesslich Heliotrope als Einstellungsobjekte benutzt sind, nächst Seitenrefraktionen des Lichtes und Auffassungsfehlern der Heliotropenlichter, sowie vielleicht einzelnen Centrirungsunsicherheiten, besonders die Theilungsfehler der Kreise betrachtet werden.”
In English: “As causes of that effect, since heliotropes were used almost exclusively as pointing targets, one must consider, besides lateral refractions of the light and errors of perception of the heliotrope lights, and perhaps single centring uncertainties, above all the graduation errors of the circles.”

Historic abstract, January 1847, Boschluis station in the Bushman Flat (p. 415). The heliostat on Keibiskow, about 80 miles away, rose above the horizon only in the early morning, when the vertical refraction was largest, so this angle could be measured only then. The margin note reads 'Effect of mirage on the Keibiskow light'. This shows the observers watched the change of refraction through the day and timed the work to it.

“The angle between the Keibiskow and Kamies-Sector Berg station detained me there until the 11th, for the top of Keibiskow could only be seen during the maximum refraction. Introduction to Section 9, Observed Zenith Distances of Stations (p. 591). A zenith distance is the angle between the vertical and the line of sight. The tables name the instrument (D = Dollond repeating circle, B = Beaufort theodolite), give the height of the target above the station surface, mark heliostat targets with H, and reduce excentric set-ups to the angle point by a printed formula.

“The letters D and B in the third column distinguish the instruments employed in the measurement of the zenith distances,—viz., the Dollond repeating circle and the Beaufort theodolite. In the eighth column is given the height of the object observed above the surface of the station ; and when the object was a heliostat, the letter H is annexed to the name of the station in column five. The observations with the Dollond circle were for the most part made at excentric stations, and require on this account special reductions to the trigonometric or angle point.”

Paragraph 56 (p. 20). When a distant station was often hidden, a white rod 2 to 3 miles away, in the same vertical plane, stood in for it in the round; the distant beacon was tied to the rod by micrometer whenever it could be seen. Verloren Vlei was observed this way from Mare's Kop and Langekloof.

“56. A satisfactory method of including in the round of observations a distant station which was frequently being obscured by mist or grass-fire smoke was to set up a signal, usually a straight rod, two inches in diameter and painted white, at a distance from the observing point of between 2 and 3 miles, and, as nearly as possible, in the vertical of the distant station. This rod was regarded as the distant station, and included in the usual round of observations. The beacon at the latter was then referred to the rod, at suitable opportunities, by means of the micrometer of the observing telescope, by simple vertical movement of the latter.”

Towers, scaffolds and high stations Vertical refraction coefficients

Same page. Roy records the state of the air (pressure and temperature) against each observation in the table facing p. 246, then states why he did not turn these readings into a correction: the two ends of a line were not observed at the same time with two instruments. He then states the main result of the table.

“The heights of the barometer and thermometer are inserted on the days on which the observations were made, merely to shew what was nearly the state of the atmosphere at the respective times. But we have not attempted to apply any correction on that account, because it could not be done in a satisfactory manner, and consequently could not be useful, unless the circumstances had permitted reciprocal observations to have been made at corresponding times with double sets of instruments, which in our situation was impossible. By attending to the results in the table, it will in general be seen, that terrestrial as well as celestial refraction certainly diminishes as the heights of the stations above the sea increase”

“Proportionable Part.”
Reading the table. Columns: height of the telescope above the sea in feet at each end (letters A, R, H, L etc. are the station initials); distance of the stations in fathoms; contained arc nearly (minutes, seconds); mean refraction (minutes, seconds); proportionable part (fraction of the contained arc). Upper part: from 1/2 and 1/3 (Allington Knoll and Ruckinge, 329 and 37.4 ft) to 1/24 (Dover Castle and Folkestone Turnpike, 469 and 575.3 ft). Lower part: Folkestone and Calais 1/6 and 1/7, Dover and Calais 1/15 and 1/16, Folkestone and Montlambert 1/17. 1795: moist vapours near the ground named as the principal cause of unusual refraction, tested by the bending line of pickets on a dewy morning
Trigonometrical Survey of England and Wales (Ordnance), Williams, Mudge and Dalby 1791-1799 · p. 587 · strength ★★★
Towers, scaffolds and high stations

Same remarks, after Dalby's account of a hill top that seemed to lift off the ground on a dewy day in the Isle of Wight. The pickets were posts driven in a straight line 100 feet apart for the Hounslow Heath base. Seen through the telescope on a dewy, sunny morning they appeared curved; in the afternoon the curve was gone. This links the irregular refraction to moisture and evaporation over the ground.

“Here, and also on Hounslow Heath, the rays of light passed near the earth's surface a great way before they arrived at the eye; and it is more than probable, that moist vapours were the principal cause of the very unusual refractions: the truth of which conjecture seems to be verified by the following circumstance. In measuring the base on Hounslow Heath, we had driven into the ground, at the distance of 100 feet from each other, about 30 pickets, so that their heads appeared through the boning telescope to be in a right line: this was done in the afternoon. The following morning proved uncommonly dewy, and the sun shone bright; when having occasion to replace the telescope, we remarked that the heads of the pickets exhibited a curve, concave upwards, the farthermost pickets rising the highest”
Williams, E., Mudge, W., & Dalby, I. (1795). An account of the trigonometrical survey carried on in the years 1791, 1792, 1793, and 1794. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, 85, 414-591., p. 587

Ordnance Trigonometrical Survey of Great Britain and Ireland, Principal Triangulation · p. 550 · strength ★★★
Vertical refraction coefficients Towers, scaffolds and high stations

Conclusion of the refraction section. The levelled-height table and the reciprocal table are combined. Clarke separates rays over the sea from rays over land, and treats short lines near the ground separately because their refraction is larger and irregular.

“With one or two exceptions, all the coefficients in the preceding tables are derived from observed zenith distances of very distant objects; and the results are, upon the whole, tolerably consistent. The same consistency, however, is not found to exist among coefficients of refraction deduced from the observations of objects at short distances: the values are very irregular, and, indeed, cannot be represented with precision by any mean quantity. A great deal depends upon the nature of the ground over which the ray passes: as a general rule, when the distances are small the ray passes near the ground, which would tend to increase the coefficient of refraction, as is evident from Struve's formula (page 512); and this agrees with observation, for the mean value at short distances is certainly not under 0.1000, one-tenth of the arc-distance, with an uncertainty of at least half that quantity.”
Clarke, A. R. (1858). Ordnance trigonometrical survey of Great Britain and Ireland: Account of the observations and calculations of the principal triangulation. London: Eyre and Spottiswoode., p. 550

Chapter VI, section 5. The heights of 109 points were carried by zenith distances from the New Russia points Popovka and Kadamovka to a mark on the Caspian shore at Naryshkina Kosa. This gives the difference between the levels of the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea. Struve's computation of the 1836 and 1837 Caspian to Black Sea levelling expedition (Fuss, Sabler and Savich) gives a second, independent value. The two differ by 0.643 sazhen.

“При исчисленіи высотъ 109 пунктовъ отъ начальнаго до Нарышкиной Косы, найдено, что разность поверхности морей Чернаго и Каспійскаго = — 12, 850 саж. Директоръ Пулковской Обсерваторіи Струве исчисливъ съ строжайшею точностію наблюденія, сдѣланныя въ 1836 и 1837 годахъ, для разрѣшенія ученаго вопроса относительно уровней этихъ морей нашелъ, что Каспійское море ниже Чернаго на = — 12, 207 саж. Разность обоихъ опредѣленій = 0, 643 саж.”
In English: “In computing the heights of 109 points from the starting point to Naryshkina Kosa it was found that the difference of the surfaces of the Black and Caspian Seas = -12.850 sazhen. The Director of the Pulkovo Observatory, Struve, having computed with the strictest accuracy the observations made in 1836 and 1837 to resolve the scientific question of the levels of these seas, found that the Caspian Sea is lower than the Black by -12.207 sazhen. Difference of the two determinations = 0.643 sazhen.”
Worked out here: 12.850 - 12.207 = 0.643 sazhen. 1 sazhen = 2.1336 m, so 0.643 sazhen = 1.37 m. 950 versts at 1.0668 km = about 1013 km.

Heft I, § 12, the Russian (Polish) triangulation under General Tenner. In the southern Warsaw to Czenstochau connection the average number of sets was 11.4. The closures of all 219 Polish triangles give a mean angle error of ±0.73″. Tenner found this somewhat high and gave as reasons the high signals (pyramids 6 to 20 m, and 20 to 50 m in 148 cases) and measurement in unfavourable air that could not always be avoided. The rule for such air and strong wind was 18 to 24 sets. The sum of the 219 closures, +9.73″, shows no bias to positive or negative.

“Als Erklärungsgrund werden die hohen Signale, welche meist nothwendig waren, sowie die mehrfach nicht zu vermeidende Messung bei ungünstiger Luft angeführt. (Bei ungünstiger Luft und starkem Wind sollten 18—24 Sätze genommen werden.) Die Summe der 219 Widersprüche ist + 9″,73, so dass keine Neigung zu positiven oder negativen Schlussfehlern zu erkennen ist.”
In English: “The high signals, which were mostly necessary, and the measurement in unfavourable air, which several times could not be avoided, are given as the explanation. (In unfavourable air and strong wind 18 to 24 sets were to be taken.) The sum of the 219 closures is +9.73″, so that no tendency to positive or negative closure errors can be seen.”
Worked out here: √(354.1 / (219 × 3)) = √0.539 = 0.734″ (printed ±0.73″). Per direction 0.73/√2 = 0.52″ (printed).

Heft I, § 5, French channel stations of 1862. At Harlettes Beaux observed on a 21 m scaffold in wind under very unfavourable conditions, so Helmert doubled all q (halved all weights). “Harlettes. Die Beobachtungen wurden 1862 von Beaux wegen Wind unter sehr ungünstigen Umständen auf einem 21 m hohen Gerüst ausgeführt, weshalb ich hier alle q verdoppelt habe. ... Letzterer Werth ist verdoppelt worden, weil jene 60 Rep. an einem einzigen Tage erhalten sind.”

Lateral refraction named as the most important outside influence on horizontal angles; larger on plains and over jungle
GTS Bombay Longitudinal Series (Southern Trigon) · p. 100 · strength ★★★
Towers, scaffolds and high stations

Chapter III, the weights of the angles. Lateral refraction is the sideways bend of a ray passing close to ground or objects; it affects horizontal angles. The survey did not correct each angle for it; it measured its effect through the scatter of angles in each group and weighted the groups accordingly. Station height above ground is named as the control.

“Disparity of circumstance necessarily occurs whenever there are very marked variations in the general elevation of the observing and signal stations above the level of the ground; for on this condition freedom from grazing rays—and their concomitant lateral refractions—greatly depends. [...] and of these there can be little doubt that the most important is lateral refraction, which is liable to be greater in the plains than in the hills, and much greater in tracts of country which are covered with dense forest and jungle, than in tracts which are open and cultivated.”
Great Trigonometrical Survey of India. (1890). Account of the operations of the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India, Vol. XII: The Southern Trigon. Dehra Dun: Trigonometrical Branch, Survey of India., p. 100

Part III, introduction to the Indiana series. "Positions of the circle" are the different settings of the graduated circle, used so that graduation errors average out. "Broken series" are series in which some signals could not be seen, so the series had to be repeated.

“It was through this section that our highest towers were needed, and even then considerable cutting had to be resorted to. All the observations were made on lights at night. The total length of the series between the base-net lines is nearly 216 kilometres (or 135 statute miles); the number of stations is 15; the average length of a side is 32 kilometres (or 19.9 statute miles); the number of series of measures at a station (mean of telescope D. and R.) exceeds 34,* and the usual number of the positions of the circle is 17. [...] *The intention was to observe each direction 34 times, but owing to the presence of broken series their total number is much greater.”
Reading the table. The crop also shows the first station abstract of the series (Oblong, Illinois, 1879): dates, theodolite, telescope height above ground (30.94 m), observer, and for each direction the station-adjusted value and the corrections from the base-net and figure adjustments.
Worked out here: 34 series / 17 positions = 2 series in each circle position.

Part II, fifth section to Mobile Bay. The probable errors from the triangle closures are compared across four sections observed by different observers, instruments, heights and hours.

“The country being well timbered and cutting impracticable, it was necessary to elevate the theodolite on scaffolds ranging from 12m.4 to 46m.5 in height, with several 37m high. All observing was done at night on signal lights. The mean closing error derived from 28 triangles composing the figure equals sqrt(38.23/28) = +/- 1".17; the mean error of an angle is +/- 0".68, and the probable error of a direction, 0.674 x 1.17/sqrt(6) = +/- 0".34. For the several sections these last values are very nearly equal notwithstanding the number of observers, of instruments, and methods, and other circumstances, such as elevation of instruments, day or night observations, etc. The values of the probable error of a direction for the second, third, fourth, and fifth sections average +/- 0".34, which indicates that the triangulation of Alabama is of a high degree of accuracy.”

Robinson's report, paragraphs 20-21 (p. 165). Heights carried by vertical angles from Zwartkop, Natal, are compared with heights from spirit levelling from Delagoa Bay at four stations, next to the theoretical probable error (0.35 foot per mile times the square root of the miles). Same section, after the table. Roy states that the ray height above the ground changes the refraction even for the same arc, and that a full study would be a separate operation on high mountains near the sea, with heights fixed by levelling (he names Ben Nevis; the 1858 account later observed there).

“If the circumstances had permitted the refraction on the distance between Dover and Calais to have been repeatedly tried, at the bottom of the cliff, at the top of the cliff, and again at the top of the castle, we should probably have found the refraction at the three stations considerably different, with the same length of arc, or one only varying insensibly. Section on placing the instrument. Raising the instrument lifts the line of sight clear of the ground over flat country. The inner scaffold for the instrument was separate from the outer one for the observer, so neither the observer's movements nor the wind on the hut reached the instrument.

“The high stage used for the great instruments is 32 feet high, but has been only used in cases of absolute necessity. ... Many instances of high scaffolding occurred in the triangulation of the Eastern Counties, where, the country being flat, the stations were over church-towers. ... Thus the instrument, at the height of 178 feet above ground, was insulated, and not affected by the movements of the observer, or the action of the wind upon the observatory.”

“The amount of terrestrial refraction is very variable and not to be expressed by any simple law: the path of a ray of light, inasmuch as it depends on the refractive power of the atmosphere at every point through which it passes, is necessarily very irregular. Tome II, Chapter I, terrain of Finland. Between Uleaborg and Tornea the stations stand on low islands; Rontti and Ulkogrunni are only 1.2 and 3.2 toises (about 2.3 and 6.2 m) above the sea. Abnormally strong vertical refraction lifts distant objects above the horizon. Struve states that Woldstedt very often had to wait for these extraordinary refractions to see the stations, and stayed nearly two months on Ulkogrunni to complete one station.

“M. Woldstedt a dû très-souvent profiter des réfractions extraordinaires pour atteindre son but; aussi voyons nous, dans ses journaux, que pour achever les observations d'une seule de ces stations, Ulkogrunni, il a dû faire un séjour de près de deux mois sur cette île déserte.”
In English: “Mr Woldstedt very often had to take advantage of the extraordinary refractions to reach his aim; we also see in his journals that, to complete the observations of only one of these stations, Ulkogrunni, he had to stay nearly two months on this deserted island.”
Worked out here: 1 toise = 1.949 m: 1.2 toise = 2.3 m, 3.2 toises = 6.2 m.

Introduction, season 1862-63. Finding old station marks destroyed, Haig re-observed the old triangles as well as the new ones. A station built too low left a ray close to a hill; the extra refraction of evening did not lift it clear, so the station had to be raised.

“he therefore determined not only to observe the angles of the new triangles which had been approximately laid down by Mr. McGill, but to re-observe those of all the old ones, [...] The second delay was occasioned by Kem Station not having been built sufficiently high; there was a hill on which the ray to Wápla grazed, but which was so close to Kem, that the increased refraction in the evening produced scarcely any perceptible effect in raising the ray clear of the hill, which was covered with large laterite boulders.”

Small triangulation near Klyp Fonteyn, La Caille's base (p. 49). The relative heights of the base ends were found with an 18-inch level, and the refraction entered the computed altitudes. Zenith distances were taken from both ends of the base and the mean used, so the refraction on the line is found from the line itself.

“Lieutenant Williams and myself examined the relative heights of the base-line and corn-floor with an excellent 18-inch level, sent out by Capt. Beaufort for these inquiries. We found the north end 72·2 feet, and the south end 68·3 feet, lower than the corn-floor. The axis of the repeating circle was four feet above the floor. These quantities are taken into account in the computation of the altitudes, together with the refraction : the zenith distances having been observed at both ends of the base, the mean of the results was taken.”

“as only two base lines (Belfast and Kroonstad) were directly connected with the mean sea level, the heights above mean sea level of the others were entirely dependent on the results of the vertical angles, and that the probable errors of these heights compared to the radius of the earth should not exceed the probable error of the measurement of the base lines; or, in other words and assuming that the probable error of a measurement is one millionth of the length, that the probable error of a vertical height should not exceed 21 feet. Delambre's two remedies against a possible lateral refraction: wait for favourable moments, and repeat at different hours and conditions
Delambre and Méchain, meridian arc Dunkirk to Barcelona (Base du système métrique) · T1 Discours préliminaire p. 106 · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours Repetition over days and hours Night lamps and heliotropes

Discours préliminaire, section on signals. Lateral refraction is a sideways bend of the line of sight, which would change horizontal angles. Delambre says he was at times tempted to believe in it, that night lamps would be equally subject to it, and that the defence is to observe at good moments and to repeat at other hours and in other conditions, so that a sideways error does not repeat in the same direction.

“S'il existe une réfraction latérale, comme j'ai été par fois tenté de le croire, les réverbères y seroient également sujets, et l'on n'a pour se garantir de cette illusion que deux moyens qui ne sont pas infaillibles, l'un est d'attendre les instans favorables ; l'autre, de répéter les observations à des heures et dans des circonstances différentes.”
In English: “If a lateral refraction exists, as I have at times been tempted to believe, reverberatory lamps would be equally subject to it, and there are only two means, not infallible, to guard against this illusion: one is to wait for favourable moments; the other, to repeat the observations at different hours and in different circumstances.”
Méchain, P., & Delambre, J.-B. J. (1806). Base du système métrique décimal, ou mesure de l'arc du méridien compris entre les parallèles de Dunkerque et Barcelone (Vol. 1). Paris: Baudouin., T1 Discours préliminaire p. 106
Zenith distances: one series of ten per target, more when doubtful; in bad weather angles were repeated instead; the zenith distance nearest in hour to the angle was used
Delambre and Méchain, meridian arc Dunkirk to Barcelona (Base du système métrique) · T1 Discours préliminaire p. 113 · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours Repetition over days and hours

Discours préliminaire, section Observations. A zenith distance is the vertical angle between the plumb-line direction straight up (the zenith) and the target. A series is a run of repeated readings on the repeating circle; ten angles means the circle was turned ten times and the total divided by ten. Delambre gives his rule and the reason: in bad weather the variations of refraction make zenith distances less sure. For steep sights he took the zenith distance just before or after the angle, or at several hours, and used the one nearest in time. Méchain repeated zenith distances more than Delambre.

“je me suis contenté de faire pour chaque distance au zénith une seule série de dix angles, excepté dans les cas où quelque circonstance rendoit l'observation douteuse. Quand le temps étoit beau, j'aimois mieux répéter l'observation des angles de position, et, s'il étoit mauvais, les variations de la réfraction terrestre auroient rendu les distances au zénith plus incertaines. Quand ces distances sont plus grandes que 91 degrés, ou plus petites que 89, il conviendroit de les observer en même temps que l'angle de position ; mais cela n'est guère possible. Il falloit donc se contenter de les observer immédiatement avant ou après, ou à plusieurs heures du jour, afin de choisir pour la réduction des angles à l'horizon la distance dont l'heure étoit la plus voisine, et où l'on avoit lieu de croire la réfraction terrestre moins différente.”
In English: “I was content to make for each zenith distance a single series of ten angles, except in cases where some circumstance made the observation doubtful. When the weather was fine I preferred to repeat the observation of the angles of position, and if it was bad, the variations of terrestrial refraction would have made the zenith distances more uncertain. When these distances are greater than 91 degrees or less than 89, they should be observed at the same time as the angle of position; but that is hardly possible. So one had to be content to observe them immediately before or after, or at several hours of the day, in order to choose for the reduction of the angles to the horizon the distance whose hour was nearest, and where there was reason to believe the terrestrial refraction least different.”
Méchain, P., & Delambre, J.-B. J. (1806). Base du système métrique décimal, ou mesure de l'arc du méridien compris entre les parallèles de Dunkerque et Barcelone (Vol. 1). Paris: Baudouin., T1 Discours préliminaire p. 113

Tome I, Observations géodésiques, station of Fiefs. For each angle every series is printed: the number of repetitions, the total arc in grades, the single angle, the reduction to the centre, the observer and circle (D. = Delambre, F. = Lalande, B. = Bellet; n° 1 or n° 4 = circle number), the date and hours, and a remark on visibility, sun and wind. One series is marked 'série à rejeter' (series to be rejected) for strong wind, a faint and curved target and undulations. The remark on Sauti says that phases (the side lighting of a spire by the sun) moved the apparent target.

“D. n° 1 + première place. Grand vent ; Sauti foible et courbe ; ondulations au Mesnil ; fils en + série à rejeter. ... Le clocher de Sauti et les flèches voisines nous ont fort exercés par leurs phases différentes. ... D. n° 1. 3 juillet, 5h 40' — 7h 20'. Objets éclairés du soleil ; Sauti tout-à-fait courbe. ... F. n° 4. 4 juillet, 3h 10' — 5h 45'. Objets assez beaux en commençant ; ils l'étoient moins vers le milieu.”
In English: “D. circle no. 1, first place. Strong wind; Sauti faint and curved; undulations at Mesnil; wires in +; series to be rejected. ... The steeple of Sauti and the neighbouring spires gave us much trouble by their different phases. ... D. circle no. 1. 3 July, 5h 40' to 7h 20'. Objects lit by the sun; Sauti quite curved. ... F. circle no. 4. 4 July, 3h 10' to 5h 45'. Objects rather fine at the start; less so towards the middle.”
Reading the table. Each block is one series: first number = repetitions (20 or 12 here); then the total arc in grades, the single angle in grades, and the same in degrees; the line 'Au centre' gives the angle reduced to the centre of the station. Below: circle and observer, date, hours, remarks on the air. The angle between Mesnil and Sauti has three series of 20; the mean of the first three is reduced to the horizon (+0.58") to give 42° 59' 48.72". Bonnières-Sauti has series of 20, 20 and 12 on 3 and 4 July at different hours. A typical angle in Delambre's north part has 2 to 5 series of 12 to 30 repetitions (e.g. Dunkerque, Watten-Cassel: 20 + 16 + 30).
Worked out here: Mesnil-Sauti series reduced to centre: 42° 59' 49.68" and 42° 59' 55.07" (the rejected series is 5.4" higher).
