Tome I, station of Boiscommun (frimaire an 2, December 1793). Delambre observed the zenith distance of the weathercock of Châteauneuf on seven days, one series of ten each, and printed with each the hour, the barometer (in pouces and lignes), the thermometer (as a fraction of the ice-to-boiling interval, converted to Réaumur degrees), and the sky: rain, fine or poor horizon, damp fog. He also stayed half an hour at the telescope to see whether refraction changed the distance. This is a direct record of humidity and pressure with each vertical angle.

“24 frimaire, 12h ¼. Bar. 27p 1l9. Therm. 0.099 = 7d92. A 1h ¼ la distance étoit encore la même. ... Le baromètre et le thermomètre étoient placés environ 1t8 au-dessous de la lunette. Après ces observations je suis resté pendant une demi-heure à la lunette, pour voir si la réfraction ne changeroit pas la distance : je n'ai pas vu la moindre variation. Horizon très-pur, point de soleil. ... 25 frimaire, 3h ¾. Bar. 27p 4l. Therm. + 0.11 = 8d8. Temps pluvieux ; horizon assez beau. ... 30 frimaire, 3h ½. Bar. 27p 3l. Therm. + 0.067 = 5d36. Brouillard humide.”
In English: “24 frimaire, 12h ¼. Barometer 27 pouces 1.9 lignes. Thermometer 0.099 = 7.92 degrees. At 1h ¼ the distance was still the same. ... The barometer and thermometer were placed about 1.8 toises below the telescope. After these observations I stayed half an hour at the telescope to see whether refraction would change the distance: I did not see the least variation. Very clear horizon, no sun. ... 25 frimaire, 3h ¾. Barometer 27 pouces 4 lignes. Thermometer +0.11 = 8.8 degrees. Rainy weather; horizon fairly fine. ... 30 frimaire, 3h ½. Barometer 27 pouces 3 lignes. Thermometer +0.067 = 5.36 degrees. Damp fog.”
Reading the table. Each line: number of repetitions (10), total arc in grades, single zenith distance in grades, the same in degrees; then date, hour, barometer, thermometer, remarks. Seven series on seven days (24 to 30 frimaire) to the same target. The page continues on p. 167 with 1, 2 and 7 nivôse.
Worked out here: Seven zenith distances of the Châteauneuf weathercock range from 90° 5' 46.0" (28 frimaire) to 90° 6' 6.1" (30 frimaire, damp fog): spread 20.1".

Boiscommun: observations repeated many times to test barometer and hygrometer effects; fog found to be the main cause, its values set aside
Delambre and Méchain, meridian arc Dunkirk to Barcelona (Base du système métrique) · T2 p. 775 · strength ★★★
Rejecting readings in unsteady air Vertical refraction coefficients Repetition over days and hours

Tome II, remarks on the n table. A hygrometer measures air humidity. Delambre repeated the reciprocal observations at Boiscommun many times to see whether changes of the barometer and hygrometer affected refraction, and left the instrument pointed at Châteauneuf for several hours. He found fog to be the main factor (n of 0.14 to 0.17) and set the fog observations aside.

“A Boiscommun j'ai répété les observations un grand nombre de fois, pour voir si les changemens du baromètre et de l'hygromètre influoient sur la réfraction : je n'ai rien pu remarquer. J'ai laissé pendant plusieurs heures l'instrument bien callé et la lunette dirigée sur Châteauneuf, dans l'intervalle des observations de distances au zénith, et je n'ai pas vu de variations sensibles dans la hauteur ... Il paroît que c'est le brouillard qui influe surtout sur les réfractions, et qui donne pour n des valeurs de 0.14 à 0.17. Je laisse donc à part les observations non numérotées de Boiscommun.”
In English: “At Boiscommun I repeated the observations a great many times to see whether changes of the barometer and the hygrometer affected refraction: I could notice nothing. I left the instrument firmly set for several hours with the telescope pointed at Châteauneuf, between the zenith-distance observations, and I saw no noticeable variation in the height ... It appears that it is fog above all that affects refraction, and gives for n values of 0.14 to 0.17. I therefore set aside the unnumbered observations of Boiscommun.”
Méchain, P., & Delambre, J.-B. J. (1807). Base du système métrique décimal, ou mesure de l'arc du méridien compris entre les parallèles de Dunkerque et Barcelone (Vol. 2). Paris: Baudouin., T2 p. 775
Instruction: zenith distances from at least three series at different hours, mainly near midday, simultaneous where possible, with barometer readings; first-order series to the twentieth repetition
Parallel of Paris, Brest to Strasbourg (Henry east part, Bonne west part), Nouvelle carte de France · 28 · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours Repetition over days and hours

Instruction of the commission of the Dépôt de la Guerre for the new map of France, printed by Puissant. It sets the observing rules for the first-order chains, including the parallel of Paris. A conjugate observation is one repetition of the angle on the repeating circle. Simultaneous observations are reciprocal zenith distances taken at both ends at the same time, so that both see the same state of the air.

“Les distances zénithales relatives à ces chaînes seront elles-mêmes le résultat de trois séries au moins, prises à des heures différentes, et surtout vers le milieu du jour, afin qu'elles puissent donner les différences de niveau avec toute l'exactitude désirable, et, autant qu'il sera possible, par le concours d'observations simultanées : celles-ci seront accompagnées d'observations barométriques. ... Toutes les séries du premier ordre seront, autant que possible, prolongées jusqu'à la vingtième observation conjuguée ; toutes celles du deuxième ordre s'arrêteront à la dixième.”
In English: “The zenith distances for these chains will themselves be the result of at least three series, taken at different hours, and above all towards the middle of the day, so that they can give the level differences with all desirable accuracy, and, as far as possible, by the combination of simultaneous observations: these will be accompanied by barometric observations. ... All first-order series will, as far as possible, be carried to the twentieth conjugate observation; all those of the second order will stop at the tenth.”
Puissant, L. (1832). Nouvelle description géométrique de la France (Première partie). Paris: Ch. Picquet., 28

Brousseaud, narrative of the French part (1811-1823). A repetition is one turn of the repeating circle; a series is the set of repetitions whose total gives one value of the angle. Because results sometimes varied even when the view seemed the same, the number of series for each angle was set by how far the first five or six series disagreed. The sentence continues on p. 158 (item fr_45n_02).

“A cet effet on prit la résolution, ainsi qu'il a été déjà signalé page 32, de multiplier les observations d'angles entre les objets terrestres trente fois au moins par chaque série, et de répéter ces séries à des heures et à des jours différens. On avait remarqué depuis long-temps que, malgré tous les soins apportés dans les observations angulaires, les résultats variaient quelquefois d'une quantité considérable, quoique les circonstances de la vision parussent les mêmes. En conséquence le nombre des séries jugées nécessaires à la mesure d'un angle fut déterminé par le nombre de secondes dont les cinq ou six premiers résultats différaient entre eux”
In English: “To this end it was resolved, as already noted on page 32, to multiply the observations of angles between terrestrial objects at least thirty times per series, and to repeat these series at different hours and on different days. It had long been noticed that, despite all the care taken in angular observations, the results sometimes varied by a considerable amount, although the conditions of vision seemed the same. Consequently the number of series judged necessary for the measurement of an angle was set by the number of seconds by which the first five or six results differed among themselves”
Brousseaud (Colonel). (1839). Mesure d'un arc du parallèle moyen entre le pôle et l'équateur. Limoges: F. Chapoulaud., 157
When the first six series differed by 15 to 20 seconds, the angle was carried to twelve or fifteen series; differences of 25 to 35 decimal seconds between days at the same hour
Brousseaud, arc of the mean parallel (45 N) across France, with link to the Austro-Sardinian chain · 158 · strength ★★★
Repetition over days and hours

Brousseaud, p. 158, continuing the rule of p. 157. Decimal seconds are centesimal seconds (1 decimal second = 0.324 sexagesimal second). The author reports, without hiding it, that series of the same angle at the same hour on different days differed by 25 to 35 decimal seconds even when both targets were seen well, and that more series were added to reduce these errors.

“[si, de la première à la sixième série (par exemple), les angles conclus variaient de quinze à] vingt secondes, on les continuait jusqu'à la douzième ou quinzième série afin d'atténuer le plus possible ces erreurs inexplicables. On a remarqué des différences de vingt-cinq à trente-cinq secondes décimales entre les résultats des séries d'un même angle observé à la même heure et à des jours différens, quoique les deux objets sur lesquels on pointait se vissent parfaitement dans des circonstances semblables.”
In English: “[if, from the first to the sixth series (for example), the concluded angles varied by fifteen to] twenty seconds, they were continued to the twelfth or fifteenth series in order to reduce these unexplained errors as much as possible. Differences of twenty-five to thirty-five decimal seconds were noticed between the results of series of the same angle observed at the same hour and on different days, although the two objects pointed at were seen perfectly in similar circumstances.”
Worked out here: 25 to 35 decimal seconds = 8.1" to 11.3" sexagesimal.
Brousseaud (Colonel). (1839). Mesure d'un arc du parallèle moyen entre le pôle et l'équateur. Limoges: F. Chapoulaud., 158
Zenith distances of the signal tops always taken between eleven and one o'clock, in at least six or eight series of ten
Brousseaud, arc of the mean parallel (45 N) across France, with link to the Austro-Sardinian chain · 158 · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours Repetition over days and hours

Brousseaud, p. 158. A zenith distance is the vertical angle between the plumb-line direction straight up (the zenith) and the target. The hours near noon were chosen because vertical refraction is then smallest and steadiest. Six to eight series of ten single angles give 60 to 80 readings per zenith distance.

“Les distances au zénith de l'extrémité des signaux ont toujours été prises entre onze heures et une heure du soir, et répétées au moins par six ou huit séries de dix angles simples chaque.”
In English: “The zenith distances of the tops of the signals were always taken between eleven o'clock and one in the afternoon, and repeated in at least six or eight series of ten single angles each.”
Brousseaud (Colonel). (1839). Mesure d'un arc du parallèle moyen entre le pôle et l'équateur. Limoges: F. Chapoulaud., 158
French part: angles from six to fourteen series of thirty to forty repetitions on different days and hours; zenith distances repeated sixty to a hundred times between eleven and noon; all series kept; largest closure 4 seconds
Brousseaud, arc of the mean parallel (45 N) across France, with link to the Austro-Sardinian chain · 36 · strength ★★★
Repetition over days and hours Steady-air hours

Brousseaud, summary of the three parts of the arc of the mean parallel. For the French part (34 triangles, Mont Granier to Marennes) the author states the number of series and repetitions, that every series was kept in the mean without exception, and the largest triangle closure error (the amount by which the sum of the three angles missed its true value).

“Les valeurs des angles ont été déterminées par six, huit, dix, douze quatorze séries de trente à quarante répétitions chaque, faites à des jours et à des heures différens. Les distances au zénith ont aussi été répétées de soixante à cent fois, entre onze heures et midi, afin d'avoir avec exactitude la hauteur absolue des signaux placés sur les hautes montagnes de la France et de la Savoie. Le résultat adopté pour chaque angle de ces trente-quatre triangles provient de la moyenne entre tous les résultats fournis par les séries relatives à cet angle, et prises sans exception. Cependant, malgré ces soins, la plus grande erreur de la somme des trois angles des triangles s'élève encore à 4" de degré.”
In English: “The values of the angles were determined by six, eight, ten, twelve, fourteen series of thirty to forty repetitions each, made on different days and at different hours. The zenith distances were also repeated sixty to a hundred times, between eleven and noon, to obtain accurately the absolute height of the signals placed on the high mountains of France and Savoy. The result adopted for each angle of these thirty-four triangles is the mean of all the results given by the series for that angle, taken without exception. Yet, despite these precautions, the largest error of the sum of the three angles of the triangles still reaches 4" of a degree.”
Worked out here: 6 to 14 series x 30 to 40 repetitions = 180 to 560 repetitions per angle.
Brousseaud (Colonel). (1839). Mesure d'un arc du parallèle moyen entre le pôle et l'équateur. Limoges: F. Chapoulaud., 36
Roy: in hot weather only short morning and evening periods were good enough; a whole day could go for one satisfactory angle
Anglo-French triangulation of 1787 (Greenwich to Paris junction), English side by Roy · p. 170 · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours Repetition over days and hours Rejecting readings in unsteady air

Roy, Art. I of the section on the triangles, explaining why the angles were repeated less often than planned. 'Tremulous motion or boiling in the air' is the shimmer caused by heated air near the ground, which makes a distant object dance in the telescope. Roy observed only when the objects were distinct, and he did not change the zero (the starting point on the divided circle) at those times because each change needed a new levelling of the instrument.

“At particular times, especially in hot weather, there was such a tremulous motion or boiling in the air, that it was only during a very short space, chiefly in the mornings and evenings, that the objects were sufficiently distinct to be observed with accuracy. So difficult it is to do any thing perfectly good in this way, that a whole day has frequently been spent, after watching with anxious care, in obtaining a single one that was perfectly satisfactory!”
Roy, W. (1790). An account of the trigonometrical operation, whereby the distance between the meridians of the Royal Observatories of Greenwich and Paris has been determined. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, 80, 111-270 (with Dalby, I., Remarks, pp. 593-614)., p. 170
Roy: fewer repetitions than planned, but a few very good observations beat a mean of many hurried ones, as the base of verification shows
Anglo-French triangulation of 1787 (Greenwich to Paris junction), English side by Roy · p. 171 · strength ★★★
Repetition over days and hours

Same article, p. 169 to p. 171. Roy had planned to measure each angle many times on different parts of the circle (to average out errors of division of the scale). He states that this was often impossible in practice. He gives the close agreement between the measured and the computed length of the base of verification (the Romney Marsh base, computed through the triangles from the Hounslow Heath base about 70 miles away) as the test of the result. On pp. 177-178 he gives that difference as about 4 1/2 inches.

“On the whole, although, for the reasons already assigned, we have repeated the observations seldomer than was at first proposed; yet it will obviously appear from the results, and particularly from the near agreement between the measured and computed length of the base of verification, that a few very good observations are greatly preferable to a mean that might perhaps have been obtained of many made in a hurry, which at best would have been but indifferent.”
Roy, W. (1790). An account of the trigonometrical operation, whereby the distance between the meridians of the Royal Observatories of Greenwich and Paris has been determined. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, 80, 111-270 (with Dalby, I., Remarks, pp. 593-614)., p. 171
1795: angles observed on different arcs and repeated till their truth became certain; doubtful night observations re-observed with fresh lights
Trigonometrical Survey of England and Wales (Ordnance), Williams, Mudge and Dalby 1791-1799 · p. 448 · strength ★★★
Repetition over days and hours Night lamps and heliotropes

Section on the instrument and method. 'Different arcs' means different parts of the divided circle, so that errors of division average out. Staffs were poles at stations up to about fifteen miles away; lamps and white lights were used at night. When only one of two white lights was seen, the observation was kept only if it showed no error beyond the division error of the instrument; otherwise new lights were sent and the angle observed again.

“namely, that of observing the angles upon different arcs. When staffs were erected, which was generally the case when the stations were not more remote than fifteen miles, the angles were repeated till their truth became certain, and the same was also done, when angles were determined by the lamps; but it sometimes happened, that only one of the two white lights, which were burned at the distant stations, was seen; in which case, if the observation appeared to be made without any error, but that which an inequality in the division of the instrument might be supposed to produce, it was considered as sufficient; otherwise fresh lights were sent to the station and observed.”
Williams, E., Mudge, W., & Dalby, I. (1795). An account of the trigonometrical survey carried on in the years 1791, 1792, 1793, and 1794. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, 85, 414-591., p. 448

Same remarks. The sentence before records that at one station the depression of Chanctonbury Ring varied from 1' 41" to 2' 30" (repeated observations of one angle). The authors state when the tabled observations were made, and they reject the idea that pressure and temperature at the station explain the changes when the ray runs close to the ground.

“The observations, however, on which the tables are founded, were made in close cloudy days, or toward the evenings, when the tremulous motion in the air is commonly the least. It has been conjectured, that the variations in terrestrial refraction, depend on the changes in the atmosphere indicated by the barometer and thermometer: this, however, cannot be the case when the rays of light pass near the earth's surface for any considerable distance.”
Williams, E., Mudge, W., & Dalby, I. (1795). An account of the trigonometrical survey carried on in the years 1791, 1792, 1793, and 1794. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, 85, 414-591., p. 586
Mudge 1799: one station's angle changed while the other's did not, so a local stratum, not dew, caused it; a long series is needed
Trigonometrical Survey of England and Wales (Ordnance), Williams, Mudge and Dalby 1791-1799 · p. 188 · strength ★★★
Repetition over days and hours

Discussion of the first series. Mudge estimates the error of each angle at no more than 3". At 9 and 10 p.m. the elevation at Whiteham changed by 44" and 42" while the depression seen from White Horse Hill stayed nearly the same. Because both ends were observed at the same time, he can place the change near one station. 'Floating strata' are layers of air with different refraction.

“These changes in the observed angles of elevation at Whiteham, (44" and 42" being the differences,) without corresponding ones at White Horse Hill, prove that some partial alteration, from floating strata, had taken place in the refraction near the former station. Whoever considers the matter, must perceive a case may be constructed in which this will take place, causing a great variation in one of the angles, whilst the other apparently remains the same: and this suggested the idea, that to afford any accurate conclusions in this way, a long series of observations would be necessary. It furthermore appears, that dew could not have caused these differences at Whiteham Hill, since the same cause would equally operate to vary the observed angles at White Horse Hill; but those remained nearly the same.”
Mudge, W. (1801). An account of the operations carried on for accomplishing a trigonometrical survey of England and Wales, continued from the year 1797, to the end of the year 1799 (Vol. 2, from the Philosophical Transactions). London: W. Faden., p. 188
Clarke 1858: the method of 'arcs': every round starts and ends on the referring object, the telescope is reversed and the circle shifted; single angles were never observed
Ordnance Trigonometrical Survey of Great Britain and Ireland, Principal Triangulation · p. 50 · strength ★★★
Repetition over days and hours

Section on the method of observing with the theodolite. The referring object (R.O.) is a fixed mark near the station. An 'arc' is one full round: the observer reads the R.O., then every object in turn, then the R.O. again; the closing reading tests the steadiness of the instrument. Between arcs the telescope is reversed and the circle turned 20 to 30 degrees, so the same directions are read on other parts of the scale. Each direction is therefore observed many times.

“The method of "arcs" has been always followed; though in the earlier operations an arc contained a smaller number of points. It has never been the practice to observe single and independent angles, as in the Indian and other geodetical operations.”
Clarke, A. R. (1858). Ordnance trigonometrical survey of Great Britain and Ireland: Account of the observations and calculations of the principal triangulation. London: Eyre and Spottiswoode., p. 50

Section IV, extracts from the general abstracts. For each station the instrument, the dates, the observer and every object are listed. The range is the difference between the greatest and least single observation of that direction. The reciprocal of weight is larger for directions with fewer or more scattered observations. Footnotes reduce bearings taken to an object off the station to the station itself.

Section IV, second part: azimuthal observations in detail. Azimuth is the angle of a line from true north; it was found from the referring object and circumpolar stars at elongation (their farthest east or west point). Each row is one night's observation with its own result, so the spread can be seen. Footnote marks give the weather for individual rows. Probable error is the amount the mean is as likely to be within as outside.

Chapter VI compares the results. A probable error is the error that is as likely to be exceeded as not; here it is computed by least squares from the closures of the triangles. For all first-class triangles the probable error of one angle is 0.5997″. The main row (angles in at least 12 sets) gives 0.6019″, the Kizlyar row (6 sets) gives 0.6011″. The authors conclude that more sets did not raise the accuracy as fast as probability theory predicts, and put this down to outside conditions, above all the uneven illumination of the targets.

“Это показываетъ: что отъ увеличенія числа пріемовъ точность угла возрастаетъ не съ такою быстротою, какъ убѣждаетъ въ томъ исчисленіе вѣроятностей, и что слѣдственно тутъ, какъ надо полагать, зависитъ отъ обстоятельствъ совершенно постороннихъ, въ особенности же отъ болѣе или менѣе одинаковаго освѣщенія наблюдаемыхъ предметовъ.”
In English: “This shows that with an increase in the number of sets the accuracy of an angle grows not as fast as the calculus of probabilities leads one to expect, and that consequently it depends here, as one must suppose, on quite external circumstances, in particular on the more or less uniform illumination of the observed objects.”
Worked out here: Sum of squared closures 367.6443 for the first-class triangles. Probable error of one angle: all triangles 0.5997″; main row (119 triangles, 12 or more sets) 0.6019″; Kizlyar row (36 triangles, 6 sets) 0.6011″.

Livonia: measure only with distinct images, in the 2-hour afternoon calm; triangle closures show one Livonian set worth 8 of Bessel's
Struve Geodetic Arc (Russo-Scandinavian arc of the meridian, Danube to Fuglenaes) · T. I, p. 32 · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours Repetition over days and hours

Tome I, Chapter IV. A set (mise) is one complete round of pointings. Struve counts 833 sets for the 141 Livonian directions (5.91 per direction) against 41.77 per direction in Bessel's East Prussian survey. He then compares the two surveys by their triangle closures (the excess of the angle sum over 180 degrees plus the spherical excess): mean square 0.987 for 31 Livonian triangles and 1.179 for Bessel's 15. From this he finds one Livonian set equal in weight to 8.44 Prussian sets, and he states the Livonian rule: measure only with sufficiently distinct images, in practice in the 2-hour afternoon period of calm images.

“En Livonie la règle a été strictement observée, de ne jamais faire des mesures que par des images suffisamment distinctes des objets, c'est-à-dire presque exclusivement pendant la période de 2 heures des images calmes, qui d'ordinaire a lieu chaque après-midi (Gradmessung I. p. 88).”
In English: “In Livonia the rule was strictly kept never to make measurements except with sufficiently distinct images of the objects, that is, almost exclusively during the 2-hour period of calm images which usually occurs every afternoon (Gradmessung I. p. 88).”
Worked out here: 41.77 / 5.91 = 7.07 (printed 7.07). Weight ratio printed: 41.77 × 1.179 : 5.91 × 0.987 = 8.44 : 1.
Struve, F. G. W. (1857). Arc du méridien de 25° 20' entre le Danube et la Mer Glaciale mesuré depuis 1816 jusqu'en 1855 (Vol. 1). Imprimerie de l'Académie impériale des sciences., T. I, p. 32
Swedish part: corresponding zenith distances at every station, never fewer than 40 to 50 per station
Struve Geodetic Arc (Russo-Scandinavian arc of the meridian, Danube to Fuglenaes) · T. I, Introduction p. XXIV · strength ★★★
Repetition over days and hours

Tome I, Introduction, quoting Selander's report to the Stockholm Academy. Corresponding zenith distances are measured at both ends of a line for trigonometric levelling. From Haparanda to the Norwegian border, 40 Swedish miles, Agardh and Selander observed them at all stations with two instruments read by microscopes. The number per station was never below 40 to 50 and above 100 at some stations.

“M. Agardh, professeur d'astronomie (à l'Université de Lund), a été chargé de prendre part, des observations correspondantes des distances zénithales ont été exécutées sur toutes les stations situées depuis Haparanda jusqu'à la frontière de Norvège ... Vu que le nombre des distances zénithales, mesurées sur chaque station, n'est jamais au-dessous de 40 à 50, et s'élève pour d'autres au-delà de 100, j'ai raison d'espérer que les résultats que fournira le calcul, seront dignes de confiance.”
In English: “Mr Agardh, professor of astronomy (at the University of Lund), having been charged to take part, corresponding observations of zenith distances were made at all stations from Haparanda to the border of Norway ... Since the number of zenith distances measured at each station is never below 40 to 50, and for others rises above 100, I have reason to hope that the results the computation will give will be worthy of confidence.”
Struve, F. G. W. (1857). Arc du méridien de 25° 20' entre le Danube et la Mer Glaciale mesuré depuis 1816 jusqu'en 1855 (Vol. 1). Imprimerie de l'Académie impériale des sciences., T. I, Introduction p. XXIV
Finland instruction: any observation with indistinct or too undulating images was inadmissible; each object pointed 20 times
Struve Geodetic Arc (Russo-Scandinavian arc of the meridian, Danube to Fuglenaes) · T. II, p. 21 · strength ★★★
Rejecting readings in unsteady air Repetition over days and hours

Tome II, p. 21, continuing the instruction. Undulating images are images that shimmer because of unsteady air near the ground. The instruction rejected any observation made with indistinct or too undulating images. Struve states that it was followed so strictly that only in two cases is an object wholly missing from a set; incomplete sets were completed with extra observations when the object became visible again. Each object was pointed 4 times in each set, 20 times in all, against 12 in the Baltic arc.

“Enfin l'instruction fixait, que toute observation était inadmissible, si les images des objets étaient indistinctes ou trop ondulantes. Cette instruction a été suivie en Finlande à telle rigueur, qu'il ne se trouve que deux cas, où un objet manque entièrement dans une des mises à faire. ... En Finlande, chaque objet était pointé 4 fois dans chaque mise, donc en tout 20 fois, au lieu de 12 fois dans la mesure Baltique.”
In English: “Finally the instruction laid down that any observation was inadmissible if the images of the objects were indistinct or too undulating. This instruction was followed in Finland with such rigour that there are only two cases where an object is wholly missing from one of the sets to be made. ... In Finland each object was pointed 4 times in each set, so 20 times in all, instead of 12 times in the Baltic measurement.”
Struve, F. G. W. (1860). Arc du méridien de 25° 20' entre le Danube et la Mer Glaciale mesuré depuis 1816 jusqu'en 1855 (Vol. 2). Imprimerie de l'Académie impériale des sciences., T. II, p. 21
Always 5 sets of 4 pointings; the separate values of both halves of every set are printed for each station
Struve Geodetic Arc (Russo-Scandinavian arc of the meridian, Danube to Fuglenaes) · T. II, p. 228 · strength ★★★
Repetition over days and hours Raw tables of repeated measures

Tome II, pièces justificatives, explanation of the Finland station table. Three almost identical Munich universal instruments were used by Oberg, Melan and Woldstedt, each with an assistant on the lower telescope so the pointings of the two telescopes were simultaneous. Struve states that there were always 5 sets with 4 pointings on each object, each set in two halves, and that he prints the separate figures of the two halves at every station.

“Il y a eu constamment 5 mises observées, chacune à 4 pointés de chaque objet. Mais chaque mise était composée de deux moitiés, correspondantes aux deux positions renversées de la lunette supérieure. J'ai donné, à chaque station, les chiffres séparés des deux moitiés.”
In English: “There were always 5 sets observed, each with 4 pointings of each object. But each set was made of two halves, corresponding to the two reversed positions of the upper telescope. I have given, at each station, the separate figures of the two halves.”
Struve, F. G. W. (1860). Arc du méridien de 25° 20' entre le Danube et la Mer Glaciale mesuré depuis 1816 jusqu'en 1855 (Vol. 2). Imprimerie de l'Académie impériale des sciences., T. II, p. 228
Internal check of the zenith distances: 693 values at 84 stations; probable error of one zenith distance 1.49 seconds
Struve Geodetic Arc (Russo-Scandinavian arc of the meridian, Danube to Fuglenaes) · T. II, pp. 232-233 · strength ★★★
Repetition over days and hours

Tome II, p. 233. The zenith place Z should be the same for all targets of one set if the observations were perfect and the change of terrestrial refraction (the bending of near-horizontal rays in the air) was uniform during the set. Struve uses the scatter of Z within each set as a check. At 84 stations 693 zenith distances of 335 objects were observed, about 2 per object. From the scatter he finds the probable error of a single zenith distance, from two circle positions, as 1.49″.

“Les Z qui appartiennent à la même ligne horizontale c.-à-d. à une même mise, auraient dû être identiques, si les observations avaient été d'une exactitude parfaite, et si la variation de la réfraction terrestre avait été uniforme pendant la durée de chaque mise. Les différences entre les Z de la même ligne nous font par conséquent juger de l'exactitude des distances au zénith observées”
In English: “The Z that belong to the same horizontal line, that is, to one and the same set, would have had to be identical if the observations had been of perfect accuracy and if the variation of terrestrial refraction had been uniform during each set. The differences between the Z of the same line therefore let us judge the accuracy of the observed zenith distances”
Worked out here: 693 / 335 = 2.07 observations per object (printed 2.07).
Struve, F. G. W. (1860). Arc du méridien de 25° 20' entre le Danube et la Mer Glaciale mesuré depuis 1816 jusqu'en 1855 (Vol. 2). Imprimerie de l'Académie impériale des sciences., T. II, pp. 232-233
Station Ristisaari: the 10 half-set values of each angle, two observing parties, and zenith distances with times
Struve Geodetic Arc (Russo-Scandinavian arc of the meridian, Danube to Fuglenaes) · T. II, p. 250 · strength ★★★
Raw tables of repeated measures Repetition over days and hours

Tome II, station 17 of the Finland table. Ristisaari was occupied by Oberg and Melan in 1833 and by Woldstedt in 1843. Under 'Angles horizontaux' each column holds one angle with its 10 half-set values (5 sets, two halves each), then the mean, the reduction to centre, the reduction for the signals, and the reduced angle. Under 'Angles verticaux' each line is one set of zenith distances with the date and true solar time; Z* is the mean zenith place of the set. The note at the foot reads: in 1843 the objects very undulating.

“En 1843 les objets très-ondulants.”
In English: “In 1843 the objects very undulating.”
Reading the table. Horizontal: three angles (Mäki-päälys to Svartvira and Svartvira to Tuskas by Oberg and Melan 1833; Tuskas to Kokko-vuori by Woldstedt 1843), 10 values each. Vertical: one 1833 set at 1h 45m and two 1843 sets at 23h 17m and 23h 45m (astronomical time, counted from noon), with the zenith distance to each target and the Z value in small type; log distance at the foot.
Worked out here: Half-set ranges: angle 1 39.38″ to 41.38″ (2.00″); angle 2 46.00″ to 50.87″ (4.87″); angle 3 (1843, objects very undulating) 36.00″ to 42.25″ (6.25″).
Struve, F. G. W. (1860). Arc du méridien de 25° 20' entre le Danube et la Mer Glaciale mesuré depuis 1816 jusqu'en 1855 (Vol. 2). Imprimerie de l'Académie impériale des sciences., T. II, p. 250
Polish chains: 219 triangle closures give ±0.73 seconds; in unfavourable air and strong wind 18 to 24 sets were to be taken
European arc of the parallel in 52 N, Greenwich (Feaghmain) to Warschau · p. 29 · strength ★★★
Repetition over days and hours Towers, scaffolds and high stations Night lamps and heliotropes

Heft I, § 12, the Russian (Polish) triangulation under General Tenner. In the southern Warsaw to Czenstochau connection the average number of sets was 11.4. The closures of all 219 Polish triangles give a mean angle error of ±0.73″. Tenner found this somewhat high and gave as reasons the high signals (pyramids 6 to 20 m, and 20 to 50 m in 148 cases) and measurement in unfavourable air that could not always be avoided. The rule for such air and strong wind was 18 to 24 sets. The sum of the 219 closures, +9.73″, shows no bias to positive or negative.

“Als Erklärungsgrund werden die hohen Signale, welche meist nothwendig waren, sowie die mehrfach nicht zu vermeidende Messung bei ungünstiger Luft angeführt. (Bei ungünstiger Luft und starkem Wind sollten 18—24 Sätze genommen werden.) Die Summe der 219 Widersprüche ist + 9″,73, so dass keine Neigung zu positiven oder negativen Schlussfehlern zu erkennen ist.”
In English: “The high signals, which were mostly necessary, and the measurement in unfavourable air, which several times could not be avoided, are given as the explanation. (In unfavourable air and strong wind 18 to 24 sets were to be taken.) The sum of the 219 closures is +9.73″, so that no tendency to positive or negative closure errors can be seen.”
Worked out here: √(354.1 / (219 × 3)) = √0.539 = 0.734″ (printed ±0.73″). Per direction 0.73/√2 = 0.52″ (printed).
Helmert, F. R. (Ed.). (1893). Die europäische Längengradmessung in 52 Grad Breite von Greenwich bis Warschau. I. Heft: Hauptdreiecke und Grundlinienanschlüsse von England bis Polen. P. Stankiewicz., p. 29
Golmberg: a doubtful angle was measured again in 1889; first 16 observations rejected for poor lights; the remeasurement confirms 1880 to 0.85 seconds
European arc of the parallel in 52 N, Greenwich (Feaghmain) to Warschau · p. 186 · strength ★★★
Rejecting readings in unsteady air Steady-air hours Night lamps and heliotropes Repetition over days and hours

Heft I, Kap. 3, station record of Golmberg. In 1880 each angle was measured twice on 8 circle positions, a full set of 24 pointings per direction. The angle Collm to Golmberg differed by 2.61″ from 1871. Helmert examined the possible causes: the 1880 sights were spread over only three days, and the brightly lit tower at Collm may have pulled the pointing, since the observations were as usual made in the afternoon. General Schreiber ordered a remeasurement in 1889: 32 measurements on 16 circle positions over several days, the first 16 rejected for poor lights. The new result confirms 1880 to 0.85″.

“General Schreiber ordnete eine Neumessung des letzteren an, die im Juni und Juli 1889 durch den Landesvermessungsrath Erfurth erfolgte. Es wurden 32 Messungen angestellt, die sich auf 16 Kreisstände vertheilten und 149° 16′ 49″,72 als Resultat ergaben, dessen m. F. nach Maassgabe der Abweichungen der 16 Mittel aus Hin- und Hergang vom Gesammtmittel ± 0″,20 beträgt. (Die ersten 16 Beobachtungen sind wegen mangelhafter Lichter verworfen; sie geben 49″,74.)”
In English: “General Schreiber ordered a remeasurement of the latter, which was made in June and July 1889 by Landesvermessungsrath Erfurth. 32 measurements were made, distributed over 16 circle positions, and gave 149° 16′ 49.72″ as the result, whose mean error, from the deviations of the 16 means of forward and return runs from the overall mean, is ±0.20″. (The first 16 observations were rejected because of poor lights; they give 49.74″.)”
Reading the table. The small table in the middle of the page lists the values of the angle Collm to Golmberg: 1871 from 3 circle positions with 4 and 6 pointings (50.67″, 52.01″) and from the other angles of a pentagon (51.34″); 1880 from 16 direct measurements and from the two part angles (48.65″, 49.21″) and from a quadrilateral (51.24″).
Worked out here: 1889: 49.72″; 1880 mean 48.87″; difference 0.85″ (printed). 1871 mean 51.48″.
Helmert, F. R. (Ed.). (1893). Die europäische Längengradmessung in 52 Grad Breite von Greenwich bis Warschau. I. Heft: Hauptdreiecke und Grundlinienanschlüsse von England bis Polen. P. Stankiewicz., p. 186

Clarke's appendix on the longitude stations Feaghmain and Haverfordwest. The table prints the observations with the 18-inch theodolite at Feaghmain, one line per arc (one position of the circle), with the date and the time of day. Observations to which the observer added a remark of a poor bisection (pointing) of the object were given half weight and are marked 1/2 after the seconds.

“those observations to which the observer has appended a remark, indicating a not very satisfactory bisection of the object from whatever cause, are considered as having half weight, and are characterized in the tables following by the fraction ½ following the decimals of seconds.”
Reading the table. Columns: arc number; date (1862); time (hours and minutes, A.M. or P.M.); seconds of the reading on each target (Gurrana referring object, Brandon, Baurtregaum, Knocknadober, Knightstown, Knocknagante, Kilbeg Hill), with the degrees and minutes in the heading; x, the correction of the arc. Arc 1 is on 25 July at 5:15 P.M.; arcs 2 to 12 are on 26 July from 10:35 A.M. to 5:20 P.M. Values marked ½ have half weight.
Worked out here: Gurrana R.O. over 12 arcs: 37.78″ to 41.05″, range 3.27″.
Clarke, A. R. (1867). Determination of the positions of Feaghmain and Haverfordwest, longitude stations on the great European arc of parallel: Being an appendix to the account of the principal triangulation of Great Britain and Ireland. Eyre and Spottiswoode for HMSO., p. 4
Vapour over the Madras base flat: all angles repeatedly taken; only one clear morning
Great Arc of India, Lambton's meridional arc (Coromandel coast to Punnae and north to about 18 N) · p. 165 · strength ★★★
Repetition over days and hours Rejecting readings in unsteady air

Below the triangles that connect the Madras base with St. Thomas's Mount. The two routes gave slightly different distances, and Lambton gives the reason. The vapour he describes is near-ground haze over the flat, which made the flag-staffs unsteady. His response was to repeat the angles and to use the clear morning of 7 October.

“It may be necessary to notice here, that there was great difficulty in taking all these angles, on account of the very thick vapour which constantly floated near the surface of the flat where the base line runs, almost immediately after day-light, to very near the time of sun-setting. All the angles, and particularly at the north and south end of the base line, have been repeatedly taken, and the only time when the flag-staff appeared distinctly, was in the morning of the 7th of October,”
Lambton, W. (1808). An account of the measurement of an arc on the meridian on the coast of Coromandel, and the length of a degree deduced therefrom in the latitude 12° 32'. Asiatic Researches, 8, 137 ff., p. 165
Lambton's rule: repeat hazy angles; reject any angle 10 seconds from the others until the triangle is complete
Great Arc of India, Lambton's meridional arc (Coromandel coast to Punnae and north to about 18 N) · pp. 176-177 · strength ★★★
Rejecting readings in unsteady air Repetition over days and hours

After the table of triangles 31 and 32 of the 1802-03 triangulation. Lambton states his own rule for horizontal angles taken in haze. The triangle closure (the amount by which the three observed angles, less the spherical excess, miss 180 degrees) is the test he applies before an angle is kept or rejected. The rule continues on p. 177 with the method of trying each angle in turn.

“The angles have been taken with much care, and I believe with as much accuracy as the nature of such a process admits of; difficulty, however, very frequently arose from the haziness of the weather, which rendered the objects at the very distant points extremely dull, and occasioned some irregularity in the angles. Whenever that happened, the observations were often repeated, and in case any one, in particular, was different from the other so much as ten seconds, it was rejected till the three angles of the triangle had been observed.”
Lambton, W. (1808). An account of the measurement of an arc on the meridian on the coast of Coromandel, and the length of a degree deduced therefrom in the latitude 12° 32'. Asiatic Researches, 8, 137 ff., pp. 176-177
Each angle measured three or four times, both microscopes read thrice, two separate field-books
Great Arc of India, Lambton's meridional arc (Coromandel coast to Punnae and north to about 18 N) · Appendix p. 14 · strength ★★★
Repetition over days and hours Rejecting readings in unsteady air

GTS Vol. XII appendix summary of Lambton's 1802-03 observing of horizontal angles. A microscope here is the reading microscope on the circle; reading both, three times each, reduces reading error. Two field-books were kept independently and compared.

“The angles were all measured three or four times each; both microscopes were read off thrice every time the object was observed, and two separate field-books were kept for making out the angles. If from any marked difference between two measures of the same angle the graduation of the instrument was suspected to be in error, the division between the dots was carefully examined, as also those to the right and left, and if any error was discovered, allowance was made accordingly. Difficulties however very frequently arose from the haziness of the weather occasioning irregularity in the angles, and observations in consequence had often to be repeated.”
Great Trigonometrical Survey of India. (1890). Account of the operations of the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India, Vol. XII: The Southern Trigon. Dehra Dun: Trigonometrical Branch, Survey of India., Appendix p. 14
Pole-star azimuth at Yerracondah on nine nights to a referring lamp; vapour hides the star by day
Lambton, trigonometrical operations across the Peninsula, Fort St. George to Mangalore · p. 362 · strength ★★★
Raw tables of repeated measures Repetition over days and hours Night lamps and heliotropes

Table of pole-star observations for the meridian at Yerracondah (January 1804). A referring lamp is a lamp set up as a fixed night mark near the station; the angle from the star to the lamp is measured each night and the lamp is then tied to a survey station by day. The note below says no double azimuths were possible because vapour hid the pole star by day.

“Pole-Star Observations at Yerracondah Station, reduced for determining the position of the Meridian. [...] It may be remarked here, that no double azimuths have been taken. The pole-star being so low, and the vapour in the atmosphere so great in general, that I have never, except in two instances, been able to discern it while the sun was above the horizon.”
Reading the table. Columns: date (15 to 27 January 1804, 9 nights); apparent polar distance of the star; latitude; azimuth of the star; angle between the pole star and the referring lamp; angle between the north pole and the referring lamp. Look at the last column: 9 independent nightly values from 7 16 31.49 to 7 16 36.08, mean 7 16 33.64.
Worked out here: Spread of the nightly values: 36.08 - 31.49 = 4.59".
Lambton, W. (1811). An account of trigonometrical operations in crossing the Peninsula of India, and connecting Fort St. George with Mangalore. Asiatic Researches, 10, 290-384., p. 362

Error of a single measure computed separately for hills, sandhills and plains
GTS Karachi Longitudinal Series (North-West Quadrilateral) · p. 130-B · strength ★★★
Repetition over days and hours

Investigation after the sums of squares. The e.m.s. (error of mean square) of one measure and of one zero mean is computed for each group of angles by the same observer under similar conditions. The groups are split by terrain, so the larger scatter on the plains, where rays run close to the ground, is measured rather than assumed.

“The first 47 angles were measured at hill stations on 4 pairs of zeros, face right and face left, with an average of 3.14 observations on each zero; the remaining angles, 372 in number, were measured on 5 pairs of zeros with an average of 2.11 observations on each zero, at stations on hills, and sandhillocks and in the plains. The first 47 angles form a group by themselves; the remaining angles form 8 distinct groups, which again may be collected into 3 groups, in order that the relative e. m. s. of observations on hills and sand-hillocks, and in the plains, may be shown.”
Reading the table. Table columns: Group; Instrument and Observer; Position of stations (Hills, Sandhills, Plains); interval between zeros; measures on each zero (average); number of angles, single measures, zeros; e.m.s. of a single measure; e.m.s. of graduation and observation of a single zero. Compare the e.m.s. for hill groups with the plains groups.
Worked out here: e.m.s. of a single measure as printed: hills ±0.845, 0.787, 0.833, 0.760; sandhills ±0.966, 0.844; plains ±1.028, 1.252 seconds.

Introduction, Jacob's work of 1837-38. The new signals were introduced and the Surveyor General ordered an entirely new triangulation. Heavy unseasonable rain in November held up the work.

“yet by the end of the rains most of them had become tolerably well acquainted with their new duties, and were competent to direct the heliotropes by day as well as the lamps by night. [...] In clear weather these could be seen at a distance of 40 miles. [...] With all these advantages he took the field in the end of October, 1837, and in the course of the field season, was able to re-observe all the angles of the principal triangles between the meridians of 76° and of 74°, the Surveyor General having directed that an entirely new triangulation should be made.”

Part I, in the explanation of the station (local) adjustment. A "series" is one sweep of the telescope over all visible signals, read with the telescope direct (D.) and then reversed (R.), at one setting ("position") of the horizontal circle. Schott prints two of the 152 series observed at Mount Helena, California, as an example of the raw field record that goes into each station abstract. The counts at the foot of the next page show how many separate pointings went into each direction.

“The following portions of the local adjustment at the station Mount Helena, California, will serve to illustrate the arrangement of the numerical work. [...] In the abstract proper two series only, the thirty-third and thirty-sixth, are here given out of the 152 series shown in the original computation. The first line gives the seconds of the mean reading of the three microscopes for each signal sighted with the telescope direct. The corrections for run have already been applied. The second line gives the corresponding readings with the telescope in the reverse position, when sweeping back over the same signals in the opposite direction. The third line is the mean of the first and second.”
Reading the table. Columns: the ten signals sighted from Mount Helena (Mt. Diablo, Table Mt., Snow Mt. (E), Azimuth Mark, Marysville Butte, Lola, Pine Hill, Round Top, Monticello, Vaca). Top rows: assumed directions and their arithmetic complements. Each series block (Oct. 11 a.m., circle position 12, series 33; Oct. 12 a.m., position 13, series 36) has five lines: seconds read with telescope direct, seconds read reversed, mean of the two, mean reduced to the first signal, and the value used in the observation equations. A signal not seen in a series is left blank. The continuation on p. 44 (pdf 45) gives the "No." row, the number of pointings on each signal over all 152 series: 82, 60, 81, 122, 56, 54, 55, 50, 67, 56.
Worked out here: Sum of the "No." row on p. 44: 82+60+81+122+56+54+55+50+67+56 = 683 pointings (each one a D. and R. pair) at one station. Fewest on one signal: 50 (Round Top).

What one "observation of a direction" contains: two pointings and six microscope readings, or twelve pointings with the repeater
US Transcontinental Triangulation, 39th parallel · p. 47 · strength ★★★
Repetition over days and hours

Part I, rules for reading the station abstracts. Every station abstract in Part III ends with "probable error of a single observation of a direction (D. and R.)". This passage defines that unit. A probable error is the error that half the observations exceed and half do not (0.6745 times the standard error).

“The probable error of a single observation of a direction (e) is given under the list of directions at each station as a convenient index of the accuracy of the observations. When the parenthesis (D. and R.) is used, the observations were made with a direction instrument. A single observation of a direction comprises two pointings upon the signal, one with telescope direct and one with telescope reversed, and two readings (forward and backward) of each microscope, of which there are usually three, for each pointing. [...] When the parenthesis (6 D. and 6 R.) is used, the observations were made with a repeating instrument and a single observation of an angle comprises 12 pointings upon each of two signals, 6 with telescope direct and 6 reversed”
Worked out here: One (D. and R.) observation = 2 pointings x 3 microscopes x 2 readings = 12 circle readings.
Schott, C. A. (1900). The transcontinental triangulation and the American arc of the parallel (Special Publication No. 4). U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey; Government Printing Office., p. 47

Part III, introduction to the Indiana series. "Positions of the circle" are the different settings of the graduated circle, used so that graduation errors average out. "Broken series" are series in which some signals could not be seen, so the series had to be repeated.

“It was through this section that our highest towers were needed, and even then considerable cutting had to be resorted to. All the observations were made on lights at night. The total length of the series between the base-net lines is nearly 216 kilometres (or 135 statute miles); the number of stations is 15; the average length of a side is 32 kilometres (or 19.9 statute miles); the number of series of measures at a station (mean of telescope D. and R.) exceeds 34,* and the usual number of the positions of the circle is 17. [...] *The intention was to observe each direction 34 times, but owing to the presence of broken series their total number is much greater.”
Reading the table. The crop also shows the first station abstract of the series (Oblong, Illinois, 1879): dates, theodolite, telescope height above ground (30.94 m), observer, and for each direction the station-adjusted value and the corrections from the base-net and figure adjustments.
Worked out here: 34 series / 17 positions = 2 series in each circle position.

Rocky Mountain series: 17 to 19 circle positions, two full sets each, morning and evening balanced, over twenty or more days; meteorological notes kept

Part III, Rocky Mountain series (Pikes Peak to Salt Lake, stations near 3 650 m, longest side 294 km). Heliotropes are mirrors that reflect sunlight from the far station as a bright point target. A "double zenith distance" is a vertical angle read in both circle faces. This passage gives the full observing programme for both horizontal and vertical angles.

“The horizontal directions at all the stations were observed with the 50-centimetre (20-inch) theodolite, originally in 19 and later on (since 1893) in but 17 positions of the azimuth circle. The intention was to secure two full sets in each position and to balance the number of observations of the morning and evening, but on account of unavoidable broken series their numbers had generally to be increased for each position. Respecting the time of observations, they were made from sunrise till 8 o'clock, and resumed in the afternoon at half past 4 o'clock and continued till sunset. [...] To secure observations under a variety of atmospheric conditions, observations were extended over twenty or more days. Double zenith distances for heights of stations were observed at three different periods of the day, viz. between 6 1/2 and 8 o'clock in the morning, between 11 1/2 and 1 o'clock, and again between 4 1/2 and 6 o'clock in the evening. This brought to light the fact that the minimum refraction of the day occurs late in the afternoon, even after the heat of the day has passed. As a rule these vertical angle measures were spread over not less than twelve days, at least for the main lines. [...] No simultaneous reciprocal zenith distances were obtained. [...] The triangulation party also made observations of the magnetic declination, dip, and intensity, and meteorological notes were regularly kept.”
Worked out here: Minimum per direction from the stated plan: 17 positions x 2 sets = 34 observations (38 with 19 positions), each a D. and R. pair.
Schott, C. A. (1900). The transcontinental triangulation and the American arc of the parallel (Special Publication No. 4). U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey; Government Printing Office., p. 553
Nevada series from 1880: forenoon and afternoon measures equalized to guard against lateral refraction
US Transcontinental Triangulation, 39th parallel · p. 573 · strength ★★★

Part III, Nevada and California series. Lateral (horizontal) refraction is a sideways bend of the line of sight caused by unequal air temperature across the line, for example air heated on one side of a slope. Its sign changes between morning and afternoon heating, so equal numbers of forenoon and afternoon measures tend to cancel it.

“The equalization of the number of measures of horizontal directions at a station taken in the forenoon and in the afternoon was first put into execution in 1880 in this section; its purpose was to eliminate any effect of unequal heating of the theodolite as well as to provide against possible lateral refraction along the lines of sight. Observations of zenith distances were made at three different periods of the day, as stated in the case of the Rocky Mountain work.”
Schott, C. A. (1900). The transcontinental triangulation and the American arc of the parallel (Special Publication No. 4). U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey; Government Printing Office., p. 573

Part I, Epping base net (Maine). A repeating theodolite measures one angle several times in a row on the circle and divides the total. Schott gives the probable error from the 20 measures of each angle and, separately, from the closing errors of the 46 triangles of the net. The footnote compares the two instrument types.

“In case of repetitions the probable error will depend upon the comparison of a resulting angle with each of its 20 measures (each of 3 repetitions direct and 3 repetitions reversed), from which an average and approximate value of the probable error of a single measure of an angle and of a direction has been derived [...] If we deduce the probable error of a direction from the closing errors in the sum of the angles of the 46 triangles, we find from the sum of the squares of these errors the mean closing error of a triangle = sqrt(54.49/46) = +/- 1".09, hence the probable error of a direction = 0.674 x 1.09/sqrt(6) = +/- 0".30. [...] The mean of the 4 values of e_1 derived from a single measure (D. and R.) with the 75cm theodolite is +/- 1".04 and the mean of the 5 values of e_1 derived from a single measure (3 D. and 3 R.) with the 25cm repeating theodolite is +/- 1".16, or one measure with the first instrument is about equal in accuracy to three with the latter.”
Worked out here: Per angle: 20 measures x 6 repetitions = 120 pointings on each signal.

Weights of base-line angles carry the loss of precision from undulating signals over hot ground
Maclear's verification and extension of La Caille's arc of meridian, Cape of Good Hope · p. 338 · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours Repetition over days and hours

Section 7, part 4, of the base verification by triangulation (Zwartland base). Maclear explains how the weight of each angle was found: the square of the number of partial measures divided by twice the sum of squares of the differences from the mean. A partial measure is the mean of a group of repetitions; the weight is a number that is larger when the results agree better. He states that over flat ground the signals undulate, except in gloomy and moist weather or early morning and late evening, and that this error must enter the weights. So the state of the air is measured in the scatter of the results, not ignored.

“The weight of each angle was calculated by dividing the square of the number of partial measures by twice the sum of the squares of the differences from the mean, assuming the theodolite errors of division to be insensible, an assumption which is not strictly correct. The method pursued when measuring, of stepping the divided circle, eleminates the division errors from the mean result; they are restored in the weight as above calculated ; but that factor cannot justly be represented by the number of measures alone,—where, as in the present instance, the triangulation is carried over flat ground,—the line of sight passing in close proximity to heated sand and bush, causing the signals to undulate so much, except during gloomy and moist weather, or early in the morning and late in the evening, as to materially diminish the precision of the pointing : it is therefore necessary to introduce this element of error.”
Maclear, T. (1866). Verification and extension of La Caille's arc of meridian at the Cape of Good Hope (Vol. 1). London: Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty., p. 338
Number of partial results set by the air; bad definition and lateral refraction cut the weight from 360 to 11
Maclear's verification and extension of La Caille's arc of meridian, Cape of Good Hope · p. 400 · strength ★★★
Repetition over days and hours

Description of the Beaufort theodolite method (p. 400). Each angle was measured by repetition, the verniers read at every tenth repetition; the mean of ten repetitions is one partial result. Maclear says the number of partial results depended on the importance of the angle and on the atmosphere. Definition is how sharp and steady the signal looks in the telescope; probable error is the error that has an even chance of being exceeded. Five results in first-rate definition (Simon's Berg, 19 November 1845) gave 0.05"; sixteen results in bad definition and lateral refraction (Kapoc Berg, 12 February 1846) gave 0.3". The footnotes giving these stations and dates are at the foot of the same page and inside the crop.

“The mean of every tenth repetition being regarded as one partial result, the required number of such results depended upon the importance of the angle, and the atmospheric circumstances during the time when measuring. The value of the latter may be gathered from the fact of five results obtained during first-rate definition, giving a probable error of 0"·05 and weight 360 (a) ; whereas during bad definition and lateral refraction, 16 results gave a probable error of 0"·3, and weight 11 (b). ... (a) Simon's Berg, Nov. 19, 1845. (b) Kapoc Berg, Feb. 12, 1846.”
Worked out here: 5 results = 50 repetitions; 16 results = 160 repetitions. Weight = 1/P^2 (p. 419): 1/0.3^2 = 11.1, printed 11. 1/0.05^2 = 400; the printed 360 corresponds to P = 0.0527, which rounds to the printed 0.05.
Maclear, T. (1866). Verification and extension of La Caille's arc of meridian at the Cape of Good Hope (Vol. 1). London: Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty., p. 400
Definition of the angle weights: reciprocal of the squared probable error from the partial results
Maclear's verification and extension of La Caille's arc of meridian, Cape of Good Hope · p. 419 · strength ★★★
Repetition over days and hours

Same page. For the Beaufort theodolite the weight of an angle is 1/P^2, where P is the probable error computed from the spread of the partial results (each partial result = 10 repetitions). For the Fuller theodolite, where errors from the atmosphere and the eye are mixed with instrument errors, the weight is the number of partial means. Maclear states that the two methods are not homogeneous. This rule is why angles measured in unsteady air (larger scatter) count less in the adjustment.

“The weight annexed to each angle observed with the Beaufort theodolite is the reciprocal of the square of the probable error (P), derived from the formula : P = √(Σ.ε × 0·454936 / (n²—n)) where Σ.ε is the sum of the squares of the differences from the mean of each partial result,—10 repetitions being taken for the unit; 0·454936 = 2 ρ², derived from the theory of probabilities (ρ = ·476936). The weight annexed to the final determination of an angle is the sum of the weights of the separate determinations. ... With respect to the Fuller theodolite, the errors depending upon the state of the atmosphere and the eye, are mixed up with instrumental errors of a different order to errors of observation. The precision of the partial measures have therefore been regarded as equal, and the weight annexed to each angle is the sum of the partial means from which it is derived.”
Worked out here: Check with the 1 December 1846 group on p. 421: n = 13 partial results, sum of squares 4.5708. P = sqrt(4.5708 x 0.454936 / (169 - 13)) = sqrt(0.013330) = 0.1155 (printed 0.1155). Weight = 1/0.1155^2 = 75.0 (printed 75.02).
Maclear, T. (1866). Verification and extension of La Caille's arc of meridian at the Cape of Good Hope (Vol. 1). London: Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty., p. 419

The printed type example for the Beaufort theodolite: the angle at Kamies-Sector Berg between the Keibiskow heliostat (about 80 miles away) and Bokkeveld Berg, 1, 3 and 4 December 1846. Each row is one partial result of 10 repetitions with the hour and a remark on the definition of the signals. The remarks record the air: wind direction, 'hot temperature: about 85 deg.', 'therm. 90 deg.', and 'Definition in the morning not good, towards 11h it became much worse'. Half the work was measured forward with the Y bearings right, half backward with Y left. The final angle comes from 260 measures with weight 131.99.

“Angle at Kamies-Sector Berg, West Rock Station; between Keibiskow and Bokkeveld Berg : measured with the Beaufort Theodolite. ... Middling definition. ... Northerly wind, perhaps 1 point E. of N. Hot temperature : about 85°. ... Bad definition and bad signaling at Bokkeveld ... Wind west, next S.W., and lastly south; this afternoon very hot, therm. 90°. ... Excellent do., points. ... Definition in the morning not good, towards 11h it became much worse. ... Resulting angle from 260 meas. = 23°32′1″·98 Weight = 131·99”
Reading the table. Columns: date (1846) and hour (A.M./P.M.); remarks on definition, wind and temperature; No. of repetitions (10 per row); pointer degrees and minutes; seconds on verniers A, D, B, C; mean reading; angle seconds for the row (left) and running mean (right), all after 23 deg 32'. Under each day: sum of squares of errors, probable error of 10 measures, probable error of the day's total, and the weight. 1 Dec: 13 rows (130 repetitions), 3 Dec: 7 rows, 4 Dec: 6 rows (130 repetitions). Row seconds range from 0.65" to 3.35". Look at how the remarks change with the hour and how the weight of each day follows its scatter.
Worked out here: Combination printed at foot: 1.96 x 75.02 = 147.039; 2.00 x 56.97 = 113.940; 75.02 + 56.97 = 131.99; 260.979 / 131.99 = 1.977 -> 1.98". The day weight above it is printed 56.77 (1/0.1327^2 = 56.8), so the 56.97 in the combination differs from it by 0.2.

The printed type example for the Fuller theodolite (pp. 422-426): the angle at Riebeek's Kasteel between the Kapoc Berg signal rock heliostat and the east end of the base, 17 to 26 February 1842. Each block is a couplet: the angle measured twice with the circle stepped, giving one partial mean. The remarks column gives the definition ('Beautiful definition', 'Good definition. “54 Couplets = 33°50′58″·524. ☾ 20th February.—In general cloudy, with misty horizon,—none of the heliostats now visible at the same time. Cape Town seen twice, Kapoc Berg once, east end of Base for an hour. N.W. wind and dense fog in the afternoon. ♄ 26th February.—Violent wind from E. by S. came on, on Thursday night and continued until 9 o'clock yesterday morning, then died away; but towards 4 o'clock it returned, last night and this morning it may be called a strong gale. Yesterday and last night the canvas and instrument were removed for security, but time being valuable, an attempt to observe was made at 10h 30m this morning. Bad images, the instrument not free from danger.”

Morris's report, paragraph 53 (p. 19). An arc is one complete measure of the round of directions with the circle set to a given zero; CL and CR are circle left and circle right (the telescope turned over). Captain Gordon and Mr. Simms used eight arcs at every point, with zeros near 0, 45, 90, 135, 23, 67, 113 and 157 deg. When an arc was repeated, the same circle readings were kept.

“53. Captain Gordon and Mr. Simms observed at all points of their work with the zeros of the horizontal arc set as follows :— Arc 1 {C L 0 C R 180} Arc 2 {C R 270 C L 90} Arc 3 {C L 45 C R 225} Arc 4 {C R 315 C L 135} Arc 5 {C L 23 C R 203} Arc 6 {C R 293 C L 113} Arc 7 {C L 67 C R 247} Arc 8 {C R 337 C L 157} not, of necessity, accurately to the foregoing, but in their near proximity; and whenever any particular arc had to be repeated, either as a whole, or partially, the circle readings for that arc as recorded were always adhered to.”

Measurement of angles (p. 182). A round is one sighting of every station in azimuth order; a double set is a round in one face and the return round with the telescope reversed. Rounds were spread over different parts of the graduated circle to remove graduation errors. No PDF of this paper is in the project; the item points to the OCR text file, so no crop is possible. Wording checked against a page image of p. 182 held elsewhere in the project.

“The method of measuring angles, followed during the earlier years of the survey of New South Wales, was to observe the direction of one point as a referring mark and then to sight to each station consecutively in order of azimuth, completing the surround by again observing the referring mark ; the instrument was then reversed and the same round of stations was observed in this position, similar rounds being taken after moving the graduated circle so that each station was observed upon different parts of the arc in order to eliminate graduation errors. About twenty observations on to each station were deemed sufficient. In the later angle measures, the method has been to reverse the telescope after each round and observe in reverse order of azimuth back to referring mark, twenty such double sets being altogether observed on different parts of the circle.”

Altitudes of stations (p. 204). Furber states that simultaneous observation at both ends is the ideal, because only then is the refraction certain to be the same at both ends. That was not possible, so the reciprocal observations were made at the same time of day. Each set is two rounds of elevations, face left and face right, with a level along the line read at every sighting. He adds that more sets would be better. No PDF of this paper is in the project; the item points to the OCR text file, so no crop is possible. Quote from the text layer, one OCR word break corrected ('reciprocal observations').

“The simultaneous observation at each end of the line involved, which is necessary to an ideal determination of relative heights (for by that means only is it made certain that the co-efficients of refraction at the two ends of the line are the same) has, of course, been impracticable. The work, however, is performed always at the same time of the day, so as to secure, as far as possible, the same atmospheric conditions in the reciprocal observations. The actual field work consists in the measurement, with a theodolite having a 10-inch circle, of the elevations of all the stations in the surround, noting, at the time of sighting to each, the reading of a level the axis of which is in the direction of the line being sighted, any variations of the level being subsequently applied to the circle reading. The instrument is then reversed and a similar round taken, each such pair of rounds constituting a set from which the differences of height may be derived.”
No page image: this source is held as a text layer only.
Furber, T. F. (1898). The trigonometrical survey of New South Wales, with mention of similar surveys in the other Australian colonies. Report of the Australasian Association for the Advancement of Science, 7, Section A, 176-237., p. 204
An angle is never taken from one single measurement
Middleton, Chadwick and Bogle, A Treatise on Surveying (textbook) · p. 191 · strength ★★★
Repetition over days and hours

The book's rule for measuring angles: two methods, repetition and reiteration, both measure the angle many times. In repetition the angle is added up on the circle several times and the total is divided by the number of readings. In reiteration the angle is measured separately at different parts of the circle (a different zero each time) and the results are averaged.

“It will be assumed therefore that before commencing the observation of angles, it is practically in perfect adjustment. There are two methods of observing angles, by which more correct values can be obtained than is possible with one single measurement. These are 'repetition' and 'reiteration.'”
Middleton, R. E., Chadwick, O., & Bogle, J. du T. (1904). A treatise on surveying: Part I (2nd ed.). E. & F. N. Spon., p. 191

Tome II, remarks on the n table. Delambre states how the southern zenith distances were taken: by Méchain, with several series for each distance, rarely after October, and from mountain stations where the line of sight stayed clear of the ground.

“A commencer de 135 toutes les observations sont de M. Méchain qui a toujours fait plusieurs séries pour la même distance, et qui, à l'exception de quelques stations de Nore au Vernet, n'a guère observé passé le mois d'octobre, et presque toujours sur des montagnes où le rayon visuel ne rasoit pas le sol.”
In English: “From 135 on, all the observations are by M. Méchain, who always made several series for the same distance, and who, except for some stations from Nore to Le Vernet, hardly observed after October, and almost always on mountains where the line of sight did not graze the ground.”

Night lamps and heliotropes Repetition over days and hours Steady-air hours

Same page. A flag-staff is a pole set over the station; to 'bisect' it is to set the telescope cross-wire on its centre. White lights were short-burning flares fired at agreed times at the distant stations. Roy compares the two kinds of target and states which lines needed the night lights.

“In very favourable circumstances of the weather a good observation by day is preferable to one by the white lights at night; because, in the first case, the observer has time at his leisure nicely to bisect a fine flag-staff, and repeatedly to read off the angle; whereas, in the short duration of the burning of the light, he is somewhat hurried, from the fear of losing some of the lights at other distant stations, if two of them happened to come together, which now and then they did, from the irregularity of the rates of the watches of the artillery-men attending at the different stations. It was, however, by the assistance of the white lights only, that the most distant stations could be rendered visible”
Roy, W. (1790). An account of the trigonometrical operation, whereby the distance between the meridians of the Royal Observatories of Greenwich and Paris has been determined. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, 80, 111-270 (with Dalby, I., Remarks, pp. 593-614)., p. 170

Art. VII, General Remarks, introducing the refraction table. 'Double observations' are an elevation and a depression on the same line, one from each end. Roy states that refraction was a secondary object of the operation and that his table shows mainly how variable refraction is.

“These results are not however offered as being free from error; on the contrary, if the circumstances had permitted this to become a principal object in our operation, the successive repetition of the observations for many times would, no doubt, have furnished still more satisfactory conclusions. It is hoped, nevertheless, that these, such as they are, may have their use, were it only by shewing the variableness of terrestrial refraction”

Ordnance Trigonometrical Survey of Great Britain and Ireland, Principal Triangulation · p. 48 · strength ★★
Towers, scaffolds and high stations Night lamps and heliotropes Repetition over days and hours

Section on placing the instrument. Raising the instrument lifts the line of sight clear of the ground over flat country. The inner scaffold for the instrument was separate from the outer one for the observer, so neither the observer's movements nor the wind on the hut reached the instrument.

“The high stage used for the great instruments is 32 feet high, but has been only used in cases of absolute necessity. ... Many instances of high scaffolding occurred in the triangulation of the Eastern Counties, where, the country being flat, the stations were over church-towers. ... Thus the instrument, at the height of 178 feet above ground, was insulated, and not affected by the movements of the observer, or the action of the wind upon the observatory.”
Clarke, A. R. (1858). Ordnance trigonometrical survey of Great Britain and Ireland: Account of the observations and calculations of the principal triangulation. London: Eyre and Spottiswoode., p. 48

Ordnance Trigonometrical Survey of Great Britain and Ireland, Principal Triangulation · p. 52 · strength ★★
Night lamps and heliotropes Repetition over days and hours

Section on observing. A heliostat is a mirror that reflects the sun from a distant station so that it shows as a bright point. Rewards were paid for each sighting, graded by distance, with smaller sums for the second and third arcs on the same day. The passage shows the effort to get repeated observations on long lines.

“A watch is always kept in the camp for distant heliostats. ... The propriety of this allowance will be readily admitted when it is remembered that as long a period as a month has very frequently occurred between consecutive observations of very distant points.”
Clarke, A. R. (1858). Ordnance trigonometrical survey of Great Britain and Ireland: Account of the observations and calculations of the principal triangulation. London: Eyre and Spottiswoode., p. 52

Same page. The vertical circle was read after the horizontal reading in each observation (p. 510), so the zenith distances come in the same arcs as the horizontal directions. 'Under all circumstances' means at all hours and in all weather in which horizontal work was done, so the mean includes the daily range.

“The vertical observations with the larger theodolites are generally numerous (at least in the more modern observations), and taken under all circumstances.”

Chapter II, the general review of the work. A set (приёмъ) is one complete round of pointings on the targets in both positions of the telescope; the angle is the mean of all sets. The passage gives the instruments used at the 161 first-class points and the minimum number of sets per angle: 12 in the Main and Krasnoyarsk rows, 6 in the Kizlyar row.

“Измѣреніе на нихъ первоклассныхъ угловъ произведено: на 74-хъ универсальными инструментами, на 70-ти терристрическимъ теодолитомъ и на 16-ти теодолитомъ Порта, дѣлая для каждаго угла въ Главномъ и Красноярскомъ ряду не менѣе 12 пріемовъ, а въ Кизлярскомъ не менѣе 6.”
In English: “The measurement of the first-class angles at them was made: at 74 with universal instruments, at 70 with the terrestrial theodolite and at 16 with Porta's theodolite, making for each angle in the Main and Krasnoyarsk rows not fewer than 12 sets, and in the Kizlyar row not fewer than 6.”
Voenno-topograficheskoe depo. (1861). Zapiski Voenno-topograficheskago depo, Chast' XXII, Otd. II: Privolzhskoe trigonometricheskoe izmerenie. Voenno-topograficheskoe depo., Zapiski XXII, Otd. II, p. 19
