Chapter II, continued. A zenith distance is the angle between the vertical and the line of sight to a target. Measured at both ends of a line, the two zenith distances give the height difference and show the bend of the ray on that line. The passage states that zenith distances were measured at all first-class points, and that the verification base near Astrakhan was joined to the net by three triangles whose angles were measured in 12 and more sets.

“Зенитныя разстоянія измѣрены на всѣхъ первоклассныхъ точкахъ, а на второклассныхъ только въ Сарпинскомъ ряду.”
In English: “Zenith distances were measured at all first-class points, and at second-class points only in the Sarpinsky row.”
Voenno-topograficheskoe depo. (1861). Zapiski Voenno-topograficheskago depo, Chast' XXII, Otd. II: Privolzhskoe trigonometricheskoe izmerenie. Voenno-topograficheskoe depo., Zapiski XXII, Otd. II, p. 20

Chapter III describes the field methods. Canvas screens against wind and an umbrella against the sun protected the instrument. Horizontal angles were measured in sets by W. Struve's method: pointings left to right, then with the telescope turned through the zenith, right to left. Zenith distances for the height differences were measured with double pointing and in two positions of the vertical circle, so that the index error of the circle cancels.

“Зенитныя разстоянія, для опредѣленія разностей высотъ пунктовъ, измѣрялись двойнымъ наведеніемъ на предметы и въ двухъ различныхъ положеніяхъ вертикальнаго круга.”
In English: “The zenith distances, for determining the height differences of the points, were measured with a double pointing on the objects and in two different positions of the vertical circle.”
Voenno-topograficheskoe depo. (1861). Zapiski Voenno-topograficheskago depo, Chast' XXII, Otd. II: Privolzhskoe trigonometricheskoe izmerenie. Voenno-topograficheskoe depo., Zapiski XXII, Otd. II, p. 22
The closure of each triangle was shared among its angles in proportion to the scatter of their sets
Russian arc of the parallel of 47.5 N, Privolzhsk triangulation (Kishinev to Astrakhan arc, eastern part) · Zapiski XXII, Otd. II, p. 130 · strength ★★
Repetition over days and hours

Chapter V, computation of the triangulation. m is the mean deviation of the single sets of an angle from the mean of all its sets. The closure error of each triangle was divided among its three angles in proportion to their m, so a less consistent angle took a larger share. The worked example is triangle 52: closure -3.35″, m = 2.0, 1.0 and 1.1, corrections -1.63″, -0.82″ and -0.90″.

“чтобы соразмѣрять поправку съ достоинствомъ его измѣренія, принималось во вниманіе среднее ариѳметическое число, получаемое изъ разностей каждаго пріема съ среднимъ изъ всѣхъ пріемовъ одного и того же угла. Если это среднее ариѳметическое число означимъ чрезъ m, то погрѣшность суммы угловъ разлагалась пропорціонально тремъ m;”
In English: “to make the correction proportional to the quality of its measurement, account was taken of the arithmetic mean obtained from the differences of each set from the mean of all sets of one and the same angle. If this arithmetic mean is denoted by m, the error of the sum of the angles was distributed in proportion to the three m;”
Worked out here: -3.35 × 2.0/4.1 = -1.63; -3.35 × 1.0/4.1 = -0.82; -3.35 × 1.1/4.1 = -0.90 (sum of m = 4.1).
Voenno-topograficheskoe depo. (1861). Zapiski Voenno-topograficheskago depo, Chast' XXII, Otd. II: Privolzhskoe trigonometricheskoe izmerenie. Voenno-topograficheskoe depo., Zapiski XXII, Otd. II, p. 130
Lithuania (Tenner): each angle in two series of 20 repetitions, with three instruments
Struve Geodetic Arc (Russo-Scandinavian arc of the meridian, Danube to Fuglenaes) · T. I, p. 148 · strength ★★
Repetition over days and hours

Tome I, p. 148, § 39. Tenner's southern section used the repetition method: the angle is added on the circle many times and the total is divided by the number of repetitions. Each angle had two series of 20 repetitions, and from 1827 the repetitions were made in both directions of rotation. The difference of the two series gives an estimate of the probable error of the final angle.

“En général, il y a eu pour chaque angle deux séries, chacune de 20 répétitions. La comparaison des deux valeurs du même angle conduit à une évaluation de l'erreur probable de l'angle définitif qui est la moyenne des deux valeurs isolées.”
In English: “In general there were for each angle two series, each of 20 repetitions. The comparison of the two values of the same angle leads to an estimate of the probable error of the final angle, which is the mean of the two separate values.”
Struve, F. G. W. (1857). Arc du méridien de 25° 20' entre le Danube et la Mer Glaciale mesuré depuis 1816 jusqu'en 1855 (Vol. 1). Imprimerie de l'Académie impériale des sciences., T. I, p. 148
Finland instruction: 5 sets 18 degrees apart on the circle, each set in two halves with the telescope reversed
Struve Geodetic Arc (Russo-Scandinavian arc of the meridian, Danube to Fuglenaes) · T. II, p. 20 · strength ★★
Repetition over days and hours

Tome II, Chapter V, § 78, observing methods of Finland. Horizontal angles were measured by reiteration: each set starts on a different part of the circle, so graduation errors average out. Struve replaced the 6 sets of the Baltic arc by 5 sets 18 degrees apart. Each set has two halves (vertical circle east, then west), and in each half every object is pointed twice with the two opposite motions of the slow-motion screw. The pointing order is reversed in the second half.

“Seulement je remplaçai les 6 mises, adoptées pour l'arc Baltique, par 5 mises, distantes de 18° à 18° sur le limbe, chaque mise étant partagée en deux moitiés, relatives aux deux positions de l'axe horizontal, le cercle vertical étant ou à l'est, ou à l'ouest. Dans ces moitiés chaque objet fut observé deux fois de suite, par les deux mouvements opposés de la vis de rappel.”
In English: “Only I replaced the 6 sets adopted for the Baltic arc by 5 sets, 18° apart on the circle, each set being divided into two halves, relating to the two positions of the horizontal axis, the vertical circle being either east or west. In these halves each object was observed twice in succession, by the two opposite motions of the slow-motion screw.”
Struve, F. G. W. (1860). Arc du méridien de 25° 20' entre le Danube et la Mer Glaciale mesuré depuis 1816 jusqu'en 1855 (Vol. 2). Imprimerie de l'Académie impériale des sciences., T. II, p. 20
Prussian nets: 36 pointings in 18 sets for each object; Bessel used 12 sets 15 degrees apart
European arc of the parallel in 52 N, Greenwich (Feaghmain) to Warschau · p. 20 · strength ★★
Repetition over days and hours

Heft I, § 7. The Rhenish, Hessian and Märkisch-Thuringian nets were observed under General Baeyer's instruction of 9 April 1868. It prescribes direction observations after Bessel, with a zero mark (a distant fixed target in every set) and 36 pointings in 18 sets on each object, on 6 circle positions 30 degrees apart. Bessel's East Prussian arc used 12 sets 15 degrees apart.

“unterscheidet sich aber von Bessels Methode einestheils durch die Einführung der Nullmarke, einem einige Kilometer entfernten, meist künstlichen Objekt, welches in jedem Satze Aufnahme finden sollte, anderntheils durch Vertheilung der 36 Einstellungen (in 18 Sätzen) für jedes Objekt auf nur 6 Stände des Horizontalkreises mit 30° Intervall.”
In English: “but differs from Bessel's method partly by the introduction of the zero mark, an object some kilometres away, usually artificial, which was to be included in every set, and partly by the distribution of the 36 pointings (in 18 sets) for each object over only 6 positions of the horizontal circle at 30° intervals.”
Helmert, F. R. (Ed.). (1893). Die europäische Längengradmessung in 52 Grad Breite von Greenwich bis Warschau. I. Heft: Hauptdreiecke und Grundlinienanschlüsse von England bis Polen. P. Stankiewicz., p. 20

Same page as ga_01. Lambton states how the vertical angles for the Madras height were taken. Collimation error is the small offset of the telescope line of sight; turning the telescope over and the circle half round cancels it. He also records the weather during these observations.

“The angles of elevation and depression were taken by the circular instrument, from a mean of several observations, and the error of collimation was corrected by turning the transit over, and the horizontal plate half-round. But the weather was rather dull, during the whole of these operations.”

Section VII, latitude of Paudree by the zenith sector. A zenith sector measures the zenith distance (angle from the vertical) of a star as it crosses the meridian. Lambton reports the monsoon weather, the number of nights, and that the weaker nights were rejected before the latitude was taken.

“The time I commenced observing at Paudree station was during the heavy part of the monsoon, which occasioned frequent interruptions: and although I had intended observing by at least three fixed stars, I only succeeded to my satisfaction in one, which was Aldebaran. With that star I had a fortunate succession for about sixteen nights; some few of those observations being less favourable than the others, were rejected, and the rest, from which the latitude was determined, appear in the following table,”

Walker quotes Lambton's manuscript General Report on how he measured the horizontal angles of this period (1802-1808). It adds his method when a triangle did not close: each angle in turn was held correct and the sides were recomputed, and no angle was dropped without cause.

““ As to the angles in general they have been taken three and four times, and every time that the object was observed, both microscopes were read off thrice, and two separate field-books kept for making out the angles. [...] This however has rarely happened, and when it did, great precaution was used, and no angle was rejected without some reason appeared to render it doubtful”.”

Season 1848-49, start of the series near Sironj. The observers found instrument faults because repeated measures disagreed, repaired them, and re-did the affected work.

“The progress in the observations however, during that month was small, owing to defects in the Instrument, (Troughton and Simms' 36-inch Theodolite) which could only be detected from the discrepancies they occasioned in the observations, and which had to be remedied after a careful investigation of their causes. [...] The time lost by these alterations, and in the consequent revision of work, caused great delay [...] Subsequently, the observations were continued till the second week in May, when the atmosphere became so decidedly unfavorable, that no further work could be obtained.”

Method of zeros: readings at equal intervals round the circle, face left and face right
GTS Bombay Longitudinal Series (Southern Trigon) · p. 11 · strength ★★
Repetition over days and hours

Chapter II. Everest's method of horizontal angles. Face left and face right means the vertical circle is on the observer's left in one set and on his right in the other; a pair cancels collimation error. Shifting the circle between sets spreads the readings over the graduations.

“The method of observing horizontal angles was that introduced by Colonel Everest, and had for its object the giving of readings at equal intervals round the azimuthal circle, with a view to the cancellation of periodic errors of graduation. [...] A single measure on each of the two zero-settings constitute a pair of collimated observations, the face of the vertical circle being to the left of the observer at one setting and to his right at the other.”
Great Trigonometrical Survey of India. (1890). Account of the operations of the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India, Vol. XII: The Southern Trigon. Dehra Dun: Trigonometrical Branch, Survey of India., p. 11

GTS Bombay Longitudinal Series (Southern Trigon) · p. VIII-B · strength ★★

Introduction, season 1862-63. Finding old station marks destroyed, Haig re-observed the old triangles as well as the new ones. A station built too low left a ray close to a hill; the extra refraction of evening did not lift it clear, so the station had to be raised.

“he therefore determined not only to observe the angles of the new triangles which had been approximately laid down by Mr. McGill, but to re-observe those of all the old ones, [...] The second delay was occasioned by Kem Station not having been built sufficiently high; there was a hill on which the ray to Wápla grazed, but which was so close to Kem, that the increased refraction in the evening produced scarcely any perceptible effect in raising the ray clear of the hill, which was covered with large laterite boulders.”
Great Trigonometrical Survey of India. (1890). Account of the operations of the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India, Vol. XII: The Southern Trigon. Dehra Dun: Trigonometrical Branch, Survey of India., p. VIII-B

Gordon's Rhodesia junction chain: unsteady images from irregular refraction, grass-fire haze, rain; four arcs
Geodetic Survey of the Transvaal and Orange River Colony (Morris; preface and introduction by Gill) · p. xxvii · strength ★★
Repetition over days and hours

Captain Gordon's report on the 1906-1907 chain joining the Transvaal survey to Simms' Rhodesia survey, printed in Gill's introduction (p. xxvii). Over the flat bushed country near the Zoutpansberg the images were unsteady from irregular refraction; haze from grass fires lasted through July and August, and rain fell from November. Each station had measures on four arcs only.

“Passing southwards through the heavy granite country of the M'Patem, one emerges on the flat heavily bushed tract which stretches continuously to the heights of the Zoutpansberg in the Transvaal. In this last country the work of observation became very tedious and difficult by reason of the unsteadiness of the images produced by irregular refraction. The absence of roads and the density of the bush in this section gave rise to much difficulty and delay in the earlier work of the reconnaissance, the trouble being in no way lightened by the constant thick haze prevailing during the months of July and August as the result of the numerous grass fires incidental to that season. During November heavy rains began to fall, and continued intermittently to the close of the work. ... Pressure of circumstances necessitated limiting the instrumental work at each station to a series of measures on four arcs only; the zero reference point of the circle being successively placed about the divisions of 0°, 45°, 90°, and 135°.”
Morris, W. G. (1908). Reports on the geodetic survey of the Transvaal and Orange River Colony (Geodetic Survey of South Africa, Vol. 5; preface and introduction by D. Gill). London: Harrison and Sons., p. xxvii

The observations have been all made by Mr. Sprent, and with the same twelve-inch instrument. Refraction named as the main difficulty in trigonometrical levelling; Bessel weights by the number of days at both ends
Trigonometrical Survey of New South Wales · p. 205 · strength ★★
Repetition over days and hours

pp. 204-205. Furber names the irregular change of refraction as the main difficulty, cites the Indian experience of zenith distances varying through nine minutes at 10 to 12 miles, and argues that a large spread is the reason to observe over more days. Bessel's weight for a reciprocal line has the factor n1 x n2, the numbers of days observed at the two ends. No PDF of this paper is in the project; the item points to the OCR text file, so no crop is possible. Quote from the text layer; the subscripts of n are garbled there and are written n₁, n₂.

“There is little doubt that the principal source of difficulty in trigonometrical levelling lies in the considerable and irregular changes in the atmospheric refraction. This cannot be better illustrated than by the experience obtained in India, where apparent zenith distances of points only 10 or 12 miles away varied under certain circumstances through a range of as much as nine minutes. At first sight it might appear to be useless to go on duplicating such apparently wild observations, yet consideration of the nature of the question will show that the great range among the observations forms, itself, the reason for extending them to cover a longer period of time. Bessel's opinion on this subject may be gathered from his estimate of the relative weights to be assigned to such observations, the principal factor in the weight being n₁ n₂, where n₁ and n₂ are the number of days on which observations are made at opposite ends of the same line.”
No page image: this source is held as a text layer only.
Furber, T. F. (1898). The trigonometrical survey of New South Wales, with mention of similar surveys in the other Australian colonies. Report of the Australasian Association for the Advancement of Science, 7, Section A, 176-237., p. 205
What repeating an angle does and does not remove
Middleton, Chadwick and Bogle, A Treatise on Surveying (textbook) · p. 191 · strength ★★
Repetition over days and hours

The authors explain the limits of repetition: it reduces graduation and pointing errors, but past a point it stops helping, and it cannot remove a displaced signal. This is why the surveys also changed the circle zero, the hour and the day, rather than only repeating on one occasion.

“There is a limit beyond which repetition produces no improvement. Errors due to slip and flexure, accumulate and prevent extreme accuracy, though a moderate number of repetitions reduce graduation error, by measuring the angle at different parts of the circle. To some extent it reduces errors in bisecting the objects aimed at, for it is reasonable to suppose that the cross-wire will not be always laid on the same side of the true centre. Repetition, however, does not eliminate the most serious source of error of all, namely displacement of the signal observed to.”
Middleton, R. E., Chadwick, O., & Bogle, J. du T. (1904). A treatise on surveying: Part I (2nd ed.). E. & F. N. Spon., p. 191

Tome I, Observations géodésiques, station of Fiefs. For each angle every series is printed: the number of repetitions, the total arc in grades, the single angle, the reduction to the centre, the observer and circle (D. = Delambre, F. = Lalande, B. = Bellet; n° 1 or n° 4 = circle number), the date and hours, and a remark on visibility, sun and wind. Le clocher de Sauti et les flèches voisines nous ont fort exercés par leurs phases différentes. ... D. n° 1. 3 juillet, 5h 40' — 7h 20'. Objets éclairés du soleil ; Sauti tout-à-fait courbe. ... F. n° 4. 4 juillet, 3h 10' — 5h 45'. Objets assez beaux en commençant ; ils l'étoient moins vers le milieu.”

Reading the table. Each block is one series: first number = repetitions (20 or 12 here); then the total arc in grades, the single angle in grades, and the same in degrees; the line 'Au centre' gives the angle reduced to the centre of the station. Below: circle and observer, date, hours, remarks on the air. The angle between Mesnil and Sauti has three series of 20; the mean of the first three is reduced to the horizon (+0.58") to give 42° 59' 48.72". Bonnières-Sauti has series of 20, 20 and 12 on 3 and 4 July at different hours. Boiscommun: observations repeated many times to test barometer and hygrometer effects; fog found to be the main cause, its values set aside
Delambre and Méchain, meridian arc Dunkirk to Barcelona (Base du système métrique) · T2 p. 775 · strength ★★★
Rejecting readings in unsteady air Vertical refraction coefficients Repetition over days and hours

Tome II, remarks on the n table. A hygrometer measures air humidity. Delambre repeated the reciprocal observations at Boiscommun many times to see whether changes of the barometer and hygrometer affected refraction, and left the instrument pointed at Châteauneuf for several hours. He found fog to be the main factor (n of 0.14 to 0.17) and set the fog observations aside.

“A Boiscommun j'ai répété les observations un grand nombre de fois, pour voir si les changemens du baromètre et de l'hygromètre influoient sur la réfraction : je n'ai rien pu remarquer. J'ai laissé pendant plusieurs heures l'instrument bien callé et la lunette dirigée sur Châteauneuf, dans l'intervalle des observations de distances au zénith, et je n'ai pas vu de variations sensibles dans la hauteur ... Il paroît que c'est le brouillard qui influe surtout sur les réfractions, et qui donne pour n des valeurs de 0.14 à 0.17. Je laisse donc à part les observations non numérotées de Boiscommun.”
In English: “At Boiscommun I repeated the observations a great many times to see whether changes of the barometer and the hygrometer affected refraction: I could notice nothing. I left the instrument firmly set for several hours with the telescope pointed at Châteauneuf, between the zenith-distance observations, and I saw no noticeable variation in the height ... It appears that it is fog above all that affects refraction, and gives for n values of 0.14 to 0.17. I therefore set aside the unnumbered observations of Boiscommun.”
Méchain, P., & Delambre, J.-B. J. (1807). Base du système métrique décimal, ou mesure de l'arc du méridien compris entre les parallèles de Dunkerque et Barcelone (Vol. 2). Paris: Baudouin., T2 p. 775

Rejecting readings in unsteady air Steady-air hours Night lamps and heliotropes

Puissant, eastern part of the parallel (Colonel Henry, from 1818). The first-order angles were observed at night at Laplace's wish. Comparable zenith distances (those that should agree, such as the reciprocal pair on one line) disagreed so much that the night zenith distances were rejected and the heights were taken from day measures at second-order stations tied to the first-order ones.

“Le premier des deux tableaux ci-après présente l'ensemble des triangles du premier ordre dont les angles furent observés de nuit, dès l'année 1818, d'après le désir de l'illustre président de la commission royale, dans l'espérance qu'il en résulterait une plus grande exactitude. Mais l'énorme discordance que présentèrent sur cette ligne la plupart des distances zénithales comparables, mirent dans la nécessité de rejeter ces observations nocturnes pour déterminer les différences de niveau par d'autres mesures angulaires recueillies de jour, à différentes stations du second ordre, liées à celles du premier ordre.”
In English: “The first of the two tables below presents all the first-order triangles whose angles were observed at night, from 1818, at the wish of the illustrious president of the royal commission, in the hope of greater accuracy. But the enormous discordance shown on this line by most of the comparable zenith distances made it necessary to reject these night observations and to determine the level differences by other angular measures taken by day at various second-order stations tied to the first-order ones.”
Puissant, L. (1832). Nouvelle description géométrique de la France (Première partie). Paris: Ch. Picquet., 208
Roy: in hot weather only short morning and evening periods were good enough; a whole day could go for one satisfactory angle
Anglo-French triangulation of 1787 (Greenwich to Paris junction), English side by Roy · p. 170 · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours Repetition over days and hours Rejecting readings in unsteady air

Roy, Art. I of the section on the triangles, explaining why the angles were repeated less often than planned. 'Tremulous motion or boiling in the air' is the shimmer caused by heated air near the ground, which makes a distant object dance in the telescope. Roy observed only when the objects were distinct, and he did not change the zero (the starting point on the divided circle) at those times because each change needed a new levelling of the instrument.

“At particular times, especially in hot weather, there was such a tremulous motion or boiling in the air, that it was only during a very short space, chiefly in the mornings and evenings, that the objects were sufficiently distinct to be observed with accuracy. So difficult it is to do any thing perfectly good in this way, that a whole day has frequently been spent, after watching with anxious care, in obtaining a single one that was perfectly satisfactory!”
Roy, W. (1790). An account of the trigonometrical operation, whereby the distance between the meridians of the Royal Observatories of Greenwich and Paris has been determined. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, 80, 111-270 (with Dalby, I., Remarks, pp. 593-614)., p. 170

Rejecting readings in unsteady air

Chapter I gives the year-by-year account of the Privolzhsk triangulation, the eastern part of the 47.5 N arc. The closure of a triangle is the amount by which the sum of its three measured angles differs from 180 degrees plus the spherical excess. Triangle no. 64 closed with more than 7 seconds. The computers found that the angles at the station Nomardzhin had been observed in foggy weather and judged them unreliable. In the 1856 orders on the same page, Captain Napersnikov is told to remeasure the angle at Nomardzhin of triangle no. 64.

“При вычисленіи главнаго ряда треугольниковъ оказалось, что погрѣшность суммы 3-хъ угловъ въ треугольникѣ № 64 составляла свыше 7″, по этому и почтено за необходимость переизмѣрить углы на пунктѣ Номарджинъ, оказавшіеся неблагонадежными, потому, что наблюденія на этомъ пунктѣ произведены въ туманную погоду.”
In English: “In computing the main row of triangles it was found that the error of the sum of the 3 angles in triangle no. 64 was above 7″, and for this reason it was thought necessary to remeasure the angles at the point Nomardzhin, which proved unreliable because the observations at this point had been made in foggy weather.”
Voenno-topograficheskoe depo. (1861). Zapiski Voenno-topograficheskago depo, Chast' XXII, Otd. II: Privolzhskoe trigonometricheskoe izmerenie. Voenno-topograficheskoe depo., Zapiski XXII, Otd. II, p. 13

Tome I, Chapter I, on the signals of the Baltic arc. The signals were painted dark so that the vertical beam, not the sunlit face of the pyramid, was pointed. A phase is a false apparent centre of a target caused by side lighting. Struve states that angle measurement had already stopped before sunset, because the images then always undulate, and gives the summer period of calm images as 0.5 to 0.8 of the interval from noon to sunset.

“Mais à cette époque la mesure des angles a déjà cessé, parce que près du coucher du soleil les objets sont toujours très ondulants, le calme des images ayant lieu en été, dans nos climats, entre 0,5 à 0,8 de l'intervalle de temps entre midi et le coucher du soleil.”
In English: “But at that time the measurement of the angles has already stopped, because near sunset the objects are always very undulating, the calm of the images taking place in summer, in our climates, between 0.5 and 0.8 of the interval of time between noon and sunset.”
Struve, F. G. W. (1857). Arc du méridien de 25° 20' entre le Danube et la Mer Glaciale mesuré depuis 1816 jusqu'en 1855 (Vol. 1). Imprimerie de l'Académie impériale des sciences., T. I, p. 14

Tome II, p. 21, continuing the instruction. Undulating images are images that shimmer because of unsteady air near the ground. The instruction rejected any observation made with indistinct or too undulating images. Struve states that it was followed so strictly that only in two cases is an object wholly missing from a set; incomplete sets were completed with extra observations when the object became visible again. Each object was pointed 4 times in each set, 20 times in all, against 12 in the Baltic arc.

“Enfin l'instruction fixait, que toute observation était inadmissible, si les images des objets étaient indistinctes ou trop ondulantes. Cette instruction a été suivie en Finlande à telle rigueur, qu'il ne se trouve que deux cas, où un objet manque entièrement dans une des mises à faire. ... En Finlande, chaque objet était pointé 4 fois dans chaque mise, donc en tout 20 fois, au lieu de 12 fois dans la mesure Baltique.”
In English: “Finally the instruction laid down that any observation was inadmissible if the images of the objects were indistinct or too undulating. This instruction was followed in Finland with such rigour that there are only two cases where an object is wholly missing from one of the sets to be made. ... In Finland each object was pointed 4 times in each set, so 20 times in all, instead of 12 times in the Baltic measurement.”

Heft I, Kap. 3, station record of Golmberg. In 1880 each angle was measured twice on 8 circle positions, a full set of 24 pointings per direction. The angle Collm to Golmberg differed by 2.61″ from 1871. Helmert examined the possible causes: the 1880 sights were spread over only three days, and the brightly lit tower at Collm may have pulled the pointing, since the observations were as usual made in the afternoon. General Schreiber ordered a remeasurement in 1889: 32 measurements on 16 circle positions over several days, the first 16 rejected for poor lights. The new result confirms 1880 to 0.85″.

“General Schreiber ordnete eine Neumessung des letzteren an, die im Juni und Juli 1889 durch den Landesvermessungsrath Erfurth erfolgte. Es wurden 32 Messungen angestellt, die sich auf 16 Kreisstände vertheilten und 149° 16′ 49″,72 als Resultat ergaben, dessen m. F. nach Maassgabe der Abweichungen der 16 Mittel aus Hin- und Hergang vom Gesammtmittel ± 0″,20 beträgt. (Die ersten 16 Beobachtungen sind wegen mangelhafter Lichter verworfen; sie geben 49″,74.)”
In English: “General Schreiber ordered a remeasurement of the latter, which was made in June and July 1889 by Landesvermessungsrath Erfurth. 32 measurements were made, distributed over 16 circle positions, and gave 149° 16′ 49.72″ as the result, whose mean error, from the deviations of the 16 means of forward and return runs from the overall mean, is ±0.20″. (The first 16 observations were rejected because of poor lights; they give 49.74″.)”
Reading the table. Below the triangles that connect the Madras base with St. Thomas's Mount. The two routes gave slightly different distances, and Lambton gives the reason. The vapour he describes is near-ground haze over the flat, which made the flag-staffs unsteady. His response was to repeat the angles and to use the clear morning of 7 October.

“It may be necessary to notice here, that there was great difficulty in taking all these angles, on account of the very thick vapour which constantly floated near the surface of the flat where the base line runs, almost immediately after day-light, to very near the time of sun-setting. All the angles, and particularly at the north and south end of the base line, have been repeatedly taken, and the only time when the flag-staff appeared distinctly, was in the morning of the 7th of October,”

Continuation of ga_03. Lambton found that all angles referred to the south end of the base at Perumbauk hill were 10 to 12 seconds too large, a micrometer reading error. He replaced those angles by the supplement of the other corrected angles. A side computed through two different triangles is a check: if the angles are good, both routes give the same length.

“It was discovered, that at Perumbauk hill, there had been an error in reading off the south end of the base, most probably of 10" from the micrometers, as all the angles which had a reference to that point, exceeded what they ought to have been by ten or twelve seconds. In consequence of this disagreement, I chose to take the supplemental angle in the second and fourth triangles, after the other angles had been corrected. [...] it appears that the latter distance comes out within 0,4 of a foot to what had been brought by the first triangle; and that, the distance from the south end of the base to Perumbauk hill, derived from the second and fourth triangles, differ only ,14 of a foot.”
Lambton, W. (1808). An account of the measurement of an arc on the meridian on the coast of Coromandel, and the length of a degree deduced therefrom in the latitude 12° 32'. Asiatic Researches, 8, 137 ff., p. 166

After the table of triangles 31 and 32 of the 1802-03 triangulation. Lambton states his own rule for horizontal angles taken in haze. The triangle closure (the amount by which the three observed angles, less the spherical excess, miss 180 degrees) is the test he applies before an angle is kept or rejected. The rule continues on p. 177 with the method of trying each angle in turn.

“The angles have been taken with much care, and I believe with as much accuracy as the nature of such a process admits of; difficulty, however, very frequently arose from the haziness of the weather, which rendered the objects at the very distant points extremely dull, and occasioned some irregularity in the angles. Whenever that happened, the observations were often repeated, and in case any one, in particular, was different from the other so much as ten seconds, it was rejected till the three angles of the triangle had been observed.”
Lambton, W. (1808). An account of the measurement of an arc on the meridian on the coast of Coromandel, and the length of a degree deduced therefrom in the latitude 12° 32'. Asiatic Researches, 8, 137 ff., pp. 176-177

GTS Vol. XII appendix summary of Lambton's 1802-03 observing of horizontal angles. A microscope here is the reading microscope on the circle; reading both, three times each, reduces reading error. Two field-books were kept independently and compared.

“The angles were all measured three or four times each; both microscopes were read off thrice every time the object was observed, and two separate field-books were kept for making out the angles. If from any marked difference between two measures of the same angle the graduation of the instrument was suspected to be in error, the division between the dots was carefully examined, as also those to the right and left, and if any error was discovered, allowance was made accordingly. Difficulties however very frequently arose from the haziness of the weather occasioning irregularity in the angles, and observations in consequence had often to be repeated.”

Introduction to the Karachi Longitudinal Series, season 1851-52. Mirage is strong refraction near hot or wet ground. The observers tried to fix the height of the Runn (a salt marsh) from Akoria station and did not use the result. The desert itself was free of mirage in that season.

“The desert was found perfectly free from mirage at the season it was visited; but the Runn of Cutch, on the southern flank of the series, was greatly affected by this atmospheric phenomenon, which prevented the ascertainment of the height of the Runn with respect to the sea level. [...] To determine this point, a secondary station was selected in the Runn, and vertical angles taken to it from Akoria station, on the edge of the tract, but the secondary point could not be connected, and the vertical angles were so affected by mirage, as to be untrustworthy.”

Part II, eastern Colorado, after the table of m for each line (pp. 262-263) and in the remarks on the heights (p. 267). The two passages show that the observers knew the warm air layer at the ground changes the bend of short, low lines, and that they dropped observations taken while refraction was far above its daily minimum.

“The tabular values of m show an apparent dependence upon the length of lines s, viz: the shorter s, the smaller m. This fact may be explained by the circumstance of the line of sight being nearer the heated ground the shorter the distance. The comparatively warm stratum of air is quite close to the ground, particularly during insolation. [...] The ground is barren and treeless over the entire region and the climate is very dry, especially during the summer. The instrument was only elevated sufficiently to overcome the earth's curvature and permit the visibility of the distant object. [p. 267:] As a rule (with some exceptions) the early observations-say those made before 9 or 10 a. m.-and some late ones in the afternoon could not be included, the refraction being then much above its ordinary minimum daily amount.”

Part II, heights across the Sacramento and San Joaquin valleys. The older long lines were observed at different hours, months and years, so equal refraction at the two ends could not be relied on. In 1898 the observers measured both ends at the same time over shorter lines, and the long lines were removed from the height results.

“The difficulty experienced when attempting the determination of heights on the crest of the Sierra Nevada by means of zenith distances measured over the long lines spanning the great valley of California rendered it necessary to supplement the older measures. This was done in the summer of 1898, by strictly simultaneous reciprocal measures over shorter lines, along which the variations of refraction are less injurious. [p. 305:] If, further, we reflect that the resulting zenith distances, as tabulated, were taken mostly at different hours of the day, in different months of the year, and in different years, with only the new (1898) measures simultaneous; it does not seem surprising that it became necessary to exclude the resulting differences of height over the several long lines across the valley which range up to 229 kilometres or 142 statute miles.”

Vertical heights (p. 151). Mutual vertical angles are elevation angles measured from each end of a line toward the other. The formula h' - h = s tan 1/2 (alpha - alpha') uses both, and the refraction drops out when it is the same at both ends. Table M gives the coefficient of refraction found on each line, so the bend was measured line by line. Values in brackets were left out of the chain mean; on this page they are all lines of 4.9 to 12.9 miles. The definition of the coefficient is not printed in the report.

“17. The differences of height were computed by the formula h′ — h = s . tan ½ (α — α′) where s = the length of the line in feet α, α′ = the angles of elevation of each point from the other. ... 1. Under the margin heading "Perturbation of Atmosphere in Hot Climates". Boiling is the shimmer of heated air near the ground. The instruction is to stop observing while it lasts, because the signal moves about and accurate work is impossible.

“In hot climates the atmosphere often 'boils' at certain times of the day. When this takes place it is useless to observe, the signal will dance about and become distorted in so erratic a manner, that accurate work is impossible. To attempt to observe under these conditions merely amounts to loss of time and temper.”

Refraction varies with hour, temperature and pressure; horizontal deviation happens
Middleton, Chadwick and Bogle, A Treatise on Surveying (textbook) · p. 226 · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours Rejecting readings in unsteady air

The authors list what changes refraction: the hour (least about 3h 45m p.m. in the tropics), temperature and barometric pressure, and heated ground, where the ray can even curve the other way (mirage). They also state that sideways (horizontal) deviation is common. Their conclusion: under strong disturbance do not observe at all, and otherwise rely on reciprocal angles in similar conditions.

“Now the value of error of refraction though usually small, is very uncertain. It varies at different hours of the day, being least (in the tropics) at about 3h. 45m. P.M. It varies also with temperature, and barometric pressure. Over highly heated arid plains, it becomes exceedingly irregular, the curve sometimes being actually convex towards the earth, so that objects are depressed and not raised. [...] Horizontal deviation is also very common. A series of rods, ranged out in a straight line at one time, have presented the appearance of a curve at another time. When disturbance is so great as this, accurate observation of any kind is obviously impracticable. At any time, however, the effect of refraction is uncertain, and accurate results can only be arrived at, by taking reciprocal angles under similar atmospheric conditions.”
Middleton, R. E., Chadwick, O., & Bogle, J. du T. (1904). A treatise on surveying: Part I (2nd ed.). E. & F. N. Spon., p. 226

Tome II, remarks after the n table. Delambre explains the single negative n (no. 12, Fiefs-Bonnières): July, very hot and stormy weather, a poorly visible steeple. He states that refraction was nearly zero at the moment of the two observations, and notes that three observations of the same morning hour gave different refraction for different directions.

“Le 12e est négatif. Les deux observations sont du mois de juillet. A Fiefs le temps étoit très-chaud et orageux, et le clocher de Bonnières se voyoit mal. Cette dernière circonstance devoit augmenter la distance au zénith de quelques secondes. En diminuant de 9" la distance observée on auroit n = 0.0020 ; mais il n'en est pas moins sûr qu'à l'instant des deux observations la réfraction étoit à peu près nulle.”
In English: “The 12th is negative. The two observations are from July. At Fiefs the weather was very hot and stormy, and the steeple of Bonnières was poorly seen. This last circumstance must have increased the zenith distance by a few seconds. Reducing the observed distance by 9" would give n = 0.0020; but it is no less certain that at the moment of the two observations the refraction was nearly nil.”
Méchain, P., & Delambre, J.-B. J. (1807). Base du système métrique décimal, ou mesure de l'arc du méridien compris entre les parallèles de Dunkerque et Barcelone (Vol. 2). Paris: Baudouin., T2 p. 773

Parallel of Paris, Brest to Strasbourg (Henry east part, Bonne west part), Nouvelle carte de France · 28 · strength ★★
Rejecting readings in unsteady air

Same Instruction, added considerations. Vapours are visible moisture or haze near the ground; undulations are the trembling of the target image in unsteady air; phases are the uneven sunlight on one side of a signal that shifts its apparent centre. The rule tells observers to wait for steady, clear air before measuring angles.

“On évitera, autant que possible, de faire des observations d'angles dans les momens où il y a beaucoup de vapeurs et d'ondulations, et dans ceux où le soleil donnerait aux signaux des phases prononcées qui rendraient le pointé trop incertain.”
In English: “One will avoid, as far as possible, observing angles at moments when there are many vapours and undulations, and at those when the sun would give the signals marked phases that would make the pointing too uncertain.”
Puissant, L. (1832). Nouvelle description géométrique de la France (Première partie). Paris: Ch. Picquet., 28
Roy: a doubtful observation was left blank in the triangle table, not filled in
Anglo-French triangulation of 1787 (Greenwich to Paris junction), English side by Roy · pp. 170-171 · strength ★★
Rejecting readings in unsteady air

Same page, at the foot. The 'column of observed angles' is in the triangle tables that follow (pp. 172-182). The sentence continues on p. 171: 'But no bad consequence has arisen on that account, there being always such other checks from the collateral stations, as to leave nothing doubtful.' Collateral stations are neighbouring stations whose angles close the same figures.

“Sometimes an observation has been entirely lost, or at least that which had been obtained was not thought a very good one. In such cases a blank has been left in the column of observed angles, and also in that expressing the error.”
Roy, W. (1790). An account of the trigonometrical operation, whereby the distance between the meridians of the Royal Observatories of Greenwich and Paris has been determined. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, 80, 111-270 (with Dalby, I., Remarks, pp. 593-614)., pp. 170-171
Clarke 1858: all observations equal weight unless the observer's own remark condemns one; observations seldom taken in decidedly unfavourable conditions
Ordnance Trigonometrical Survey of Great Britain and Ireland, Principal Triangulation · p. 50 · strength ★★
Rejecting readings in unsteady air

Same page. The rule for rejection was decided at the station by the observer, who wrote remarks on the air and the target against each reading (see the observation-book item). The office did not discard readings because they looked bad afterwards (p. 67 repeats this rule).

“All observations, when received in the office, are considered of equal weight, unless a remark of the observer against any observation condemns it as to be rejected. Observations under favourable circumstances are doubtless more valuable than observations under less favourable circumstances; but how to assign their relative numerical value is a question that admits of no general solution. Observations are seldom taken under decidedly unfavourable circumstances, if it can be avoided.”
Clarke, A. R. (1858). Ordnance trigonometrical survey of Great Britain and Ireland: Account of the observations and calculations of the principal triangulation. London: Eyre and Spottiswoode., p. 50
Zenith sector: about sixteen nights on Aldebaran in the monsoon; less favourable nights rejected
Great Arc of India, Lambton's meridional arc (Coromandel coast to Punnae and north to about 18 N) · p. 180 · strength ★★
Rejecting readings in unsteady air Repetition over days and hours

Section VII, latitude of Paudree by the zenith sector. A zenith sector measures the zenith distance (angle from the vertical) of a star as it crosses the meridian. Lambton reports the monsoon weather, the number of nights, and that the weaker nights were rejected before the latitude was taken.

“The time I commenced observing at Paudree station was during the heavy part of the monsoon, which occasioned frequent interruptions: and although I had intended observing by at least three fixed stars, I only succeeded to my satisfaction in one, which was Aldebaran. With that star I had a fortunate succession for about sixteen nights; some few of those observations being less favourable than the others, were rejected, and the rest, from which the latitude was determined, appear in the following table,”
Lambton, W. (1808). An account of the measurement of an arc on the meridian on the coast of Coromandel, and the length of a degree deduced therefrom in the latitude 12° 32'. Asiatic Researches, 8, 137 ff., p. 180
Lambton's general report: angles taken three and four times, field-books compared, doubtful angles rejected only with reason
Lambton, trigonometrical operations across the Peninsula, Fort St. George to Mangalore · p. XVIII · strength ★★
Repetition over days and hours Rejecting readings in unsteady air

Walker quotes Lambton's manuscript General Report on how he measured the horizontal angles of this period (1802-1808). It adds his method when a triangle did not close: each angle in turn was held correct and the sides were recomputed, and no angle was dropped without cause.

““ As to the angles in general they have been taken three and four times, and every time that the object was observed, both microscopes were read off thrice, and two separate field-books kept for making out the angles. [...] This however has rarely happened, and when it did, great precaution was used, and no angle was rejected without some reason appeared to render it doubtful”.”
Walker, J. T. (1870). Account of the operations of the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India, Vol. I: Standards of measure and base-lines. Dehra Dun: Great Trigonometrical Survey., p. XVIII
Ferrero's m from 95 primary triangles: 0.469" (0.386" without four outliers)
Trigonometrical Survey of New South Wales · p. 187 · strength ★★
Rejecting readings in unsteady air

Furber computes General Ferrero's m, the mean error of an angle found from the triangle closing errors, and lists it for many surveys (pp. 186-187), including South Africa with the 10-inch Repsold (0.495", 134 triangles) and Maclear's angles (1.140", 64 triangles). For New South Wales it is 0.469"; four triangles with abnormally large errors would be rejected by Peirce's criterion (a statistical rule for discarding outliers), giving 0.386". No PDF of this paper is in the project; the item points to the OCR text file, so no crop is possible. Wording checked against a page image of p. 187 held elsewhere in the project.

“For New South Wales, as deduced from the 95 primary triangles already observed, m = ± 0·469 while that value would be reduced to ± 0·386 by the omission of four triangles, in which the error is abnormally great, and which would be rejected by Pierce's criterion.”
No page image: this source is held as a text layer only.

Before 1890 Peirce's criterion used to reject directions; since 1890 no rejections and least-squares figure adjustment
Trigonometrical Survey of New South Wales · pp. 182-183 · strength ★★
Rejecting readings in unsteady air

Computation of triangulation (pp. 182-183). Before 1890 observed directions were tested with Peirce's criterion for rejection. After 1890 the practice of other major surveys was followed: no rejection for apparent discordance (disagreement), local adjustment at each station, and adjustment of the figures by least squares. No PDF of this paper is in the project; the item points to the OCR text file, so no crop is possible. The p. 182 part was checked against a page image held elsewhere in the project; the p. 183 part is from the text layer.

“Prior to 1890, when the survey was resumed after having been in abeyance some years, the azimuthal directions derived immediately from the observations were tabulated, without adjustment for correction of reading or bisection of referring mark, and Peirce's criterion was applied in order to determine whether any should be rejected; also, in the computation, no adjustment for "figure" conditions was made except in the case of one or two quadrilaterals. In the primary work done since the year named, the practice in other surveys of similar importance of making local adjustment and permitting no rejections on account of apparent discordance has been followed, and, in the series of triangles south from the Lake George base to the boundary of the Colony, adjustment to meet the geometrical conditions of such figure has been made by the method of least squares.”
No page image: this source is held as a text layer only.

The printed tables themselves, with what each column means.

Four reciprocal zenith-distance pairs measure the total refraction on lines of 9 to 35.5 minutes of arc
Cassini de Thury and Lacaille, verification of the Paris meridian and the arc of the parallel near 43.5 N · x-xj (Troisième partie), footnote · strength ★★★
Raw tables of repeated measures Vertical refraction coefficients

Footnote continued on p. xj. For four lines the zenith distance was observed at both ends. Reciprocal zenith distances are taken from each end of a line toward the other; their sum exceeds 180 degrees by the arc between the two verticals, less the bend of the ray at both ends, so the pair measures the refraction on that line itself. For each pair the authors print the two zenith distances, the apparent arc given by their sum, the true arc from the triangles, and the difference, which is the total refraction of both ends.

“Au fignal de Ste Victoire, la diftance apparente du fommet de la Montagne des Houpies au zenith fut obfervée de 90° 41' 40". A la Montagne des Houpies la diftance de Ste Victoire au zenith fut trouvée de 89° 43' 15". La fomme 180° 24' 55" donne 24' 55" pour l'arc itinéraire apparent, au lieu que le véritable eft de 28' 15"½. Il y avoit donc 3' 20"½ de réfraction, fur un arc de 28'.”
In English: “At the signal of Sainte-Victoire, the apparent zenith distance of the top of the Montagne des Houpies was observed as 90° 41' 40". At the Montagne des Houpies the zenith distance of Sainte-Victoire was found as 89° 43' 15". The sum 180° 24' 55" gives 24' 55" for the apparent itinerary arc, whereas the true one is 28' 15"½. So there were 3' 20"½ of refraction on an arc of 28'.”
Reading the table. Four printed pairs in running text: Sainte-Victoire / Houpies (90° 41' 40", 89° 43' 15"; 3' 20"½ on 28'); Aigues-Mortes / Houpies (89° 50' 19", 90° 40' 20"; 4' 57" on 35'½); Carcassonne / foot of Alaric signal (89° 1' 25", 91° 10' 5"; 1' 22" on 13'); Perpignan / foot of Tautavel tower (88° 36' 55", 91° 31' 20"; 43" on 9'). Each pair: zenith distance at A, zenith distance at B, apparent arc, true arc, total refraction. One value per station; the number of readings is not printed.
Worked out here: Refraction at one end as a fraction of the arc: 200.5/1695.5/2 = 0.059; 297/2136/2 = 0.070; 82/772/2 = 0.053; 43/538/2 = 0.040.

Tome I, Observations géodésiques, station of Fiefs. For each angle every series is printed: the number of repetitions, the total arc in grades, the single angle, the reduction to the centre, the observer and circle (D. = Delambre, F. = Lalande, B. = Bellet; n° 1 or n° 4 = circle number), the date and hours, and a remark on visibility, sun and wind. One series is marked 'série à rejeter' (series to be rejected) for strong wind, a faint and curved target and undulations. The remark on Sauti says that phases (the side lighting of a spire by the sun) moved the apparent target.

“D. n° 1 + première place. Grand vent ; Sauti foible et courbe ; ondulations au Mesnil ; fils en + série à rejeter. ... Le clocher de Sauti et les flèches voisines nous ont fort exercés par leurs phases différentes. ... D. n° 1. 3 juillet, 5h 40' — 7h 20'. Objets éclairés du soleil ; Sauti tout-à-fait courbe. ... F. n° 4. 4 juillet, 3h 10' — 5h 45'. Objets assez beaux en commençant ; ils l'étoient moins vers le milieu.”
In English: “D. circle no. 1, first place. Strong wind; Sauti faint and curved; undulations at Mesnil; wires in +; series to be rejected. ... The steeple of Sauti and the neighbouring spires gave us much trouble by their different phases. ... D. circle no. 1. 3 July, 5h 40' to 7h 20'. Objects lit by the sun; Sauti quite curved. ... F. circle no. 4. 4 July, 3h 10' to 5h 45'. Objects rather fine at the start; less so towards the middle.”
Reading the table. Each block is one series: first number = repetitions (20 or 12 here); then the total arc in grades, the single angle in grades, and the same in degrees; the line 'Au centre' gives the angle reduced to the centre of the station. Below: circle and observer, date, hours, remarks on the air. The angle between Mesnil and Sauti has three series of 20; the mean of the first three is reduced to the horizon (+0.58") to give 42° 59' 48.72". Bonnières-Sauti has series of 20, 20 and 12 on 3 and 4 July at different hours. A typical angle in Delambre's north part has 2 to 5 series of 12 to 30 repetitions (e.g. Dunkerque, Watten-Cassel: 20 + 16 + 30).
Worked out here: Mesnil-Sauti series reduced to centre: 42° 59' 49.68" and 42° 59' 55.07" (the rejected series is 5.4" higher).

Zenith distances at Boiscommun on seven days, each with hour, barometer, thermometer and state of the air, including 'brouillard humide'

Tome I, station of Boiscommun (frimaire an 2, December 1793). Delambre observed the zenith distance of the weathercock of Châteauneuf on seven days, one series of ten each, and printed with each the hour, the barometer (in pouces and lignes), the thermometer (as a fraction of the ice-to-boiling interval, converted to Réaumur degrees), and the sky: rain, fine or poor horizon, damp fog. He also stayed half an hour at the telescope to see whether refraction changed the distance. This is a direct record of humidity and pressure with each vertical angle.

“24 frimaire, 12h ¼. Bar. 27p 1l9. Therm. 0.099 = 7d92. A 1h ¼ la distance étoit encore la même. ... Le baromètre et le thermomètre étoient placés environ 1t8 au-dessous de la lunette. Après ces observations je suis resté pendant une demi-heure à la lunette, pour voir si la réfraction ne changeroit pas la distance : je n'ai pas vu la moindre variation. Horizon très-pur, point de soleil. ... 25 frimaire, 3h ¾. Bar. 27p 4l. Therm. + 0.11 = 8d8. Temps pluvieux ; horizon assez beau. ... 30 frimaire, 3h ½. Bar. 27p 3l. Therm. + 0.067 = 5d36. Brouillard humide.”
In English: “24 frimaire, 12h ¼. Barometer 27 pouces 1.9 lignes. Thermometer 0.099 = 7.92 degrees. At 1h ¼ the distance was still the same. ... The barometer and thermometer were placed about 1.8 toises below the telescope. After these observations I stayed half an hour at the telescope to see whether refraction would change the distance: I did not see the least variation. Very clear horizon, no sun. ... 25 frimaire, 3h ¾. Barometer 27 pouces 4 lignes. Thermometer +0.11 = 8.8 degrees. Rainy weather; horizon fairly fine. ... 30 frimaire, 3h ½. Barometer 27 pouces 3 lignes. Thermometer +0.067 = 5.36 degrees. Damp fog.”
Reading the table. Each line: number of repetitions (10), total arc in grades, single zenith distance in grades, the same in degrees; then date, hour, barometer, thermometer, remarks. Seven series on seven days (24 to 30 frimaire) to the same target. The page continues on p. 167 with 1, 2 and 7 nivôse.
Worked out here: Seven zenith distances of the Châteauneuf weathercock range from 90° 5' 46.0" (28 frimaire) to 90° 6' 6.1" (30 frimaire, damp fog): spread 20.1".

Tome I, station of Rieupeyroux in Méchain's southern part (thermidor an 6, July-August 1798; M. et A. = Méchain and his assistant). Each target has two series of ten on different days and hours, with the thermometer reading and remarks: calm or strong wind, sun or shade, undulations or none. The mean is then corrected for half the wire thickness and for the height of the signal (dH) 'for the level difference and the refraction'.

“M. et A. 24 thermidor, à 5h ½ du soir. Thermomètre + 13d6 en 80d. Calme. L'objet est dans l'ombre ; on le voit bien. ... M. et A. 18 thermidor, à 6h ¼ du soir. Thermomètre 15d0. Soleil. Le grand vent agite le niveau, et le signal est difficile à distinguer. ... M. et A. 21 thermidor, à 7h ¾ du matin. Thermomètre 15d0. Calme. Objet assez net ; il n'y a point d'ondulations.”
In English: “M. and A., 24 thermidor, at 5h ½ in the evening. Thermometer +13.6 degrees (80-degree scale). Calm. The object is in shadow; it is seen well. ... M. and A., 18 thermidor, at 6h ¼ in the evening. Thermometer 15.0 degrees. Sun. The strong wind shakes the level, and the signal is hard to make out. ... M. and A., 21 thermidor, at 7h ¾ in the morning. Thermometer 15.0 degrees. Calm. Object fairly sharp; there are no undulations.”
Reading the table. Per target (Rodez statue, signal of La Gaste): two series of 10, each with date, hour (evening and morning), thermometer and remarks. 'Milieu des deux séries' / 'Moyenne' = mean used for the reduction to the horizon; then 'Demi-épaisseur du fil' (half wire thickness, +3") and dH (signal height correction) give the value used 'pour la différence de niveau et la réfraction'.
Worked out here: La Gaste: evening series 89° 57' 37.9", morning series 89° 57' 27.2"; difference 10.7".

Raw tables of repeated measures

Tome I, Tableau des triangles. For each triangle the table gives the observed angles with the register page, the spherical excess (the amount by which the angles of a triangle on the curved earth exceed 180 degrees) and the 'Somme des erreurs', which is the closure error: the sum of the three observed angles minus 180 degrees minus the excess. A star marks an angle concluded, not observed. Closure errors are a direct internal check on the horizontal angles.

“Somme des erreurs . . — 1"18 ... L'astérisque est la marque d'un angle conclu.”
In English: “Sum of the errors -1.18" ... The asterisk marks a concluded angle.”
Reading the table. Columns: No. of triangle; station names; register page; observed angles; spherical excess; spherical angles; angles of the chords; mean angles. Under each fully observed triangle, 'Somme des erreurs' gives the closure error. Triangle 1 (Dunkerque, Watten, Cassel): -1.18"; triangle 3 (Watten, Cassel, Fiefs): -0.90".
Worked out here: Triangle 1: observed sum 180° 0' 0.00", excess 1.18", closure -1.18". Triangle 3: observed sum 180° 0' 0.77", excess 1.67", closure -0.90".

For each line of the chain where zenith distances were taken from both ends, the table gives the factor n = r/C (refraction at one end divided by the angle between the verticals). Reading the table. Two columns of station pairs with the factor n. Numbering in fives at the left margin (5, 10, ... 80). The leading '0.' is dropped after the first entry of each group of five. Montjouy tower: six sea-horizon heights compared with a direct levelling; the levelling is kept
Delambre and Méchain, meridian arc Dunkirk to Barcelona (Base du système métrique) · T2 p. 759 · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours Raw tables of repeated measures

Tome II, heights above the Mediterranean. The height of the battlements of the Montjouy tower had been measured by direct levelling (105.1 toises). Delambre computes it again from six zenith distances of the sea horizon and prints each result. The mean agrees with the levelling within 0.5 toise, but single values scatter. He states the observations were all near sunset, when refraction raises the sea, and that one isolated sea-horizon observation can be wrong by 5 to 6 toises; he keeps the levelling.

“toutes ces observations ayant été faites vers le coucher du soleil, la réfraction devoit élever la mer plus que dans l'état moyen et faire paroître la hauteur de la tour trop petite. Elles prouvent qu'une observation de l'horizon de la mer prise isolément peut donner une erreur de 5 à 6 toises. Nous nous en tiendrons donc au résultat du nivellement”
In English: “all these observations having been made towards sunset, refraction must have raised the sea more than in the mean state and made the height of the tower appear too small. They prove that an isolated observation of the sea horizon can give an error of 5 to 6 toises. We shall therefore keep to the result of the levelling”
Reading the table. Columns: zenith distance of the sea horizon (90° 23' to 90° 25'); height computed with n = 0.08 and the correction for each; resulting height H in toises (100.5 to 107.5). Milieu 105.2; plus 0.4 for half the wire thickness gives 105.6, against Nivellement 105.1; difference 0.5 toise.

Raw tables of repeated measures

Art. II, Calculation of the Triangles, the first page of the table that runs to p. 182. Spherical excess is the amount by which the three angles of a triangle on a curved surface exceed 180 degrees; it is computed from the area. The 'error' is the difference between the observed excess and the computed one, so it is a check on each triangle. On p. 169 Roy introduces the table: 'a column is inserted containing the spherical excess; and another for the difference or error between that and the excess of the sum of the observed angles above 180°'.

“Art. II. Calculation of the Triangles.”
Reading the table. Columns: number of the triangle; names of the stations; observed angles (degrees, minutes, seconds) with their sum below; spherical excess in seconds; difference or error in seconds; angles corrected for calculation; distances in feet. Triangle I: observed sum 179 59 59, excess 0.29, error -1.29. Triangle II: sum 179 59 59.6, excess 0.21, error -0.61. Each angle is a single printed value (Roy gives the means only); the error column is the test.

Art. II, Heights of Rook's Hill and Butser Hill. Each of three stations observed the other two, so every line has an angle from each end (reciprocal angles). From these the mean refraction of each line follows (see the rules in the 1797 item). The heights round the triangle do not close exactly: 228 feet by the lines across the water against 208 feet by the direct reciprocal line, and the authors share the 20 feet between the refractions.

“From these observations, the mean refraction between Dunnose and Rook's Hill will be found 1' 58"; between Dunnose and Butser Hill 2' 16"; and between Butser Hill and Rook's Hill 39"; which are about 1/12, 1/10, 1/15 of the contained arcs respectively, as in the table.”
Reading the table. Rows: at Dunnose, Rook's Hill and Butser Hill, the depression (or elevation) of the ground at each other station, in minutes and seconds; then the three contained arcs (23' 31", 23' 3", 9' 59"). The flagstaff at Rook's Hill was 20 feet high and the telescope axis about 5 1/2 feet above the ground. One value per direction is printed.
Worked out here: Dunnose-Rook's Hill: depressions 12' 14" + 7' 37" = 19' 51" = 1191". Reducing each to the telescope axis (5.5 ft at about 1411" x 101.4 ft = 143,100 ft subtends 7.9") removes about 16": 1175". Arc 23' 31" = 1411". (1411 - 1175)/2 = 118" = 1' 58", as printed. 118/1411 = 0.084 = 1/12.

Section IV, second part: azimuthal observations in detail. Azimuth is the angle of a line from true north; it was found from the referring object and circumpolar stars at elongation (their farthest east or west point). Each row is one night's observation with its own result, so the spread can be seen. Footnote marks give the weather for individual rows. Probable error is the amount the mean is as likely to be within as outside.

“Cloudy and misty. Cloudy. Very misty; partial sun. Very clear in all directions.”
Reading the table. Columns: date (5 Aug to 14 Sep 1846); star and elongation (51 Cephei, Polaris, delta and lambda Ursae Minoris, E or W); reading of star; computed level and collimation correction; corrected reading; reading of R.O.; computed azimuth of star at elongation; resulting azimuth of R.O. (81° 52' plus 15.09" to 32.33"). Mean of eastern elongations 24.23", western 20.28", general mean 81° 52' 22".51, probable error ±0".60. The quote is the four footnotes on weather.

Section IX, 'Coefficient of Refraction'. Where both heights are known by levelling, the true zenith distance Z can be computed. The observed z differs from Z only by refraction, so k = (Z - z)/v is measured directly on that line. The weight w grows with the square root of the distance and with the number of observations.

“In the former case, the coefficient required is simply the ratio of the excess of the observed above the true zenith distance to the angle subtended by the two stations at the centre of the earth.”
Reading the table. Columns: number of the line; stations; levelled height (ft); observed zenith distance z; number of observations (4 to 29, e.g. Ben Nevis 19, Merrick 29, Pertinny 20); logarithmic distance; v (angle at the earth's centre, seconds); true zenith distance Z; Z - z (seconds); k; weight w; k times w. Values from 0.0649 (High Willhays) to 0.1058 (Swyre Barrow). Printed mean k = 0.0792.
Clarke, A. R. (1858). Ordnance trigonometrical survey of Great Britain and Ireland: Account of the observations and calculations of the principal triangulation. London: Eyre and Spottiswoode., p. 542

Ordnance Trigonometrical Survey of Great Britain and Ireland, Principal Triangulation · p. 543 · strength ★★★
Raw tables of repeated measures Vertical refraction coefficients

Next table. For two stations that observed each other, the sum of the two zenith distances exceeds 180° by the arc v when there is no refraction; refraction makes the sum smaller. So 1 - 2k = (z + z' - 180°)/v gives the bend on that line from the two angles alone, without knowing the heights. The weights follow the distance and the number of observations at each end.

“The weights assumed for the separate determinations are directly as the square root of the distance and inversely as the sum of the reciprocals of the numbers of observations at the two observing stations. The following table contains the calculation of 112 values of k:”
Reading the table. Columns: number; the two stations; observed zenith distance at each; number of observations at each (e.g. Monach 8 and Ben Clibrig 10; Corryhabbie 31 and 35; Jura 28); logarithmic distance; v; z + z' - 180°; 1 - 2k; k; weight w; kw. The table runs to p. 548. Group means printed on p. 548: 0.0801 (rays mostly over sea), 0.0778 (partly over sea), 0.0744 (inland).

This is the key to Table A, the computation of the triangles. Column 3 gives the number of sets for each angle, column 4 the measured angle (mean of all sets, reduced to centre), column 5 the angle after the base correction of 0.28″, column 6 the value m, the mean deviation of the single sets from the mean of the angle. The first triangle of the main row is shown under the key with 14, 12 and 12 sets and m = 1.6, 1.2 and 1.4.

“3. Число пріемовъ, сдѣланныхъ для измѣренія угла. ... 6. Величину m, то есть среднюю разность угловъ, полученныхъ изъ каждаго пріема, отъ средней величины угла.”
In English: “3. Number of sets made for measuring the angle. ... 6. The quantity m, that is, the mean difference of the angles obtained from each set from the mean value of the angle.”

Table B gives the heights above the sea of the first-class points and of the Sarpinsky row. Reciprocal zenith distances are the two zenith distances of one line, one measured from each end. For each new point the table prints the zenith distance from the point to a known point (column 4) and from the known point back (column 5), the height obtained from each known point (column 6) and the mean (column 7). Two different known points give two independent heights for the same point.

“4. Зенитное разстояніе, измѣренное съ пункта опредѣляемаго на пунктъ, котораго номеръ выставленъ въ столбцѣ третьемъ. 5. Зенитное разстояніе измѣренное съ пункта, котораго № выставленъ въ столбцѣ 3-мъ на пунктъ опредѣляемый.”
In English: “4. Zenith distance measured from the point being determined to the point whose number is given in the third column. 5. Zenith distance measured from the point whose number is given in column 3 to the point being determined.”
Reading the table. Columns: 1 number; 2 point; 3 known point it is computed from; 4 forward zenith distance; 5 backward zenith distance; 6 height of the signal top from that known point (sazhen); 7 mean of the two heights; 8 height of the foot of the pyramid. Each new point is computed from two known points.
Worked out here: Two heights per point (sazhen): Mokry Log 76.871 and 76.145 (difference 0.726); Melekhovskaya 60.955 and 60.866 (0.089); Razdorskaya 70.191 and 70.188 (0.003); Krymskaya 85.484 and 85.404 (0.080).

Tome II, pièces justificatives, explanation of the Finland station table. Three almost identical Munich universal instruments were used by Oberg, Melan and Woldstedt, each with an assistant on the lower telescope so the pointings of the two telescopes were simultaneous. Struve states that there were always 5 sets with 4 pointings on each object, each set in two halves, and that he prints the separate figures of the two halves at every station.

“Il y a eu constamment 5 mises observées, chacune à 4 pointés de chaque objet. Mais chaque mise était composée de deux moitiés, correspondantes aux deux positions renversées de la lunette supérieure. J'ai donné, à chaque station, les chiffres séparés des deux moitiés.”
In English: “There were always 5 sets observed, each with 4 pointings of each object. But each set was made of two halves, corresponding to the two reversed positions of the upper telescope. I have given, at each station, the separate figures of the two halves.”
Struve, F. G. W. (1860). Arc du méridien de 25° 20' entre le Danube et la Mer Glaciale mesuré depuis 1816 jusqu'en 1855 (Vol. 2). Imprimerie de l'Académie impériale des sciences., T. II, p. 228

End of the triangle tables of the southern arc (Punnae to Putchapolliam). A base of verification is a second measured base: its length carried through the triangles from the first base is compared with its measured length. The table also shows the method: observed angles, the difference column, the spherical excess, and the error (closure) of each triangle, for example +0.83" and +2.46".

“In the two last triangles, the distance Sekundermalli from Suddragherry will be found common: then, by taking the mean and referring to the 29th triangle, it will appear, that there is a difference of 4 1/10 feet, in the same side Suddragherry from Sekundermalli; from whence it may be inferred, that had the base been computed from bringing down the triangles from the northward, it would have exceeded the measurement by 10 inches, nearly.”

Table of pole-star observations for the meridian at Yerracondah (January 1804). A referring lamp is a lamp set up as a fixed night mark near the station; the angle from the star to the lamp is measured each night and the lamp is then tied to a survey station by day. The note below says no double azimuths were possible because vapour hid the pole star by day.

“Pole-Star Observations at Yerracondah Station, reduced for determining the position of the Meridian. [...] It may be remarked here, that no double azimuths have been taken. The pole-star being so low, and the vapour in the atmosphere so great in general, that I have never, except in two instances, been able to discern it while the sun was above the horizon.”
Reading the table. Columns: date (15 to 27 January 1804, 9 nights); apparent polar distance of the star; latitude; azimuth of the star; angle between the pole star and the referring lamp; angle between the north pole and the referring lamp. Look at the last column: 9 independent nightly values from 7 16 31.49 to 7 16 36.08, mean 7 16 33.64.
Worked out here: Spread of the nightly values: 36.08 - 31.49 = 4.59".
Lambton, W. (1811). An account of trigonometrical operations in crossing the Peninsula of India, and connecting Fort St. George with Mangalore. Asiatic Researches, 10, 290-384., p. 362

US Transcontinental Triangulation, 39th parallel · p. 43 · strength ★★★
Raw tables of repeated measures Repetition over days and hours

Part I, in the explanation of the station (local) adjustment. A "series" is one sweep of the telescope over all visible signals, read with the telescope direct (D.) and then reversed (R.), at one setting ("position") of the horizontal circle. Schott prints two of the 152 series observed at Mount Helena, California, as an example of the raw field record that goes into each station abstract. The counts at the foot of the next page show how many separate pointings went into each direction.

“The following portions of the local adjustment at the station Mount Helena, California, will serve to illustrate the arrangement of the numerical work. [...] In the abstract proper two series only, the thirty-third and thirty-sixth, are here given out of the 152 series shown in the original computation. The first line gives the seconds of the mean reading of the three microscopes for each signal sighted with the telescope direct. The corrections for run have already been applied. The second line gives the corresponding readings with the telescope in the reverse position, when sweeping back over the same signals in the opposite direction. The third line is the mean of the first and second.”
Reading the table. Columns: the ten signals sighted from Mount Helena (Mt. Diablo, Table Mt., Snow Mt. (E), Azimuth Mark, Marysville Butte, Lola, Pine Hill, Round Top, Monticello, Vaca). Each series block (Oct. 11 a.m., circle position 12, series 33; Oct. 12 a.m., position 13, series 36) has five lines: seconds read with telescope direct, seconds read reversed, mean of the two, mean reduced to the first signal, and the value used in the observation equations. Part III, summary of angular results. The closing error of a triangle is 180 degrees plus the spherical excess minus the sum of the three measured angles; it is a check that is independent of the station repeats. Schott lists, per series and base net, how many triangles closed plus and minus, the sums of the plus and minus errors, the mean error of an angle and the probable error of an adjusted direction.

“With respect to the closure of the triangles (pi plus spherical excess minus the sum of the angles), we find the number of cases in excess to those in defect in the ratio 36 to 34, nearly.”
Reading the table. Columns: locality; number of positive and negative closing errors; sum of positive and sum of negative closing errors (seconds); number of triangles; mean error of an angle; probable error of a resulting direction. Totals: 357 positive, 343 negative, 701 triangles (one closes exactly), mean error of an angle +/- 0.77", probable error of a direction from 1 660 directions +/- 0.44". The intro sentence is on p. 612 (pdf 642).
Worked out here: Mean closing error per triangle from sums: (383.21 + 359.60) / 701 = 1.06" (average size of a closure, sign ignored).

Part II, general remarks. The coefficient of refraction m is the bend of the line of sight expressed as a fraction of the arc between the stations (m = k/2 in the usual notation). Reciprocal zenith distances are vertical angles measured from each end of a line toward the other; from the pair, m is computed for that line, so the refraction is measured on the line itself, not assumed. Special hourly series were run day and night to find the daily cycle.

“For the sake of easy reference, we shall give here in tabular form and also exhibit by diagrams the resulting hourly values of the coefficient of refraction, m, from four experimental series [...] The tabular values were deduced under the supposition of equal refraction angles at lower and upper stations.”
Reading the table. Table 1: local hour (midnight to midnight) against m for Bodega Head-Ross Mountain (22.48 km, 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. only), Martinez East-Mount Diablo (24.26 km), Jackson Butte-Round Top (72.37 km) and the sea horizon from Ragged Mountain. Table 2: hourly departure from the daily mean. Daily means: 0.1000, 0.0646, 0.0849; daily ranges 0.0333, 0.0168, 0.0293. The first sentence of the quote is on p. 254 (pdf 257).
Worked out here: Jackson Butte-Round Top: maximum 0.0711 (2 a.m.), minimum 0.0557 (2 to 3 p.m.).
