The printed type example for the Beaufort theodolite: the angle at Kamies-Sector Berg between the Keibiskow heliostat (about 80 miles away) and Bokkeveld Berg, 1, 3 and 4 December 1846. Each row is one partial result of 10 repetitions with the hour and a remark on the definition of the signals. The remarks record the air: wind direction, 'hot temperature: about 85 deg.', 'therm. 90 deg.', and 'Definition in the morning not good, towards 11h it became much worse'. Half the work was measured forward with the Y bearings right, half backward with Y left. The final angle comes from 260 measures with weight 131.99.

“Angle at Kamies-Sector Berg, West Rock Station; between Keibiskow and Bokkeveld Berg : measured with the Beaufort Theodolite. ... Middling definition. ... Northerly wind, perhaps 1 point E. of N. Hot temperature : about 85°. ... Bad definition and bad signaling at Bokkeveld ... Wind west, next S.W., and lastly south; this afternoon very hot, therm. 90°. ... Excellent do., points. ... Definition in the morning not good, towards 11h it became much worse. ... Resulting angle from 260 meas. = 23°32′1″·98 Weight = 131·99”
Reading the table. Columns: date (1846) and hour (A.M./P.M.); remarks on definition, wind and temperature; No. of repetitions (10 per row); pointer degrees and minutes; seconds on verniers A, D, B, C; mean reading; angle seconds for the row (left) and running mean (right), all after 23 deg 32'. Under each day: sum of squares of errors, probable error of 10 measures, probable error of the day's total, and the weight. 1 Dec: 13 rows (130 repetitions), 3 Dec: 7 rows, 4 Dec: 6 rows (130 repetitions). Row seconds range from 0.65" to 3.35". Look at how the remarks change with the hour and how the weight of each day follows its scatter.
Worked out here: Combination printed at foot: 1.96 x 75.02 = 147.039; 2.00 x 56.97 = 113.940; 75.02 + 56.97 = 131.99; 260.979 / 131.99 = 1.977 -> 1.98". The day weight above it is printed 56.77 (1/0.1327^2 = 56.8), so the 56.97 in the combination differs from it by 0.2.

The last page (shown) gives the total, 54 couplets, and the weather diary: misty horizon, dense fog in the afternoon on the 20th, and a gale with bad images on the 26th.

“54 Couplets = 33°50′58″·524. ☾ 20th February.—In general cloudy, with misty horizon,—none of the heliostats now visible at the same time. Cape Town seen twice, Kapoc Berg once, east end of Base for an hour. N.W. wind and dense fog in the afternoon. ♄ 26th February.—Violent wind from E. by S. came on, on Thursday night and continued until 9 o'clock yesterday morning, then died away; but towards 4 o'clock it returned, last night and this morning it may be called a strong gale. Yesterday and last night the canvas and instrument were removed for security, but time being valuable, an attempt to observe was made at 10h 30m this morning. Bad images, the instrument not free from danger.”

Calculation of the differences of altitude (p. 598). Reciprocal zenith distances are measured from each end of the same line toward the other; their sum exceeds 180 deg by the earth's curvature minus the bending of the ray, so they give the actual refraction on that line. Maclear prints the formula for m (the coefficient of refraction as a fraction of c, the angle at the earth's centre) and the 10 lines with the zenith distance at each end, the number of observations at each end (4 to 86), z + z' - 180 deg, c and m. The values run from .0667 to .0842; the mean .0712 was adopted for the altitudes.

“The following formulæ have been employed in the calculation of the co-efficient of refraction, and the altitudes of the points observed : ... then h′—h = s cot. (z + m c — ½ c) (1 + (h′+h)/2ν). and m = ½ (1 — (z+z′—180°)/c). The calculation of m from 10 sets of reciprocal zenith distances is contained in the following table : ... The mean value of m from the above is ·0712.”
Reading the table. Columns: reference number in the preceding abstract; station (the two ends of each line); true zenith distance at each end; No. of observations at each end; log distance; z + z' - 180 deg (seconds); c (seconds); coefficient of refraction m. Observation counts per end: 68 and 82, 84 and 48, 66 and 44, 44 and 48, 48 and 86, 52 and 20, 38 and 32, 8 and 48, 8 and 12, 21 and 12.
Worked out here: East End of Base - Kapoc Berg: m = 0.5 x (1 - 646.1/746.2) = 0.5 x 0.13415 = 0.0671 (printed .0671). In the usual k = 2m form the mean is 0.1424.

Vertical heights (p. 151). Mutual vertical angles are elevation angles measured from each end of a line toward the other. The formula h' - h = s tan 1/2 (alpha - alpha') uses both, and the refraction drops out when it is the same at both ends. Table M gives the coefficient of refraction found on each line, so the bend was measured line by line. Values in brackets were left out of the chain mean; on this page they are all lines of 4.9 to 12.9 miles. The definition of the coefficient is not printed in the report.

“17. The differences of height were computed by the formula h′ — h = s . tan ½ (α — α′) where s = the length of the line in feet α, α′ = the angles of elevation of each point from the other. ... 1. The coefficients of refraction and the mean coefficient for each chain Quantities in brackets are omitted in the mean (Table M). ... Table M. Coefficients of Refraction determined from Mutual Vertical Angles.”

Chains on this page: Newcastle to Belfast (two columns, mean .065 at 27.5 miles average) and Belfast to Ottoshoop (mean .065, 37.9 miles). About 85 lines on this page. Robinson's report, paragraphs 20-21 (p. 165). Heights carried by vertical angles from Zwartkop, Natal, are compared with heights from spirit levelling from Delagoa Bay at four stations, next to the theoretical probable error (0.35 foot per mile times the square root of the miles). The differences L - V are of the size of the theoretical probable errors. This tests the vertical-angle heights, and so the refraction treatment, against an independent method.

“20. Assuming the average probable error of an adjusted difference of height to be ± 0·35 feet per mile, it is interesting to compare the theoretical probable errors with discordances between results from vertical angles and from actual levelling from Delagoa Bay. Taking Zwartkop, Natal, where the discordance is only 1·6 feet, as a datum, we have the following comparisons at other stations :— ... S. end Belfast base .. 280 6391·4 6399·9 + 8·5 ± 5·8 Muckleneuk .. .. 400 4739·8 4748·6 + 8·8 ± 7·0 Observatory Hill .. 460 5930·0 5936·1 + 6·1 ± 7·5 E. end Kroonstad base 670 4691·7 4684·4 — 7·3 ± 9·1”
Reading the table. Columns: station; distance from Zwartkop through the chains (miles); height from vertical angles (feet); height by levelling (feet); L - V (feet); theoretical probable error of the vertical height (feet). The second table gives the probable errors of the five base heights (5.8 to 10.1 feet).
Worked out here: 0.35 x sqrt(280) = 5.86 (printed 5.8); 0.35 x sqrt(670) = 9.06 (printed 9.1). 8.5 ft in 6399.9 ft of height after 280 miles of chain; 7.3 ft after 670 miles.

Cotton's later addition (p. 88). The Longford base was computed from the Ralph's Bay base through four different series of triangles, and series 1 was also computed by Mr. Sprent. The results differ from the measured length by -2.2 to +0.5 feet; the series of the largest and best-shaped triangles agrees best.

“Measured Length of Longford Base reduced to the Level of the Sea. Feet. 25,745·7 Difference in Feet. Length as computed by 1st series of triangles 25,746·0 + ·3 Do. do. 4th series 25,746·2 + ·5 Do. do. 2nd series 25,744·5 — 1·2 Do. do. 3rd series 25,743·5 — 2·2 1st Series computed by Mr. Sprent 25,746·01 + ·29 1st Series varied in one triangle computed by Mr. Sprent 25,745·35 — ·35 ... The results of the other two series are very satisfactory, and give abundant proof that both the measurements and the observations are good.”
Reading the table. Columns: series of triangles used; computed length of the Longford base (feet); difference from the measured length 25,745.7 feet.
Worked out here: Largest difference 2.2 ft in 25,745.7 ft = 1 part in 11,700; spread of the four series 25,743.5 to 25,746.2 = 2.7 ft.

Extract from the field book of the 12-inch instrument at Dromedary station, 1851 (p. 95). It shows the vernier readings of a horizontal angle measured with 1 and then 7 repetitions, star elongations (a star at its greatest east or west position, used for the meridian), and the vertical angle to Rumney's Hill from six readings. The barometer (27.016 inches) and the attached and detached thermometers (46 deg) were recorded with the vertical angle, which is the information needed for a refraction allowance.

“Extract from Field Book of 12-inch Altitude and Azimuth Instrument, as adopted by Mr. Sprent at the Main Stations. Dromedary Station. ... Horizontal Angles. ... Reading the table. Horizontal angles: names of stations; no. of repetitions; reading in degrees and minutes; seconds of three verniers; mean reading; angle. Elongations: reading, verniers, mean, level readings, date (5 June 1851). Elevations and depressions: barometer; thermometer attached (on the barometer) and detached (air); circle reading; vernier seconds; mean of verniers; angle. Six readings give the vertical angle, three in each face.

Struve Geodetic Arc (Russo-Scandinavian arc of the meridian, Danube to Fuglenaes) · T. II, p. 232 · strength ★★
Raw tables of repeated measures

Tome II, p. 232. Struve prints one complete vertical-angle observation at the north end of the Elimä base, 5 September 1844, true solar time 3h 26m, on three targets. For each target he gives the level readings and two vernier readings with the circle right and with the circle left, the level correction, and the means a and b. Half the difference (a - b)/2 is the zenith distance z; half the sum (a + b)/2 is the zenith place Z, the circle reading of the vertical, which should be the same for all targets of one set.

“J'ai ajouté partout dans le texte le lieu du zénith (a+b)/2 = Z, qu'a donné chaque observation complète d'un objet, en le plaçant en parenthèses, et en types mineurs, à côté de son z.”
In English: “I have added everywhere in the text the zenith place (a+b)/2 = Z given by each complete observation of an object, placing it in parentheses and in small type beside its z.”
Reading the table. Rows: level (two ends of the bubble), first and second vernier, mean, correction for the level, for circle right and circle left. Then the corrected means a and b, (a - b)/2 = zenith distance, (a + b)/2 = zenith place, the reduction to the centre of the station, and the reduced z as entered in the station table.
Worked out here: Zenith places Z for the three targets: 0°53′48.0″, 0°53′52.9″, 0°53′54.4″; spread 6.4″ within one set.
Struve, F. G. W. (1860). Arc du méridien de 25° 20' entre le Danube et la Mer Glaciale mesuré depuis 1816 jusqu'en 1855 (Vol. 2). Imprimerie de l'Académie impériale des sciences., T. II, p. 232

Introduction to Section 9, Observed Zenith Distances of Stations (p. 591). A zenith distance is the angle between the vertical and the line of sight. The tables name the instrument (D = Dollond repeating circle, B = Beaufort theodolite), give the height of the target above the station surface, mark heliostat targets with H, and reduce excentric set-ups to the angle point by a printed formula.

“The letters D and B in the third column distinguish the instruments employed in the measurement of the zenith distances,—viz., the Dollond repeating circle and the Beaufort theodolite. In the eighth column is given the height of the object observed above the surface of the station ; and when the object was a heliostat, the letter H is annexed to the name of the station in column five. The observations with the Dollond circle were for the most part made at excentric stations, and require on this account special reductions to the trigonometric or angle point.”

Rule for refraction on computed zenith distances, founded on observations with an instrument checked by reversal
Cassini de Thury and Lacaille, verification of the Paris meridian and the arc of the parallel near 43.5 N · x (Troisième partie), with footnote; sentence ends on p. xj · strength ★★★
Vertical refraction coefficients

Same page. Where a zenith distance could not be observed at the far station, it was computed from the one observed at the near station and the itinerary arc (the arc between the two places, 1 minute for 951 toises). The authors state that refraction makes this computation inexact and give a rule: take 2 or 3 minutes off the arc when it exceeds 20 minutes. The footnote says the rule rests on observations made with a quadrant checked by reversal (turning the instrument over to remove its index error), made on purpose to measure terrestrial refraction.

“Il eft vrai que la réfraction empêche que ce calcul ne foit exact ; mais on peut y avoir égard , en quelque façon (*), en ôtant deux ou trois minutes de l'arc de la [diftance itinéraire , s'il excéde 20'] ... (*) Pour faire voir fur quoi eft fondée la correction que nous difons ici qu'on peut faire , nous allons rapporter quelques obfervations qui ont été faites avec un Inftrument vérifié exprès par le renverfement, pour connoitre la quantité de la réfraction horifontale, qui rend incertains les grands nivellemens.”
In English: “It is true that refraction prevents this calculation from being exact; but one can allow for it in some fashion (*) by taking two or three minutes off the arc of the [itinerary distance, if it exceeds 20']. (*) To show what the correction we say can be made here is founded on, we shall report some observations made with an instrument checked expressly by reversal, to learn the amount of horizontal refraction, which makes long levellings uncertain.”
Cassini de Thury, C.-F. (1744). La méridienne de l'Observatoire Royal de Paris vérifiée dans toute l'étendue du Royaume par de nouvelles observations. Paris: H.-L. Guérin & J. Guérin., x (Troisième partie), with footnote; sentence ends on p. xj

Tome II, chapter on inclined distances and terrestrial refraction. Reciprocal zenith distances are taken from each end of a line toward the other; their sum exceeds 180 degrees by the arc between the two verticals, less the bend of the ray at both ends, so the pair measures the refraction on that line itself. Delambre writes the observed zenith distances as δ and δ'' and the angle between the two verticals as C, and derives r, the refraction at each end. The ratio r/C is the coefficient n used in the table of 189 pairs. The only assumption is that the bend is the same at both ends.

“Ces dernières sont diminuées de la réfraction terrestre, qui est supposée proportionnelle à l'angle des deux normales ou à l'angle M, et qui par conséquent est égale pour les deux observations. Soit r cette réfraction”
In English: “These are diminished by terrestrial refraction, which is supposed proportional to the angle between the two normals or to the angle M, and which is therefore equal for the two observations. Let r be this refraction”
Worked out here: From the printed equations: 2r = 180° + C - δ - δ''; r/C = 1/2 - (δ + δ'' - 180°)/(2C) (eq. 64).

Tome II, remarks on the n table. A hygrometer measures air humidity. Delambre repeated the reciprocal observations at Boiscommun many times to see whether changes of the barometer and hygrometer affected refraction, and left the instrument pointed at Châteauneuf for several hours. He found fog to be the main factor (n of 0.14 to 0.17) and set the fog observations aside.

“A Boiscommun j'ai répété les observations un grand nombre de fois, pour voir si les changemens du baromètre et de l'hygromètre influoient sur la réfraction : je n'ai rien pu remarquer. J'ai laissé pendant plusieurs heures l'instrument bien callé et la lunette dirigée sur Châteauneuf, dans l'intervalle des observations de distances au zénith, et je n'ai pas vu de variations sensibles dans la hauteur ... Il paroît que c'est le brouillard qui influe surtout sur les réfractions, et qui donne pour n des valeurs de 0.14 à 0.17. Je laisse donc à part les observations non numérotées de Boiscommun.”
In English: “At Boiscommun I repeated the observations a great many times to see whether changes of the barometer and the hygrometer affected refraction: I could notice nothing. I left the instrument firmly set for several hours with the telescope pointed at Châteauneuf, between the zenith-distance observations, and I saw no noticeable variation in the height ... It appears that it is fog above all that affects refraction, and gives for n values of 0.14 to 0.17. I therefore set aside the unnumbered observations of Boiscommun.”
Méchain, P., & Delambre, J.-B. J. (1807). Base du système métrique décimal, ou mesure de l'arc du méridien compris entre les parallèles de Dunkerque et Barcelone (Vol. 2). Paris: Baudouin., T2 p. 775

Puissant, Discours préliminaire, formulas of trigonometric levelling. Reciprocal zenith distances are taken from each end of a line toward the other; their sum exceeds 180 degrees by the arc between the two verticals, less the bend of the ray at both ends, so the pair measures the refraction on that line itself. The formula at the top of the page gives n from the two apparent zenith distances δ, δ' and the angle C between the verticals. Puissant states its condition: both distances must see the same atmosphere, so they should be simultaneous; he also names the constant error of the instrument as a second effect to separate.

“Il est à remarquer que les deux distances zénithales apparentes δ, δ' sont supposées répondre au même état de l'atmosphère ; circonstance qui n'a lieu en général que quand ces distances sont observées à la même époque. Il y a plus, ces mêmes distances ne sont pas seulement influencées par la réfraction, elles peuvent être affectées de l'erreur constante de l'instrument qui a servi à leur mesure”
In English: “Note that the two apparent zenith distances δ, δ' are supposed to correspond to the same state of the atmosphere; a circumstance which in general holds only when these distances are observed at the same time. Moreover, these distances are not only influenced by refraction; they may be affected by the constant error of the instrument used to measure them”
Worked out here: Printed formula: n = (½C - ½(δ + δ' - 200g))/C.
Puissant, L. (1832). Nouvelle description géométrique de la France (Première partie). Paris: Ch. Picquet., 55

Brousseaud, p. 160. The absolute heights of the chain come from a succession of reciprocal zenith distances starting at the Cordouan lighthouse (68.445 m above mean sea, mean of four measures). Reciprocal zenith distances are taken from each end of a line toward the other; their sum exceeds 180 degrees by the arc between the two verticals, less the bend of the ray at both ends, so the pair measures the refraction on that line itself. Each height is the mean of two results that rarely differ by more than a metre. A discordance of about 9 m at the east end was traced to long sights from Bossivre and to signal caps too small to see at noon, and Puissant removed it by using heights from other stations. The coefficient of refraction found along the whole levelling lies between 0.0563 and 0.097.

“Partant de ce point, chacune des hauteurs absolues rapportées dans le deuxième tableau est la moyenne entre deux résultats, dont la différence dépasse rarement un mètre (1). ... a cependant présenté une discordance qui s'est accrue de 9m environ à l'extrémité orientale de la chaîne ... 2° que, sur toute son étendue, la valeur du coefficient de la réfraction est renfermée entre 0,0563 et 0,097, et se trouve généralement de 0,08, ainsi que Delambre l'avait déduit de ses observations.”
In English: “Starting from this point, each of the absolute heights given in the second table is the mean of two results whose difference rarely exceeds one metre (1). ... nevertheless showed a discordance that grew to about 9 m at the eastern end of the chain ... 2nd that, over its whole extent, the value of the coefficient of refraction lies between 0.0563 and 0.097, and is generally 0.08, as Delambre had deduced from his observations.”

Same section. The 'comprehended arc' (or contained arc) is the angle at the centre of the earth between the two stations. Earlier authors gave one fixed fraction of this arc for refraction. Roy's reciprocal observations showed a wide range, so a single adopted value was not reliable.

“for from these observations it will appear, that terrestrial refraction, instead of being 1/9th of the comprehended arc, according to M. Bouguer, 1/10th according to Dr. Maskelyne, 1/14th according to M. Lambert, varies from 1/3 to 1/24th part of that arc; and perhaps, if it had been possible for us to have tried it on heights considerably more elevated, we should have found it almost wholly to vanish.”

“The heights of the barometer and thermometer are inserted on the days on which the observations were made, merely to shew what was nearly the state of the atmosphere at the respective times. But we have not attempted to apply any correction on that account, because it could not be done in a satisfactory manner, and consequently could not be useful, unless the circumstances had permitted reciprocal observations to have been made at corresponding times with double sets of instruments, which in our situation was impossible. Ordnance Trigonometrical Survey of Great Britain and Ireland, Principal Triangulation · p. 509 · strength ★★★
Vertical refraction coefficients

Opening of Section IX on zenith distances and heights. A zenith distance is the angle of a line of sight from the vertical (90° minus the elevation). The coefficient of refraction k is the refraction at one station divided by the angle at the earth's centre between the stations. Clarke shows that an error of .02 in k gives 5.1 feet in height at 14 miles but 127.4 feet at 70 miles, because the height error grows with the square of the distance.

“The co-efficient of refraction is a quantity so variable, that at great distances the average of any number of observations, however large, cannot be entirely relied upon. When the determination of altitudes becomes a matter of primary importance, the stations must be within a short distance of each other, or no very consistent or accurate results can be obtained; for the uncertainty of refraction being as the distance, the uncertainty of difference of height is as the square of the distance. ... The precision of the results is very much increased by simultaneous and reciprocal zenith distances. This case, however, does not exist in the Ordnance Survey, for the observations, though generally reciprocal, are not simultaneous.”
Clarke, A. R. (1858). Ordnance trigonometrical survey of Great Britain and Ireland: Account of the observations and calculations of the principal triangulation. London: Eyre and Spottiswoode., p. 509

Section IX, 'Coefficient of Refraction'. Where both heights are known by levelling, the true zenith distance Z can be computed. The observed z differs from Z only by refraction, so k = (Z - z)/v is measured directly on that line. The weight w grows with the square root of the distance and with the number of observations.

“In the former case, the coefficient required is simply the ratio of the excess of the observed above the true zenith distance to the angle subtended by the two stations at the centre of the earth.”
Reading the table. Columns: number of the line; stations; levelled height (ft); observed zenith distance z; number of observations (4 to 29, e.g. Ben Nevis 19, Merrick 29, Pertinny 20); logarithmic distance; v (angle at the earth's centre, seconds); true zenith distance Z; Z - z (seconds); k; weight w; k times w. Values from 0.0649 (High Willhays) to 0.1058 (Swyre Barrow). Printed mean k = 0.0792.

Next table. For two stations that observed each other, the sum of the two zenith distances exceeds 180° by the arc v when there is no refraction; refraction makes the sum smaller. So 1 - 2k = (z + z' - 180°)/v gives the bend on that line from the two angles alone, without knowing the heights. The weights follow the distance and the number of observations at each end.

“The weights assumed for the separate determinations are directly as the square root of the distance and inversely as the sum of the reciprocals of the numbers of observations at the two observing stations. The following table contains the calculation of 112 values of k:”
Reading the table. Conclusion of the refraction section. The levelled-height table and the reciprocal table are combined. Clarke separates rays over the sea from rays over land, and treats short lines near the ground separately because their refraction is larger and irregular.

“With one or two exceptions, all the coefficients in the preceding tables are derived from observed zenith distances of very distant objects; and the results are, upon the whole, tolerably consistent. The same consistency, however, is not found to exist among coefficients of refraction deduced from the observations of objects at short distances: the values are very irregular, and, indeed, cannot be represented with precision by any mean quantity. A great deal depends upon the nature of the ground over which the ray passes: as a general rule, when the distances are small the ray passes near the ground, which would tend to increase the coefficient of refraction, as is evident from Struve's formula (page 512); and this agrees with observation, for the mean value at short distances is certainly not under 0.1000, one-tenth of the arc-distance, with an uncertainty of at least half that quantity.”

Struve Geodetic Arc (Russo-Scandinavian arc of the meridian, Danube to Fuglenaes) · T. II, p. 480 · strength ★★★
Vertical refraction coefficients

Tome II, Lindhagen's memoir on the Finmarken heights. Reciprocal zenith distances measured at the same time cancel the refraction if it is equal both ways; Lindhagen says that, when they cannot be simultaneous, they are still the best method if both are measured at the same, most favourable time of day. The great heights of the stations made the refraction very constant. Many surplus zenith distances gave a refraction constant, which was solved together with the heights. Barometer and thermometer readings were recorded at every vertical-angle measurement and were used in computing the refraction for the main net.

“In den Tagebüchern sind die Barometer- und Thermometerstände, welche zu den Zeiten der Vertikalwinkelmessungen stattfanden, regelmässig annotirt. Bei der Berechnung des Einflusses der Refraction auf die Zenithdistanzen im Hauptdreiecksnetze sind dieselben, so wie auch die Abhängigkeit der Refraction von den höheren Potenzen des Winkels, welchen die beiden Lothlinien, durch den Beobachtungsort und das Beobachtungsobject, mit einander machen, auf eine Weise berücksichtigt worden, zu deren Auseinandersetzung hier nicht der geeignete Ort ist.”
In English: “In the journals the barometer and thermometer readings that held at the times of the vertical angle measurements are regularly noted. In computing the influence of refraction on the zenith distances in the main triangle net these were taken into account, as was the dependence of the refraction on the higher powers of the angle that the two plumb lines, through the place of observation and the object observed, make with each other, in a way that this is not the proper place to set out.”
Struve, F. G. W. (1860). Arc du méridien de 25° 20' entre le Danube et la Mer Glaciale mesuré depuis 1816 jusqu'en 1855 (Vol. 2). Imprimerie de l'Académie impériale des sciences., T. II, p. 480

Great Arc of India, Lambton's meridional arc (Coromandel coast to Punnae and north to about 18 N) · p. 148 · strength ★★★
Vertical refraction coefficients

Section on the reduction of the Madras base (1802) to sea level. Lambton measured the depression of a flag on the beach from the race-stand and the elevation of the race-stand from the beach. A reciprocal pair is two vertical angles taken from each end of the same line toward the other end. The contained arc is the angle at the centre of the earth between the two stations. Half the excess of the contained arc over the sum of the two vertical angles gives the bend of the ray on that line, here 5.5 seconds.

“And the difference between the depression and elevation being 2' 58", we have (3' 9" - 2' 58")/2 = 5",5 for the terrestrial refraction.”
Worked out here: Contained arc 3' 9" = 189". Depression minus elevation as used here 2' 58" = 178". (189 - 178)/2 = 5.5". 5.5/189 = 0.029 of the contained arc.

Appendix to GTS Vol. XII, Account of Colonel Lambton's operations, quoting a letter of 1814. Lambton reports the range of the refraction he measured on reciprocal lines over ten years, names moisture as the cause, explains why barometer readings do not help in India (pressure hardly changes), and calls for hygrometer readings and a table of low-altitude refractions from observation.

“In the course of my observations during the last ten years, I have at times found the terrestrial refraction to be as much as 1/4 of the contained arc, and occasionally as low as 1/20. This great irregularity I attribute to the different degrees of moisture in the atmosphere at different times. A knowledge of the laws of refraction is yet a desideratum in physical science. In climates remote from the equator, where the weight of the atmosphere is constantly changing, the barometer has been called in to indicate the pressure of a column of air, and rules investigated whereby to correct the mean celestial refraction according to the different heights of the mercury in the barometer. But in tropical climates this method can never apply owing to a well-known fact, that the weight of the atmosphere suffers very little variation, and while a barometer remains at the same station, it will not alter the 1/10 of an inch for several months together, excepting in the case of some great convulsion in the atmosphere. Other principles must therefore be adverted to. The hygrometer will be a necessary instrument to indicate the degree of moisture.”
Great Trigonometrical Survey of India. (1890). Account of the operations of the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India, Vol. XII: The Southern Trigon. Dehra Dun: Trigonometrical Branch, Survey of India., Appendix p. 37

A comparison between the new values and the old exhibited discrepancies with a range of 43 feet. The reciprocal angles are also employed to determine the co-efficient of refraction, to be used in reducing unreciprocated vertical angles ; [...] and φ/C gives the terrestrial refraction in decimals of contained arc—or in other words the co-efficient of refraction—for each pair of reciprocated observations.”
Worked out here: Formula as printed: φ = 1/2 {C - (Da + Db) + β}; coefficient = φ/C.

Part II, general remarks. The coefficient of refraction m is the bend of the line of sight expressed as a fraction of the arc between the stations (m = k/2 in the usual notation). Reciprocal zenith distances are vertical angles measured from each end of a line toward the other; from the pair, m is computed for that line, so the refraction is measured on the line itself, not assumed. Special hourly series were run day and night to find the daily cycle.

“For the sake of easy reference, we shall give here in tabular form and also exhibit by diagrams the resulting hourly values of the coefficient of refraction, m, from four experimental series [...] The tabular values were deduced under the supposition of equal refraction angles at lower and upper stations.”
Reading the table. Table 1: local hour (midnight to midnight) against m for Bodega Head-Ross Mountain (22.48 km, 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. only), Martinez East-Mount Diablo (24.26 km), Jackson Butte-Round Top (72.37 km) and the sea horizon from Ragged Mountain. Table 2: hourly departure from the daily mean. Daily means: 0.1000, 0.0646, 0.0849; daily ranges 0.0333, 0.0168, 0.0293. The first sentence of the quote is on p. 254 (pdf 257).
Worked out here: Jackson Butte-Round Top: maximum 0.0711 (2 a.m.), minimum 0.0557 (2 to 3 p.m.).

US Transcontinental Triangulation, 39th parallel · p. 256 · strength ★★★
Steady-air hours Vertical refraction coefficients

Part II, directly after the hourly table. Schott draws the observing rule from the measured cycle: refraction is largest and most irregular at night and changes little through the middle of the day.

“It shows that the refraction is greater and more irregular during the night hours than during the day; the maximum value is reached within two or three hours from midnight and the minimum value at sometime within 2 hours from noon-before noon at the coast stations after noon at the interior stations. The average amount (mean of 24 hours) is greater the nearer the line of sight is to the sea level, being some function of the altitude. The refraction changes but little, comparatively, between the hours of 10 a. m. and 5 1/2 p. m. and the intervening time is best suited for observing zenith distances for altitudes, so far as refraction is concerned; but in other respects, as for telescopic visions, the hours about noon are unfavorable on account of faint, unsteady, and distorted images being then more prevalent.”
Schott, C. A. (1900). The transcontinental triangulation and the American arc of the parallel (Special Publication No. 4). U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey; Government Printing Office., p. 256

“The tabular values of m show an apparent dependence upon the length of lines s, viz: the shorter s, the smaller m. [...] The ground is barren and treeless over the entire region and the climate is very dry, especially during the summer. The instrument was only elevated sufficiently to overcome the earth's curvature and permit the visibility of the distant object. Steady-air hours Night lamps and heliotropes Vertical refraction coefficients

End of the quoted manual. The heliotrope limits daytime work to about 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. Vertical angles (the up-down angles used for heights) are to be taken between 2½ and 3½ p.m., the time of least refraction. The manual says vertical angles taken at other hours are so irregular that heights from them are nearly worthless. It also says luminous targets are observed more correctly than opaque ones.

“the only limit to the times at which observations can be made will be from 9 o'clock A.M. to 2½ or 3 o'clock P.M. But the heliotrope is more particularly recommended for the purpose of taking vertical angles with certainty between the hours of 2½ and 3½ afternoon, which is the time of minimum refraction, because verticals taken at any other time are subject to great irregularities, whereby heights deduced from them are nearly worthless. Luminous objects are much more correctly, rapidly, and comfortably observed than opaque ones, which, if distant, are always faint, and disappear when brought near the wire of the telescope.”
Middleton, R. E., Chadwick, O., & Bogle, J. du T. (1904). A treatise on surveying: Part I (2nd ed.). E. & F. N. Spon., pp. 190-191
Why a sight line bends: pressure and irregular heating
Middleton, Chadwick and Bogle, A Treatise on Surveying (textbook) · p. 224 · strength ★★★
Vertical refraction coefficients

Start of the section "Effect of Refraction on Vertical Angles". Air density changes with pressure and heating, so a nearly horizontal ray curves, usually concave to the ground. A target then appears higher than it is. Fig. 129 shows the true line O A, the curved path O C A, and the apparent direction A O₁. The angle O₁ A O is the refraction error.

“The effect of refraction has now to be considered. Rays of light passing through the atmosphere, nearly parallel to the earth's surface, do not travel in a straight line as they do in space (fig. 128). Owing to the varying density of the air, due to differences of pressure, and to irregular heating, they travel in a curved line. Usually, almost invariably, the path of the ray is concave towards the earth's surface, the effect of this being to make an object appear higher than it really is.”
Middleton, R. E., Chadwick, O., & Bogle, J. du T. (1904). A treatise on surveying: Part I (2nd ed.). E. & F. N. Spon., p. 224
Reciprocal angles measure the bend on each line
Middleton, Chadwick and Bogle, A Treatise on Surveying (textbook) · p. 225 · strength ★★★
Vertical refraction coefficients

The method used to find refraction on a line. The vertical angle is observed from each end toward the other (reciprocal angles). On a curved earth, the two angles and the angle θ at the earth's centre are related, so the refraction error ρ comes out of the observed angles: ρ = (θ − (D − A)) ÷ 2, where D is the depression and A the elevation. The bend is measured on that line, in that air, not taken from a model. The book adds that observing both ends at the same time, or in similar conditions on different days, determines it well enough for practical purposes.

“By taking reciprocal angles, 'refraction errors' may be eliminated, by thus ascertaining their values, and applying the same as corrections. [...] If the refraction be fairly regular, and if the reciprocal angles be observed simultaneously, or under similar conditions of the atmosphere on different days, the refraction will be determined with sufficient accuracy for all practical purposes, for the correction for refraction is usually but small. It is generally expressed as a fraction of the subtended arc, and amounts to about one-fifteenth part thereof (vide infra).”
Middleton, R. E., Chadwick, O., & Bogle, J. du T. (1904). A treatise on surveying: Part I (2nd ed.). E. & F. N. Spon., p. 225

Delambre and Méchain, vol. 3, review of the 1739 meridian. Delambre takes five 1739 observations of the sea horizon from the terrace of the Sainte-Victoire hermitage and computes the terrace height with mean refraction. The five results agree within about 7 toises, and their mean is 42 toises below the height printed in 1744. He states that the 1744 calculation neglected terrestrial refraction, and that with the mean coefficient 0.08 the heights come much closer.

“Mais, dans le calcul, on négligeoit la réfraction terrestre : ainsi l'on trouvoit toutes les hauteurs trop grandes. C'est ce qu'on peut aussi remarquer dans la méridienne de 1718. En refaisant tous les calculs avec la réfraction moyenne 0.08, j'ai trouvé des nombres beaucoup plus rapprochés de ceux qu'on a vus”
In English: “But in the calculation terrestrial refraction was neglected: so all the heights were found too large. This can also be seen in the meridian of 1718. Redoing all the calculations with the mean refraction 0.08, I found numbers much closer to those we have seen”
Worked out here: Five heights 444.3, 447.4, 440.0, 446.3, 440.9 toises; range 7.4 toises; mean 443.8 against 486.0 printed, difference 42.2 toises (printed).

Delambre and Méchain, vol. 3, p. 534, quoting a note by Lacaille found in the 1740 registers. Lacaille states that terrestrial refraction is regular enough to be allowed for and too large to neglect in heights, and proposes finding it by observation and building a table. He names humidity over the sea as one cause of the irregular dip of the sea horizon. The dip is the angle by which the visible sea horizon lies below the horizontal.

“1° que cette réfraction n'est pas si irrégulière qu'on ne puisse trouver le moyen d'y avoir égard d'une manière satisfaisante ; 2° que la réfraction terrestre est trop grande pour être négligée dans le calcul des hauteurs des objets au-dessus de l'horizon ... Quand je dis que la réfraction horizontale des objets terrestres n'est pas si irrégulière qu'on pense, j'en excepte celle de l'abaissement de l'horizon de la mer. ... 2°. que l'air qui est au-dessus de la mer, est beaucoup plus humide que sur la terre.”
In English: “1st that this refraction is not so irregular that one cannot find a way to allow for it satisfactorily; 2nd that terrestrial refraction is too large to be neglected in computing the heights of objects above the horizon ... When I say that the horizontal refraction of terrestrial objects is not as irregular as people think, I except that of the dip of the sea horizon. ... 2nd that the air above the sea is much more humid than over the land.”

Tome II, table of heights. Delambre states the range of the coefficient n over the arc and the size of the error it can cause (one or two toises at 18 000 toises). He separates heights found from two different points, which check each other, from heights found from a single point.

“Le coefficient n, que nous avons supposé 0.08, pouvant varier de 0.07 à 0.09, et même quelquefois à 0.10 ... ce qui peut produire une ou deux toises d'erreur quand la distance est de 18000 toises. ... Presque toutes les hauteurs de la table précédente ont été déterminées de deux points différens. Middleton, Chadwick and Bogle, A Treatise on Surveying (textbook) · p. 227 · strength ★★
Vertical refraction coefficients

The convention used across the surveys: refraction is expressed as a fraction of the arc between the two stations at the earth's centre (θ). The book gives about 1/15 as usual. Where reciprocal angles cannot be had (for example an inaccessible peak), an assumed value must be used.

“It may, however, happen that it is impossible to obtain reciprocal observations. For example, it may be required to determine the height of an inaccessible peak, the distance of which has been determined by intersection. In this case the only plan is to assume a value for the correction for refraction. It is the general practice of geodetic writers to express this value as a fraction of the 'subtended arc,' that is, the angle subtended at the centre of the earth between the two stations, or the angle θ in fig. 130. Usually, this fraction is found to be about 1/15.”
Worked out here: 1/15 = 0.067 per arc; the surveys' printed values have median 0.078.
Middleton, R. E., Chadwick, O., & Bogle, J. du T. (1904). A treatise on surveying: Part I (2nd ed.). E. & F. N. Spon., p. 227

What the numbers stand for

Diagrams: horizontal and vertical angles, reciprocal zenith distances, lateral refraction, closures, observing hours
Without refraction: zA + zB = 180° + C
With refraction, each target looks higher by r: zA + zB = 180° + C − 2r
So the refraction on that line: r = (180° + C − zA − zB) ÷ 2, and per arc = r ÷ C

Worked out here from the figure. Example: Maclear's mean per arc, 0.0712, on a line with C = 10′ (600″) gives r = 0.0712 × 600″ ≈ 42.7″ at each end. The two zenith distances need not be read at the same moment; Clarke (1858) and Schott (1900) note that theirs were not.

Survey overviews

Cassini de Thury and Lacaille, verification of the Paris meridian and the arc of the parallel near 43.5 N 1739-1744

Horizontal angles were taken with a quadrant and reduced to the horizon with zenith distances known to 3 or 4 minutes, which is enough for that reduction; no lateral refraction correction is stated. The chains were checked by a second chain (5 toises over Dunkirk to Amiens) and by bases computed through the triangles (about one foot at Paris). For vertical angles, the authors measured refraction directly on four lines with reciprocal zenith distances from a quadrant checked by reversal, and from these set a rule of 2 to 3 minutes for computed zenith distances. They warn that the printed zenith distances are not precise enough for heights, and Delambre (1810) showed that the 1744 heights had neglected refraction.

Cassini de Thury, C.-F. (1744). La méridienne de l'Observatoire Royal de Paris vérifiée dans toute l'étendue du Royaume par de nouvelles observations. Paris: H.-L. Guérin & J. Guérin. Méchain, P., & Delambre, J.-B. J. (1810). Base du système métrique décimal (Vol. 3). Paris: Baudouin.
Delambre and Méchain, meridian arc Dunkirk to Barcelona (Base du système métrique) 1792-1798

Every horizontal angle was measured in several series of 10 to 30 repetitions on the repeating circle, at different hours and days; each series is printed with observer, circle, date, hours and remarks on wind, sun and undulations, and bad series are marked for rejection. Lateral refraction was met by waiting for steady air and repeating at other hours; vertical refraction enters horizontal angles only through the reduction to the horizon. Refraction on each line was measured by reciprocal zenith distances: the table of 189 lines gives n from about 0 to 0.17, with barometer, thermometer and fog recorded at the stations, and the fog and rainy lines rejected (mean 0.07876). Checks include triangle closures of about 1 second, the Perpignan base computed from Melun through 53 triangles within 0.160 toise, and sea-horizon heights compared with a direct levelling.

Méchain, P., & Delambre, J.-B. J. (1806). Base du système métrique décimal, ou mesure de l'arc du méridien compris entre les parallèles de Dunkerque et Barcelone (Vol. 1). Paris: Baudouin. Méchain, P., & Delambre, J.-B. J. (1807). Base du système métrique décimal, ou mesure de l'arc du méridien compris entre les parallèles de Dunkerque et Barcelone (Vol. 2). Paris: Baudouin. Méchain, P., & Delambre, J.-B. J. (1810). Base du système métrique décimal, ou mesure de l'arc du méridien compris entre les parallèles de Dunkerque et Barcelone (Vol. 3). Paris: Baudouin.
Parallel of Paris, Brest to Strasbourg (Henry east part, Bonne west part), Nouvelle carte de France 1818-1823

The Instruction set first-order series of 20 repetitions, avoidance of vapours and undulations, and zenith distances from at least three series at different hours near midday, simultaneous where possible, with barometer readings. Night angles on lamps, tried at Laplace's wish, gave larger discordances and triangle errors no smaller than by day, so Puissant judges them as much affected by refraction; the night zenith distances of the eastern part were rejected and heights taken by day. Each angle has 100 to about 300 observations, every triangle prints its closure error, and the Plouescat base computed from Melun through 33 triangles agrees with its measurement to 0.00 m. Heights of the western part come from reciprocal simultaneous zenith distances, printed series by series with date, hour and the coefficient n (0.061 to 0.090).

Puissant, L. (1832). Nouvelle description géométrique de la France (Première partie). Paris: Ch. Picquet.
Brousseaud, arc of the mean parallel (45 N) across France, with link to the Austro-Sardinian chain 1811-1827

Horizontal angles were not corrected for refraction; instead each angle was measured in six to fourteen series of thirty to forty repetitions at different hours and days, with more series when the first six disagreed, and all series were kept in the mean. The largest triangle closure in the French part is 4 seconds, and three measured bases agree through the chains within 0.03 to 0.35 m. Zenith distances were always taken between eleven and one o'clock in six to eight series of ten, with a barometer and thermometers. Heights from the Cordouan tower to the Alps come from reciprocal zenith distances; the coefficient of refraction found on these lines lies between 0.0563 and 0.097, generally 0.08.

Brousseaud (Colonel). (1839). Mesure d'un arc du parallèle moyen entre le pôle et l'équateur. Limoges: F. Chapoulaud.
Anglo-French triangulation of 1787 (Greenwich to Paris junction), English side by Roy 1784-1788

Roy measured horizontal angles with Ramsden's great theodolite and did not correct them for refraction. He controlled the effect of unsteady air by observing only when the objects were distinct, chiefly in the mornings and evenings, and by night observations of white lights for the long lines. He checked the angles by the error of each triangle against the spherical excess and by the agreement of the Hounslow Heath and Romney Marsh bases, which differ by about 4 1/2 inches. For vertical angles he observed elevations and depressions at both ends of each line, at different times, and found the refraction on each line from these reciprocal angles and from heights fixed by levelling. He printed the barometer and thermometer for each day but applied no correction from them, because simultaneous observations with two instruments were not possible. Legendre's French memoir (1789) is not used here because no page image of its refraction pages (pp. 355-357) is available locally.

Roy, W. (1790). An account of the trigonometrical operation, whereby the distance between the meridians of the Royal Observatories of Greenwich and Paris has been determined. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, 80, 111-270 (with Dalby, I., Remarks, pp. 593-614).
Trigonometrical Survey of England and Wales (Ordnance), Williams, Mudge and Dalby 1791-1799 1791-1799

The horizontal angles were measured on different parts of the circle and repeated until their truth became certain, by day on staffs and by night on lamps and white lights. Bearings of minor objects were taken in the morning or evening, when the air was free from vapour and from the midday quivering. The angles were checked by triangle errors and by the base of verification on Salisbury Plain, whose length computed from Hounslow Heath came within about an inch of the measurement. For vertical angles the survey used reciprocal elevations and depressions, reduced to the telescope axis, and printed the mean refraction of each line as a fraction of the contained arc. In 1799 Mudge made hourly simultaneous reciprocal observations, regulated by signals and watches, with barometer, thermometer and weather remarks for each hour. The authors state that moist vapours near the ground were the principal cause of irregular refraction and that no dependence can be placed on single vertical observations. Roy's work of 1784-1788 is under anglo_french_1787.

Williams, E., Mudge, W., & Dalby, I. (1795). An account of the trigonometrical survey carried on in the years 1791, 1792, 1793, and 1794. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, 85, 414-591. Williams, E., Mudge, W., & Dalby, I. (1797). An account of the trigonometrical survey carried on in the years 1795 and 1796. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, 87, 432-541. Mudge, W. (1801). An account of the operations carried on for accomplishing a trigonometrical survey of England and Wales, continued from the year 1797, to the end of the year 1799 (Vol. 2, from the Philosophical Transactions). London: W. Faden.
Ordnance Trigonometrical Survey of Great Britain and Ireland, Principal Triangulation 1783-1853 (published 1858)

Each horizontal direction was observed in many 'arcs' (full rounds of all objects, with the telescope reversed and the circle shifted between rounds), never as single angles. The observer wrote the atmospheric state against each observation; an observation was rejected only when the observer's own remark condemned it. The angles were checked by the triangle errors (rarely over 3.4 seconds), by six bases measured against their computed lengths (within 5 inches for the two main bases), and by a Salisbury Plain base computed from Lough Foyle in Ireland. Vertical angles were reciprocal but not simultaneous; Clarke found the refraction coefficient from levelled heights (31 values) and from 112 reciprocal pairs, and adopted 0.0809 over sea and 0.0750 over land. He gives the daily variation of refraction, attributes the morning and evening excess to aqueous vapour near the ground, and states that no vertical observations should be taken early in the morning.

Clarke, A. R. (1858). Ordnance trigonometrical survey of Great Britain and Ireland: Account of the observations and calculations of the principal triangulation. London: Eyre and Spottiswoode.
Textbook guidance of the period on terrestrial refraction 1848-1880

Clarke (1880) states that refraction acts almost wholly in the vertical plane and that lateral refraction affects horizontal angles only to a very small extent, although it can be persistent from local ground shape. For that reason he takes the probable error of an angle from triangle closures, not from the scatter at one station. For heights he defines the coefficient k, prints Ordnance Survey values with the number of observations, gives the mean of 144 values with its probable error, separates rays over sea and over land, and recommends simultaneous reciprocal zenith distances, which remove k. Airy (1848) rejects a refraction correction to geodetic lines as a needless refinement and records Everest's preference for night signals in India.

Clarke, A. R. (1880). Geodesy. Oxford: Clarendon Press. Airy, G. B. (1848). Figure of the Earth. In Encyclopaedia of astronomy (Encyclopaedia Metropolitana, vol. 5). London: J. J. Griffin.
Russian arc of the parallel of 47.5 N, Privolzhsk triangulation (Kishinev to Astrakhan arc, eastern part) 1855-1858 (field), published 1861

Horizontal angles were measured by W. Struve's method in at least 12 sets per angle in the main row (6 in the Kizlyar row), with every reading entered in field journals that record the hour, the sky, the wind and the visibility of the targets. Angles observed in fog were remeasured, the closure of each triangle was divided in proportion to the scatter of its sets, and the net was checked against the measured Astrakhan base (difference 0.541 sazhen) before that difference was spread over the angles. Zenith distances were measured at all first-class points with double pointing in both circle positions, mostly reciprocally, with barometer, thermometer and the steadiness of the object noted. Table B prints both reciprocal zenith distances for every line, and the resulting heights over about 950 versts agree with the 1836-37 Caspian levelling to 0.643 sazhen.

Voenno-topograficheskoe depo. (1861). Zapiski Voenno-topograficheskago depo, Chast' XXII, Otd. II: Privolzhskoe trigonometricheskoe izmerenie. Voenno-topograficheskoe depo.
Struve Geodetic Arc (Russo-Scandinavian arc of the meridian, Danube to Fuglenaes) 1816-1855

For horizontal angles Struve controlled the air by time of day and by rejection: in Livonia angles were measured almost only in the 2-hour afternoon period of calm images, and in Finland any observation with indistinct or too undulating images was inadmissible. Each Finnish angle was observed in 5 sets of two halves (20 pointings per object), and the station table prints all 10 half-set values with the dates and observers. Lateral refraction was tested against the triangle closures; Struve finds no sign of it in the Baltic arc, and the computed and measured bases agree as closely as the stated errors predict. For vertical angles, zenith distances were taken at every station with true solar time and checked by the scatter of the zenith place within each set; the Swedish and Norwegian parts recorded 40 to over 100 zenith distances per station with barometer and thermometer, and Lindhagen solved a refraction constant from surplus zenith distances.

Struve, F. G. W. (1857). Arc du méridien de 25° 20' entre le Danube et la Mer Glaciale mesuré depuis 1816 jusqu'en 1855 (Vol. 1). Imprimerie de l'Académie impériale des sciences. Struve, F. G. W. (1860). Arc du méridien de 25° 20' entre le Danube et la Mer Glaciale mesuré depuis 1816 jusqu'en 1855 (Vol. 2). Imprimerie de l'Académie impériale des sciences.
European arc of the parallel in 52 N, Greenwich (Feaghmain) to Warschau 1825-1893 (national triangulations compiled by Helmert 1893)

Helmert's volume re-adjusts the national nets and prints, for each, the mean angle error from the triangle closures and the base-to-base misclosures with their expected errors. Horizontal angles are not corrected for refraction; lateral refraction is named as a systematic error source and is handled by weights: angles exposed to it, observed in wind on high scaffolds, or taken all on one day received lower weights, and measurements of different years at one station were treated as separate stations. Doubtful angles were measured again, as at Golmberg in 1889, where poor-light observations were rejected and the remeasurement confirmed the earlier value to 0.85 seconds. The Polish chains took 18 to 24 sets in unfavourable air and strong wind. Vertical angles do not enter the volume except for reducing French oblique angles to the horizon.

Helmert, F. R. (Ed.). (1893). Die europäische Längengradmessung in 52 Grad Breite von Greenwich bis Warschau. I. Heft: Hauptdreiecke und Grundlinienanschlüsse von England bis Polen. P. Stankiewicz. Clarke, A. R. (1867). Determination of the positions of Feaghmain and Haverfordwest, longitude stations on the great European arc of parallel: Being an appendix to the account of the principal triangulation of Great Britain and Ireland. Eyre and Spottiswoode for HMSO.
Great Arc of India, Lambton's meridional arc (Coromandel coast to Punnae and north to about 18 N) 1802-1820

Lambton measured horizontal angles three or four times each, read both microscopes three times, kept two field-books, and rejected any angle 10 seconds from the others until the triangle closed; haze and vapour forced repeated observation and he waited for clear mornings. Horizontal angles were not corrected for refraction; checks came from triangle closures, sides computed by two routes, and bases of verification (Tinnevelly, about 10 inches). Station heights came from reciprocal elevations and depressions on each line, so the refraction was measured line by line and printed as a fraction of the contained arc, from about 1/4 to 1/40. The chain of heights closed at the sea at Punnae with 10.2 ft. Lambton attributed the variation of refraction to moisture and judged the barometer useless in the tropics; vertical angles in this period were taken at any hour.

Lambton, W. (1808). An account of the measurement of an arc on the meridian on the coast of Coromandel, and the length of a degree deduced therefrom in the latitude 12° 32'. Asiatic Researches, 8, 137 ff.; Lambton, W. (1816). An account of the measurement of an arc on the meridian, comprehended between the latitudes 8° 9' 38" and 10° 59' 48" north. Asiatic Researches, 12, 1-101.; Lambton, W. (1816). An account of the measurement of an arc on the meridian extending from latitude 10° 59' 49" to 15° 6' 0" north. Asiatic Researches, 12, 286-356.; Great Trigonometrical Survey of India. (1890). Account of the operations of the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India, Vol. XII: The Southern Trigon. Dehra Dun: Trigonometrical Branch, Survey of India.; Walker, J. T. (1870). Account of the operations of the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India, Vol. I: Standards of measure and base-lines. Dehra Dun: Great Trigonometrical Survey.
Lambton, trigonometrical operations across the Peninsula, Fort St. George to Mangalore 1802-1808

Horizontal angles followed Lambton's rules (three or four measures, two field-books, rejection of doubtful angles with reason) and were checked by triangle closures and by a southern branch that closed on the northern branch with 3.7 ft on a 12-mile side. Heights of all great stations from coast to coast came from reciprocal vertical angles; the refraction on each line is printed as a fraction of the arc, 1/7 to 1/40, and the chain closed on the measured height of a Mangalore beach station with 8.6 ft. Astronomical zenith distances used mean refraction tables without barometer or thermometer, because no table for the climate existed. Vapour hid the pole star by day, so azimuths were taken at night to a referring lamp on nine nights.

Lambton, W. (1811). An account of trigonometrical operations in crossing the Peninsula of India, and connecting Fort St. George with Mangalore. Asiatic Researches, 10, 290-384.; Warren, J. (1811). An account of astronomical observations near Fort St. George. Asiatic Researches, 10.; Great Trigonometrical Survey of India. (1890). Account of the operations of the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India, Vol. XII: The Southern Trigon. Dehra Dun: Trigonometrical Branch, Survey of India.; Walker, J. T. (1870). Account of the operations of the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India, Vol. I: Standards of measure and base-lines. Dehra Dun: Great Trigonometrical Survey.
GTS Karachi Longitudinal Series (North-West Quadrilateral) 1849-1855

Horizontal angles were measured on 4 or 5 pairs of zeros, face left and face right, with every single reading to heliotrope or lamp printed; a typical angle has 20 to 32 readings, and the error of a single measure was computed separately for hills, sandhills and plains. Horizontal angles were not corrected for lateral refraction; towers and ray tracing kept rays off the ground. Heights came from reciprocal vertical angles of 4 to 6 observations each, mostly in the afternoon, with the refraction printed in seconds and as a decimal of the arc for each pair, including near-zero and negative values and .168 for a pair observed near sunset. Mirage made angles over the Runn of Cutch untrustworthy and they were not used; over the plains spirit levelling replaced vertical angles. The Karachi base of verification differed from its triangulated length by 10.45 inches (23 millionths).

Walker, J. T. (Ed.). (1873). Account of the operations of the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India, Vol. III: The principal triangulation, North-West Quadrilateral. Dehra Dun: Great Trigonometrical Survey.; Walker, J. T. (1870). Account of the operations of the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India, Vol. I: Standards of measure and base-lines. Dehra Dun: Great Trigonometrical Survey.
GTS Bombay Longitudinal Series (Southern Trigon) 1822-1885

The early work (1828-1836) used poles and straw fires and was re-observed from 1837 with heliotropes by day and lamps by night, and again by Haig in 1862. Horizontal angles were measured on 6 to 10 zeros with at least two or three rounds each and repeated when measures disagreed; every reading is printed. Lateral refraction was treated through the weights of angle groups, being larger on plains and over jungle. Vertical angles were measured between 1 and 3 p.m. so both ends were equally refracted; the coefficient was found from each reciprocal pair (mostly .043 to .068, one negative value on a short ray), independent height values were compared and outliers rejected, and old heights taken at other hours were revised by spirit levels. After the simultaneous reduction the error dispersed on the series side was about 0.02 inch per mile.

Great Trigonometrical Survey of India. (1890). Account of the operations of the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India, Vol. XII: The Southern Trigon. Dehra Dun: Trigonometrical Branch, Survey of India.; Walker, J. T. (1870). Account of the operations of the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India, Vol. I: Standards of measure and base-lines. Dehra Dun: Great Trigonometrical Survey.
GTS Guzerat Longitudinal Series (South-West Quadrilateral, Vol. XIV) 1851-1877

Only page images of Vol. XIV are held. Horizontal angles were measured on 12 zeros with two readings each, to heliotropes and lamps, and every reading is printed. The positions and sides were carried by two independent routes from the Karachi Longitudinal Series and closed with 2.4 ft and 1.0 ft on sides of about 10.6 and 12.8 miles. Heights from vertical angles were tested against spirit-levelled stations and showed cumulative errors of +3, +2 and -3 ft, which were dispersed by proportion. The vertical angle tables of Vol. XIV are not in the local set, so no coefficients for this series are given.

Great Trigonometrical Survey of India. (1890). Account of the operations of the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India, Vol. XIV: The South-West Quadrilateral (Guzerat Longitudinal Series). Dehra Dun: Trigonometrical Branch, Survey of India.
US Transcontinental Triangulation, 39th parallel 1844-1898

Horizontal directions were not corrected for refraction. Lateral refraction was controlled by the observing scheme: many series in 7 to 19 circle positions (typically 34 or more observations of each direction), forenoon and afternoon measures balanced from 1880, night observing on lights in Indiana and Illinois, heliotropes in early morning and late afternoon in the mountains, and high towers and scaffolds in the plains and woods. Persistent lateral refraction is named as an error that only the triangle closures can show, and the closures (701 triangles, mean error of an angle 0.77") and the base-to-base accord (1 in 25 700 to 1 in 724 000) are printed as the check. Heights west of First View come from reciprocal zenith distances; the coefficient m was computed for each line from the two opposite zenith distances, with pressure and temperature recorded, and three special hourly series (with full barometer, wet and dry bulb, wind and sky records at Jackson Butte and Round Top) fixed the daily cycle and the best observing hours. Lines with doubtful refraction were rejected or re-measured simultaneously in 1898, and the Mount Lola trigonometric height agrees with spirit levels to 0.7 m.

Schott, C. A. (1900). The transcontinental triangulation and the American arc of the parallel (Special Publication No. 4). U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey; Government Printing Office.
US Eastern Oblique Arc, Calais to New Orleans 1833-1898

The report does not correct horizontal directions for refraction and names persistent lateral refraction among the triangle-combination errors that show only in the closures. Angles were measured many times (20 sets of 3 direct and 3 reversed repetitions with the repeating circles; 35 series or more with Hassler's and Boutelle's direction theodolites, up to 132 series at one station with two instruments). From 1888 all primary directions in Alabama were observed at night on lights, with the theodolite on scaffolds up to 46.5 m, and the probable errors came out nearly equal whatever the height or hour. The checks are printed: 483 triangles with mean error of an angle 0.82", and base accords of 57 and 26 units (New England), 24 units (Kent Island to Atlanta) and 1.5 units of the 7th log decimal over 677 km (Atlanta to Dauphin Island). The report has no heights part and prints no refraction coefficient.

Schott, C. A. (1902). The eastern oblique arc of the United States and osculating spheroid (Special Publication No. 7). U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey; Government Printing Office.
Maclear's verification and extension of La Caille's arc of meridian, Cape of Good Hope 1840-1850 (published 1866)

Horizontal angles were measured by repetition with the Fuller theodolite and the Beaufort theodolite, and Maclear prints the number of measures for every angle. He applied no correction for lateral refraction; instead the number of partial results depended on the state of the air, and the weights came from the scatter of the partial results, so angles measured in unsteady air got low weights. He prints the full field record of one angle for each instrument, with hour, definition, wind and temperature remarks. For heights, zenith distances were observed with the Dollond repeating circle and the Beaufort theodolite, with date, hour and number of observations, and the coefficient of refraction was computed from 10 sets of reciprocal zenith distances (mean m = .0712). The base was verified by triangulation, section by section.

Maclear, T. (1866). Verification and extension of La Caille's arc of meridian at the Cape of Good Hope (Vol. 1). London: Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty.
Geodetic Survey of the Transvaal and Orange River Colony (Morris; preface and introduction by Gill) 1902-1907 (report 1908)

Every horizontal angle was measured on eight arcs (four circle zeros, each with face left and face right), or on four arcs in some chains. The observer was told to take half the arcs in the early morning and half in the late afternoon, the hours of clearest and steadiest air; mist, haze and grass-fire smoke often stopped the morning work. No lateral refraction correction is applied; the triangle errors and probable errors per observer are printed as the check (0.30" on eight arcs, 0.39" on four arcs). Vertical angles were observed in the afternoon near sunset, mutual (from both ends of each line), and the heights used h' - h = s tan 1/2 (alpha - alpha'); Table M lists a coefficient of refraction for every line. Heights from vertical angles were checked against spirit levelling at four stations (differences 6.1 to 8.8 feet over 280 to 670 miles of chain).

Morris, W. G. (1908). Reports on the geodetic survey of the Transvaal and Orange River Colony (Geodetic Survey of South Africa, Vol. 5; preface and introduction by D. Gill). London: Harrison and Sons.
Trigonometrical Survey of Van Diemen's Land (Tasmania) survey in progress at the 1855 report (field-book extract 1851)

Cotton gives no treatment of terrestrial refraction. Every angle was measured by repetition with reverse observations, and the field-book extract prints the number of repetitions and the barometer and thermometer readings with the vertical angles. Angles of elevation and depression were observed at every principal station, but no refraction coefficient or reduction method is printed. The check is the base-to-base verification: the Longford base computed from the Ralph's Bay base through four separate series of triangles agrees with its measured length within 0.3 to 2.2 feet.

Cotton, H. C. (1855). On the trigonometrical survey of Van Diemen's Land. Papers and Proceedings of the Royal Society of Van Diemen's Land, 3, 82-107.
Trigonometrical Survey of New South Wales 1867-1898 (paper read January 1898)

Furber applies no lateral refraction correction to the New South Wales angles, but he reports Gill's South African finding that lateral refraction was larger than the pointing errors, and Gill's remedy of combining morning and afternoon observations. Horizontal angles were observed in about twenty double sets on different parts of the circle; one full station register (Kosciusko, 30 rounds) is printed. Heights came from zenith distances observed at both ends of the lines at the same time of day (usually 2 to 4 p.m.), and the coefficient of refraction was computed from reciprocal observations on nearly a hundred lines; Furber found that it grows with the length of the line. The paper is available here only as an OCR text layer, so its items have no page crops.

Furber, T. F. (1898). The trigonometrical survey of New South Wales, with mention of similar surveys in the other Australian colonies. Report of the Australasian Association for the Advancement of Science, 7, Section A, 176-237.
Middleton, Chadwick and Bogle, A Treatise on Surveying (textbook) 1899 (1st ed.), 1904 (2nd ed.)

A surveying textbook for British and colonial surveyors. It quotes the Survey of India manual on signals and observing hours, gives the rules for repeated measurement of angles, and treats refraction on vertical angles by reciprocal observation. Pages cited are from the 1904 second edition scan; the first edition of 1899 has the same text on the same pages (pp. 224 to 227 compared).

Middleton, R. E., Chadwick, O., & Bogle, J. du T. (1904). A treatise on surveying: Part I (2nd ed.). E. & F. N. Spon.
